question: Defending Dante to a Latin tutor, an apprentice scribe insists: 'It is not just MY enthusiasm. The Comedy's plotting, the precision of every line — these are real strengths the work has, whether the reader perceives them or not.' Which view is the scribe defending?
answer: Aesthetic realism — real qualities (craft, structure, depth) make a work genuinely better than another, beyond taste.
choices: Aesthetic realism — real qualities (craft, structure, depth) make a work genuinely better than another, beyond taste.
Subjectivism — 'better' just means 'pleases me'; there is no fact about merit outside the listener's own response.
Hume's standard of taste — trained judges converge on real merit even though personal taste varies between listeners.
Aesthetic skepticism — no claim about better or worse can be settled, because every standard rests on an untested assumption.
context: Aesthetic realism holds works carry real merits and demerits independent of any reader's response. Critics ask how merit could be 'there' if no one perceived it. Hume (1757) routes around the worry: convergent trained judgment is the practical mark of real qualities, without proof.

question: Trying to settle a fashion debate, Sara suggests: 'It's not purely in the outfit, and not purely how I feel. It's the FIT — between real features of the outfit and a trained eye that can see them.' Which view of beauty is Sara defending?
answer: Beauty as relation — beauty is neither pure object nor pure response, but the fit between features and a trained viewer.
choices: Beauty as relation — beauty is neither pure object nor pure response, but the fit between features and a trained viewer.
Beauty as real property — beauty is IN the object; its features make it beautiful whether or not anyone is looking.
Beauty as response — beauty is a feeling produced in the viewer; without a viewer the object isn't beautiful.
Beauty as social label — what counts as beautiful is whatever the people around us — critics, taste-makers — call beautiful.
context: Relational views of beauty (later developments of Hume's and Kant's response-side theories) say beauty arises in the fit between features of an object and a viewer prepared to see them. The view honors both sides of the property-vs-response debate without collapsing into either extreme.

question: Two herald-painters argue about a rival's new banner. One shrugs: 'It's striking to me, garish to you. End of story. Calling either of us right or wrong about art is a confused way to talk — there is no fact underneath, only our two reactions.' Which view is the herald defending?
answer: Subjectivism — 'better' just means 'pleases me'; there is no fact about merit outside the listener's own response.
choices: Subjectivism — 'better' just means 'pleases me'; there is no fact about merit outside the listener's own response.
Hume's standard of taste — trained judges converge on real merit even though personal taste varies between listeners.
Cultural relativism — quality is whatever a culture treats as quality; standards are internal to a community, not universal.
Aesthetic skepticism — no claim about better or worse can be settled, because every standard rests on an untested assumption.
context: Subjectivism reduces 'beautiful' or 'ugly' to reports about the speaker's response. It is simple and avoids hard metaphysics. Critics ask why we argue about art at all, and why trained reviewers' judgments seem to weigh more. Hume (1757) tries to answer both without giving up on real merit.

question: Reading a Bach fugue at the harpsichord, an apprentice corrects her brother who calls it 'dry math.' 'Look at how the voices weave — the balance of answer against subject, the way each entry weights the texture. The arrangement is the whole point.' Which view is she defending?
answer: Formalism — art's value lies in its formal structure (shape, balance) and the satisfaction of seeing how parts fit.
choices: Formalism — art's value lies in its formal structure (shape, balance) and the satisfaction of seeing how parts fit.
Expressionism — art's value lies in what it expresses emotionally; technique without feeling is skill, not art.
Aesthetic realism — real qualities (craft, structure, depth) make a work genuinely better than another, beyond taste.
Subjectivism — 'better' just means 'pleases me'; there is no fact about merit outside the listener's own response.
context: Formalism (Clive Bell, 1914) fits Bach naturally: counterpoint is the play of voices in formal relation. Bell's 'significant form' was developed for post-Impressionist painting but his framework was meant to extend to music and architecture too. Expressionists object that fugues do have an emotional weight Bell undervalues.

question: A wandering minstrel argues with a court tutor about a song from the eastern caliphate. 'It isn't NOT music — you've never sat in the courts where this scale grew up. Different tradition, different standard.' Which view is the minstrel defending?
answer: Cultural relativism — quality is whatever a culture treats as quality; standards are internal to a community, not universal.
choices: Cultural relativism — quality is whatever a culture treats as quality; standards are internal to a community, not universal.
Subjectivism — 'better' just means 'pleases me'; there is no fact about merit outside the listener's own response.
Aesthetic realism — real qualities (craft, structure, depth) make a work genuinely better than another, beyond taste.
Hume's standard of taste — trained judges converge on real merit even though personal taste varies between listeners.
context: Cultural relativism treats aesthetic standards as community-relative. Music is a strong test case because tunings, scales, and rhythms vary widely between traditions. Critics still ask whether trained cross-cultural ears converge on quality more than naive ones — a Humean pressure on the relativist.

question: Two squires argue about tournament heraldry. The captain of the lists rules: 'Senior heralds — who've judged a thousand banners — converge on which paintings are strong. Their convergence isn't proof, but it tracks something real.' Which view is the captain defending?
answer: Hume's standard of taste — trained judges converge on real merit even though personal taste varies between listeners.
choices: Hume's standard of taste — trained judges converge on real merit even though personal taste varies between listeners.
Aesthetic realism — real qualities (craft, structure, depth) make a work genuinely better than another, beyond taste.
Subjectivism — 'better' just means 'pleases me'; there is no fact about merit outside the listener's own response.
Cultural relativism — quality is whatever a culture treats as quality; standards are internal to a community, not universal.
context: Hume's 'Standard of Taste' (1757) treats convergent skilled judgment as the practical mark of real merit. The senior heralds play the role Hume assigns to skilled critics: wide exposure, careful attention, fair temperament. The view lies between subjectivism and pure realism.

question: A YouTuber reviews two films. The first is technically masterful but emotionally hollow. The second is rough but deeply moving. The reviewer concludes: 'The second is the better work — technique without expression is empty craft.' Which view of art's value is she defending?
answer: Expressionism — art's value lies in what it expresses emotionally; technique without expression is mere skill, not real art.
choices: Expressionism — art's value lies in what it expresses emotionally; technique without expression is mere skill, not real art.
Formalism — art's value lies in its formal structure and the satisfaction of perceiving that pattern; emotion is incidental, not the point.
Realism — art's value lies in how truly it captures the world; the films succeed or fail by accuracy of depiction, not by feeling or technique.
Institutional theory — art's value is whatever the artworld recognizes; the reviewer's verdict is one institutional voice among many others.
context: Expressionism (Tolstoy, What Is Art? 1897; Croce 1902; Collingwood 1938) holds art transmits feeling artist-to-audience. Without that transmission, only craft remains. Formalism is its main rival in twentieth-century debate about what makes art valuable.

question: A school newspaper critic reviews an abstract painting: 'You don't need to know what it represents or what the artist felt. The arrangement of lines and color does the work — that pattern is what makes it valuable.' Which view of art's value is she defending?
answer: Formalism — art's value lies in the arrangement of formal elements (line, color, shape); pattern attended to is what matters.
choices: Formalism — art's value lies in the arrangement of formal elements (line, color, shape); pattern attended to is what matters.
Expressionism — art's value lies in what it expresses emotionally; the work succeeds by transmitting the artist's feeling to the viewer.
Realism — art's value lies in how truly it depicts the world; an abstract work that depicts nothing fails the basic standard.
Cognitivism — art's value lies in the knowledge it offers about the world; pattern alone, without learning, does not yet make it valuable.
context: Formalism is most associated with Clive Bell (Art, 1914), who coined 'significant form,' and Roger Fry. The view emerged partly to defend abstract and non-representational art from charges of emptiness — pattern itself, attended to, is what matters.

question: A debate-club captain argues: 'A great portrait succeeds by showing the person as she really was. A landscape succeeds by showing the place as it really is. The point of art is faithful depiction of the world.' Which view of art's value is she defending?
answer: Realism (mimetic theory) — art's value lies in faithful depiction of the world; successful art accurately captures its subject.
choices: Realism (mimetic theory) — art's value lies in faithful depiction of the world; successful art accurately captures its subject.
Expressionism — art's value lies in what it expresses emotionally; depiction matters only as the vehicle that carries feeling to a viewer.
Formalism — art's value lies in formal structure (line, color, composition); fidelity to the subject is incidental to that structure.
Institutional theory — art's value is whatever the artworld accepts; depiction is one stylistic choice among many an artworld may recognize.
context: Mimetic theory traces to Plato (Republic) and Aristotle (Poetics, c. 335 BC), who held art is imitation (mimesis). The view dominated Western aesthetics into the nineteenth century; photography and abstraction in the twentieth century forced its revision.

question: A YouTuber covers a controversial gallery show: a urinal signed and displayed as art. She argues: 'What makes it art isn't beauty or skill — it's that a qualified gallery presented it as a candidate for appreciation. The artworld decides.' Which view of art is she defending?
answer: Institutional theory — art is what artworld members present as candidates for appreciation; status is conferred by the institution, not by skill.
choices: Institutional theory — art is what artworld members present as candidates for appreciation; status is conferred by the institution, not by skill.
Realism — art is faithful depiction of the world; objects that do not depict anything fail the basic standard for being art at all.
Expressionism — art is the transmission of feeling artist to viewer; objects that express nothing are not art regardless of any gallery's verdict.
Formalism — art is significant form arranged for perception; objects without formal merit are not art, however a gallery's curators frame them.
context: Institutional theory of art (George Dickie, Art and the Aesthetic, 1974) was developed partly to account for cases like Duchamp's 'Fountain' (1917) — a urinal exhibited as art. The theory says artworld conferral, not any intrinsic property, makes art art.

question: Two siblings argue. One insists a famous sculpture is genuinely great. The other replies: 'It only seems great to people trained to see it that way. There's no fact about beauty beyond how people respond to a thing.' Which view of beauty is the second sibling defending?
answer: Subjectivism — beauty is response-dependent; 'beautiful' just means 'producing certain responses in viewers,' not a fact about the object.
choices: Subjectivism — beauty is response-dependent; 'beautiful' just means 'producing certain responses in viewers,' not a fact about the object.
Aesthetic realism — beauty is a real feature of objects; trained perception tracks something genuinely there, beyond personal response.
Hume's standard of taste — trained judges converge over time on real merit; untrained reactions are evidence but not the final standard here.
Cognitivism — beauty is tied to what a work teaches; works that yield knowledge are beautiful in virtue of that yield, not because of response.
context: Subjectivism about beauty (sometimes called 'in the eye of the beholder') makes aesthetic value a fact about viewers, not objects. Hume's middle path ('Of the Standard of Taste,' 1757) accepts response is involved but argues trained taste converges on merit.

question: A school newspaper critic argues: 'Taste varies, but trained critics across centuries keep landing on the same masters — Shakespeare, Bach, Rembrandt. That convergence shows trained judgment tracks real merit; novices' reactions are weaker evidence.' Which view of taste is she defending?
answer: Hume's standard of taste — trained judges with experience converge on real merit; that convergence is the best evidence beauty is genuine.
choices: Hume's standard of taste — trained judges with experience converge on real merit; that convergence is the best evidence beauty is genuine.
Subjectivism — beauty is response-dependent; novice and expert reactions count equally, since neither tracks an objective feature of the work.
Cultural relativism — quality is whatever a culture treats as quality; the convergence the critic notes reflects shared tradition, not real merit.
Institutional theory — art is what the artworld accepts; the critic mistakes continued recognition of Shakespeare for evidence of real merit.
context: Hume's 'Of the Standard of Taste' (1757) addresses the puzzle that taste varies yet some works persist across centuries. Hume argues qualified critics — practiced, comparative, free of prejudice — converge on real merit; their consensus is the standard.

question: A debate-club captain argues: 'A great novel teaches you something you couldn't have learned any other way — what it's like to live an unfamiliar life. Art's value is the genuine knowledge of human experience it gives.' Which view of art's value is she defending?
answer: Cognitivism — art's value lies in the genuine knowledge it provides about human experience and the world that other inquiry cannot deliver.
choices: Cognitivism — art's value lies in the genuine knowledge it provides about human experience and the world that other inquiry cannot deliver.
Expressionism — art's value lies in transmitting the artist's feeling; the novel succeeds by sharing experience, not by providing real knowledge.
Formalism — art's value lies in formal structure; what the novel teaches is incidental to the patterned arrangement of plot and theme.
Aesthetic empiricism — art's value lies in the viewer's response; whatever the novel produces in the reader is the value, nothing further.
context: Cognitivism about art (Nelson Goodman, Languages of Art, 1968; Martha Nussbaum, Love's Knowledge, 1990) holds art is a serious vehicle of knowledge. Novels in particular teach the texture of lives a reader could never live, an epistemic role science cannot fill.

question: A peer-review reader replies to a classmate who says a sloppy painting is 'just as good if you like it': 'Craft, composition, control of medium — those are real qualities. Liking doesn't make them appear or disappear.' Which view of aesthetic value is she defending?
answer: Aesthetic realism — real qualities (craft, structure, control) make one work better than another; quality is a fact about the work itself.
choices: Aesthetic realism — real qualities (craft, structure, control) make one work better than another; quality is a fact about the work itself.
Subjectivism — 'better' and 'worse' just mean 'more pleasing to me'; there is no fact about quality outside individual preference and taste.
Cultural relativism — quality is whatever a culture treats as quality; the peer-review reader's criteria are local conventions presented as universal.
Hume's standard of taste — trained judges converge on merit over time; quality is not in the work itself but in convergent critical response.
context: Aesthetic realism holds that artworks have mind-independent value-relevant qualities (craft, originality, structure). Subjectivism reduces 'better' to 'more pleasing.' Hume carves a middle: response-involving but converging. The peer-reviewer takes the realist line.

question: A YouTuber on film interpretation argues: 'You can't read a movie however you want. The director MADE the film mean something — the meaning is partly fixed by what the maker intended. Ignoring that gets the work wrong.' Which view of artistic meaning is she defending?
answer: Author-intent view — the maker's intention partly constitutes a work's meaning; readings that ignore intention can mistake what the work says.
choices: Author-intent view — the maker's intention partly constitutes a work's meaning; readings that ignore intention can mistake what the work says.
Aesthetic empiricism — only the viewer's response constitutes meaning; the maker's intention is biography, not part of what the work itself says.
Reader-response theory — meaning is whatever the audience makes of the work; every interpretation is legitimate within each viewer's experience.
Institutional theory — meaning is whatever the artworld accepts; intention is one input critics consider, never authoritative on its own.
context: The author-intent view (Wollheim, Painting as an Art, 1987; Jerrold Levinson) holds the maker's intention is partly constitutive of meaning. Wimsatt and Beardsley's 'intentional fallacy' (1946) is the classic opposing argument: only the work itself is the proper object.

question: A school newspaper critic argues: 'What the artist intended doesn't change what the work IS. Two viewers with identical experiences in front of a painting get the same work. The work just is whatever it gives the viewer.' Which view of art is she defending?
answer: Aesthetic empiricism — only the viewer's response constitutes the work; intent is biography, irrelevant to what the work itself actually is.
choices: Aesthetic empiricism — only the viewer's response constitutes the work; intent is biography, irrelevant to what the work itself actually is.
Author-intent view — the maker's intention partly constitutes a work's meaning; identical-looking responses can still pick out different works.
Institutional theory — art is what the artworld accepts; the critic's reduction to private response leaves out the social conferral that makes art.
Cognitivism — art's value lies in what it teaches; the response matters only as evidence of the knowledge the work delivers about experience.
context: Aesthetic empiricism (Monroe Beardsley, Aesthetics, 1958) holds the work is what the viewer experiences; the maker's intention is biography, not constitutive. The AI-art debate sharpens this — if response is identical, does the absence of intention matter?

question: A YouTuber argues: 'Art is whatever a society has set up rules and roles to recognize as art — painters, galleries, exhibitions, audiences trained to respond. There's no underlying essence; it's all conventional practice.' Which view of art is she defending?
answer: Convention theory — art is the social practice around a recognized category; what counts as art varies with each society's set conventions.
choices: Convention theory — art is the social practice around a recognized category; what counts as art varies with each society's set conventions.
Realism — art is faithful depiction of the world; the convention theorist mistakes the social setting of art for its standard of success.
Expressionism — art is transmission of feeling; convention theory misses that genuine artwork must do emotional work, beyond mere convention.
Formalism — art is significant form arranged for perception; conventions surround art but do not constitute it, since formal value is intrinsic.
context: Convention theory overlaps with institutional theory but emphasizes the rule-governed practice over the institutional fact of conferral. Both treat art as a constructed category. Wittgenstein's 'family resemblance' approach (Philosophical Investigations, 1953) influenced both.

question: A debate-club captain argues: 'Art is defined by what it DOES: it provokes reflection, refines sensibility, passes culture along. Anything that performs those functions counts as art, however unusual the medium or maker.' Which view of art is she defending?
answer: Functionalism — art is defined by the social functions it performs (reflection, sensibility, cultural transmission), not by intrinsic features.
choices: Functionalism — art is defined by the social functions it performs (reflection, sensibility, cultural transmission), not by intrinsic features.
Institutional theory — art is what the artworld accepts; the functionalist view leaves out the social conferral that settles what counts as art today.
Author-intent view — art is partly constituted by the maker's intentions; functions performed without intent can mimic art's effects without being art.
Formalism — art is significant form arranged for perception; function-language is imprecise compared to formal qualities of the work.
context: Functionalism in aesthetics (sometimes called the 'functional definition' of art) identifies art by what it does rather than by intrinsic properties or institutional status. Critics worry: many things perform those functions (advertising, propaganda) without being art.

question: A school newspaper critic reviews a beautifully shot film celebrating a historical atrocity: 'However polished the craft, the moral failure is also an aesthetic failure. A work that endorses cruelty is worse as art.' Which view of art and morality is she defending?
answer: Moralism in criticism — moral merit and defect bear directly on aesthetic merit; a work's ethical failures count against it as art, not just as ethics.
choices: Moralism in criticism — moral merit and defect bear directly on aesthetic merit; a work's ethical failures count against it as art, not just as ethics.
Autonomism — moral and aesthetic merit are independent; an immoral work can be great art, since the two domains evaluate by different standards.
Formalism — art's value lies in formal structure alone; moral content is one subject matter and does not affect the work's value as form.
Aesthetic empiricism — art's value lies in viewer response; finding a work morally troubling is one response, no privileged standard there.
context: Moralism (Berys Gaut, 'The Ethical Criticism of Art,' 1998; Noel Carroll's 'moderate moralism') holds ethical defects count as aesthetic defects. Autonomism (Beardsley, early formalists) denies this — Riefenstahl's 'Triumph of the Will' is the standard test case.

question: A YouTuber on film history argues: 'A movie can be morally repugnant and still be a masterpiece of cinema. Composition, pacing, performance — these are the standards of cinematic merit, and the moral question is a separate question.' Which view of art and morality is she defending?
answer: Autonomism — moral and aesthetic merit are independent dimensions; a moral failure leaves aesthetic merit untouched, since the two are separate.
choices: Autonomism — moral and aesthetic merit are independent dimensions; a moral failure leaves aesthetic merit untouched, since the two are separate.
Moralism in criticism — moral merit bears directly on aesthetic merit; the YouTuber wrongly partitions what is in fact one combined evaluation.
Cognitivism — art's value lies in knowledge it provides; a film endorsing falsehood fails as knowledge, so endorsement counts against value.
Formalism — art's value lies in formal structure; subject matter is incidental to form, but distorting subject still counts against the work.
context: Autonomism holds the aesthetic and moral domains evaluate by separate standards. Strong autonomism (Beardsley) treats them as fully independent. Moderate moralism (Carroll) and ethicism (Gaut) deny independence to varying degrees. The test cases are propaganda films.

question: A debate-club captain argues that the graffiti murals downtown count as real art: 'A serious community treats them as art — they get curated tours, written criticism, gallery shows. That recognition is what art-status consists in.' Which view of art is she defending?
answer: Institutional theory — art is what qualified members of the artworld present for appreciation; the recognition cited is the art-conferring fact.
choices: Institutional theory — art is what qualified members of the artworld present for appreciation; the recognition cited is the art-conferring fact.
Aesthetic realism — art is identified by real intrinsic qualities (craft, structure, originality); recognition is evidence, not constitutive.
Expressionism — art is transmission of feeling artist to audience; recognition may track success of transmission, but cannot constitute art.
Functionalism — art is defined by what it does (reflection, sensibility); the captain mistakes social setting for the function-based criterion.
context: Whether street art counts as art has been a live test case for institutional theory. Dickie's view (Art and the Aesthetic, 1974) predicts: as galleries and critics recognize street art, it becomes art. The case sharpens debate between institutional and intrinsic-quality views.

question: A school newspaper critic writes about a sunset: 'The sky's colors aren't beautiful in themselves — beauty is what happens when a sensitive observer responds to them. Without observers, just photons.' What, on this view, makes the sunset beautiful — a property of it, or a response in us?
answer: Response-dependence — beauty is constituted by the response of qualified observers; real, but a relation between objects and viewers.
choices: Response-dependence — beauty is constituted by the response of qualified observers; real, but a relation between objects and viewers.
Aesthetic realism — beauty is an intrinsic property of objects; sensitive observers detect a quality already there, without constituting it.
Subjectivism — beauty is whatever any individual finds pleasing; there is no fact of beauty beyond particular preferences of viewers.
Formalism — beauty is significant form arranged for perception; the sunset is beautiful in virtue of pattern, not any observer's response.
context: Response-dependent accounts of beauty (Hume, McDowell) treat beauty as a real relation between objects and qualified observers — neither purely 'in the object' nor merely 'in the eye.' The view sits between aesthetic realism and subjectivism, with features of both.

question: A YouTuber on global cinema argues: 'There's no universal standard for great film. What counts as a masterpiece in one tradition would seem slow or strange in another. Each culture's standards are valid within its own frame.' Which view of aesthetic value is she defending?
answer: Cultural relativism — aesthetic standards are valid only within the culture that holds them; cross-cultural ranking misses the framework.
choices: Cultural relativism — aesthetic standards are valid only within the culture that holds them; cross-cultural ranking misses the framework.
Hume's standard of taste — trained judges across cultures converge over time; disagreement reflects training, not absence of real merit.
Aesthetic realism — works have real merit-relevant qualities independent of culture; disagreement is varying access, not varying merit.
Institutional theory — art is what each artworld accepts; the YouTuber mistakes institutional variation for the metaphysics of aesthetic value.
context: Cultural relativism about taste holds aesthetic standards are framework-relative — no view-from-nowhere. Hume's standard of taste is the classical opposing position: convergence of trained judges across cultures is itself evidence beauty is a real quality.

question: A peer-review reader argues: 'A great novel can teach you what grief feels from the inside — what no statistic about bereavement could convey. Art delivers a kind of knowledge that other modes of inquiry actually cannot reach.' Which view of art's value is she defending?
answer: Cognitivism about art — art provides genuine knowledge (especially of inner experience) that other modes of inquiry cannot deliver.
choices: Cognitivism about art — art provides genuine knowledge (especially of inner experience) that other modes of inquiry cannot deliver.
Expressionism — art's value lies in transmission of feeling artist to audience; the novel shares feeling, not establishes real knowledge.
Aesthetic empiricism — art's value lies in viewer response; the novel's effect is the response, with no further fact about knowledge.
Formalism — art's value lies in formal arrangement; what the novel teaches is incidental to the patterned structure that constitutes the work.
context: Cognitivism (Goodman, Nussbaum, Carroll) holds art is a vehicle for knowledge — especially the texture of inner experience. The view answers an old worry: if art is valuable, what does it deliver? Expressionism gives feeling-transmission; cognitivism gives knowledge.

question: A school newspaper critic writes about a found-object sculpture: 'It has no craft, no skill, no expression. But the museum displays it, curators write about it, critics evaluate it. That's enough to make it art.' Which view of art is she defending?
answer: Institutional theory — art is what qualified members of the artworld present for appreciation; conferral by the institution makes art art.
choices: Institutional theory — art is what qualified members of the artworld present for appreciation; conferral by the institution makes art art.
Aesthetic realism — art requires real merit-relevant qualities (craft, originality); the reduction to conferral leaves out what art is.
Expressionism — art requires transmission of feeling; the object transmits nothing, so institutional acceptance cannot make it art.
Formalism — art requires significant form arranged for perception; an object lacking formal merit is not art, however a museum frames it.
context: Dickie's institutional theory was developed to handle cases where intrinsic-quality tests fail — readymades, found objects, conceptual pieces. Critics object that the view leaves art-status entirely to the artworld's say-so, making 'art' whatever the gatekeepers approve.

question: Two siblings debate. One says: 'Saying a painting is great isn't reporting a fact — it's expressing your own positive attitude toward it. Aesthetic claims don't describe; they vent.' Which view of aesthetic judgment is she defending?
answer: Non-cognitivism — aesthetic judgments express attitudes rather than describe facts; 'great' vents approval, so disagreement is clash of attitude.
choices: Non-cognitivism — aesthetic judgments express attitudes rather than describe facts; 'great' vents approval, so disagreement is clash of attitude.
Aesthetic realism — aesthetic judgments report mind-independent facts; calling a work great is true or false depending on real qualities of the work.
Hume's standard of taste — aesthetic judgments report convergent judgment of qualified critics; 'great' is true if trained judges agree.
Cognitivism — aesthetic judgments report what the work delivers as knowledge; calling a work great is true if it teaches its audience well.
context: Aesthetic non-cognitivism parallels ethical non-cognitivism (Ayer, Stevenson). Aesthetic judgments are treated as expressions of attitude, not statements of fact. Critics note the difficulty of accounting for apparent aesthetic reasoning and disagreement on this view.

question: On an arts podcast, host Petra asks: 'If beauty is just subjective, why do critics across centuries converge on the same masterpieces?' Philosopher Halsey replies: 'Beauty tracks the responses of well-trained sensibilities under suitable conditions.' Which view best handles this agreement without collapsing into objectivism?
answer: Response-dependent view - beauty tracks the converging responses of qualified observers (delicate sense, practice, comparison) under good conditions, real but not measurable as a property.
choices: Response-dependent view - beauty tracks the converging responses of qualified observers (delicate sense, practice, comparison) under good conditions, real but not measurable as a property.
Pure aesthetic realism - convergence shows beauty is a mind-independent property of objects like mass or shape, and critical agreement is accurate detection of what was there all along.
Strict subjectivism - convergence is sociological (training, prestige, market) rather than aesthetic, and critics agree only because they share culture, education, and economic pressures.
Pure formalism - convergence is explained by shared response to significant form (line, color, composition) alone, with no reference to qualified observers or historically situated taste.
context: David Hume's 'Of the Standard of Taste' (1757) argues that beauty isn't a quality in the object yet isn't merely arbitrary either: it tracks the verdicts of qualified judges (delicate sense, practice, comparison, freedom from prejudice). Convergence over time is evidence of standard, not of mind-independent aesthetic properties.

question: An op-ed columnist writes: 'A painting can move me whether or not I want to own it, eat it, or use it for anything.' Critic Yves replies: 'Yes - genuine aesthetic pleasure has a structure: it isn't tied to appetite or use, and yet we expect others to feel it too.' Which view best handles this combination of detachment and shared demand?
answer: Kantian aesthetics - aesthetic judgment is disinterested (not tied to appetite or use) and yet claims universal validity, demanding agreement from others without resting on personal stake.
choices: Kantian aesthetics - aesthetic judgment is disinterested (not tied to appetite or use) and yet claims universal validity, demanding agreement from others without resting on personal stake.
Hedonism about art - aesthetic value just is pleasure of any kind that art produces in the viewer, with no special structure separating it from culinary pleasure or pleasures of possession.
Strict subjectivism - aesthetic responses are wholly personal, and any 'demand' that others share them is a polite illusion masking what is in fact merely private preference and habit.
Aesthetic moralism - aesthetic value derives from the moral worth of the work's content, and the 'detachment' the columnist notes is illusory once moral content is brought into view.
context: Kant's Critique of the Power of Judgment (1790) defines aesthetic judgment as disinterested pleasure (no stake in the object's existence) that nevertheless claims subjective universality: the judge speaks 'with a universal voice.' The structure separates beauty from the agreeable (private) and the good (interested).

question: A gallery exhibits a stack of plain bricks arranged on the floor. Visitor Rolf says: 'Bricks are bricks - calling it art changes nothing.' Curator Mira answers: 'The bricks have been presented as a candidate for appreciation by a recognized member of the artworld; that is what classifies them.' Which view of art is Mira defending?
answer: Institutional theory of art - what makes an object art is conferred status from an artworld institution (artists, curators, critics) presenting it as a candidate for appreciation.
choices: Institutional theory of art - what makes an object art is conferred status from an artworld institution (artists, curators, critics) presenting it as a candidate for appreciation.
Aesthetic experience theory - what makes an object art is its capacity to produce a distinctive aesthetic experience in attentive viewers, regardless of placement or label.
Imitative theory of art - what makes an object art is skillful representation of a subject; absent representation, bricks remain bricks wherever exhibited or by whom they are presented.
Expression theory of art - what makes an object art is the artist's embodied expression of feeling, and bricks without expressed feeling do not become art by curatorial choice alone.
context: George Dickie's Art and the Aesthetic (1974) develops the institutional theory: a work is art if conferred candidate-for-appreciation status by a person acting on behalf of the artworld. Carl Andre's brick works (Equivalent VIII, 1966) at the Tate are a real test case. Critics charge the account is circular; defenders deny it.

question: Two boxes sit side by side - one a supermarket shipping carton, the other Warhol's identical-looking Brillo box sculpture. A critic says: 'They are visually indiscernible, yet one is art and the other isn't. The difference lies in interpretation, theory, and art-historical context.' Which view of art is the critic defending?
answer: Danto's artworld theory - what makes something art is an atmosphere of theory and art-historical context that interpret it as art; visual properties alone do not settle the question.
choices: Danto's artworld theory - what makes something art is an atmosphere of theory and art-historical context that interpret it as art; visual properties alone do not settle the question.
Formalism - what makes something art is its possession of significant form (line, color, composition); two visually indiscernible objects would be aesthetically equivalent on this view.
Aesthetic experience theory - what makes something art is its capacity to produce a distinctive aesthetic experience; if objects are indiscernible, both should produce the same experience.
Imitative theory of art - what makes something art is representation of some subject; both boxes equally represent Brillo packaging, so the imitative theory cannot mark the difference.
context: Arthur Danto's 'The Artworld' (Journal of Philosophy, 1964) and The Transfiguration of the Commonplace (1981) argue that art requires an atmosphere of theory: an interpretation locating the work in art history. The Brillo Box case (Warhol, 1964) shows that two visually identical objects can have different art-statuses.

question: On a critic-vs-defender panel, philosopher Sten argues: 'Art's value isn't its market price or its institutional pedigree, but the unified, intense, complex experience it affords an attentive viewer when she gives it sustained attention.' Which view of aesthetic value is Sten defending?
answer: Aesthetic experience theory - art's value lies in its capacity to afford a unified, intense, complex experience to an attentive viewer; the experience itself is the locus of aesthetic worth.
choices: Aesthetic experience theory - art's value lies in its capacity to afford a unified, intense, complex experience to an attentive viewer; the experience itself is the locus of aesthetic worth.
Institutional theory of art - aesthetic value derives from conferred status by the artworld (artists, critics, curators), and viewer experience is downstream of that institutional fact.
Expression theory of art - aesthetic value lies in the work's embodiment of the artist's expressed feeling; viewer experience matters only as it picks up that expression accurately.
Formalism - aesthetic value lies in the formal properties of the work (line, color, composition) themselves, regardless of whether any particular viewer's experience is unified or intense.
context: Monroe Beardsley's Aesthetics: Problems in the Philosophy of Criticism (1958) develops the aesthetic-experience account: art's value is its capacity to produce experiences marked by unity, intensity, and complexity. Critics (Dickie, Danto) press that some art (conceptual, minimalist) doesn't aim at experience in this sense.

question: On a podcast on art and meaning, novelist Eira insists: 'Art is the conscious transmission of feeling from one human being to another - through line, sound, or word - so that the recipient comes to feel what the artist felt.' Which view of art is Eira defending?
answer: Tolstoyan expression theory - art is the deliberate transmission of a feeling from artist to audience through an external medium, so that the receiver comes to share the original feeling.
choices: Tolstoyan expression theory - art is the deliberate transmission of a feeling from artist to audience through an external medium, so that the receiver comes to share the original feeling.
Collingwood expression theory - art is the artist's clarification of an indistinct emotion in the act of making the work, with transmission to an audience a secondary or optional outcome.
Formalism - art's value lies in significant form (line, color, composition), not in any feeling transmitted; emotional response is a byproduct of formal perception, not the aim of the work.
Institutional theory of art - art is whatever is presented as a candidate for appreciation by an artworld actor; transmission of feeling is neither necessary nor sufficient for art-status.
context: Leo Tolstoy's What Is Art? (1897) defines art as the transmission of feeling: the artist evokes a feeling in herself, then expresses it through external signs so others feel the same. Tolstoy uses the account to reject much elite art as inauthentic. R. G. Collingwood's Principles of Art (1938) is the rival expression theory.

question: A composer tells an interviewer: 'When I began, I had only a vague unease; the piece is how I found out what I felt. The writing wasn't communication of a known emotion - it was the emotion becoming clear to me, through the work itself.' Which view of art is the composer defending?
answer: Collingwood expression theory - art is the artist's clarification of an initially indistinct emotion in the act of making the work; the work is how an inchoate feeling becomes determinate.
choices: Collingwood expression theory - art is the artist's clarification of an initially indistinct emotion in the act of making the work; the work is how an inchoate feeling becomes determinate.
Tolstoyan expression theory - art is the deliberate transmission of an already-felt emotion to an audience through external signs, so the audience comes to share the feeling the artist had.
Aesthetic experience theory - art's value lies in the unified, intense experience it affords an attentive viewer, regardless of what the artist did or did not know while making the work.
Formalism - art's value lies in significant form (line, color, sound, composition) alone, and what the artist did or did not feel while making the work is irrelevant to aesthetic worth.
context: R. G. Collingwood's The Principles of Art (1938) distinguishes expressing emotion (clarifying a vague feeling into a determinate one through the act of making) from arousing emotion or transmitting an already-known feeling (the Tolstoyan account). On this view the artist often does not know what she feels until the work exists.

question: A critic dismisses a representational painting: 'Lovely subject matter doesn't make a good picture.' Painter Inese answers: 'What moves us in any genuine artwork - from a Byzantine icon to a Cezanne still life - is the arrangement of lines, shapes, and colors itself.' Which view of art is Inese defending?
answer: Formalism - what makes a work art is significant form (the arrangement of lines, shapes, and colors that moves the trained eye), independent of subject matter, story, or external reference.
choices: Formalism - what makes a work art is significant form (the arrangement of lines, shapes, and colors that moves the trained eye), independent of subject matter, story, or external reference.
Expression theory of art - what makes a work art is its embodiment of the artist's feeling through an external medium; the formal properties matter only as the vehicle of expressed emotion.
Imitative theory of art - what makes a work art is skillful representation of some subject in the world; the relationship between artwork and subject is what aesthetic value tracks here.
Aesthetic experience theory - what makes a work art is its capacity to produce a unified, intense, complex experience in attentive viewers; the formal properties are means to that end.
context: Clive Bell's Art (1914) introduced 'significant form' - the arrangement of lines and colors that produces 'aesthetic emotion' in those sensitive to it. Bell took this to cut across cultures and periods. Roger Fry's Vision and Design (1920) developed the view further. Critics charge the account is circular; modernists embraced it.

question: A traveler describes standing under a thousand-foot cliff in a storm: 'Awe, dread, and a strange exhilaration all at once. Not beauty exactly - something other.' Aesthetician Calder says: 'The response to vast power perceived safely - terror without imminent danger - is its own category.' Which view of the sublime is Calder defending?
answer: Burkean sublime - the sublime is the delightful kind of terror produced by vast power or magnitude perceived in safety, sharply distinguished from beauty as a separate category of response.
choices: Burkean sublime - the sublime is the delightful kind of terror produced by vast power or magnitude perceived in safety, sharply distinguished from beauty as a separate category of response.
Kantian mathematical sublime - the sublime arises when imagination fails to grasp magnitude and reason supplies the idea of infinity, locating it in the mind's faculties, not in the object.
Kantian dynamical sublime - the sublime arises when nature's power exceeds physical resistance but reason recognizes a moral vocation above it, locating the sublime in moral self-awareness.
Romantic sublime as union - the sublime is the dissolution of the boundary between self and world in moments of overwhelming nature, beyond Burke's safety condition and Kant's analysis.
context: Edmund Burke's A Philosophical Enquiry into the Origin of Our Ideas of the Sublime and Beautiful (1757) treats the sublime as a physiological response: terror is sublime when distance or safety removes actual danger, producing 'delight' distinct from beauty. Kant later reworks the account, locating the sublime in the mind.

question: A philosopher describes the night sky: 'I cannot grasp the number of stars; my imagination fails. But the very failure summons in me an idea of the infinite my senses cannot supply. The sublime is in this movement, not in the stars themselves.' Which view of the sublime is the philosopher defending?
answer: Kantian mathematical sublime - the sublime arises when imagination fails to grasp magnitude and reason supplies the idea of infinity; it lives in the mind's faculties, not in the object.
choices: Kantian mathematical sublime - the sublime arises when imagination fails to grasp magnitude and reason supplies the idea of infinity; it lives in the mind's faculties, not in the object.
Burkean sublime - the sublime is the delightful kind of terror produced by vast power or magnitude perceived in safety, a physiological response rather than a faculty-of-reason matter.
Kantian dynamical sublime - the sublime arises when nature's power exceeds resistance but reason recognizes a moral vocation, locating it in our moral self-awareness, not in cognition.
Longinian sublime - the sublime is the elevated rhetorical effect of great writing that transports the audience; the location is in language and oratorical force, not in nature or the mind.
context: Kant's Critique of the Power of Judgment (1790) divides the sublime into mathematical (overwhelming magnitude - sky, mountains) and dynamical (overwhelming power - storms, volcanoes). In both, the sublime is located in the relation between imagination's failure and reason's idea of the absolute, not in the natural object.

question: A novel is widely admired for its prose, but a critic argues: 'The book's casual contempt for its female characters is a defect of the work AS art, not merely a separate moral problem. The same callousness shaping its sentences shapes its world.' Which view of art-and-morality is the critic defending?
answer: Aesthetic moralism - moral defects in a work can be aesthetic defects of it, because the same attitudes that shape moral content also shape the formal and imaginative texture of the work.
choices: Aesthetic moralism - moral defects in a work can be aesthetic defects of it, because the same attitudes that shape moral content also shape the formal and imaginative texture of the work.
Strict autonomism - aesthetic value is wholly independent of moral content; a work's moral defects, however serious, cannot count against its standing as art on the autonomist view of value.
Cognitivism about art - art's value lies in the genuine knowledge it gives us about the world or human experience, and moral defects matter only as they distort what the art teaches us.
Aesthetic immoralism - moral defects in a work can sometimes enhance its aesthetic value by securing imaginative resistance, complexity, or transgressive force unavailable to wholesome work.
context: Aesthetic moralism is defended by Berys Gaut ('The Ethical Criticism of Art,' 1998 - the 'ethicism' thesis) and Noel Carroll ('Moderate Moralism,' 1996). Strict autonomism (Oscar Wilde's preface to Dorian Gray, 1891) holds aesthetic value is independent of moral content. Immoralism is the symmetric opposing position.

question: A debate-show panelist argues: 'Whether a film glorifies violence is a moral question. Whether it succeeds as cinema is an aesthetic one. Confusing the two leads us to admire bad movies because they preach well and dismiss good ones because their politics offend us.' Which view is the panelist defending?
answer: Strict autonomism - aesthetic value is independent of moral content, and judgments about a work's moral message are separate from judgments about its accomplishment as art on its own terms.
choices: Strict autonomism - aesthetic value is independent of moral content, and judgments about a work's moral message are separate from judgments about its accomplishment as art on its own terms.
Aesthetic moralism - moral defects in a work can be aesthetic defects of it, since the attitudes shaping moral content also shape the formal and imaginative texture of the work as a whole.
Aesthetic immoralism - moral defects in a work can sometimes enhance its aesthetic value by securing imaginative resistance, transgressive force, or complexity unavailable to wholesome work.
Cognitivism about art - art's value lies in the genuine understanding it gives us about the world or human experience, so moral content matters only when it bears on what art teaches.
context: Strict autonomism (echoing Wilde's preface to Dorian Gray, 1891: 'There is no such thing as a moral or an immoral book...') holds moral and aesthetic value are independent. Modern defenders include Richard Posner ('Against Ethical Criticism,' 1997). The view contrasts with moralism (Gaut, Carroll) and immoralism (Eaton).

question: A flawless forgery of a Vermeer hangs beside the original. The two are visually indistinguishable today. Curator Yulia argues: 'Even so, they aren't aesthetically equivalent: knowing one is the work and one the copy will reshape what trained eyes actually see in each.' Which view of forgery is Yulia defending?
answer: Goodman on forgery - awareness that two paintings differ in provenance can reshape the trained perceiver's experience of each, so equivalence isn't settled by visual indiscernibility.
choices: Goodman on forgery - awareness that two paintings differ in provenance can reshape the trained perceiver's experience of each, so equivalence isn't settled by visual indiscernibility.
Strict visual equivalence - if two paintings cannot be distinguished by any observer today, they are aesthetically equivalent, since aesthetic value is fixed by what can presently be seen.
Institutional theory of art - the forgery's status depends on whether artworld actors confer art-status as candidate for appreciation, which they refuse for a known forgery however it looks.
Aesthetic moralism - the forgery is aesthetically diminished because forgery is a moral wrong (deception), and moral defects in a work can count as aesthetic defects of the work itself.
context: Nelson Goodman's Languages of Art (1968) argues that knowledge of which painting is original can train the eye to detect differences not yet visible to it, so present visual indistinguishability does not yet settle aesthetic equivalence. The argument turns on perceptual learning, not on moral or institutional facts.

question: Reader Alvaro insists a poem 'really means' whatever its author later said she had in mind. Critic Esme answers: 'What the poet intended to say is one thing; what the poem on the page actually achieves is another. The poem must stand or fall on its own verbal performance.' Which view is Esme defending?
answer: Intentional fallacy - the author's intention is neither available nor decisive for what the work means; meaning resides in the work's verbal performance, not in any intentions behind it.
choices: Intentional fallacy - the author's intention is neither available nor decisive for what the work means; meaning resides in the work's verbal performance, not in any intentions behind it.
Intentionalism - the work's meaning is fixed by what the author intended, and recovering authorial intention is the legitimate aim of literary interpretation where intention is recoverable.
Hypothetical intentionalism - meaning is fixed by what an ideal audience would attribute to the historical author given everything publicly available, not by what was privately in mind.
Reader-response theory - meaning is constituted in the reader's encounter with the text and the reader's situation, so neither author intention nor the text alone settles what it means.
context: W. K. Wimsatt and Monroe Beardsley's 'The Intentional Fallacy' (Sewanee Review, 1946) is the canonical New Critical statement that author intention is irrelevant to the work's meaning. Later positions (E. D. Hirsch's intentionalism, Levinson's hypothetical intentionalism) defend versions of the role of intention in interpretation.

question: A conceptual artist exhibits only the certificate of an idea - no physical object. Visitor Bram complains: 'There's nothing TO see.' Curator Lila answers: 'The work is the proposal itself, situated in an art-historical conversation about what art has been; the certificate is the medium.' Which view of art is Lila defending?
answer: Danto artworld theory - art-status depends on an art-historical context and an atmosphere of theory that interpret the work, so a non-perceptual proposal can be art if so situated.
choices: Danto artworld theory - art-status depends on an art-historical context and an atmosphere of theory that interpret the work, so a non-perceptual proposal can be art if so situated.
Aesthetic experience theory - art exists to afford a unified, intense, complex experience to the senses, so a certificate without a perceptual object cannot count as an artwork on this view.
Formalism - art is significant form (line, color, composition) discernible by trained perception; a certificate with no formal properties cannot count as a work on the formalist view of art.
Imitative theory of art - art is skillful representation of a subject in the world; a bare proposal without representational content cannot count as a work of art on the imitative theory.
context: Sol LeWitt's 'Paragraphs on Conceptual Art' (1967) holds 'the idea becomes a machine that makes the art.' Lawrence Weiner's Statements (1968) reduced works to verbal propositions. Danto's 'The Artworld' framework (1964) is the philosophical home for such cases: art-historical context, not visual appearance, classifies.

question: On a panel, classicist Iona defends an old view: 'Tragedy represents serious human action and arouses pity and fear in the audience, working through those emotions toward a kind of release. Imitation isn't a defect of art - it is what art does and how it instructs.' Which view of art is Iona defending?
answer: Aristotelian mimesis - art represents human action and, through representation, produces cognitive and emotional effects (catharsis) that teach the audience about character and feeling.
choices: Aristotelian mimesis - art represents human action and, through representation, produces cognitive and emotional effects (catharsis) that teach the audience about character and feeling.
Platonic suspicion of mimesis - art is imitation of imitation, twice removed from the real, and arouses passions reason should govern; the philosopher-ruler is right to restrict it.
Tolstoyan expression theory - art is the deliberate transmission of feeling from artist to audience, and what matters is the moral quality of feeling transmitted, not the imitative content.
Formalism - art's value lies in significant form (line, color, composition, dramatic shape), and representational or imitative content of the work is incidental to aesthetic worth.
context: Aristotle's Poetics (c. 335 BC) develops mimesis as art's distinctive contribution: tragedy represents serious action and produces catharsis - a working-through of pity and fear. Plato's Republic Book X (c. 375 BC) is the contrasting suspicion of mimesis. The dispute is the founding debate of Western aesthetics.

question: Critic Tibor argues: 'Some films are aesthetically valuable PARTLY because of their morally troubling features - the imaginative resistance the viewer must work through is itself an achievement no morally tame film could match.' Which view is Tibor defending?
answer: Aesthetic immoralism - moral defects in a work can sometimes enhance its aesthetic value by securing imaginative resistance, transgressive force, or complexity unavailable to tame work.
choices: Aesthetic immoralism - moral defects in a work can sometimes enhance its aesthetic value by securing imaginative resistance, transgressive force, or complexity unavailable to tame work.
Aesthetic moralism - moral defects in a work are aesthetic defects of it, because the attitudes that shape its moral content also shape its formal and imaginative texture for the worse.
Strict autonomism - moral and aesthetic value are simply independent; moral defects neither enhance nor diminish aesthetic value, and the two questions should be kept clear of each other.
Cognitivism about art - art's value lies in the genuine understanding it gives about the world; moral content matters only as it advances or distorts what the work teaches the viewer.
context: Aesthetic immoralism is defended by Anne Eaton ('Robust Immoralism,' 2012) and Matthew Kieran ('Forbidden Knowledge,' 2003). The view is the symmetric opposite of Berys Gaut's ethicism: where Gaut holds moral defects always count as aesthetic defects, immoralism holds they can sometimes count as merits.

question: On a podcast, philosopher Rinaldo argues: 'The harmony of a Bach fugue or the proportion of a Doric column is not a fact ABOUT us. It is a fact about the work itself, which our responses succeed or fail in tracking.' Which view of aesthetic value is Rinaldo defending?
answer: Aesthetic realism - aesthetic properties are mind-independent features of works, and qualified responses succeed or fail by tracking those features, much as perception succeeds or fails.
choices: Aesthetic realism - aesthetic properties are mind-independent features of works, and qualified responses succeed or fail by tracking those features, much as perception succeeds or fails.
Response-dependent view - aesthetic properties are constituted by converging responses of qualified observers under suitable conditions; real but not independent of human sensibility.
Strict subjectivism - aesthetic 'properties' are sociological projections of taste; there is no independent fact about a fugue's harmony that critical agreement is tracking when they agree.
Kantian view - aesthetic judgments are responses (disinterested pleasure) claiming universal validity, but do not pick out mind-independent properties of the object in the realist's sense.
context: Aesthetic realism (Frank Sibley, 'Aesthetic Concepts,' 1959; Eddy Zemach, Real Beauty, 1997) holds aesthetic properties are real features of works. Response-dependent views (Hume, modern neo-Humeans) deny mind-independence but preserve objectivity through qualified-observer convergence. The dispute is ongoing.

question: An untrained recluse spends fifty years filling notebooks with extraordinary drawings, never shown to anyone. After her death they are discovered. Critic Wim says: 'These were art the whole time, with or without an artworld; the perceptual depth is intrinsic to the works themselves.' Which view of art is Wim defending?
answer: Aesthetic experience theory - works are art by their capacity to afford the distinctive aesthetic experience to attentive viewers, regardless of any institutional recognition ever received.
choices: Aesthetic experience theory - works are art by their capacity to afford the distinctive aesthetic experience to attentive viewers, regardless of any institutional recognition ever received.
Institutional theory of art - works become art only when conferred candidate-for-appreciation status by an artworld actor, so they become art on rediscovery, not in the recluse's lifetime.
Danto artworld theory - art-status requires an art-historical context and atmosphere of theory; works produced wholly outside such a context cannot count as art until context is supplied.
Tolstoyan expression theory - art requires successful transmission of feeling from artist to an audience, so works that never reached any audience in their making cannot have been art.
context: The outsider-art case (Henry Darger's discovered notebooks; the Vivian Maier photographs) is a standard test of institutional vs. aesthetic-experience accounts. Beardsley-style theorists say the works are art intrinsically; Dickie-style institutionalists say art-status is conferred, so the question becomes when the conferral occurred.

question: A novelist tells an interviewer: 'My books aim to do something no essay can - let the reader inhabit a kind of life and learn, from inside, what living that life is like. The value of literature, for me, is this distinctive knowledge.' Which view of art is the novelist defending?
answer: Cognitivism about art - art's distinctive value lies in the genuine understanding it gives us about the world, ourselves, or what living a particular kind of life is like from inside.
choices: Cognitivism about art - art's distinctive value lies in the genuine understanding it gives us about the world, ourselves, or what living a particular kind of life is like from inside.
Aesthetic experience theory - art's value lies in the unified, intense, complex experience the work affords an attentive perceiver; any knowledge gained is a byproduct rather than the value.
Tolstoyan expression theory - art's value lies in transmission of feeling from artist to audience through external signs, with knowledge claims a secondary effect rather than the chief aim.
Formalism - art's value lies in significant form (line, color, composition, dramatic shape) discernible by trained perception; didactic or cognitive content is incidental to aesthetic worth.
context: Cognitivism about art (Catherine Wilson, 'Literature and Knowledge,' 1983; Martha Nussbaum, Love's Knowledge, 1990) holds literature and other arts deliver distinctive understanding (perspectival, particular, imaginative) unavailable to argument. Anti-cognitivists (Jerome Stolnitz, Peter Lamarque) deny art has a special cognitive role.

question: A defender of generative art argues on a panel: 'What matters in evaluating an image is the work itself — its composition, its rhythm, its perceptible qualities — not who or what produced it. If a viewer would judge an AI-generated and human-made image identically on its perceptible features, then they have identical aesthetic value.' Which theory of art is she defending?
answer: Aesthetic empiricism — Beardsley holds only the work itself constitutes its aesthetic object; production history is irrelevant once perceptible features are fixed, so identical features yield identical value.
choices: Aesthetic empiricism — Beardsley holds only the work itself constitutes its aesthetic object; production history is irrelevant once perceptible features are fixed, so identical features yield identical value.

Intentionalism — Wollheim and Levinson make the maker's intention partly constitutive of art, so identical-looking outputs from a non-intentional process can only mimic art's appearance, not share its nature.

Institutional theory — Dickie holds art is status conferred within artworld practices; identical-looking outputs may differ in art-status depending on the institutional context that confers candidacy upon them.

Historical-functional theory — Levinson holds art is anything intended to be regarded as previous artworks were regarded; the same image counts as art only when situated in the right historical regard-relations.
context: Monroe Beardsley's Aesthetics (1958) and 'The Intentional Fallacy' (with W.K. Wimsatt, 1946) ground aesthetic empiricism: the work itself is the proper object of aesthetic evaluation, not the artist's biography or intention. Intentionalist replies (Wollheim, Levinson) make intention partly constitutive of meaning; the AI case sharpens the disagreement.

question: An art critic argues at a gallery talk: 'Two indiscernible canvases — one painted by a Renaissance master, one produced by chance splashes — are not the same artwork even though their visible features coincide. What the maker did, intended, and was responding to is part of what the work IS.' Which view of art is she defending?
answer: Intentionalism — Wollheim makes the maker's intentional activity partly constitutive of an artwork, so two indiscernible objects can be different works because their generative intentions differ.
choices: Intentionalism — Wollheim makes the maker's intentional activity partly constitutive of an artwork, so two indiscernible objects can be different works because their generative intentions differ.

Aesthetic empiricism — Beardsley holds only the work's perceptible features constitute its aesthetic object, so two visually indiscernible canvases must yield identical aesthetic value regardless of how each came to exist at all.

Institutional theory — Dickie holds art-status is conferred within the artworld; whether the chance canvas is art depends not on intention but on whether the artworld confers candidacy upon it, which is a separate question.

Cluster theory — Gaut holds art has no single defining feature; whether the chance splashes count depends on how many cluster properties they exhibit, with intentional history being only one among many of the relevant properties.
context: Richard Wollheim's Art and Its Objects (1968, 2nd ed. 1980) and Jerrold Levinson's 'Defining Art Historically' (1979) develop intentionalist accounts on which the maker's intention is partly constitutive of artwork-identity. Beardsley's anti-intentionalism is the opposing classical position; Danto's Transfiguration of the Commonplace (1981) presses the indiscernibles question from a different angle.

question: A curator defends including a urinal-on-a-pedestal in a major art exhibition: 'Whether something is art is not a matter of its physical features or even the artist's intention in isolation — it is whether the artworld, through its practices of exhibition, criticism, and recognition, has conferred candidacy upon it for appreciation.' Which theory of art is the curator defending?
answer: Institutional theory — Dickie holds art is what the artworld confers status upon; candidacy for appreciation is conferred through exhibition, recognition, and the practices of artworld participants.
choices: Institutional theory — Dickie holds art is what the artworld confers status upon; candidacy for appreciation is conferred through exhibition, recognition, and the practices of artworld participants.

Aesthetic empiricism — Beardsley holds the perceptible features of the work itself constitute its aesthetic object; whether the artworld confers any status on a urinal is irrelevant to whether the object has aesthetic value.

Intentionalism — Wollheim and Levinson make the artist's intention partly constitutive of art; the urinal counts as art because Duchamp intended it as such, not because the artworld subsequently conferred any institutional status.

Functionalism — Beardsley and Gaut hold art is defined by the function of affording aesthetic experience; the urinal is or is not art depending on whether it can afford such experience, not on artworld institutional recognition.
context: George Dickie's institutional theory, developed across Art and the Aesthetic (1974) and The Art Circle (1984), frames art as a status conferred within the practices of the artworld. The view responds to Duchamp's readymades and Warhol's Brillo Boxes: objects indiscernible from non-art become art through institutional placement. Critics: Beardsley, Carroll, Levinson.

question: A philosopher of art writes about Warhol's Brillo Boxes: 'What makes these objects art when ordinary Brillo boxes are not cannot be anything visible — the difference lies in an atmosphere of theory, a knowledge of the history of art, an artworld that gives the gesture its meaning.' Which view of art is he advancing?
answer: Dantonian artworld theory — Danto argues the difference between art and indiscernible non-art lies in an interpretive context — an atmosphere of theory and art-history — that confers artwork-status.
choices: Dantonian artworld theory — Danto argues the difference between art and indiscernible non-art lies in an interpretive context — an atmosphere of theory and art-history — that confers artwork-status.

Aesthetic empiricism — Beardsley holds the work's perceptible features constitute its aesthetic object; indiscernible objects must have identical aesthetic status, and a theoretical atmosphere differentiates nothing.

Intentionalism — Wollheim and Levinson make the maker's intention partly constitutive of art; Warhol's intention differentiates his boxes from Brillo's commercial ones, not the atmosphere of art-historical theory surrounding them.

Cluster theory — Gaut holds art has no single defining feature but a cluster; whether Warhol's boxes count depends on how many cluster properties they exhibit, with art-historical placement being only one among many.
context: Arthur Danto's 'The Artworld' (Journal of Philosophy, 1964) and The Transfiguration of the Commonplace (1981) respond to Warhol's Brillo Boxes (1964) by arguing the art/non-art distinction cannot be perceptual. Danto's view shaped Dickie's institutional theory; the two diverge on whether artworld is interpretive (Danto) or institutional (Dickie).

question: A philosopher at a seminar argues: 'No single feature — not intention, not artworld recognition, not aesthetic function — is necessary or sufficient for being art. Art has a cluster of typical properties (expressive content, formal complexity, imagination, skill), and something counts as art if enough of them hold.' Which view of art is she defending?
answer: Cluster theory — Gaut holds art has no single defining feature; an object counts as art when it exhibits enough of a cluster of typical art-properties, no individual property being needed.
choices: Cluster theory — Gaut holds art has no single defining feature; an object counts as art when it exhibits enough of a cluster of typical art-properties, no individual property being needed.

Institutional theory — Dickie holds art is what the artworld confers status upon; candidacy for appreciation is conferred through institutional practices of recognition, which the cluster account treats as just one property.

Intentionalism — Wollheim and Levinson make the maker's intention partly constitutive; on this view intention is necessary, whereas the cluster account treats intentional history as only one among several art-properties.

Aesthetic functionalism — Beardsley and the early Gaut hold art is defined by the capacity to afford aesthetic experience; the function unifies the class, whereas the cluster view denies any single defining property at all.
context: Berys Gaut's 'The Cluster Account of Art' (2000) and Denis Dutton's earlier cluster proposals (1979) adapt Wittgenstein's family-resemblance thinking to the definition of art. The view replies to repeated failures of single-property definitions (intentionalist, institutional, functionalist) by giving up the search for necessary-and-sufficient conditions.

question: A philosopher at an aesthetics conference argues: 'Art is anything intended by its maker to be regarded in the way that previous artworks were regarded — a backward-looking definition that ties new works to the historical tradition of regard, rather than to any timeless feature like beauty or expression.' Which view is she defending?
answer: Historical-functional theory — Levinson defines art recursively: a thing is art if intended to be regarded in ways previous artworks were regarded, anchoring novelty to regard-relations.
choices: Historical-functional theory — Levinson defines art recursively: a thing is art if intended to be regarded in ways previous artworks were regarded, anchoring novelty to regard-relations.

Institutional theory — Dickie holds art is what the artworld confers status upon; the historical view replaces institutional conferral with intentional placement in a regard-tradition the artworld may or may not recognize.

Intentionalism — Wollheim's broader intentionalism makes intention partly constitutive, but does not require the backward-looking historical structure Levinson builds in; intention can be present with no reference to past art.

Aesthetic empiricism — Beardsley holds the work's perceptible features constitute its aesthetic object; both historical tradition and maker's intention are irrelevant to value once the perceptible features are fully fixed.
context: Jerrold Levinson's 'Defining Art Historically' (British Journal of Aesthetics, 1979) and the essays in Music, Art, and Metaphysics (1990) develop the historical-functional definition. The view tries to combine intentionalism's force with the institutional theory's appreciation of historical practice, without requiring an explicit artworld conferral.

question: A literary scholar argues at a panel on aesthetic disagreement: 'Beauty is not a property in the object alone, but neither is taste merely whatever happens to please. The standard is what would please qualified judges — those of practiced delicacy, freed from prejudice — and their convergence gives us all the objectivity we need.' Which view is she defending?
answer: Humean response-dependent standard — Hume grounds objectivity in the converging verdicts of qualified judges (delicate, practiced, unprejudiced), not in a property of the object alone.
choices: Humean response-dependent standard — Hume grounds objectivity in the converging verdicts of qualified judges (delicate, practiced, unprejudiced), not in a property of the object alone.

Aesthetic realism — beauty is a real property of the object, independent of any response; trained judges approximate the truth about it but do not constitute it, so convergence is evidence, not the standard itself.

Pure subjectivism — beauty is whatever pleases the individual; no judges are more qualified than any others, and the convergence of trained judges only describes what they happen to share, not any standard binding on others.

Kantian disinterested pleasure — beauty is what is judged with universal validity in disinterested pleasure; the standard lies in the structure of the judgment itself, not in the historical convergence of any class of judges.
context: David Hume's 'Of the Standard of Taste' (1757) navigates between aesthetic realism and pure subjectivism by grounding objectivity in the response of qualified judges: those with practiced delicacy, freed from prejudice, comparing widely. The view is response-dependent without being individualistic. Kant's Critique of Judgment (1790) offers the rival transcendental account.

question: A philosopher of aesthetics writes: 'The judgment that something is beautiful is universally communicable not because it tracks a property of the object, but because it expresses a pleasure free of all interest — neither in the object's existence nor in its utility — that anyone with the same faculties would share.' Which view of the aesthetic judgment is she defending?
answer: Kantian disinterested pleasure — Kant grounds beauty's claim to universal validity in the disinterested free play of imagination and understanding, communicable across subjects with shared faculties.
choices: Kantian disinterested pleasure — Kant grounds beauty's claim to universal validity in the disinterested free play of imagination and understanding, communicable across subjects with shared faculties.

Humean response-dependence — Hume grounds aesthetic objectivity in the converging verdicts of qualified judges of practiced delicacy, but the route runs through historical convergence rather than the structure of the judgment.

Aesthetic realism — beauty is a real property in the object, independent of any response in subjects; the judgment tracks the property rather than expressing a communicable pleasure of disinterested contemplation.

Sibley's aesthetic concepts — aesthetic properties (grace, balance, elegance) are perceived directly though they are not reducible to non-aesthetic features; the framework concerns concept-acquisition, not pleasure's structure.
context: Immanuel Kant's Critique of the Power of Judgment (1790) treats the judgment of beauty as singular yet universally communicable: a free harmony of imagination and understanding, accompanied by disinterested pleasure. The view contrasts with Hume's empirical response-dependence and with classical realism; modern Kantians (Guyer, Allison) develop the transcendental machinery in detail.

question: A philosophy seminar discusses art-critical language: 'Properties like grace, balance, and unity are perceived by trained sensitivity in particular works, but no description of the work's non-aesthetic features (its lines, colors, measurements) entails that it is graceful or balanced. The aesthetic is supervenient on the non-aesthetic but not derivable from it.' Which view is being defended?
answer: Sibley's aesthetic concepts — Sibley argues aesthetic properties (grace, balance) supervene on non-aesthetic features but are not condition-governed by them; perception requires trained sensitivity.
choices: Sibley's aesthetic concepts — Sibley argues aesthetic properties (grace, balance) supervene on non-aesthetic features but are not condition-governed by them; perception requires trained sensitivity.
