Students who eat breakfast probably also have other advantages, so the study's finding may be confounded, though this would hold across studies.
The newspaper may have selected a study that confirmed what the reporter already believed; reporters do not always cover contradicting findings.
context: The replication crisis (Ioannidis 2005, OSC 2015) revealed that many single-study findings fail to replicate. Knowledge claims about effects should defer to convergent evidence, not lean on the latest headline study.

question: A YouTuber learns that a particular diet works because she watched a video by a credentialed doctor — who sells that same diet plan and earns a commission from every sign-up. The diet works for some people. Did she KNOW the diet works?
answer: No — credentials and commercial incentive pulled in opposite directions, and she never weighed the conflict that should have lowered her trust.
choices: No — credentials and commercial incentive pulled in opposite directions, and she never weighed the conflict that should have lowered her trust.
Yes — the doctor was credentialed, the doctor said it works, and it does work for some people; this combination is what learning-from-doctors means.
Yes — credentials transfer warrant directly to the listener whenever the credentialed person has said something true; commissions are irrelevant.
No — testimony from any video source can never deliver knowledge regardless of credentials; only personal clinical consultation would ever count.
context: Source assessment requires weighing credentials AGAINST conflicts of interest. A credentialed-but-commissioned source is not on the same footing as an unconflicted one; ignoring this lowers epistemic warrant.

question: A viral post claims a celebrity said something outrageous in an interview. Screenshots and short clips circulate, but the full interview is not linked anywhere in the post or its comments. What's the most careful question to ask before believing the claim?
answer: Whether the full interview, in its original context, actually contains the line and means what the clip suggests, since clips often cut context.
choices: Whether the full interview, in its original context, actually contains the line and means what the clip suggests, since clips often cut context.
Whether the celebrity has said similar things in past interviews, since a history of similar statements makes the new claim more plausible directly.
Whether the post has gone viral enough that mainstream news has covered it, since high public attention generally tracks the underlying truth.
Whether the celebrity has issued a denial of the claim, since the presence or absence of a public denial is the standard signal for belief.
context: Context-collapse is the hallmark of viral misquotation: a short clip removes the surrounding qualifications and conditions. The careful epistemic move is to find the full original source before treating the clipped claim as known.

question: A student is convinced she will get an A on the math test because she wore her 'lucky' shirt and that always works for her. She does get an A. Did she really KNOW she would get the A before the test?
answer: No — her shirt had no connection to her math performance, so her belief was wishful thinking, not anything that tracked whether she would succeed.
choices: No — her shirt had no connection to her math performance, so her belief was wishful thinking, not anything that tracked whether she would succeed.
Yes — her confidence was strong, the outcome matched the prediction, and strong-confidence-plus-matching-outcome is what 'knowing in advance' means.
Yes — wearing the lucky shirt may have boosted her real confidence and performance, and since the boost made the prediction reliable it counts.
No — predictions about future test results can never count as knowledge regardless of evidence; only the returned graded paper is knowable.
context: A lucky charm has no causal connection to test outcomes. Belief formed from lucky-shirt reasoning is wishful even when it happens to land right. Reasons that don't track the truth deliver coincidence, not knowledge.

question: A YouTuber argues a particular conspiracy theory is true because she's read many articles supporting it. Pressed, she admits she only reads articles from sites that share her view, and dismisses skeptical pieces unread. What's STILL the strongest reason to doubt her knowledge claim?
answer: Reading only what agrees with you guarantees confidence rises with the article count, regardless of whether the underlying claim is even true.
choices: Reading only what agrees with you guarantees confidence rises with the article count, regardless of whether the underlying claim is even true.
Conspiracy theories are sometimes correct, so the YouTuber might accidentally be right about this case; her method is wrong but the result could hold.
Articles online vary in quality from site to site, and even a YouTuber with terrible reading habits could be lucky enough to land on truth.
Confidence in any conspiracy theory tends to fade when the believer stops thinking about it; the YouTuber's belief may not even persist as knowledge.
context: Confirmation bias (Wason 1960) systematically inflates confidence: each agreeing article adds subjective weight, but the filtered diet was never in contact with the disconfirming evidence that would test the belief.

question: A debate-club captain spots her friend Mira waving from across the cafeteria and concludes 'Mira is at lunch today.' Mira IS at lunch — at the other end of the room. The person who waved was Mira's visiting twin sister. Did the captain really KNOW Mira was at lunch?
answer: No — her belief that Mira was at lunch was true, but the person she saw was the twin; her justification had no link to Mira's actual location.
choices: No — her belief that Mira was at lunch was true, but the person she saw was the twin; her justification had no link to Mira's actual location.
Yes — she formed a confident belief from a clear visual identification and the belief turned out true; identifying a familiar friend is what knowing means.
Yes — Mira's twin looks enough like Mira that mistaking one for the other is reasonable; a reasonable identification leading to truth is knowledge.
No — knowledge about another person's location can never rest on a single glance regardless of resemblance; only verbal confirmation would count.
context: Twin and look-alike cases are textbook Gettier examples: justified true belief that misses knowledge because the source of justification (the twin) is not the source of the truth (Mira's actual location elsewhere).

question: Columnist Mira glances at the wall clock in her newsroom — it reads 3:14 — and forms the belief 'It's 3:14.' It actually IS 3:14, but unknown to her the clock stopped exactly twelve hours earlier and has read 3:14 the whole time. Did Mira actually KNOW the time?
answer: No — Mira's belief is true and felt reasonable, but it didn't track the time; she would have read 3:14 no matter what hour it actually was, so the truth is accidental.
choices: No — Mira's belief is true and felt reasonable, but it didn't track the time; she would have read 3:14 no matter what hour it actually was, so the truth is accidental.
Yes — Mira had a justified true belief, and on the classical analysis of knowledge that combination (justified true belief, or JTB) is what knowledge IS, by definition.
Yes — Mira looked at a clock she had every reason to trust and arrived at a true belief by ordinary means, and ordinary reliable means producing truth counts as knowledge.
No — Mira's belief was unjustified because she did not double-check the clock against another source, and unverified beliefs never count as knowledge regardless of truth.
context: Edmund Gettier (1963) showed that justified true belief is insufficient for knowledge. The Russell-style stopped-clock case is a textbook variant: the believer's reasons track only the clock face, not the time, so the truth of the belief is an accident.

question: An op-ed columnist writes: 'No historical claim about life before written records can really be KNOWN — we have only fragmented inference.' A philosopher replies: 'By that standard, you can never really know what happened in your own kitchen yesterday — you have only fragmented memory.' What survives the columnist's standard?
answer: No — almost nothing survives; the columnist's bar, applied consistently, dissolves both ancient history and ordinary memory, which most readers treat as a reductio against the bar.
choices: No — almost nothing survives; the columnist's bar, applied consistently, dissolves both ancient history and ordinary memory, which most readers treat as a reductio against the bar.
Yes — only direct perceptual experience survives; anything beyond the present sensory moment, ancient or yesterday's, falls outside what the columnist's bar lets us call knowledge.
Yes — propositions of pure logic survive; the columnist's bar bites only empirical claims, leaving mathematical and analytic truths untouched as the residue of certain knowledge.
No — yesterday's kitchen survives but ancient history does not; the parallel is overdrawn because recent memory tracks reality with a reliability that ancient inference lacks.
context: The philosopher's move is a 'tu quoque' against the skeptical standard: if the bar for knowing about pre-literate times is set high enough to exclude them, it excludes ordinary memory too. Either we lower the bar or we slide into near-total skepticism.

question: Reporter Henk is told by a normally reliable colleague: 'The mayor resigned this morning.' Henk forms the belief that the mayor resigned. Unknown to Henk, the colleague mistook a satirical headline for a real one, but as it happens the mayor did actually resign earlier on a different issue. Does Henk KNOW the mayor resigned?
answer: No — Henk's belief is true and his trust in the colleague was justified, but the route through a satirical-headline mistake means his belief didn't track the actual resignation.
choices: No — Henk's belief is true and his trust in the colleague was justified, but the route through a satirical-headline mistake means his belief didn't track the actual resignation.
Yes — Henk relied on a generally reliable colleague and arrived at a true belief, and reliabilism (knowledge as true belief from a reliable process) endorses that result.
Yes — Henk had no reason to suspect the testimony and his belief was true and well-supported by the available evidence, which under the JTB analysis is precisely what knowledge is.
No — Henk lacks knowledge because the resignation is not yet a matter of public record at the moment he forms the belief, and unpublished events cannot be known prior to verification.
context: Defeaters come in two flavors: rebutting defeaters (which support the negation of the claim) and undercutting defeaters (which neutralize the reason without speaking to the claim). Henk lacks the undercutting defeater that would have removed his justification.

question: An expert poultry-sexer reliably sorts day-old chicks into male and female at near-perfect rates, but cannot articulate the cues he uses — when asked, he says, 'I just see it.' He sorts a chick correctly as male without being able to justify why. Does the sexer KNOW the chick is male?
answer: Yes — on reliabilism (knowledge as true belief from a reliable process), the sexer's near-perfect track record makes his unarticulated verdict count as knowledge.
choices: Yes — on reliabilism (knowledge as true belief from a reliable process), the sexer's near-perfect track record makes his unarticulated verdict count as knowledge.
No — on internalism (justification must consist in reasons the believer can access), the sexer's inability to articulate cues prevents his true belief from counting as knowledge.
Yes — the sexer's belief is true and was formed without obvious error, and any true belief formed in normal conditions, regardless of access to grounds, counts as knowledge.
No — the sexer's verdict is a habit rather than a reasoned judgment, and habitual sortings cannot constitute knowledge however reliable the underlying mechanism turns out to be.
context: Reliabilism (Alvin Goldman, 'What Is Justified Belief?', 1979) is externalist about knowledge: it doesn't require the believer to access the reasons. The chicken-sexer is a stock test case — internalists deny he KNOWS, reliabilists insist he does.

question: A podcast host interviews two equally credentialed epidemiologists on a contested public-health question — same training, same data access, sharp disagreement. Each thinks the other is reasoning carefully. After the exchange, should a non-expert listener feel more or less confident in the host's preferred view?
answer: No — when recognized epistemic peers disagree on shared evidence, conciliationism says each should reduce confidence in their own verdict, and the non-expert listener should reduce too.
choices: No — when recognized epistemic peers disagree on shared evidence, conciliationism says each should reduce confidence in their own verdict, and the non-expert listener should reduce too.
Yes — on the steadfast view of peer disagreement, each peer may rationally retain their original confidence after disagreement, and a listener tracking the host's reasoning may share it.
Yes — listeners should defer to whichever expert has the more recent publication record, treating the more-recently-published expert's verdict as the rational anchor for non-expert belief.
No — listeners should defer to the majority of epidemiologists outside the podcast frame and treat one-on-one expert disagreement as an irrelevant pairwise sample of the wider field's view.
context: Peer disagreement (David Christensen 2007, Adam Elga 2007) divides into conciliationist and steadfast camps. Conciliationists hold that recognizing your interlocutor as a genuine peer is in tension with retaining your prior confidence after they disagree.

question: Auditor Pell is told by a normally reliable database that 999 of 1,000 transactions in a month were legitimate. She picks one transaction at random and forms the belief 'This transaction is legitimate.' The transaction in fact IS legitimate. Does Pell KNOW the transaction is legitimate?
answer: No — Pell's belief tracks only the 99.9% base rate, not this transaction; high statistical probability without individuating evidence is widely held insufficient for knowledge.
choices: No — Pell's belief tracks only the 99.9% base rate, not this transaction; high statistical probability without individuating evidence is widely held insufficient for knowledge.
Yes — Pell's belief is true and supported by extremely strong probabilistic evidence, and any belief with that probability of correctness, formed in good faith, counts as knowledge.
Yes — Pell relied on a reliable database and arrived at a true belief, and reliabilism (knowledge as true belief from a reliable process) clearly endorses her belief as knowledge.
No — Pell lacks knowledge because the database is a secondary source rather than direct perception, and only beliefs formed by firsthand observation can ever count as knowledge here.
context: The lottery paradox and 'proof paradox' (Cohen 1977, Buchak 2014) press the intuition that statistical evidence — however high the probability — doesn't deliver knowledge of an individual case. Courts of law track this asymmetry: pure statistics rarely convict.

question: A self-help guru on a podcast adopts a radical-doubt move: 'You can't really know anything external to your mind — every perception could be a dream or hallucination.' A listener presses: granted the radical-doubt frame, what proposition WOULD still be certain at every moment the guru entertained the doubt?
answer: Yes — the proposition 'I am now thinking' survives, because the very act of entertaining the doubt is itself a thought; the doubter cannot doubt without thinking (Descartes's cogito).
choices: Yes — the proposition 'I am now thinking' survives, because the very act of entertaining the doubt is itself a thought; the doubter cannot doubt without thinking (Descartes's cogito).
Yes — the claim that an external world exists survives, because perceptual experience presupposes a world generating the appearances, and any coherent doubt presupposes the world it doubts.
No — nothing survives radical doubt, because once any source of belief is suspended the doubter has no basis at all left for any positive claim, including claims about her own mind.
Yes — the truths of mathematics survive radical doubt because they hold in any possible world, including dream worlds and demon-deceived worlds the doubter contemplates in this case.
context: Descartes (Meditations on First Philosophy, 1641) located the cogito as the one proposition the radical doubter cannot coherently doubt: the act of doubting is a thought, so 'I think' is certain. Critics like Lichtenberg pressed back on the 'I.'

question: A weather columnist confidently tells viewers tomorrow will be sunny, citing his rooftop barometer. Tomorrow IS sunny. What he hasn't noticed, though it sits in a memo on his desk, is that his barometer has been broken for a week and has been stuck at one reading. Did the columnist KNOW it would be sunny?
answer: No — the columnist had an accessible undercutting defeater (the memo), which would have removed his reason for trusting the barometer; believers must check easily-accessible defeaters.
choices: No — the columnist had an accessible undercutting defeater (the memo), which would have removed his reason for trusting the barometer; believers must check easily-accessible defeaters.
Yes — the columnist's belief is true and was formed by what he took to be a reliable instrument, and his ignorance of the broken barometer absolves him of any obligation to dig further.
Yes — on reliabilism (knowledge as true belief from a reliable process), the columnist's track record with the barometer makes today's reading count as knowledge despite the malfunction.
No — the columnist's belief is unjustified because barometers are inherently unreliable, and anyone relying on a single rooftop barometer cannot count as having knowledge of weather.
context: Undercutting defeaters (John Pollock 1986) neutralize a justification without supporting the negation of the knowledge claim. The 'no-defeaters' clause in epistemology is often qualified: easily-accessible defeaters must be checked.

question: An op-ed writer claims to 'know' his flight leaves at 6pm because he checked his calendar. Confronted with the prospect that missing the flight would cost a billion-dollar deal, he says, 'Well — I'd better double-check.' On contextualism (knowledge ascriptions vary with stakes), does he KNOW the time before he checks?
answer: No — on contextualism, the stakes that prompt his hesitation raise the standard for knowledge in that conversational context, and his single calendar glance falls below the new bar.
choices: No — on contextualism, the stakes that prompt his hesitation raise the standard for knowledge in that conversational context, and his single calendar glance falls below the new bar.
Yes — on contextualism, the writer's calendar check delivers knowledge in any context, because the truth-conditions of 'know' are fixed by the believer's evidence and not by the stakes.
Yes — the calendar is a reliable source and the writer's belief is true and undefeated, which on the JTB analysis is precisely what knowledge requires regardless of conversational stakes.
No — the writer doesn't know because no single calendar check ever delivers knowledge of one's own schedule, since all calendar entries require independent cross-source verification first.
context: Epistemic contextualism (Stewart Cohen 1986, Keith DeRose 1995, David Lewis 1996) holds the truth-conditions of 'S knows that P' shift with conversational context — raise the stakes or salient error possibilities, and the bar for ascribing knowledge rises.

question: A traveler driving through unfamiliar country sees a barn and forms the belief 'There's a barn there.' There IS a barn — but unknown to him, the surrounding countryside is dotted with cleverly painted barn facades that would have fooled him equally well. He happened to point at the one real barn. Does the traveler KNOW it's a barn?
answer: No — the belief is true and his vision works, but the environment is full of indistinguishable fakes; the belief could easily have been false, and that fragility blocks knowledge.
choices: No — the belief is true and his vision works, but the environment is full of indistinguishable fakes; the belief could easily have been false, and that fragility blocks knowledge.
Yes — the traveler's vision is reliable and he formed a true belief through ordinary perception, and ordinary perception producing truth simply IS what knowledge consists of.
Yes — the traveler had a justified true belief based on direct visual perception of the barn, and the JTB analysis of knowledge is satisfied here regardless of any unseen fakes nearby.
No — the traveler lacks knowledge because perception alone never delivers knowledge of distant objects, and any belief about distant objects requires corroborating non-visual evidence first.
context: Alvin Goldman's fake-barn case (1976) showed that even reliable faculties producing true belief can fail to deliver knowledge when the environment is full of fakes. Sensitivity and safety conditions (Nozick 1981, Sosa 1999) were developed to capture this.

question: A non-expert reader of climate research, without specialized training, forms the belief that average global temperatures have risen significantly over the last century — on the basis that climate scientists overwhelmingly say so. Her belief is true. Does she KNOW average temperatures have risen?
answer: Yes — reliance on a strong professional consensus among credentialed scientists is itself a reliable process, and on reliabilism that delivers knowledge to the rational layperson.
choices: Yes — reliance on a strong professional consensus among credentialed scientists is itself a reliable process, and on reliabilism that delivers knowledge to the rational layperson.
No — only those who can personally evaluate the underlying climate data and statistical methodology can know what the data show; a non-expert can never have knowledge by deferral alone.
Yes — the reader's belief is true and was formed by ordinary perception of expert statements, and any true belief formed by ordinary perceptual contact with the world counts as knowledge.
No — the reader's belief depends on testimony from many experts she has never personally met, and beliefs based on chains of unmet testifiers cannot rise to the standard of knowledge.
context: Testimony as a route to knowledge (Coady, Testimony, 1992; Lackey 2008) is now broadly accepted; the question shifts to WHEN testimony is reliable. Strong professional consensus, supported by the practice's track record, is a paradigm reliable case.

question: Reader Avi forms the belief that he did NOT win the lottery — a sensible belief given one-in-100-million odds — and he is in fact correct. Some philosophers note: Avi would form exactly the same belief even if he HAD won and not yet learned of it. Does Avi KNOW he didn't win?
answer: No — on the sensitivity condition (S's belief that P counts as knowledge only if S would not believe P were P false), Avi's belief is insensitive: he'd believe he hadn't won even if he had.
choices: No — on the sensitivity condition (S's belief that P counts as knowledge only if S would not believe P were P false), Avi's belief is insensitive: he'd believe he hadn't won even if he had.
Yes — Avi's belief is true and extraordinarily well-supported probabilistically, and any belief with that probability of correctness formed in good faith counts as knowledge under JTB.
Yes — the lottery has a definite answer at the moment Avi forms the belief, and on reliabilism Avi's belief was produced by a reliable process (statistical reasoning) and so is knowledge.
No — the lottery's outcome is in principle unknowable until publicly announced; any belief about a not-yet-announced lottery result is unjustified regardless of probability or sensitivity.
context: Robert Nozick's sensitivity condition (Philosophical Explanations, 1981) requires that S's belief track the truth across nearby possible worlds. Ernest Sosa (1999) proposed the related 'safety' condition. Lottery cases sharpen the divergence between the two.

question: Reader Coen reads in a science magazine that a certain mineral is found in deep ocean vents. Coen forms the belief, and it happens to be true. A week later he learns the magazine has been credibly accused of fabricating sources for that very article. He hasn't yet checked whether his claim is among the fabrications. Does Coen still KNOW?
answer: No — the credible accusation acts as an undercutting defeater for the magazine's testimony on this article; once the source's reliability is in question, the justification is suspended.
choices: No — the credible accusation acts as an undercutting defeater for the magazine's testimony on this article; once the source's reliability is in question, the justification is suspended.
Yes — Coen's belief was acquired through reading at the time, and later discrediting of the source cannot retroactively remove knowledge that was genuinely possessed when it was formed.
Yes — on reliabilism (knowledge as true belief from a reliable process), magazine articles remain a reliable enough process that Coen's belief still satisfies the reliabilist's standard.
No — Coen's belief was never knowledge to begin with, because no belief acquired through printed media can ever rise to the standard of knowledge regardless of the source's track record.
context: Defeaters can arrive after a belief is formed: once you learn your source is unreliable on the question at issue, the original justification is undercut. Whether the belief was knowledge at any prior moment is a separate question from whether it is now.

question: Two equally credentialed nutrition scientists publish opposing reviews of a popular diet. Reporter Sela later learns one is paid as a consultant by the diet's manufacturer while the other has no financial connection. Should Sela still treat the disagreement as a case of genuine peer disagreement requiring conciliation?
answer: No — once the financial-incentive asymmetry is known, the two are no longer epistemic peers on this question, and the conciliationist equal-weight rule only applies to genuine peers.
choices: No — once the financial-incentive asymmetry is known, the two are no longer epistemic peers on this question, and the conciliationist equal-weight rule only applies to genuine peers.
Yes — credentials and training are the only criteria for peer status, and any review article from someone with equivalent training counts as peer-level evidence regardless of interest.
Yes — disagreement between any two credentialed experts always demands conciliation, since financial ties are downstream of training and qualifications and cannot themselves alter peerhood.
No — Sela should defer entirely to the funded consultant, because manufacturer-side scientists have access to proprietary data the independent reviewer does not, regardless of incentives.
context: Peer disagreement frameworks (Christensen 2007, Elga 2007) require that the disputants really BE peers on the question. Conflicts of interest, asymmetric access to evidence, or differential track records can defeat the peerhood that triggers the conciliation demand.

question: A small-business owner forms and holds the belief 'My books are clean,' but consistently avoids looking at any of the reports that would either confirm or refute it. The books are in fact clean. A skeptic asks whether avoiding evidence undermines the owner's claim to KNOW. Does the owner know?
answer: No — avoiding available evidence acts as a self-imposed defeater; on internalist views, the believer must engage evidence she could easily access for the belief to count as knowledge.
choices: No — avoiding available evidence acts as a self-imposed defeater; on internalist views, the believer must engage evidence she could easily access for the belief to count as knowledge.
Yes — the owner's belief is true and was formed in ordinary background trust, and on reliabilism (knowledge as true belief from a reliable process) trust in one's own systems is reliable.
Yes — the owner's belief is justified by her experience running the business and turned out to be true, and the JTB analysis is satisfied regardless of whether she examined the books.
No — the owner cannot know her books are clean without a third-party audit; self-assessment of one's own books is constitutively unreliable and never yields knowledge here regardless.
context: Internalists about justification (BonJour, Conee-Feldman) emphasize the believer's responsibility to engage available evidence. 'Epistemic akrasia' — knowing you should check but not checking — undermines the kind of cognitive ownership knowledge requires.

question: Suppose a person reliably forms true beliefs about distant events by what feels to her like a vivid hunch — she has no evidence the hunches work and no theory of why, but a long track record shows they're nearly always right. She hunches that a fire is burning in a distant town, and there is. Does she KNOW about the fire?
answer: Yes — on reliabilism (knowledge as true belief from a reliable process), her track record makes the hunch-mechanism a reliable process, and the resulting belief counts as knowledge.
choices: Yes — on reliabilism (knowledge as true belief from a reliable process), her track record makes the hunch-mechanism a reliable process, and the resulting belief counts as knowledge.
No — on internalism (justification must consist in reasons the believer can access), her inability to articulate why the hunches work prevents the true beliefs from counting as knowledge.
Yes — she has formed a true belief in the ordinary course of her mental life and is sincerely confident, and any sincere confident true belief produced this way counts as knowledge.
No — clairvoyant powers don't exist in real cases, so the question is malformed; questions presupposing impossible mechanisms cannot generate genuine epistemological verdicts at all.
context: Laurence BonJour's clairvoyance case (The Structure of Empirical Knowledge, 1985) is designed to put pressure on reliabilism: if any reliable process delivers knowledge regardless of access, that seems to count clairvoyants as knowers, which troubles internalists.

question: A student argues: 'I know I have hands. I know that if I have hands, I am not a brain in a vat (since a vat-brain has no hands). So I know I'm not a brain in a vat.' A skeptic claims the chain breaks somewhere. On the closure principle (knowledge transfers across known entailment), does the student really KNOW the conclusion?
answer: Yes — closure is the default principle (S knows P, knows P entails Q, so S knows Q); the student's argument is closure applied, and rejecting the conclusion costs the principle itself.
choices: Yes — closure is the default principle (S knows P, knows P entails Q, so S knows Q); the student's argument is closure applied, and rejecting the conclusion costs the principle itself.
No — closure fails on skeptical-hypothesis arguments; the student's belief in her hands does not transmit to anti-skeptical conclusions, since hand-belief can't track the vat-brain question.
Yes — but only because she has independent evidence against the brain-in-a-vat scenario from her perception, not because of any transmission of knowledge across the logical entailment here.
No — closure fails for all knowledge claims, since the entailment relation never transmits epistemic standing from any belief to any other belief, whether the believer notices it or not.
context: The closure principle is a long-standing battleground. Nozick (1981) rejects closure to save common-sense knowledge from skepticism; Stewart Cohen and others defend closure and locate the skeptical pressure elsewhere. The student's argument is the classic version.

question: A talk-radio columnist writes: 'No moral claim can really be KNOWN — disagreement across cultures is too deep.' A philosopher objects that the same standard applied to empirical claims would dissolve all empirical knowledge, since cross-cultural disagreement exists on those too. Would any moral claim survive the columnist's standard?
answer: No — almost no moral claims survive consistently; the bar cuts so deep that even shared judgments (like the wrongness of gratuitous cruelty) dissolve, which most readers treat as a reductio.
choices: No — almost no moral claims survive consistently; the bar cuts so deep that even shared judgments (like the wrongness of gratuitous cruelty) dissolve, which most readers treat as a reductio.
Yes — only purely definitional moral claims survive (such as 'unjust acts are by definition wrong'); the columnist's bar leaves only this tautological residue of moral knowledge intact.
Yes — claims about one's own present moral sentiments survive ('I feel revulsion at this act'), since first-person psychological reports don't depend on cross-cultural agreement for warrant.
No — only moral claims grounded in religious revelation survive, since the columnist's bar targets only secular moral reasoning and leaves religious moral knowledge untouched by the move.
context: The structural move is the same as historical-skepticism tu quoque: a standard for knowing that cuts too deep is its own reductio. Cross-cultural disagreement is a feature of empirical knowledge too; consistent skepticism dissolves both or neither.

question: A scientist publishes a paper concluding that a new drug works, while noting she could be wrong (her data has the usual confidence intervals). A philosopher of science argues the admission of possible error is incompatible with knowledge — to know is to be certain. Does the scientist's caveat preclude her KNOWING the drug works?
answer: No — on fallibilism (knowledge does not require absolute certainty), a believer can know that P and acknowledge possible error, since knowledge requires good evidence but not infallibility.
choices: No — on fallibilism (knowledge does not require absolute certainty), a believer can know that P and acknowledge possible error, since knowledge requires good evidence but not infallibility.
Yes — knowledge requires certainty, and admitting a non-zero probability of error means the believer cannot strictly claim to know; the scientist should retract the claim as mere belief.
No — but only because scientific knowledge is a special category exempted from the certainty rule; ordinary everyday knowledge genuinely does require the absolute certainty disclaimed here.
Yes — the scientist's caveat is a rhetorical flourish that doesn't actually undermine her knowledge, since published scientific claims are by convention always taken to assert certainty.
context: Fallibilism — most associated with Charles Sanders Peirce — is now the orthodoxy in philosophy of science and most contemporary epistemology. Few claim knowledge requires Cartesian certainty; the interesting debate is what level of justification IS required.

question: A statistician finalizes an analysis showing a drug works. A colleague then privately reveals: 'You've been working without sleep for forty hours.' The statistician is confident the analysis is sound but recognizes sleep-deprivation as a known source of errors she might not detect. Should she retain her original confidence in the result?
answer: No — higher-order evidence (the disclosure her judgment may itself be unreliable now) is a defeater that doesn't contradict her first-order analysis; the rational response is to step back.
choices: No — higher-order evidence (the disclosure her judgment may itself be unreliable now) is a defeater that doesn't contradict her first-order analysis; the rational response is to step back.
Yes — her first-order analysis is the actual evidence for the drug working; meta-level worries about her cognitive state cannot count as evidence about whether the drug actually works.
Yes — on reliabilism (knowledge as true belief from a reliable process), her statistical methods remain reliable regardless of current sleep state, so the original confidence is justified.
No — sleep deprivation always renders any judgment formed during the deprivation period entirely worthless; the analysis must be discarded, since partial confidence reduction is not enough.
context: Higher-order evidence (David Christensen 2010, Maria Lasonen-Aarnio 2014) is evidence about whether one's first-order evidence has been correctly evaluated. Its existence complicates Bayesian updating, because it doesn't change first-order probabilities directly.

question: A forecaster looks at the broken weather station's dial reading 23°C — a temperature it has shown for three days because the needle is stuck. By coincidence, today's actual temperature is 23°C. He records the reading in his log: 'Temperature 23°C, confident.' Did the forecaster KNOW the temperature?
answer: No — his belief is true and he had a reason for it, but the reason did not track the truth; the station would have shown 23°C regardless, so the correctness is accidental rather than knowledge-conferring.
choices: No — his belief is true and he had a reason for it, but the reason did not track the truth; the station would have shown 23°C regardless, so the correctness is accidental rather than knowledge-conferring.

Yes — justified true belief is what knowledge has always meant, and the forecaster had all three: a true belief, a reason from a normally reliable instrument, and the correct outcome that confirms his record entry.

No — knowledge requires direct observation of the world, not instrument readings, so the forecaster never knew the temperature even on days when the station worked correctly and the dial moved with conditions.

Yes — the forecaster was justified in trusting the station, the belief turned out true, and accidental correctness is no obstacle since knowledge tracks the believer's epistemic position rather than external luck.
context: Edmund Gettier's three-page paper (1963) showed that justified-true-belief is not quite knowledge. Variants like Russell's stopped-clock and Goldman's fake-barn country (1976) sharpen the point: when the truth of the belief is a coincidence relative to the believer's reasons, knowledge fails to obtain.

question: A philosophy student is told to strip away every belief that could conceivably be the product of a systematic deception: senses, memories, mathematical intuitions, even the apparent existence of an external world. What, if anything, would still be certain after this exercise?
answer: That something is doing the doubting — the very activity of doubt requires a doubter, so the bare existential fact that some thinking thing exists survives even a demon's deception about its content.
choices: That something is doing the doubting — the very activity of doubt requires a doubter, so the bare existential fact that some thinking thing exists survives even a demon's deception about its content.

That the external world exists in some form — sensations must come from somewhere, so even under deception the world causing the sensations must be real on some level, even if not as the sensations represent it.

That mathematical truths hold regardless of any deceiver — the structure of arithmetic and logic cannot be falsified by an external trickster, since these truths are necessary and the demon's power is contingent.

That moral truths remain certain whatever the deception — ethics depends on pure reason rather than sensory evidence, so the moral law would survive any cognitive interference that targeted only empirical beliefs.
context: Descartes's Meditations (1641) runs this thought experiment: the 'evil demon' could be deceiving you about everything. The one bedrock survivor is the cogito — 'I think, therefore I am.' Whether anything else survives (e.g., math, God's existence) is debated; Descartes's own further moves remain contested.

question: A chicken-sexer reliably sorts day-old chicks by gender with 99% accuracy but cannot articulate any reason for her judgments — she just 'sees' it. An evidentialist on the panel says she does not have knowledge; a reliabilist says she does. Which conception of knowledge does her case challenge?
answer: Evidentialism — Conee and Feldman's view ties justification to evidence the agent has and can deploy, so the sexer's inarticulate reliability fails the requirement even though her process produces the truth.
choices: Evidentialism — Conee and Feldman's view ties justification to evidence the agent has and can deploy, so the sexer's inarticulate reliability fails the requirement even though her process produces the truth.

Reliabilism — Goldman's view ties justification to the reliability of the belief-forming process, so the sexer's high success rate confers justification regardless of whether she can articulate any evidence at all.

Virtue epistemology — Sosa's view ties knowledge to cognitive achievement attributable to the agent's skill, so the sexer's reliable competence over years counts as the kind of credit-conferring success required.

Contextualism — DeRose's view ties 'knows' to context-set standards of evidence, so whether the sexer knows depends on how strict the conversational standard is and not on the inner structure of her evidence.
context: The chicken-sexer case is from BonJour and others arguing against externalism: process reliability isn't enough without internal justification. Reliabilists (Goldman, Process Reliabilism, 1979) reply that the case actually establishes their view. Conee and Feldman defend evidentialism in Evidentialism (2004).

question: A driver glances out at a barn and forms the belief 'that is a barn.' He has in fact looked at a real barn — but he is in fake-barn country, where nearly all the structures by the road are convincing facades. Had he looked at any neighboring structure he would have formed the same false belief. Did he KNOW?
answer: No — his belief is true but unsafe: in close possible worlds where he looked slightly differently the belief would have been false, so a safety condition (belief could not easily have been wrong) is violated.
choices: No — his belief is true but unsafe: in close possible worlds where he looked slightly differently the belief would have been false, so a safety condition (belief could not easily have been wrong) is violated.

Yes — the actual barn is real and his perceptual faculties were functioning normally; nearby counterfactuals are irrelevant to whether his perceptual belief in the actual case constitutes knowledge of what he saw.

No — perception alone cannot ground knowledge in environments designed to deceive, so the driver lacked the testimony or inference required to convert his sensory state into something more than mere appearance.

Yes — reliabilism is satisfied because the driver's perceptual system functions reliably under normal conditions, and the fake-barn environment is too unusual to undercut the process's general reliability rating.
context: Goldman introduced fake-barn country (1976) as a Gettier variant: the belief is true, but the environment makes its truth lucky. Sosa and Pritchard developed the safety condition: in nearby possible worlds the belief should not easily have been false. The driver fails safety even though the actual barn he saw is real.

question: Before the draw, a ticket-holder believes 'my ticket will lose' on the basis of the very long odds. His ticket does in fact lose. A philosopher on the panel says: 'Yet he did not KNOW it would lose.' Which conception of knowledge does the philosopher's verdict appeal to?
answer: Sensitivity — Nozick's condition requires that if p were false the agent would not believe p, so the lottery belief fails because the agent would have believed 'my ticket will lose' just the same had he won.
choices: Sensitivity — Nozick's condition requires that if p were false the agent would not believe p, so the lottery belief fails because the agent would have believed 'my ticket will lose' just the same had he won.

Reliabilism — Goldman's condition requires the belief to issue from a process with high truth-ratio, and lottery beliefs based on long odds satisfy this since the process gets a true belief with very high frequency.

Evidentialism — Conee and Feldman's condition requires justification to fit the agent's evidence, and the lottery evidence does justify the belief that the ticket will probably lose, so the verdict is too strict.

Virtue epistemology — Sosa's condition requires cognitive achievement attributable to the agent's skill, and forming probabilistic beliefs from odds counts as that kind of competence-driven achievement on the view.
context: Nozick's Philosophical Explanations (1981) defends sensitivity: knowledge requires you would not believe p in close worlds where p is false. The lottery is the canonical pressure: probabilistic belief satisfies reliability but fails sensitivity. Safety (Sosa, Pritchard) was developed in part to handle the lottery cases differently.

question: Friday morning, casually: 'I know the bank is open Saturday — I was there last Saturday and they were.' Friday afternoon, with the mortgage check that must clear, the same speaker hesitates: 'I don't actually KNOW the bank is open tomorrow.' Same evidence, same speaker. Which conception best explains the shift?
answer: Contextualism — DeRose's view holds 'knows' has a context-sensitive standard that rises with the stakes of the conversation, so the same evidence underwrites 'knows' in casual context and fails to in the high-stakes one.
choices: Contextualism — DeRose's view holds 'knows' has a context-sensitive standard that rises with the stakes of the conversation, so the same evidence underwrites 'knows' in casual context and fails to in the high-stakes one.

Pragmatic encroachment — Stanley and Hawthorne hold that practical stakes affect whether the subject knows, so the speaker actually does not know in the afternoon, not merely that 'knows' fits less under afternoon standards.

Sensitivity invariantism — knowledge requires the belief would not be held if false; the speaker's belief is sensitive both mornings, so the apparent shift in 'knows' is just talk and not a real change in epistemic status.

Strict invariantism — 'knows' has a single very high standard; the morning self misspeaks rather than knowing, and the afternoon correction merely catches up to what the constant standard required all along.
context: Keith DeRose's 'Solving the Skeptical Problem' (1995) and 'The Case for Contextualism' (2009) develop the bank case. Stanley's Knowledge and Practical Interests (2005) and Hawthorne's Knowledge and Lotteries (2004) defend pragmatic encroachment as the rival explanation. Both reject simple invariantism, but on different grounds.

question: Two epistemic peers — equally trained, equal access to the same data — arrive at opposite credences in a forecasting question after long deliberation. One epistemologist says each should move significantly toward the other. A second says each may rationally retain her first-order judgment. Which conception does the first defend?
answer: Conciliationism — Christensen's view that higher-order evidence of peer disagreement requires significant credence revision toward the peer, since the disagreement is evidence that one's own reasoning may be flawed.
choices: Conciliationism — Christensen's view that higher-order evidence of peer disagreement requires significant credence revision toward the peer, since the disagreement is evidence that one's own reasoning may be flawed.

Steadfastness — Kelly's view that first-order reasons retain rational weight against the higher-order pressure of disagreement, so each peer may rationally hold position when her own evidence supports it on review.

Total-evidence equal-weight — Elga's view that one's prior probability of being correct equals one's peer's, so each should move exactly to the midpoint regardless of how detailed the first-order reasons appear.

Justificationism — Lackey's view that disagreement defeats justification only when the peers share evidence and reasoning, with idealized peerhood rare enough that most real disagreements leave first-order standing intact.
context: David Christensen's 'Epistemology of Disagreement' (2007) defends conciliationism (significant revision in response to peer disagreement). Thomas Kelly's 'Peer Disagreement and Higher-Order Evidence' (2010) defends a steadfastness-leaning view where first-order reasons retain weight. The debate is unresolved.

question: A commuter checks the schedule, sees the train is at 5:14, and forms the belief. On Monday she is going to a routine meeting; on Tuesday she is presenting at a hearing she cannot miss. Same evidence both days. On Tuesday she rechecks twice. Which conception explains the asymmetry in what she should do?
answer: Pragmatic encroachment — Stanley and Hawthorne hold that practical stakes affect what the subject is in a position to know, so on Tuesday she is not yet in a position to know what she could know on Monday.
choices: Pragmatic encroachment — Stanley and Hawthorne hold that practical stakes affect what the subject is in a position to know, so on Tuesday she is not yet in a position to know what she could know on Monday.

Contextualism — DeRose holds 'knows' has context-set standards rather than stakes-dependent thresholds on knowledge itself; the speaker's epistemic standing is the same both days, only what 'know' picks out differs.

Strict evidentialism — Conee and Feldman hold justification depends on evidence had, which is the same both days, so the asymmetry in rechecking is at most prudential rather than reflecting a real difference in knowledge.

Process reliabilism — Goldman holds knowledge tracks the reliability of the underlying process, which is fixed across the two days; the asymmetry in caution reflects risk aversion rather than the agent's epistemic position itself.
context: Jason Stanley's Knowledge and Practical Interests (2005) and John Hawthorne's Knowledge and Lotteries (2004) defend pragmatic encroachment: practical stakes affect what a subject is in a position to know. Critics (Brown, DeRose) argue the data are better explained by context-set semantic standards on 'knows.'

question: An amateur astronomer, after years of careful observation, identifies a new variable star — confirmed the next month by professional observatories. A philosopher says her belief was true because of her skill, and so constitutes knowledge in the strongest sense. Which conception is the philosopher applying?
answer: Virtue epistemology — Sosa's view holds knowledge is a cognitive achievement attributable to the agent's competence, so the astronomer's success is creditable to her observational skill rather than environmental luck.
choices: Virtue epistemology — Sosa's view holds knowledge is a cognitive achievement attributable to the agent's competence, so the astronomer's success is creditable to her observational skill rather than environmental luck.

Reliabilism — Goldman's view holds knowledge tracks reliability of the process, but it does not require the success to be creditable to the agent's skill, so the philosopher's emphasis on credit goes beyond reliabilism.

Evidentialism — Conee and Feldman's view holds justification depends on fit between belief and evidence, but the philosopher's emphasis on skill and credit shifts attention from evidence to the agent's competence.

Sensitivity invariantism — Nozick's view holds knowledge requires the belief would not be held if false, and the philosopher's emphasis on credit is distinct from this counterfactual structure of belief and truth.
context: Ernest Sosa's A Virtue Epistemology (2007) defends knowledge as 'apt belief' — true belief from competence. Linda Zagzebski's Virtues of the Mind (1996) is the other major virtue-epistemological program, emphasizing intellectual virtues. The view's signature move: shift the unit of evaluation from belief to cognitive agent.

question: A juror believes the defendant was at the scene because an eyewitness identified him. New evidence: the eyewitness viewed the lineup under lighting that has since been shown to produce unreliable identifications. The new evidence neither shows the ID was wrong nor that another person was there. What kind of defeater is this?
answer: Undercutting defeater — Pollock's term for evidence that removes the connection between the original evidence and the belief without itself showing the belief false, so the juror's reason no longer supports her belief.
choices: Undercutting defeater — Pollock's term for evidence that removes the connection between the original evidence and the belief without itself showing the belief false, so the juror's reason no longer supports her belief.

Rebutting defeater — Pollock's term for evidence that directly supports the negation of the original belief, such as evidence the defendant was elsewhere; the juror's case lacks any such directly contradicting evidence here.

No defeater at all — the juror's evidence remains exactly what it was, since the new information about lighting only affects what other eyewitnesses might say, not what this eyewitness has actually testified to.

Higher-order defeater — Christensen's term for evidence about the reliability of the agent's own reasoning, rather than evidence about the world; the juror would face this only if her own competence as juror were questioned.
context: John Pollock's Contemporary Theories of Knowledge (1986) distinguishes undercutting from rebutting defeaters: rebutting attacks the belief's truth directly; undercutting attacks the support relation. The distinction is widely used in formal epistemology and AI knowledge representation.

question: An epistemologist argues: 'You know you have hands. You know that if you have hands, you are not a handless brain-in-a-vat being fed sensory data. So by closure under known entailment you know you are not a brain-in-a-vat. Skepticism is mistaken.' Which conception is the argument deploying?
answer: Epistemic closure — the principle that if you know p and you know p entails q, you know q, applied to transmit ordinary knowledge of hands to anti-skeptical knowledge that you are not a handless envatted brain.
choices: Epistemic closure — the principle that if you know p and you know p entails q, you know q, applied to transmit ordinary knowledge of hands to anti-skeptical knowledge that you are not a handless envatted brain.

Sensitivity — Nozick's denial of closure: knowledge requires that if p were false you would not believe p, and the brain-in-a-vat belief fails this, so the argument's closure step is exactly what sensitivity rejects.

Contextualism — DeRose's view that 'knows' picks out different standards in different contexts, so the argument's premises and conclusion are not all true under one standard, and closure is preserved across single contexts only.

Pragmatic encroachment — Stanley and Hawthorne's view that practical stakes affect knowledge, so the transition from hands to anti-skeptical knowledge changes the stakes and so changes whether the subject knows.
context: G.E. Moore's 'Proof of an External World' (1939) gives the basic anti-skeptical move. Closure-based responses to skepticism are defended by Williamson, Hawthorne; rejected by Nozick and Dretske in favor of denying closure. The price of denying closure: the agent knows p but not its known consequences.

question: A journalist reports a finding from a source whose track record is reasonable but not exceptional. One epistemologist argues testimony reduces to non-testimonial evidence: I should believe only if the track record warrants it. Another says testimony is a basic source. Which conception does the first defend?
answer: Reductionism about testimony — Hume's view that testimonial justification reduces to inductive evidence about the source's reliability, so each acceptance of testimony rests on track-record support of that source.
choices: Reductionism about testimony — Hume's view that testimonial justification reduces to inductive evidence about the source's reliability, so each acceptance of testimony rests on track-record support of that source.

Anti-reductionism about testimony — Reid's view that testimony is a basic source of justification, so the hearer is entitled to believe absent positive defeaters even when she lacks an explicit track-record assessment.

Credulism about testimony — Coady's view that testimony is presumptively credible and the burden lies on doubters to provide defeaters; track records do work only when the case generates suspicion in the hearer.

Evidentialism about testimony — Conee and Feldman hold that what matters is the total evidence the agent possesses, of which testimony is just one input weighted alongside others; reduction to track records is too narrow.
context: Hume's 'Of Miracles' (Enquiry, 1748) treats testimony as inductive: trust it only when the track record supports it. Thomas Reid (Essays on the Intellectual Powers, 1785) takes testimony as a basic source. C.A.J. Coady's Testimony (1992) restarts the modern debate; Lackey's Learning From Words (2008) is a recent landmark.

question: A philosopher writes: 'Strictly, you don't know X simply — you know X rather than Y. Your evidence rules out being-a-cleverly-painted-mule, but does not rule out being-a-zebra-in-a-cleverly-designed-vat. Knowledge is a three-place relation.' Which conception is the philosopher defending?
answer: Contrastivism — Schaffer's view that 'knows' is a three-place relation K(s, p, q) where the subject knows p rather than q, with the contrast q built into the knowledge claim rather than left implicit.
choices: Contrastivism — Schaffer's view that 'knows' is a three-place relation K(s, p, q) where the subject knows p rather than q, with the contrast q built into the knowledge claim rather than left implicit.

Contextualism — DeRose's view that 'knows' has context-dependent standards, similar in shape but distinct: the contextualist varies the threshold for 'knows,' while contrastivism varies the proposition being known itself.

Relevant alternatives theory — Dretske's view that knowledge requires ruling out relevant alternatives, where relevance is fixed by context; the philosopher's three-place structure goes beyond Dretske's two-place 'knows.'

Reliabilism — Goldman's view that knowledge tracks process reliability; the philosopher's three-place structure is orthogonal to whether the process produces truth at a high ratio across the relevant range.
context: Jonathan Schaffer's 'Contrastive Knowledge' (2005) and 'From Contextualism to Contrastivism' (2004) develop contrastivism as a successor to Dretske's relevant-alternatives view. The signature claim: the implicit contrast in knowledge ascriptions should be made explicit, restructuring 'knows' as a relation Kpqr.

question: A panel reviews two physicists who fit the same data with rival theories — both empirically adequate, differing only on entities the data cannot directly probe. One panelist says: 'The data alone never force a unique theory; auxiliary commitments do the rest.' What thesis is being defended?
answer: Underdetermination of theory by data — the Quine-Duhem thesis that data alone never force a unique theoretical commitment, since auxiliary hypotheses can always be revised to preserve a chosen theory in the face of evidence.
choices: Underdetermination of theory by data — the Quine-Duhem thesis that data alone never force a unique theoretical commitment, since auxiliary hypotheses can always be revised to preserve a chosen theory in the face of evidence.

Holism about meaning — Quine's separate thesis that the meaning of terms in a theory is fixed by the theory as a whole rather than term-by-term; the panelist's claim is about evidence, not meaning composition.

Theory-ladenness of observation — Hanson's claim that observations are framed by the theoretical lens of the observer; this is distinct from the underdetermination claim about data-to-theory inference relations.

Inference to the best explanation skepticism — van Fraassen's worry that 'best' explanation is too weak to license belief; this is about explanatory virtues, not directly about auxiliary-hypothesis flexibility.
context: Pierre Duhem (The Aim and Structure of Physical Theory, 1906) argued physical theories face evidence as wholes, not piecemeal. Quine's 'Two Dogmas of Empiricism' (1951) generalized this — the Quine-Duhem thesis. Laudan and Leplin (1991) push back: underdetermination is far weaker in practice than in principle.

question: A forecaster at the end of a 20-hour shift makes a careful calculation and gets a result. A colleague tells her: 'You've been at this 20 hours; fatigued people produce errors they cannot detect from inside.' Her calculation looks fine to her. What should she rationally do with this new information?
answer: Reduce her credence in the result — higher-order evidence (evidence about the reliability of her own reasoning) defeats the first-order calculation even though no specific error has been identified yet.
choices: Reduce her credence in the result — higher-order evidence (evidence about the reliability of her own reasoning) defeats the first-order calculation even though no specific error has been identified yet.

Retain full credence in the result — the colleague's comment is not first-order evidence about the calculation itself, so unless a specific error is identified, the careful calculation's epistemic standing is untouched.

Abandon the result entirely — fatigue is a defeater, so the rational response is to set credence to the prior rather than try to weigh fatigue against the calculation's apparent quality on its own merits.

Retain full credence pending review by a fresh peer — the case is one of awaiting confirmation, not of current credence revision; the forecaster's current epistemic state is unaffected by what review might later reveal.
context: David Christensen's 'Higher-Order Evidence' (2010) gives the canonical treatment. The fatigue case is a workhorse example: evidence about the reliability of one's own reasoning rationally defeats first-order judgments, even without identifying which specific step went wrong. Critics worry the view is over-strong.

question: A philosopher accepts: 'I know I have hands.' She denies: 'I know I am not a brain-in-a-vat being fed sensory data of hands.' She insists this is consistent — closure fails. Which conception of knowledge is she defending by allowing this combination?
answer: Sensitivity-based knowledge — Nozick's tracking theory makes knowledge require that if p were false the agent would not believe p, so 'I have hands' is sensitive but 'I am not a brain-in-a-vat' is not.
choices: Sensitivity-based knowledge — Nozick's tracking theory makes knowledge require that if p were false the agent would not believe p, so 'I have hands' is sensitive but 'I am not a brain-in-a-vat' is not.

Contextualism — DeRose's view preserves closure within a context and explains the asymmetry as a shift in conversational standards, so the same speaker is not really asserting both within one set of standards.

Reliabilism — Goldman's process-reliability view preserves closure when both beliefs come from reliable processes; the philosopher's denial would require she identify a specific process failure in the anti-skeptical belief.

Virtue epistemology — Sosa's view ties knowledge to cognitive achievement, and on standard versions achievements are transmitted through known entailments, so a virtue-theoretic case for the asymmetry needs additional resources.
context: Robert Nozick (Philosophical Explanations, 1981) defends sensitivity and accepts that it requires rejecting closure: you can know ordinary perceptual claims while not knowing their anti-skeptical consequences. Critics (Sosa, Williamson) find the cost too high; the trade-off is a live debate.

question: Two epistemologists model the same forecaster: one says she believes the central bank will cut rates (graded credence 0.78); the other says she either believes it or does not (all-or-nothing). They disagree on what the correct unit of epistemic evaluation is. What is the disagreement?
answer: Credalism vs doxasticism — whether the fundamental epistemic state is graded credence subject to probability axioms (Bayesianism) or categorical belief subject to closure and threshold norms, with the rest derivative.
choices: Credalism vs doxasticism — whether the fundamental epistemic state is graded credence subject to probability axioms (Bayesianism) or categorical belief subject to closure and threshold norms, with the rest derivative.

Internalism vs externalism about justification — whether justifiers must be accessible to the agent or can include external facts about reliability; this concerns the location of justifiers, not the structure of belief itself.

Foundationalism vs coherentism — whether justification rests on basic beliefs or on coherence among beliefs; this concerns the architecture of justification, not whether the units are graded or categorical.

Reliabilism vs evidentialism — whether justification tracks process reliability or evidence-fit; this concerns what makes a belief justified, not whether the relevant doxastic states come in degrees or kinds.
context: Bayesian epistemology (Jeffrey, Probability and the Art of Judgment, 1992) takes credence as primary. Foley's Working Without a Net (1993) and Kyburg's lottery paradox motivate concerns about closure for graded belief. The 'Lockean thesis' (belief = high credence) is the bridge position; its viability is contested.

question: An expert forecaster's transcript: 'I assigned probability 0.7 to outcomes that occurred about 70% of the time, 0.3 to outcomes that occurred 30%.' Her colleague who has high accuracy on yes/no calls but gives unrelated probability numbers is criticized despite being right more often. What epistemic virtue does the first display?
answer: Calibration — the alignment of credences with frequencies, so the first forecaster's 0.7-marked claims really come true 70% of the time, which is the virtue forecasting research treats as primary even over raw accuracy.
choices: Calibration — the alignment of credences with frequencies, so the first forecaster's 0.7-marked claims really come true 70% of the time, which is the virtue forecasting research treats as primary even over raw accuracy.

Accuracy — the rate at which all-things-considered judgments turn out true, which is the virtue that favors the colleague despite poor probability assignment; accuracy and calibration come apart in just this kind of case.

Coherence — the internal consistency of the forecaster's credences across propositions in the sense the probability axioms require, which is a structural property and not the relation to outcomes the first forecaster exhibits.

Sensitivity — the property that credences would have differed had the world differed, which is necessary for forecasting to track anything but does not by itself capture the frequency-matching the transcript shows.
context: Tetlock's Superforecasting (2015) treats calibration as the central forecasting virtue and shows that calibration training matters. Brier (1950) introduced the proper-scoring framework. Calibration and accuracy come apart: high accuracy with mis-calibrated probabilities loses information for downstream decisions.

question: A hiker sees what looks like a sheep on a far hillside and forms the belief 'there is a sheep in the field.' What he saw was a sheep-shaped rock. But behind the rock, hidden from him, there is a real sheep grazing. His belief is true. Did the hiker KNOW there was a sheep in the field?
answer: No — his reason (the sheep-shaped rock he saw) does not track the truth of his belief (the hidden real sheep), so the belief is true only by accident, which is the classical Gettier failure of knowledge.
choices: No — his reason (the sheep-shaped rock he saw) does not track the truth of his belief (the hidden real sheep), so the belief is true only by accident, which is the classical Gettier failure of knowledge.

Yes — the belief is true, the hiker was justified by what he saw, and his evidence supported the right proposition; on a justified-true-belief account that ought to suffice for knowledge in just this kind of case.

No — knowledge requires direct perception of the very object the belief is about, so even on days when the hiker correctly identifies a sheep at distance he never has the knowledge of it that direct contact would provide.

Yes — reliabilism holds knowledge tracks process reliability, and the hiker's perceptual process is generally reliable for identifying sheep shapes at this distance, which on the view is enough to count as knowledge here.
context: Chisholm's sheep-in-the-field example (Theory of Knowledge, 1966) extends the Gettier point to perception: the believer's reason and the truthmaker of the belief come apart in a way that should disqualify knowledge even when accidental truth is produced. Variants like Goldman's fake-barn country (1976) push the same intuition.

question: A journalist drafts a piece on radical skepticism. She wants to identify the strongest reason a careful reader should still doubt ordinary empirical beliefs after considering the demon hypothesis — even after granting the cogito. Which is the strongest residual reason to doubt?
answer: Bridging-faculty doubt — any empirical belief beyond bare existence relies on memory, sensation, or inference, which are the very cognitive resources the demon could control, so the doubt cannot be cleanly contained.
choices: Bridging-faculty doubt — any empirical belief beyond bare existence relies on memory, sensation, or inference, which are the very cognitive resources the demon could control, so the doubt cannot be cleanly contained.

Self-undermining doubt — the deceiver hypothesis is incoherent because deception requires a world with both deceiver and deceived, so no residual doubt survives once the skeptic's own setup undercuts itself from the start.

Statistical-error doubt — empirical beliefs are reliable only on average, so any individual one might be the rare error; the demon hypothesis would render this kind of frequentist worry misplaced even if granted.

Order-of-doubt doubt — moral and aesthetic beliefs cannot survive the demon either, so empirical beliefs are protected only as long as non-empirical ones are; this runs the order backward and so is a misdirection.
context: Descartes's Meditation One (1641) gives the demon hypothesis; Meditation Two recovers the cogito; Meditations Three through Six attempt to recover the rest. The status of those further recoveries is exactly the question that defines the modern epistemological tradition, with no settled answer.

question: Mia shares half her chips with a new classmate sitting alone. She says, 'I want to be the kind of person who notices and helps.' Which view of ethics best matches Mia's reasoning?
answer: Virtue ethics — being a kind person is what good character looks like, and Mia is choosing the trait.
choices: Virtue ethics — being a kind person is what good character looks like, and Mia is choosing the trait.
Consequence ethics — what makes sharing right is whichever option produces the best total outcome.
Rule ethics — sharing is right only when a universal moral rule about giving requires it of you.
Care ethics — sharing matters because it builds a real relationship with the lonely classmate.
context: Virtue ethics (rooted in Aristotle) asks 'what kind of person should I be?' Mia's reason names a TRAIT she wants to live out — kindness — rather than calculating outcomes or following a rule.

question: Sam tells Mom that his brother broke the vase even though he promised not to tell. He says, 'If Mom doesn't know, she'll keep buying the wrong glue and break more things.' Which view of ethics matches Sam's reasoning?
answer: Consequence ethics — telling is right because it leads to a better total outcome for the household.
choices: Consequence ethics — telling is right because it leads to a better total outcome for the household.
Virtue ethics — telling reflects honesty, the trait of an admirable person who values truth-telling.
Rule ethics — telling is right because a universal rule against deception applies to every situation.
Care ethics — telling could damage the brother-relationship that matters most in moral life here.
context: Consequence ethics (Bentham, Mill) judges actions by their effects. Sam isn't claiming honesty as a virtue or invoking a rule — his stated reason is the practical outcome of Mom having accurate info.

question: When his friend asks for a peek at the answers, Ravi refuses. He says, 'Cheating is wrong, period — it doesn't matter if I'd never get caught.' Which view of ethics best matches Ravi's reasoning?
answer: Rule ethics — Ravi grounds his refusal in a universal moral rule that holds regardless of outcomes.
choices: Rule ethics — Ravi grounds his refusal in a universal moral rule that holds regardless of outcomes.
Virtue ethics — Ravi refuses because an honest person simply isn't the sort who would cheat.
Consequence ethics — Ravi refuses because the long-run results of cheating would be worse overall.
Care ethics — Ravi refuses because helping his friend cheat would hurt their real friendship most.
context: Rule ethics (associated with Kant) holds that some moral rules apply to every person in every situation. Ravi's 'period' signals the rule is binding even when consequences and character don't push.

question: Ava returns a wallet she found on the bus to its owner. She says, 'If I lost mine, I'd want someone to return it to me — so I have to do the same.' Which view of ethics best matches Ava's reasoning?
answer: Reciprocity ethics — Ava treats the owner the way she would want to be treated if she had lost it.
choices: Reciprocity ethics — Ava treats the owner the way she would want to be treated if she had lost it.
Virtue ethics — Ava returns it because honest people are the sort who give back what isn't theirs.
Consequence ethics — Ava returns it because the world is better when wallets get back to owners.
Rule ethics — Ava returns it because a universal moral rule against theft requires this of her.
context: Reciprocity ethics (the Golden Rule, present in Confucius and the Sermon on the Mount) makes the test 'how would I want to be treated?' Ava's reason runs that test, then applies the answer.

question: Leo skips practice to sit with his sick friend Owen instead. He says, 'Owen needs someone, and our friendship matters more than one practice.' Which view of ethics best matches Leo's reasoning?
answer: Care ethics — Leo grounds his choice in the relationship and the friend's real need for company.
choices: Care ethics — Leo grounds his choice in the relationship and the friend's real need for company.
Virtue ethics — Leo skips because a loyal person is the sort who shows up when a friend is sick.
Consequence ethics — Leo skips because the total good is greater with Owen comforted than at drills.
Rule ethics — Leo skips because a universal moral rule of friendship requires sitting with the ill.
context: Care ethics (developed by Nel Noddings and Carol Gilligan) centers moral life on relationships and responding to particular people in need, rather than abstract rules or aggregate good.

question: Mocked in the training yard, Ben walks away without snapping back. He explains, 'I want to be someone who keeps cool, not someone who has to win every fight.' Which view of ethics best matches Ben's reasoning?
answer: Virtue ethics — walking away expresses self-control, the kind of trait a well-formed person builds.
choices: Virtue ethics — walking away expresses self-control, the kind of trait a well-formed person builds.
Consequence ethics — walking away is right because it leads to a better total outcome at recess.
Rule ethics — walking away is right because a universal moral rule forbids responding to insults.
Reciprocity ethics — walking away is right because Ben would not want the teaser snapping at him.
context: Virtue ethics treats moral life as the long-term shaping of character. Ben's reason names a trait (staying cool) he is choosing to cultivate, not a calculation of outcomes or a rule he is obeying.

question: At her party, Nina divides her ten cookies among the nine other kids and takes none herself. She says, 'Nine smiles is more than one — that's just more good in the room.' Which view of ethics matches Nina's reasoning?
answer: Consequence ethics — Nina's reason is straightforward total good: nine smiles beats one for outcomes.
choices: Consequence ethics — Nina's reason is straightforward total good: nine smiles beats one for outcomes.
Virtue ethics — Nina divides cookies because generosity is the trait a good person practices today.
Rule ethics — Nina divides cookies because a universal moral rule requires sharing sweets in groups.
Care ethics — Nina divides cookies because the friendships in the room matter more than fairness.
context: Consequence ethics (utilitarianism) totals up the good across affected people. Nina's wording ('nine smiles is more than one') tracks the aggregate, not a trait, a rule, or a relationship.

question: Maya promised to babysit her cousin Friday. A bigger offer comes in for the same night. She tells her aunt, 'A promise is a promise — I said I would, so I'll be there.' Which view of ethics best matches Maya's reasoning?
answer: Rule ethics — Maya treats her promise as binding because keeping promises is a universal moral rule.
choices: Rule ethics — Maya treats her promise as binding because keeping promises is a universal moral rule.
Virtue ethics — Maya keeps her word because a reliable person is the sort who follows through always.
Consequence ethics — Maya keeps her word because the total outcomes will be better for everyone in it.
Care ethics — Maya keeps her word because her cousin-relationship is what matters most in deciding.
context: Rule ethics holds that moral duties bind universally and aren't traded against personal benefit. Maya's wording ('a promise is a promise') treats the promise rule as final, not as a calculation.

question: At the playground, Theo offers his swing to a smaller kid who's been waiting. He explains, 'When I was little I hated waiting for swings — so I won't make him do it.' Which view of ethics best matches Theo's reasoning?
answer: Reciprocity ethics — Theo treats the smaller kid the way he wished older kids had treated him.
choices: Reciprocity ethics — Theo treats the smaller kid the way he wished older kids had treated him.
Virtue ethics — Theo offers the swing because kindness is the kind of trait a good person grows.
Consequence ethics — Theo offers the swing because more total fun results from sharing the swings.
Care ethics — Theo offers the swing because the friendship he is building with him matters most.
context: Reciprocity ethics applies the 'how would I have wanted to be treated?' test directly. Theo explicitly remembers his own past wish and uses it as the reason to act differently now.
