question: Cal tells his dad the truth about a low test grade, though Dad would never have found out. Cal says, 'I want to be honest even when nothing forces me.' Which view of ethics matches Cal's reasoning?
answer: Virtue ethics — Cal is choosing honesty as a trait, especially because nothing external compels it.
choices: Virtue ethics — Cal is choosing honesty as a trait, especially because nothing external compels it.
Consequence ethics — Cal tells the truth because the long-run results work out better for everyone.
Rule ethics — Cal tells the truth because a universal moral rule against lying applies to every case.
Reciprocity ethics — Cal tells the truth because he'd want his dad to be honest with him in return.
context: Virtue ethics says character shows in what you do when no one is watching. Cal's stated reason centers on the trait he wants to be, not the consequences, a rule, or the Golden Rule shape.

question: Kids want to prank the bus driver by hiding everyone's pass. Jules speaks up: 'Ten kids miss school and the driver gets blamed — it isn't worth it.' Which view of ethics matches Jules's reasoning?
answer: Consequence ethics — Jules tallies the harms (ten missed days, an unjust blame) against the joke.
choices: Consequence ethics — Jules tallies the harms (ten missed days, an unjust blame) against the joke.
Virtue ethics — Jules speaks up because a fair-minded person is the trait she is choosing to live.
Rule ethics — Jules speaks up because a universal moral rule against pranks requires speaking up.
Care ethics — Jules speaks up because her relationship with the driver matters most in the choice.
context: Consequence ethics weighs the actual effects on everyone affected. Jules's wording lists concrete harms (missed school, blamed driver) and compares them — the classic utilitarian move.

question: Eli sees a dollar bill on the floor at a checkout and walks on. He tells his sister, 'It isn't mine — no one would notice, but taking it would be stealing.' Which view of ethics matches Eli's reasoning?
answer: Rule ethics — Eli applies a universal moral rule against taking what isn't his, regardless of notice.
choices: Rule ethics — Eli applies a universal moral rule against taking what isn't his, regardless of notice.
Virtue ethics — Eli walks on because honesty is the kind of trait the person he wants to be has.
Consequence ethics — Eli walks on because the total outcome works out better if dollars stay put.
Reciprocity ethics — Eli walks on because he wouldn't want a stranger pocketing a dollar he dropped.
context: Rule ethics binds even when consequences are small and detection is impossible. Eli's wording ('it doesn't matter that no one would notice') is the rule-ethics signature against outcome talk.

question: When older kids tease a new student, Hana steps in. She says, 'If I were being teased, I'd want someone to step in — so that's what I'm doing.' Which view of ethics matches Hana's reasoning?
answer: Reciprocity ethics — Hana acts the way she would want others to act if she were being teased.
choices: Reciprocity ethics — Hana acts the way she would want others to act if she were being teased.
Virtue ethics — Hana steps in because courage is the kind of trait a good person practices today.
Consequence ethics — Hana steps in because total well-being is greater when the teasing is stopped.
Care ethics — Hana steps in because her relationship with the new student matters most in choosing.
context: Reciprocity ethics runs the 'how would I want this if I were on the other side?' test as its main move. Hana's reason states the test explicitly and follows where it leads.

question: Grace's grandma had a hard week. Grace calls just to listen. She tells her brother, 'She needs someone — that's what our relationship is for.' Which view of ethics matches Grace's reasoning?
answer: Care ethics — Grace meets her grandma's particular need by attending to the relationship itself.
choices: Care ethics — Grace meets her grandma's particular need by attending to the relationship itself.
Virtue ethics — Grace calls because a compassionate person is the trait she wants to live out today.
Consequence ethics — Grace calls because the total good is greater when her grandma feels listened to.
Rule ethics — Grace calls because a universal moral rule about family requires checking on her grandma.
context: Care ethics holds that relationships are the heart of moral life — meeting the particular person in front of you. Grace's reason names the relationship itself ('what our relationship is for').

question: During a board game, Noah admits he miscounted in his own favor — no one saw. He says, 'I'd rather be straight than win by sneaking.' Which view of ethics matches Noah's reasoning?
answer: Virtue ethics — Noah is choosing the trait of straightforwardness over the unseen tactical advantage.
choices: Virtue ethics — Noah is choosing the trait of straightforwardness over the unseen tactical advantage.
Consequence ethics — Noah confesses because the total long-run results are better with honest games.
Rule ethics — Noah confesses because a universal moral rule against cheating applies in every case.
Care ethics — Noah confesses because his relationship with his fellow players matters most to him.
context: Virtue ethics treats integrity as a chosen character trait, not an effect to maximize or rule to obey. Noah's wording ('I'd rather be a person who...') is the classic virtue-ethics framing.

question: Choosing between wild tag and kickball, Kira pushes for kickball. She says, 'In tag someone always gets hurt — kickball is more total fun for everyone.' Which view of ethics matches Kira's reasoning?
answer: Consequence ethics — Kira picks kickball because it produces more total good across the players.
choices: Consequence ethics — Kira picks kickball because it produces more total good across the players.
Virtue ethics — Kira picks kickball because a careful person is the trait she wants to grow today.
Rule ethics — Kira picks kickball because a universal moral rule against risky play applies here.
Reciprocity ethics — Kira picks kickball because she'd want others to pick the safer game for her.
context: Consequence ethics compares expected outcomes for everyone affected. Kira's reason tallies up the predictable harm in tag against the broader fun of kickball — the utilitarian comparison move.

question: Tia's little brother broke a neighbor's window. The neighbor asks if she saw it; Tia says yes. She reasons, 'Lying is wrong, full stop — even when the truth costs me.' Which view of ethics matches Tia's reasoning?
answer: Rule ethics — Tia treats the rule against lying as binding regardless of what telling costs her.
choices: Rule ethics — Tia treats the rule against lying as binding regardless of what telling costs her.
Virtue ethics — Tia tells the truth because honesty is the trait the kind of person she wants has.
Consequence ethics — Tia tells the truth because in the long run total outcomes are better that way.
Care ethics — Tia tells the truth because her relationship with the neighbor matters most in choosing.
context: Rule ethics holds the rule binding even when the cost is high. Tia's 'full stop' signals the rule is doing the work — not the long-run benefit, the kind of person she is, or the relationship.

question: Asked why he's sharing his class notes with a kid who was absent, Marco shrugs: 'If I missed a week, I'd want someone to help me catch up. Same idea.' Which view of ethics best matches Marco's reasoning?
answer: Reciprocity ethics — Marco shares notes by applying the way he would want to be treated if absent.
choices: Reciprocity ethics — Marco shares notes by applying the way he would want to be treated if absent.
Virtue ethics — Marco shares because generosity is the kind of trait an admirable person practices.
Consequence ethics — Marco shares because the total outcomes are better when notes flow to absentees.
Rule ethics — Marco shares because a universal moral rule about helping classmates requires it of him.
context: Reciprocity ethics — the Golden Rule shape — runs the 'put yourself in their shoes' test. Marco's reason states the test, gets the answer (yes, I'd want help), and applies it back as the action.

question: Nora argues against ranking classmates' looks in a poll: 'It will make people we know feel awful for days.' Which view of ethics defends Nora's moral reasoning?
answer: Consequence ethics — what makes an act wrong is the harm it causes; predicted hurt to real classmates is the cost that decides it.
choices: Consequence ethics — what makes an act wrong is the harm it causes; predicted hurt to real classmates is the cost that decides it.
Virtue ethics — what makes an act wrong is the character it expresses; ranking shows a small cruelty that grows by repetition.
Rule ethics — what makes an act wrong is treating people as objects to be rated; that holds whether targets feel it or not.
Care ethics — what makes an act wrong is damage to the friendships people depend on; the poll cuts across real bonds at school.
context: Consequence ethics (Bentham, Mill — Utilitarianism, 1861) judges actions by their effects on well-being. Nora's moral focus is predicted harm to classmates, which is the consequence ethicist's central currency. Virtue, rule, and care ethics would each oppose the poll differently.

question: Asked to vouch for a friend's missing homework, Theo refuses: 'Using a teacher's trust as a tool is just off limits for me.' Which view of ethics defends Theo's moral reasoning?
answer: Rule ethics — some acts (lying, using people) are off limits whatever the result, because they fail to respect those involved.
choices: Rule ethics — some acts (lying, using people) are off limits whatever the result, because they fail to respect those involved.
Consequence ethics — Theo refuses because lying usually backfires; honesty has better long-run effects than short-term loyalty.
Virtue ethics — Theo refuses because the kind of person he wants to be doesn't tell lies, even small ones for a friend.
Care ethics — Theo refuses because lies break the trust that makes the teacher-student relationship work for everyone.
context: Kantian rule ethics (Groundwork, 1785) forbids using people merely as means — the teacher's trust is treated as a tool when Theo lies for his friend. Theo's moral focus ('using a teacher's trust as a tool') tracks the rule-based prohibition, not consequence-counting.

question: Alone with an unwatched candy display, Maya leaves it. Asked later, she says: 'I don't want to be someone who takes things just because no one's looking.' Which view of ethics defends Maya's moral reasoning?
answer: Virtue ethics — what matters is the kind of person you become through your choices; honesty alone shapes settled character.
choices: Virtue ethics — what matters is the kind of person you become through your choices; honesty alone shapes settled character.
Consequence ethics — what matters is the harm avoided; an unwatched store still loses money when small thefts add up.
Rule ethics — what matters is the rule against stealing; that rule binds whether or not anyone happens to be watching.
Care ethics — what matters is the trust between Maya and the storekeeper; small thefts unravel community bonds slowly.
context: Virtue ethics (Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics) asks 'what kind of person should I be?' rather than 'what should I do?' Maya's moral focus ('kind of person who takes things') tracks character formation — the virtue ethicist's central question.

question: Watching a fellow novice get left out at the refectory table, Priya sits with her: 'When somebody's that alone, you make space. That's what friends are for.' Which view of ethics defends Priya's moral reasoning?
answer: Care ethics — morality starts with the people in front of you; making space for someone alone is moral care made concrete.
choices: Care ethics — morality starts with the people in front of you; making space for someone alone is moral care made concrete.
Virtue ethics — morality starts with becoming kind; sitting with the classmate is the act a kind person would naturally take.
Consequence ethics — morality starts with reducing harm; the classmate's isolation hurts, so sitting with her makes it better.
Rule ethics — morality starts with respecting persons; treating the classmate as worth your time is what dignity requires.
context: Care ethics (Gilligan, In a Different Voice, 1982; Noddings, Caring, 1984) grounds morality in particular relationships and the work of attending to others. Priya's moral focus ('what friends are for') tracks care's emphasis on lived bonds, not abstract rules or outcomes.

question: Asked why the class should follow the no-phones rule they voted on, Sam answers: 'We agreed together. Breaking what we agreed to makes any rule meaningless.' Which view of ethics defends Sam's moral reasoning?
answer: Contract ethics — rules bind because the people affected agreed; the agreement itself is what gives any rule moral force.
choices: Contract ethics — rules bind because the people affected agreed; the agreement itself is what gives any rule moral force.
Rule ethics — rules bind because reason demands universal principles; the no-phones rule could be willed as a law for all.
Consequence ethics — rules bind because they produce good outcomes; the no-phones rule helps classes run better day to day.
Virtue ethics — rules bind because following them shapes responsible students; agreement is incidental to the character built.
context: Contract ethics (Hobbes, Locke, Rousseau; modernized by Rawls) grounds moral and political obligation in agreement among the affected parties. Sam's moral focus ('we agreed together') tracks the contract ethicist's central move: consent generates obligation.

question: Setting prices at the harvest fair stall, Aiden argues: 'Lower prices mean more villagers can afford a treat — more happiness today.' Which view of ethics defends Aiden's moral reasoning?
answer: Consequence ethics — the right price produces the most overall good; affordable treats means more happiness across the school.
choices: Consequence ethics — the right price produces the most overall good; affordable treats means more happiness across the school.
Virtue ethics — the right price reflects the bakers' generosity; low pricing shows the kind of people they want to be today.
Care ethics — the right price honors friendships among classmates; reachable treats keep the playground group whole at recess.
Rule ethics — the right price respects every kid as an equal; pricing too high excludes some classmates from a fair share.
context: Aiden's moral focus is straightforwardly consequence-based: aggregate happiness across the affected population is the criterion. Each other view could also support low prices — but for different REASONS. The question asks which view defends Aiden's actual moral focus.

question: In the class debate, Jordan defends an unpopular position alone. Asked why, he says: 'I'd rather be someone who says what he thinks than win by going along.' Which view of ethics defends Jordan's moral reasoning?
answer: Virtue ethics — what matters is becoming a courageous and honest person; standing alone with your view forms that character.
choices: Virtue ethics — what matters is becoming a courageous and honest person; standing alone with your view forms that character.
Rule ethics — what matters is the duty to tell the truth; switching sides for popularity is a lie about what you really think.
Consequence ethics — what matters is the long effect of speaking up; better debates happen when people share real views.
Care ethics — what matters is honest relationships in the classroom; pretending to agree corrodes trust between friends.
context: Aristotle's virtues include courage (andreia) — facing social risk for what you believe is right. Jordan's moral focus ('kind of person who says what he thinks') tracks character formation, the virtue ethicist's central concern, not duty or outcome calculus.

question: Offered a chance to peek at quiz answers, Lila refuses: 'If everyone cheated, the test would be pointless. So I shouldn't either.' Which view of ethics defends Lila's moral reasoning?
answer: Rule ethics — an action is right only if its rule could hold for everyone; cheating fails because it would destroy the quiz.
choices: Rule ethics — an action is right only if its rule could hold for everyone; cheating fails because it would destroy the quiz.
Consequence ethics — cheating is wrong because of its effects on learning; Lila's test is worth less if every classmate cheats.
Virtue ethics — cheating is wrong because it shapes a dishonest character; the rule's universality is incidental to who she is.
Care ethics — cheating is wrong because it betrays the teacher's trust; classroom relationships rest on the honesty of students.
context: Kant's Categorical Imperative (Groundwork, 1785): act only on rules you could will to be universal. Lila's moral focus ('if everyone cheated...') is a textbook universalization test — the rule ethicist's core move, not a calculation of effects or character outcomes.

question: Asked why he won't unseal the company's private letters, Eli explains: 'We all promised. Any company works because people stick to what they promised.' Which view of ethics defends Eli's moral reasoning?
answer: Contract ethics — promises bind because the group depends on each member keeping what they agreed; cooperation rests on that.
choices: Contract ethics — promises bind because the group depends on each member keeping what they agreed; cooperation rests on that.
Rule ethics — promises bind because breaking them treats people as mere instruments; respect for persons forbids the betrayal.
Virtue ethics — promises bind because keeping them shapes a trustworthy character; Eli wants to build that settled disposition.
Consequence ethics — promises bind because group chats work better when people follow them; effects of trust outweigh leaks.
context: Eli's moral focus ('we all promised... any chat works because people stick to what they promised') appeals to mutual agreement and cooperative practice — the contract ethicist's foundational move. Other views could also support keeping the promise, but Eli's actual reason is contractual.

question: Caught teasing a younger student, Marcus defends himself: 'But EVERYONE laughed when I did it.' Why is 'everyone laughed' NOT a good moral defense in ethics?
answer: Bandwagon doesn't justify — that many people enjoyed teasing doesn't make it right; popularity tracks attention, not moral merit.
choices: Bandwagon doesn't justify — that many people enjoyed teasing doesn't make it right; popularity tracks attention, not moral merit.
Consequences still count — even with audience laughter, the younger student's hurt is a real cost the laughs do nothing to erase.
Character still counts — being someone who teases for laughs is about who you are, not who happens to be watching at the moment.
Respect still counts — the younger student is a person whose dignity isn't suspended because a crowd finds his pain funny.
context: Argumentum ad populum (appeal to popularity) is a known logical fallacy in ethics: that many people approve of an act doesn't transfer to its moral status. All four answers are TRUE moral criticisms of Marcus's defense, but only the first NAMES the actual flaw in 'everyone laughed.'

question: Asked why she made fun of a classmate's clothes, Eva shrugs: 'She made fun of my shoes last week, so it's fair.' Why is 'she did it first' NOT a good moral defense in ethics?
answer: Two wrongs don't make a right — an earlier unkindness doesn't transform Eva's mockery into a justified or genuinely fair response.
choices: Two wrongs don't make a right — an earlier unkindness doesn't transform Eva's mockery into a justified or genuinely fair response.
Character is still revealed — being mocked first doesn't change who Eva becomes by retaliating; her choice still shapes her.
Harm is still done — the earlier unkindness doesn't erase the new sting of Eva's mockery; the second hurt is its own real cost.
Respect is still owed — the classmate is still a person whose dignity matters whatever she did to Eva last week at school.
context: 'Two wrongs make a right' is a recognized informal fallacy. It's close kin to tu quoque but distinct: tu quoque dodges a critic; this fallacy CLAIMS one wrong actually justifies another. All four answers are true criticisms; only the first names the specific flaw in Eva's defense.

question: Drafting a mean post about a classmate, Olivia hesitates and deletes it: 'When thousands see it, his weekend is wrecked. Too much weight for one laugh.' Which view of ethics defends Olivia's moral reasoning?
answer: Consequence ethics — Olivia weighs predicted harm (a wrecked weekend) against predicted good (one laugh) and acts on the cost.
choices: Consequence ethics — Olivia weighs predicted harm (a wrecked weekend) against predicted good (one laugh) and acts on the cost.
Virtue ethics — Olivia is shaping a character that doesn't post for cheap laughs; hesitation reveals who she wants to be.
Rule ethics — Olivia recognizes the classmate is a person, not entertainment material; respect for persons forbids the post.
Care ethics — Olivia attends to a particular human she is about to harm; that attention is what care asks her to show first.
context: Consequence ethics' hallmark is weighing predicted outcomes — costs versus benefits across the affected parties. Olivia's moral focus ('too much weight for one laugh') is explicitly outcome-weighing. The other views would support deletion too, but for non-consequence-based reasons.

question: Asked why he returned the wallet he found in the locker room, Diego shrugs: 'I want to be someone who returns wallets even when no one would ever know.' Which view of ethics defends Diego's moral reasoning?
answer: Virtue ethics — what shapes a good person is what they do when no one is watching; Diego's choice expresses settled honesty.
choices: Virtue ethics — what shapes a good person is what they do when no one is watching; Diego's choice expresses settled honesty.
Rule ethics — what shapes a moral act is the rule against keeping what isn't yours; the rule binds whether anyone sees or not.
Consequence ethics — what shapes a moral act is the harm avoided; the owner's lost wallet outweighs any benefit Diego gets.
Care ethics — what shapes a moral act is the unseen owner waiting for the wallet; Diego responds to that absent person's need.
context: 'Character is what you do when no one is watching' is a virtue-ethics commonplace. Diego's moral focus ('want to be someone who returns wallets') tracks the formation of a settled disposition — the virtue ethicist's central concern.

question: Tempted to skip his babysitting shift for a better offer, Liam declines: 'I told her I'd be there. A promise that bends for a cooler plan stops being a promise.' Which view of ethics defends Liam's moral reasoning?
answer: Rule ethics — promises create duties whose force IS the practice of promising; bending them for convenience destroys that.
choices: Rule ethics — promises create duties whose force IS the practice of promising; bending them for convenience destroys that.
Consequence ethics — promises matter because broken ones cause harm; the sister loses her sitter and Liam's reliability sinks.
Virtue ethics — promises matter because keeping them shapes a trustworthy character; bending for a cooler offer reveals less.
Care ethics — promises matter because they sustain particular relationships; Liam's bond with the family depends on showing up.
context: Kant's analysis of lying-promises (Groundwork, 1785): a rule of 'break promises when convenient' cannot be willed universally without destroying the institution of promising itself. Liam's moral focus on what a promise even means tracks the rule ethicist's universalization move.

question: When the team agrees a rotation is fairest, Noah accepts picks he hates: 'We worked out a system together. Skipping turns I dislike breaks the agreement.' Which view of ethics defends Noah's moral reasoning?
answer: Contract ethics — the rotation binds because the team agreed; agreement is what gives even disliked picks their fair claim here.
choices: Contract ethics — the rotation binds because the team agreed; agreement is what gives even disliked picks their fair claim here.
Rule ethics — the rotation binds because reason demands consistent rules for all; rotating turns is what fairness requires here.
Virtue ethics — the rotation binds because keeping it shapes a fair-minded character; Noah's tolerance forms a cooperative trait.
Consequence ethics — the rotation binds because it makes movie night go better; group happiness averages higher with the system.
context: Noah's moral focus ('we worked out a system together') tracks the contract ethicist's central claim: fair institutions get their authority from the agreement of the affected parties. Other views could defend the rotation — but for different reasons than Noah actually gave.

question: In debate, Aria opposes naming students in the discipline column: 'A named eighth-grader carries it through every grade after. Damage outweighs gossip.' Which view of ethics defends Aria's moral reasoning?
answer: Consequence ethics — predicted long-run harm to the student outweighs the short-run interest of readers; that calculus settles it.
choices: Consequence ethics — predicted long-run harm to the student outweighs the short-run interest of readers; that calculus settles it.
Care ethics — the named student is a person whose ongoing school life will hurt; close attention to him grounds the case.
Rule ethics — the student is being used as content for readers; treating a person as material for entertainment fails respect.
Virtue ethics — the paper expresses a careless character toward its subjects; carefulness is what the team should become.
context: Aria's moral focus is explicitly weighing long-run cost against short-run benefit — the consequence ethicist's calculus. The other three views could also oppose naming, each for its own moral reason; the question tests which view Aria HERSELF defends.

question: Pressured to deny what she saw in the hall, Ana refuses: 'I won't be someone who covers up things to fit in. It would just make me that person.' Which view of ethics defends Ana's moral reasoning?
answer: Virtue ethics — moral life is the project of becoming a certain kind of person; covering up reshapes who Ana would become.
choices: Virtue ethics — moral life is the project of becoming a certain kind of person; covering up reshapes who Ana would become.
Rule ethics — moral life is governed by the duty of honesty; lying about what she saw in the hall fails a rule that binds anyway.
Consequence ethics — moral life weighs the harm of cover-ups; lying about what happened makes the situation worse for everyone.
Care ethics — moral life attends to people the cover-up would hurt; loyalty to friends doesn't outweigh those it would expose.
context: Aristotle's idea of habituation: each choice shapes the next, and the person we become is built one act at a time. Ana's moral focus ('make me that person') is explicit character-formation language — the virtue ethicist's distinctive move.

question: Jay keeps 'needing' Mia to cover for homework he forgot himself. Her aunt warns: 'Helping every time isn't really helping.' Which view of ethics is the aunt defending?
answer: Virtue ethics — repeated rescue trains Jay into worse habits; a real friend supports growth, not escape from his own choices.
choices: Virtue ethics — repeated rescue trains Jay into worse habits; a real friend supports growth, not escape from his own choices.
Care ethics — responding to felt need keeps the friendship intact; the relationship matters more than the lessons Jay might miss.
Consequence ethics — Mia should weigh harm and benefit each time; if covering produces net good, she should keep doing it.
Rule ethics — friends have a universal duty to help; the rule binds Mia in every case, whatever the downstream pattern produces.
context: Virtue ethics evaluates acts by the character they shape — in helper and helped. The critique of indiscriminate caring is that it can trade short-term comfort for long-term capacity, harming the person it appears to serve.

question: An aunt gives her niece more time than other kids. She says: 'Particular obligations are real — I owe THIS child extra.' A friend objects: 'That's just bias.' Which view is the aunt defending?
answer: Partial obligations — family ties ground real duties of preference; favoring her own niece is morally grounded, not a bias to fix.
choices: Partial obligations — family ties ground real duties of preference; favoring her own niece is morally grounded, not a bias to fix.
Impartialism — every child has equal claim on adults; her preference is sentiment she should weigh as she would weigh others'.
Consequence ethics — the aunt should give where each hour produces most good; family ties count only if they track welfare.
Rule ethics — a universal duty of fair treatment binds her to all children alike; favoring her niece breaks the like-cases rule.
context: John Cottingham (Partiality and the Virtues, 1998) defends agent-relative obligations: the weight you give your own family is not a defect of impartial reasoning but a morally grounded feature of human life any plausible ethics must accommodate.

question: A debate-club captain refuses to lie for a friend even when no one will be hurt. She says: 'It's not about the consequences — it's about the kind of person I'm becoming every time I choose.' Which view of ethics is she defending?
answer: Virtue ethics — character is shaped by what you choose; lying corrupts honesty regardless of whether external harm follows from this particular act.
choices: Virtue ethics — character is shaped by what you choose; lying corrupts honesty regardless of whether external harm follows from this particular act.
Act utilitarianism — wrongness depends only on harm caused; lies that hurt no one are not wrong, since the consequence calculation comes out neutral here.
Kantian duty ethics — lying breaks a universal rule everyone must follow; the wrongness lies in the rule broken, not in what lying does to one's character.
Contract ethics — wrongness depends on whether affected parties could agree to the rule allowing it; the friend's consent here would mostly settle the matter.
context: Virtue ethics (revived by Anscombe 1958, MacIntyre 1981) judges acts by what they do to the agent's character, not just by consequences or rules. The phrase 'the kind of person I'm becoming' is the classic virtue-ethics signature.

question: A school newspaper editor argues against a clever cheat code on a graded online quiz: 'Ask yourself — what if every student did this? The system would collapse, and grades would mean nothing at all.' Which view of ethics is she defending?
answer: Kantian duty ethics — an act is wrong if you cannot will the rule allowing it to become a universal law everyone follows in the same situation.
choices: Kantian duty ethics — an act is wrong if you cannot will the rule allowing it to become a universal law everyone follows in the same situation.
Act utilitarianism — the act is wrong because aggregate harm to students outweighs personal benefit; the editor is summing costs and benefits across people.
Virtue ethics — cheating corrupts the cheater's character regardless of whether the system collapses; the universalizing question is incidental to the damage.
Care ethics — the cheater violates a relationship of trust with classmates and teachers; personal bonds matter, not abstract rules about what everyone could do.
context: Kant's Categorical Imperative (Groundwork, 1785) asks: 'Can I will the maxim of my act to become a universal law?' If universalizing the rule defeats its purpose — as with cheating or lying — the act fails the test and is wrong.

question: An online ethicist argues a stranger SHOULD jump into a cold pond to save a drowning swimmer even at the cost of expensive shoes: 'The shoes cost a hundred dollars. A life is worth incomparably more. The math is straightforward.' Which view of ethics is she defending?
answer: Act utilitarianism — the right act in this case is the one producing the most good overall; a life saved vastly outweighs the cost of ruined shoes in the trade.
choices: Act utilitarianism — the right act in this case is the one producing the most good overall; a life saved vastly outweighs the cost of ruined shoes in the trade.
Kantian duty ethics — there is a duty to help others in distress regardless of outcome; the shoes calculation is morally irrelevant to whether help is owed.
Virtue ethics — a courageous person jumps because that is what courage requires; the math frames the case but character determines the action taken here.
Contract ethics — the rule requiring rescue at small cost is one all rational people could agree to; the appeal is to what we can justify to each other.
context: Peter Singer's 'Famine, Affluence, and Morality' (1972) developed this case. Act utilitarianism (Bentham, Mill in part) judges each act by the consequences it produces; the ethicist's appeal to 'the math' is its signature pattern.

question: A peer-review essay argues: 'Even when breaking a promise WOULD produce slightly better consequences in one case, the practice of promise-keeping produces better consequences overall — so the rule should hold.' Which view of ethics is she defending?
answer: Rule utilitarianism — judge acts by rules that, if generally followed, produce the best consequences; better one-off outcomes don't justify breaking the rule.
choices: Rule utilitarianism — judge acts by rules that, if generally followed, produce the best consequences; better one-off outcomes don't justify breaking the rule.
Act utilitarianism — the right act is always whichever one maximizes good in THAT particular case; rules are useful but never override the case-by-case math.
Kantian duty ethics — promise-keeping is required because the rule is universalizable; consequences are irrelevant to whether the promise should hold.
Virtue ethics — promise-keeping is the act of an honest person; the right answer depends on the kind of character the agent is forming through her choices.
context: Rule utilitarianism (Brandt, Harsanyi) splits with act utilitarianism on exactly this case. Acts are judged by the rule they instantiate, and rules are judged by their consequences if generally followed — answering classic objections to act-utility.

question: A YouTuber defends spending her free time helping her own grandmother rather than donating that time to a charity. She says: 'The relationship itself matters — strangers aren't substitutes for the people who raised me.' Which view of ethics is she defending?
answer: Care ethics — moral obligations grow from particular relationships and their histories; the grandmother is not just one stranger among many to weigh equally.
choices: Care ethics — moral obligations grow from particular relationships and their histories; the grandmother is not just one stranger among many to weigh equally.
Act utilitarianism — the right act produces the most good overall; the YouTuber's reasoning would be wrong by this view since strangers outnumber kin.
Kantian duty ethics — duties are universal and impartial; the rule allowing favoritism toward relatives cannot be willed as a universal law for everyone.
Contract ethics — rules must be justifiable to all affected parties impartially; personal relationships should not weight obligations differently across agents.
context: Care ethics (Gilligan 1982, Noddings 1984) developed in response to impartial frameworks that treat all moral agents as interchangeable. Particular relationships — parent, child, friend — generate real obligations the impartial view misses.

question: An online ethicist explains why a small road-repair tax is justified even for drivers who never use those roads: 'No driver could reasonably reject the rule — every driver might one day need a road they didn't help build.' Which view of ethics is she defending?
answer: Contract ethics — acts are right if they follow principles no affected party could reasonably reject; the test is what rules we could agree to in advance.
choices: Contract ethics — acts are right if they follow principles no affected party could reasonably reject; the test is what rules we could agree to in advance.
Act utilitarianism — the tax is right because it produces more aggregate good than harm; the 'could agree to' phrasing is at best a useful approximation.
Kantian duty ethics — there is a universal duty of fairness, derivable from rational agency itself; the contract metaphor adds nothing the imperative lacks.
Virtue ethics — the just person pays their share willingly; what people could agree to is irrelevant if the agent's character is properly formed already.
context: Contractualism (Scanlon, What We Owe to Each Other, 1998) grounds morality in principles no one could reasonably reject. Rawls's 'veil of ignorance' (1971) is the same family: rules justified by what we could endorse not knowing our role.

question: A student argues that bullying must be fine because 'everyone does it at this school.' An ethics teacher pushes back. Why is 'everyone does it' NOT a good defense in ethics?
answer: Popularity fallacy in moral form — what most people DO is a fact about behavior; whether it OUGHT to be done is a separate question prevalence cannot answer.
choices: Popularity fallacy in moral form — what most people DO is a fact about behavior; whether it OUGHT to be done is a separate question prevalence cannot answer.
Consequence reply — bullying produces more harm than benefit summed across affected students; this answers by replacing the popularity claim with utility.
Universal-rule reply — a rule against bullying holds regardless of what others do; the popularity appeal violates the categorical structure that grounds duty.
Character reply — a bully's character is corrupted whether or not others share the flaw; what 'everyone does' is irrelevant to who the bully chooses to become.
context: The is-ought gap (Hume, Treatise 1739) grounds this point: descriptive claims about what people DO do not entail normative claims about what they SHOULD do. Popular practice may be evidence about norms — but never settles whether right.

question: A school newspaper columnist defends retaliating against a classmate's lie with a worse lie of his own: 'But she lied to me first — so I'm justified in lying back.' An ethics teacher pushes back. Why is 'they did it first' NOT a good defense in ethics?
answer: Wrongness is not transferable — a prior wrong by another person does not erase the wrongness of your own act; only the question of who started is settled by it.
choices: Wrongness is not transferable — a prior wrong by another person does not erase the wrongness of your own act; only the question of who started is settled by it.
Consequence reply — two lies produce worse outcomes than one; the columnist's calculation fails on its own utilitarian terms when summed across both parties.
Universal-rule reply — lying breaks a universal duty regardless of what others did first; universality means no prior wrongdoing releases your own obligation.
Character reply — a retaliating liar corrupts his own character; the prior lie is irrelevant to what the columnist chooses to become through his lying response.
context: This is the 'tu quoque defense' applied to ethics rather than to argument. The reasoning fails because moral wrongs do not cancel each other out; the responder is fully responsible for his own choice independent of what was done first.

question: A school principal weighs cancelling a beloved annual field trip after one parent complaint about cost. Three hundred students enjoy the trip; one family struggles to afford it. What makes cancellation right or wrong, on the utilitarian reading?
answer: Utilitarian — wrong unless cancellation produces MORE total good than the alternatives; financial aid usually beats cancelling because more benefit holds.
choices: Utilitarian — wrong unless cancellation produces MORE total good than the alternatives; financial aid usually beats cancelling because more benefit holds.
Kantian — right because cancellation respects a universal rule against exclusion on cost; the rule binds the principal regardless of how the consequences land.
Virtue ethics — right because a virtuous principal protects every student's dignity; cancellation expresses fairness as a character trait of the institution.
Contract ethics — wrong because the parent's complaint is not consent of all affected parties; rules must be justifiable to everyone the decision could touch.
context: Utilitarian analysis weighs aggregate good across affected parties (Bentham, Principles of Morals and Legislation, 1789). The right policy is whichever maximizes good — financial aid usually beats cancellation by preserving benefit.

question: A scientist considers falsifying one data point in a study — the paper will be more publishable, no one will catch it, and the conclusion is probably right anyway. What makes falsifying the data wrong, on the Kantian reading?
answer: Kantian — the maxim 'falsify data when convenient' cannot be willed as a universal law without destroying the very practice of science it depends upon.
choices: Kantian — the maxim 'falsify data when convenient' cannot be willed as a universal law without destroying the very practice of science it depends upon.
Utilitarian — falsification harms future researchers who rely on the literature; the consequence calculation comes out clearly against any falsifying of data.
Virtue ethics — a falsifying scientist corrupts her own character as a truth-tracker; what she chooses shapes the kind of researcher she is becoming over time.
Care ethics — falsification breaks an implicit trust with the scientific community; the particular bonds among researchers cannot survive routine deception.
context: Kant's universalizability test (Groundwork, 1785) is the touchstone: the maxim must be willable as a universal law without contradiction. Falsification fails because universal falsification destroys the very practice — data — it relies on.

question: A debate-club captain loses a tournament she trained months for. She tells a teammate: 'The loss isn't up to me. How I respond is. I'll prepare differently and try again, without resenting the judges.' Which view of ethics is she defending?
answer: Stoic ethics — character is formed by how we respond to externals we don't control; the loss itself is morally indifferent compared to the response chosen.
choices: Stoic ethics — character is formed by how we respond to externals we don't control; the loss itself is morally indifferent compared to the response chosen.
Act utilitarianism — the captain calculates that resenting judges yields no benefit while preparing differently raises future chances; the math drives her here.
Virtue ethics — the captain is exercising the virtue of resilience as part of building character; what's up to her or not is incidental to virtues practiced.
Kantian duty ethics — there is a universal duty to respond rationally rather than emotionally to setbacks; the captain follows the rule rather than feeling.
context: Stoicism (Epictetus, Discourses, ~108 AD; Marcus Aurelius, Meditations, ~170 AD) divides the world into what is and isn't 'up to us.' Externals are indifferent; the response is everything. The captain's framing is the classic Stoic signature.

question: A peer-review essay argues a hospital may NOT use a healthy patient for organs to save five dying ones, even if doing so saves more lives overall. The author writes: 'Some acts violate the patient's basic rights, regardless of numbers.' Which view of ethics is she defending?
answer: Rights-based ethics — persons have basic claims (life, bodily integrity) that cannot be overridden by aggregate-good calculations, no matter how favorable.
choices: Rights-based ethics — persons have basic claims (life, bodily integrity) that cannot be overridden by aggregate-good calculations, no matter how favorable.
Act utilitarianism — the right act maximizes good across affected parties; the essay's reasoning is wrong by this view since five saved lives beat one taken.
Virtue ethics — a virtuous doctor would not perform the harvest; the wrongness lies in what the act does to the doctor's character, not in any patient's rights.
Care ethics — the doctor has a particular relationship with the healthy patient that outweighs the relationship with the five strangers needing organs nearby.
context: The 'transplant case' (Thomson, Foot) is a classic objection to act-utility: rights act as 'side-constraints' (Nozick, Anarchy State and Utopia 1974) — limits on what may be done to persons regardless of good produced for others.

question: An ethics class is shown the trolley case: divert a runaway trolley to kill one instead of five. A student says: 'Always divert — five lives outweigh one.' Pressed on the organ-harvest parallel, he wavers. Which response to this dilemma holds together under scrutiny?
answer: Doing-vs-allowing — diverting redirects an existing harm; harvesting organs creates new harm from a safe person, so the cases are not morally equivalent here.
choices: Doing-vs-allowing — diverting redirects an existing harm; harvesting organs creates new harm from a safe person, so the cases are not morally equivalent here.
Bite-the-bullet harvest — the cases are identical and the student must accept harvest if he accepts diverting; consistency forces accepting both, not just one.
Bite-the-bullet refusal — the cases are identical and the student must reject diverting if he rejects harvest; consistency forces refusing intervention in both.
Numbers-only view — five lives outweigh one regardless of how the saving comes about; the student should accept the harvest result on consequence grounds alone.
context: The doing-vs-allowing distinction (Foot 1967, Thomson 1976) does real work in ethics. Diverting a trolley redirects an existing threat; harvesting creates a new one. Many philosophers reject the second while accepting the first.

question: A class debates whether lying is ever permitted: someone hides a refugee from soldiers who would kill her, and the soldiers ask the host where she is. A strict view says: 'Never lie, even here.' Which response to this dilemma holds together under scrutiny?
answer: Forfeiture view — distinguish a duty of truthfulness from a duty owed those who weaponize truth; the soldiers have forfeited any claim to honest answers here.
choices: Forfeiture view — distinguish a duty of truthfulness from a duty owed those who weaponize truth; the soldiers have forfeited any claim to honest answers here.
Strict rule view — lying is always wrong because the rule is universal; the host should tell the truth and accept that the death rests on the soldiers' account.
Consequence view — lying is permitted whenever the outcomes favor it; the host should lie here for the same reason he should lie any time the math favors lying.
Relativist view — there is no fact about whether lying is wrong; the host's choice cannot be evaluated against any standard outside his own community's rules.
context: The 'murderer at the door' case (raised against Kant by Constant, 1797) is a classic stress test for rule-based ethics. Many philosophers distinguish a general duty of truthfulness from duties owed specific persons — the latter forfeitable.

question: A YouTuber promised her grandmother she'd visit on a specific Saturday. A more lucrative paid sponsorship opens for the same day. She visits her grandmother anyway, saying: 'I keep my promises — that's who I am.' Which view of ethics is she defending?
answer: Virtue ethics — the kind of person you are is shaped by what you choose; promise-keeping expresses honesty as a trait rather than balancing consequences.
choices: Virtue ethics — the kind of person you are is shaped by what you choose; promise-keeping expresses honesty as a trait rather than balancing consequences.
Act utilitarianism — keeping the promise produces more total good than breaking it; disappointed grandmother outweighs YouTuber's sponsorship gain in the math.
Contract ethics — promise-keeping is a principle no party to the promise could reasonably reject; the wrongness lies in justification owed the grandmother.
Kantian duty ethics — there is a universal rule that promises must be kept regardless of consequence; the rule applies whether breaking is convenient or not.
context: The phrase 'that's who I am' is the virtue-ethics signature — character expression rather than rule-following or consequence-weighing. Kant, utilitarian, and contractualist views would also support keeping the promise, but for other reasons.

question: A student justifies stealing answers for a test by saying: 'I FELT like I deserved a better grade than my studying alone would get me.' An ethics teacher pushes back. Why is 'I felt I deserved it' NOT a good defense in ethics?
answer: Is-ought reply — feelings describe psychology but do not constitute moral justification; wanting an outcome more does not make wrongful pursuit any righter.
choices: Is-ought reply — feelings describe psychology but do not constitute moral justification; wanting an outcome more does not make wrongful pursuit any righter.
Consequence reply — feelings about grades produce more harm than the stolen grade benefits him; the math comes out clearly against his choice in the end.
Character reply — a virtuous student would not steal regardless of feelings; feelings are irrelevant data about psychology, not about the wrongness of acts.
Universal-rule reply — stealing answers breaks a universal rule against cheating; the rule applies to everyone regardless of how strongly anyone feels.
context: This is a version of the is-ought gap: feeling that one deserves something is a psychological fact that does not entail any moral conclusion. Strength of desire is evidence about wanting — never about whether the wanted thing is owed.

question: A student claims all moral action reduces to self-interest: 'Even people who help others do it because helping FEELS good — so they're really acting selfishly.' Another student says this proves too much. Which response to this moral dilemma holds together under scrutiny?
answer: Word-trivialization reply — if 'selfish' covers every motivated act, the word loses its grip; the FOR-self versus FOR-another distinction is silently erased.
choices: Word-trivialization reply — if 'selfish' covers every motivated act, the word loses its grip; the FOR-self versus FOR-another distinction is silently erased.
Concede-the-claim reply — the student is correct that all moral action is selfishly motivated; ethics just labels some selfish acts good based on outcomes.
Empirical-counterexample reply — the student is wrong because some people help even when it does not feel good; the claim about feelings fails on its own facts.
Virtue-ethics reply — virtuous people are motivated by character not feelings; feelings are downstream of virtue, not the motivator, so the egoist claim fails.
context: Psychological egoism (the view that all action is self-interested) is widely criticized for being unfalsifiable — any helping act can be redescribed as 'feels good.' Butler's 'Fifteen Sermons' (1726) is the classical reply: the move trivializes.

question: A philosophy student argues a particular act is wrong because it violates fairness owed every person as a rational agent. Asked WHY, she says: 'Rational agents owe each other consistency in how rules apply — that's built into reason itself.' Which view of ethics is she defending?
answer: Kantian duty ethics — moral rules are grounded in the structure of rational agency itself; what reason requires applies to every agent regardless of feelings.
choices: Kantian duty ethics — moral rules are grounded in the structure of rational agency itself; what reason requires applies to every agent regardless of feelings.
Divine command ethics — moral rules are grounded in commands from a moral authority; the appeal to rationality is really a stand-in for the lawgiver behind.
Cultural ethics — moral rules are grounded in the practices of one's community; the appeal to 'every person' is really an appeal to one community's tradition.
Sentimentalist ethics — moral rules are grounded in widely shared feelings of approval; the appeal to rationality is just a cover for fairness-feelings held.
context: Kant grounded morality in pure practical reason (Groundwork, 1785; Critique of Practical Reason, 1788). The appeal to 'rational agency' and 'consistency in rules' is the Kantian signature — distinct from divine-command and cultural views.

question: A school sports captain considers helping a struggling teammate practice after hours, even though it eats into his own training time. He decides to help. What makes the help right, on the virtue-ethics reading?
answer: Virtue ethics — it expresses generosity, a virtue forming into stable character; the right act is what a good person would do, shaping who the captain becomes.
choices: Virtue ethics — it expresses generosity, a virtue forming into stable character; the right act is what a good person would do, shaping who the captain becomes.
Utilitarian — it produces more aggregate good than not-helping when both teammates' improvements are summed; the consequence calculation favors helping.
Kantian — it instantiates a universal rule that captains should help teammates; the captain follows the rule whether or not he feels like helping in this case.
Care ethics — it honors the particular bond between captain and teammate; the relationship grounds the obligation rather than the act's effects on character.
context: Virtue ethics (Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, ~340 BC; Anscombe 1958; MacIntyre 1981) judges acts by the character traits — virtues — they express and shape. 'Expresses generosity' and 'shapes who he becomes' is the virtue-ethics signature.

question: An online ethicist argues a person should break a small promise (returning a borrowed book on time) in order to drive an injured stranger to the hospital. She writes: 'In each case, do whatever produces the most good. The book can wait.' Which view of ethics is she defending?
answer: Act utilitarianism — judge each act by its consequences in its particular case; case-by-case good-maximizing can override general rules when the math favors it.
choices: Act utilitarianism — judge each act by its consequences in its particular case; case-by-case good-maximizing can override general rules when the math favors it.
Rule utilitarianism — judge acts by rules that, if generally followed, produce best outcomes; she breaks the rule in a case her position would not actually let.
Kantian duty ethics — duties to help the injured override duties to keep small promises; the categorical imperative ranks moral rules to settle this conflict.
Care ethics — particular relationships generate obligations; the stranger's hospital need outweighs the book-lender's claim because of greater vulnerability.
context: Act utilitarianism (Bentham, Principles of Morals and Legislation, 1789) judges each act by its consequences. The phrase 'in each case, do whatever produces the most good' is the act-utility signature — rule utility would defer to the rule.

question: A teacher grants extensions every time a student cries about a deadline. A colleague pushes back: 'The pattern teaches them their tears change reality and that planning is optional.' Which view is the colleague defending?
answer: Virtue ethics — substituting distress-response for accountability trains students into worse work habits; the practice is judged by the character it cultivates.
choices: Virtue ethics — substituting distress-response for accountability trains students into worse work habits; the practice is judged by the character it cultivates.
Care ethics — meeting concrete distress is itself the moral act; the teacher's responsiveness is what an ethics of care looks like.
Consequence ethics — the colleague weighs welfare of granted versus refused extensions across the class, and concludes the math disfavors the practice.
Rule ethics — fairness requires identical treatment; the objection is that criers receive different treatment from non-criers in the class.
context: The virtue-ethics critique of indiscriminate caring is that it can systematically corrode the capacities it appears to serve. Care's central move — respond to felt distress — lacks a built-in test for when responding is itself wrong.

question: A donor funds soup kitchens in a town stuck in chronic crisis, never the policy reforms that would shrink the crisis. An economist notes: 'The soup is real care; it also makes the crisis bearable enough to persist.' Which view is the economist defending?
answer: Consequence ethics — root-cause reform is weighed against ongoing relief by total welfare; kitchen funding sustains the crisis instead of shrinking it.
choices: Consequence ethics — root-cause reform is weighed against ongoing relief by total welfare; kitchen funding sustains the crisis instead of shrinking it.
Care ethics — the donor's concrete ties with hungry townspeople are themselves the moral fact; abstract policy reform loses the particular need each meal meets.
Rule ethics — the donor has a universal duty to feed the hungry that does not depend on whether the policy regime ever changes.
Virtue ethics — the donor's character is formed by giving regardless of outcome; the practice succeeds morally whatever its effect on the crisis.
context: The consequentialist critique of care-as-relief is that responding to felt need can stabilize the conditions that generate the need. Caring acts are real moral facts, but care doesn't itself distinguish downstream relief from upstream reform.

question: Bioethicist Aris argues against a profitable but degrading reality-TV format: 'Even if the contestants consent and audiences enjoy it, repeatedly humiliating people trains producers, viewers, and contestants into worse human beings — that's what the show actually IS.' Which view of ethics is Aris defending?
answer: Virtue ethics — the show's wrong because of the kind of character it cultivates in everyone touched by it; consent and enjoyment don't redeem a habit of humiliation.
choices: Virtue ethics — the show's wrong because of the kind of character it cultivates in everyone touched by it; consent and enjoyment don't redeem a habit of humiliation.
Consequence ethics — the show is wrong only if its measurable harms to viewers and contestants outweigh the entertainment and economic benefits it produces in total.
Rule ethics — the show is wrong because humiliating people violates a universal duty to respect persons as ends, regardless of consent or downstream effects on character.
Contract ethics — the show is wrong only if rational parties choosing fair terms in advance would refuse to permit such a format under any circumstance whatsoever.
context: Virtue ethics (Aristotle, with MacIntyre's modern revival in After Virtue, 1981) evaluates acts by the character they shape. The relevant question isn't 'did anyone object?' but 'what kind of producer, viewer, contestant does this practice create over time?'

question: Op-ed writer Pell argues for diverting half the foreign-aid budget to a single antimalarial program: 'It saves the most lives per dollar — every other consideration is sentimentality. The proper question is which use of these dollars prevents the most deaths.' Which view of ethics is Pell defending?
answer: Consequence ethics — Pell weighs aid programs strictly by lives saved per dollar, treating maximizing total prevented deaths as the only ethically relevant measure of the policy.
choices: Consequence ethics — Pell weighs aid programs strictly by lives saved per dollar, treating maximizing total prevented deaths as the only ethically relevant measure of the policy.
Virtue ethics — Pell's argument turns on what kind of donor character is cultivated by the giving, with effectiveness ranked beneath the moral formation of the giver involved.
Care ethics — Pell's argument prioritizes existing relationships and concrete attentiveness to particular people the donor already knows over distant lives statistically saved by the policy.
Rule ethics — Pell's argument grounds the policy in a universal duty to respect each person as an end in themselves, regardless of what aggregate effects the policy happens to produce.
context: Act-consequentialism (Bentham, Mill, Peter Singer's Famine, Affluence, and Morality, 1972) ranks acts by total expected welfare. Critics charge that this can override duties to particular others; defenders reply that those duties already track expected welfare.

question: A medical researcher refuses to enroll vulnerable refugees in a trial that would yield high-quality data, even though they would consent: 'Using their hardship to extract data for our benefit treats them as a means to our paper, however softly we ask.' Which view of ethics is the researcher defending?
answer: Rule ethics — the researcher refuses because enrolling vulnerable refugees primarily for their data value treats them as a means rather than as ends, even with consent.
choices: Rule ethics — the researcher refuses because enrolling vulnerable refugees primarily for their data value treats them as a means rather than as ends, even with consent.
Consequence ethics — the researcher refuses because the trial's harms to refugees outweigh its expected medical benefits, in a cost-benefit calculation on welfare grounds.
Virtue ethics — the researcher refuses because participating would cultivate exploitative scientific habits in herself and her field, even if refugees were never directly harmed.
Care ethics — the researcher refuses because she has prior relationships with refugees demanding particular attentiveness, ruling out treating them as just another patient sample.
context: Kantian deontology (Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals, 1785) frames the wrong as treating persons merely as means, even with their consent. The 'humanity formulation' of the categorical imperative protects persons against being made instruments to others' projects.

question: Columnist Rasha argues for a tax proposal: 'If we had to set tax rates without knowing in advance whether we'd be born rich or poor, no rational person would agree to a system that left the worst-off with so little. THAT'S the test for a just tax code.' Which view of ethics is Rasha defending?
answer: Contract ethics — Rasha tests the tax code by what principles parties would consent to without knowing their economic position, taking reasonable agreement as the standard.
choices: Contract ethics — Rasha tests the tax code by what principles parties would consent to without knowing their economic position, taking reasonable agreement as the standard.
Consequence ethics — Rasha tests the tax code by which rate schedule maximizes total welfare or growth, treating what tiers of earners would have agreed to in advance as irrelevant.
Virtue ethics — Rasha tests the tax code by what attitudes toward wealth and citizenship it cultivates in taxpayers, judging policy by the national character it shapes over time.
Rule ethics — Rasha tests the tax code by whether it treats each taxpayer as an end in themselves, with hypothetical agreement under uncertainty an indirect route to the same conclusion.
context: Rawls (A Theory of Justice, 1971) proposed the 'original position' behind a 'veil of ignorance' as a thought experiment for testing principles of justice. T. M. Scanlon (What We Owe to Each Other, 1998) generalized this to interpersonal moral reasoning.

question: A government analyst signed a binding nondisclosure agreement, then discovered evidence of unlawful surveillance affecting millions. She tells colleagues she has decided to disclose: 'The duty of honesty I owe my employer cannot be unconditional when keeping it allows mass injury.' On her stated terms, which principle takes priority?
answer: Consequence ethics — with the harm prevented by disclosure being mass injury to millions, the analyst ranks the NDA duty as outranked by the welfare effects of staying silent.
choices: Consequence ethics — with the harm prevented by disclosure being mass injury to millions, the analyst ranks the NDA duty as outranked by the welfare effects of staying silent.
Rule ethics — the duty of honesty owed in a signed NDA is unconditional under Kantian universalizability, so the analyst would remain silent regardless of the surveillance's effects.
Virtue ethics — the analyst should ask which choice best fits the character of a trustworthy professional and let that settle the question without weighing duty against consequence.
Contract ethics — the signed NDA is itself the consent-grounded principle, and parties under fair conditions could not consent to its being overridden whenever harm to outsiders looms.
context: When duties conflict — here, contract honesty vs. preventing mass harm — the question becomes which moral principle takes priority. The analyst frames her contractual duty as conditional on its consequences (preventable mass injury), which is the consequentialist move whether or not she calls it that.

question: A trial sponsor proposes paying impoverished volunteers a year's wages to test a high-risk drug. Ethicist Soren objects: 'Even if the trial would on net save more lives than it costs, the offer instrumentalizes their poverty — that's where I draw the line.' On Soren's stated terms, which principle takes priority?
answer: Rule ethics — Soren ranks the duty not to instrumentalize the volunteers above net life-saving outcome, treating dignity as a constraint that welfare math cannot override.
choices: Rule ethics — Soren ranks the duty not to instrumentalize the volunteers above net life-saving outcome, treating dignity as a constraint that welfare math cannot override.
Consequence ethics — Soren weighs the trial's expected life-saving outcome against volunteer welfare, concluding the math favors banning trials with high payments to poor applicants.
Virtue ethics — Soren asks what kind of medical research community is cultivated by such trials, letting the answer about institutional character settle the trial's permissibility.
Care ethics — Soren prioritizes the sponsor's particular relationships with named volunteers, concluding those relationships could not survive trial conditions exploiting financial pressure.
context: When a deontological frame confronts a consequentialist one, the priority question is structural: which principle does the speaker treat as overridable? Soren explicitly concedes the welfare math but refuses to let it override the dignity constraint.

question: Donor Quill faces a choice: fund his neighborhood's struggling music program, or send the same money to a vetted overseas health charity expected to save more lives. He says: 'My ties to this neighborhood aren't a bias I should correct away — they're part of what I owe.' On Quill's terms, which principle takes priority?
answer: Care ethics — Quill ranks the moral weight of his concrete neighborhood ties above the impartial expected-lives-saved calculation, treating the relationship as ethically load-bearing.
choices: Care ethics — Quill ranks the moral weight of his concrete neighborhood ties above the impartial expected-lives-saved calculation, treating the relationship as ethically load-bearing.
Consequence ethics — Quill treats expected lives saved as the morally binding measure and his neighborhood loyalty as a sentimental preference he should correct away from impartial giving.
Rule ethics — Quill grounds the gift in a universal duty owed equally to all rational beings, with neighborhood ties a contingent feature that has no standing in his moral reasoning.
Virtue ethics — Quill asks which gift better cultivates donor virtue and ranks that question above the partiality of his ties and above the impartial expected-welfare math of the choice.
context: Care ethics treats particular relationships as moral facts. The choice between giving local and giving where expected impact is highest is one of the sharpest impartialist-vs-care debates. Both views have serious defenders; the question asks WHICH Quill is using.

question: A senior surgeon, removed from her post after a procedural dispute, writes: 'My position, my reputation, and the patients I would have served — none of these are within my control to retrieve. What remains within my control is the quality of my next day's work.' Which view of ethics is the surgeon defending?
answer: Stoic ethics — the surgeon distinguishes what is in her control (the next day's work) from what is not (reputation, patients) and treats only the controllable as moral ground.
choices: Stoic ethics — the surgeon distinguishes what is in her control (the next day's work) from what is not (reputation, patients) and treats only the controllable as moral ground.
Consequence ethics — the surgeon weighs the patients she would have served against her current options and concludes that maximizing expected medical welfare is the relevant ethical measure.
Virtue ethics — the surgeon asks what kind of physician her response is shaping and treats character development as primary, with the control distinction a less direct route to the answer.
Care ethics — the surgeon centers her ongoing relationships with patients and colleagues as moral facts the dismissal has not erased, with control over circumstances a secondary issue.
context: Stoic ethics (Epictetus, Discourses; Marcus Aurelius, Meditations) draws a sharp line between what is and isn't 'up to us.' Moral concern attaches to the former; the rest is to be met with equanimity. The view's modern revival runs through Pierre Hadot and others.

question: Theologian Brand defends a hospital's policy against physician-administered lethal injection: 'Whatever the suffering, taking innocent life directly aims against the human good itself. Some acts are wrong by what they do, regardless of motive or outcome.' Which view of ethics is Brand defending?
answer: Natural-law ethics — Brand treats directly taking innocent life as intrinsically wrong by its object, with the act's relation to human good ranked above motive or outcome in the analysis.
choices: Natural-law ethics — Brand treats directly taking innocent life as intrinsically wrong by its object, with the act's relation to human good ranked above motive or outcome in the analysis.
Consequence ethics — Brand weighs the suffering relieved by lethal injection against the lives ended and rules on the policy by which outcome ranks higher in total welfare terms.
Care ethics — Brand prioritizes the moral weight of the dying patient's relationships with family and physician and lets those concrete ties settle whether the policy is acceptable.
Stoic ethics — Brand draws a line between what the patient and physician can control and what they cannot, treating only the controllable elements of the dying process as moral matter.
context: Natural-law ethics (Aquinas, Summa Theologiae; modern revival through Finnis, Natural Law and Natural Rights, 1980) holds that some acts are wrong by their object — what they directly aim at — independent of further consequences. The doctrine of double effect is downstream of this.

question: Op-ed writer Imber argues against a billionaire's clever tax-avoidance scheme: 'The scheme is legal and harms no one visible. But imagine a rule permitting it generally — the tax base collapses. The right question isn't this act's effect, it's the effect of the RULE behind it.' Which view of ethics is Imber defending?
answer: Consequence ethics — Imber evaluates the avoidance scheme by the welfare effect of the RULE permitting it generally rather than the visible effect of this single act (rule-utilitarian).
choices: Consequence ethics — Imber evaluates the avoidance scheme by the welfare effect of the RULE permitting it generally rather than the visible effect of this single act (rule-utilitarian).
Rule ethics — Imber grounds the wrong in Kantian universalizability, asking whether the maxim of tax avoidance could be rationally willed as a universal law without contradiction.
Virtue ethics — Imber asks what kind of citizen and what kind of tax system the scheme cultivates over time and lets the answer about institutional character settle the policy question.
Contract ethics — Imber asks what tax-avoidance practices parties under a Rawlsian veil of ignorance would consent to, treating reasonable agreement as the standard rather than welfare.
context: Rule-consequentialism (Brad Hooker, Ideal Code Real World, 2000) judges acts by the welfare effects of the RULE permitting them, not the act's local effects. It captures the intuition that 'imagine if everyone did this' is doing welfare-math at the rule level, not categorical-imperative math.

question: Columnist Drei criticizes a media outlet that runs deliberately provocative headlines to drive engagement: 'Each headline is technically defensible. But the editorial habit of phrasing every story to provoke trains a newsroom — and its readers — into worse intellectual character.' Which view of ethics is Drei defending?
answer: Virtue ethics — Drei criticizes the outlet not by any single headline's effects but by the editorial habits the provocation workflow trains in newsroom staff and reader audiences over time.
choices: Virtue ethics — Drei criticizes the outlet not by any single headline's effects but by the editorial habits the provocation workflow trains in newsroom staff and reader audiences over time.
Consequence ethics — Drei sums the actual harms caused by each provocative headline across the readership and concludes the aggregate welfare effects exceed the outlet's engagement revenue.
Rule ethics — Drei grounds the criticism in a universal duty against manipulation, holding no rational party could will the maxim of provocation-headlines as a universal editorial law.
Contract ethics — Drei tests whether readers under fair conditions would consent to the outlet's provocation-driven editorial workflow as a permissible practice in their information world.
context: Virtue ethics evaluates practices by character formation. The critique here doesn't depend on tracing harms to particular readers; it claims a workflow of provoking is itself character-degrading for writers and audiences regardless of which headlines land.

question: A father plans to lie at a college-admissions interview to advantage his son. Pressed by his sister, he says: 'I'm not telling other fathers to lie. I just owe THIS to MY son.' His sister replies: 'Then what you call a duty isn't a maxim you can universalize.' On the sister's terms, which principle takes priority?
answer: Rule ethics — the sister demands the father's maxim be universalizable as a law for all rational agents, ranking that test above his particular felt duty to advantage his own son.
choices: Rule ethics — the sister demands the father's maxim be universalizable as a law for all rational agents, ranking that test above his particular felt duty to advantage his own son.
Care ethics — the sister centers the father's particular relationship to his son as moral ground and grants partial duties to one's own children priority over an abstract universal standard.
Consequence ethics — the sister weighs the welfare effects of the lie across all affected parties and concludes the costs to displaced applicants exceed the gains to the father's own son.
Virtue ethics — the sister asks what kind of father the lie cultivates and ranks that character question above universalizability as the genuinely morally informative question.
context: Kantian universalizability (categorical imperative, first formulation) tests a maxim by whether it could rationally be willed as a universal law. The sister isn't denying her brother's love for his son; she's denying that love generates a maxim he can hold against the test.

question: Policy analyst Adair argues for a moderation rule on a public platform: 'The right question isn't whether the rule produces the best total speech outcomes — it's whether it's a rule no affected user could REASONABLY reject. That's the bar a platform owes its users.' Which view of ethics is Adair defending?
answer: Contract ethics — Adair grounds the moderation rule in what affected users could not reasonably reject, treating interpersonal justification as the standard rather than aggregate welfare.
choices: Contract ethics — Adair grounds the moderation rule in what affected users could not reasonably reject, treating interpersonal justification as the standard rather than aggregate welfare.
Consequence ethics — Adair weighs the moderation rule by which version produces the best total speech welfare across the userbase, treating reasonable-rejection as a less direct measure.
Rule ethics — Adair grounds the moderation rule in a universal duty owed to each user as an end in themselves, treating dignity rather than consent under fair conditions as the basis.
Virtue ethics — Adair asks which moderation rule cultivates the best kind of user community over time and ranks character formation above aggregate welfare or interpersonal rejection.
context: Scanlon's contractualism (What We Owe to Each Other, 1998) asks not 'what could everyone consent to?' but 'what could no one reasonably REJECT?' The 'reasonable rejection' test gives weight to each affected party without aggregating welfare across persons.

question: A journalist refuses a scoop that requires breaking source confidentiality, even though no one would discover: 'The point of source protection isn't a tally of harms in this case. It's that breaking it once would not be the act of the kind of journalist I'm trying to become.' Which view of ethics is the journalist defending?
answer: Virtue ethics — the journalist refuses because breaking source confidentiality is not the act of the kind of journalist she is forming herself into, regardless of whether anyone discovers.
choices: Virtue ethics — the journalist refuses because breaking source confidentiality is not the act of the kind of journalist she is forming herself into, regardless of whether anyone discovers.
Consequence ethics — the journalist weighs the scoop's expected welfare gains against the harms to sources and concludes the aggregate calculation does not favor breaking confidentiality.
Rule ethics — the journalist refuses because breaking source confidentiality violates a universal duty owed to sources as ends in themselves under the categorical imperative's terms.
Care ethics — the journalist refuses because her particular relationships with named sources demand concrete attentiveness that breaking confidence on any one occasion would betray.
context: Virtue ethics in modern professional contexts (Alasdair MacIntyre's work on 'practices' in After Virtue) frames role-based duties as constitutive of a profession's internal goods. The relevant question is what kind of journalist a habit of breaking confidence trains.
