question: A health columnist defends individual choice on a high-sugar diet against a proposed ban: 'The only legitimate ground for compulsion is harm to others. Self-regarding choices, even foolish ones, aren't where the state's writ runs.' On the columnist's terms, which principle takes priority?
answer: Rule ethics — the columnist treats the harm principle as a near-absolute constraint limiting state coercion to other-regarding cases, ranking liberty above any welfare gain from the ban.
choices: Rule ethics — the columnist treats the harm principle as a near-absolute constraint limiting state coercion to other-regarding cases, ranking liberty above any welfare gain from the ban.
Consequence ethics — the columnist weighs the diet ban's aggregate health gains against autonomy losses, concluding the welfare math is what settles whether the ban is permissible policy.
Virtue ethics — the columnist asks what kind of citizen and civic character the ban cultivates, letting the answer about character formation settle the case apart from harm-principle talk.
Contract ethics — the columnist asks whether parties under fair conditions would consent to a paternalistic diet ban, treating harm-principle language as a less direct version of the test.
context: Mill's On Liberty (1859) frames the harm principle as a side-constraint on legitimate interference. Some readers treat Mill as a consequentialist throughout; others — and the columnist's voice here — read the harm principle as a near-deontological limit on state action.

question: A wartime commander considers planting a false story to mislead an enemy general — the deception would save thousands of lives. His chaplain objects: 'Direct lying aims at false belief in another's mind. That target is intrinsically disordered, however good the further aim.' Which view of ethics is the chaplain defending?
answer: Natural-law ethics — the chaplain treats direct lying as intrinsically wrong by its object (aiming at false belief), with the further good of lives saved unable to repair the act's disorder.
choices: Natural-law ethics — the chaplain treats direct lying as intrinsically wrong by its object (aiming at false belief), with the further good of lives saved unable to repair the act's disorder.
Consequence ethics — the chaplain weighs the lives saved by the false story against the harms of strategic deception, concluding the aggregate welfare math does not favor the report.
Rule ethics — the chaplain grounds the wrong in Kantian universalizability, holding the maxim of strategic lying could not be willed as a universal law without practical contradiction.
Stoic ethics — the chaplain separates what the commander can control from what he cannot and treats only the inner act of forming the deceptive intention as the morally relevant subject.
context: Aquinas (Summa Theologiae II-II, q.110) treats lying as intrinsically wrong by its object — aiming at false belief in another. Kant likewise condemns lying, but on universalizability grounds. The natural-law and Kantian condemnations converge on the verdict but reason there differently.

question: Podcast host Ellis describes ignoring a coordinated online harassment campaign: 'The abuse isn't within my control. The temptation to retaliate is. I attend to what's mine to attend to — my next show, my next hour — and let the rest pass through.' Which view of ethics is Ellis defending?
answer: Stoic ethics — Ellis distinguishes the harassment (not in his control) from his own response (in his control) and locates moral concern with the latter, letting the former pass through.
choices: Stoic ethics — Ellis distinguishes the harassment (not in his control) from his own response (in his control) and locates moral concern with the latter, letting the former pass through.
Virtue ethics — Ellis asks what kind of host he is forming by his response to abuse and ranks character cultivation above the control distinction as the more direct ethical question.
Care ethics — Ellis centers his relationships with listeners and collaborators as the moral ground the harassment threatens, with the control distinction a less direct way to protect them.
Consequence ethics — Ellis weighs the welfare effects of responding versus ignoring across listeners and harassers, concluding the aggregate calculus favors the no-engagement strategy.
context: The Stoic control distinction (Epictetus, Enchiridion 1) is the practical core of Stoic ethics: moral effort attaches to what is up to us; what is not up to us is met with equanimity. The view's modern revival treats this as a discipline of attention, not resignation.

question: Philanthropist Adi argues for a substantial cut in personal spending to fund international anti-malaria efforts: 'If I would wade into a pond to save a drowning child at the cost of muddy clothes, the same logic binds me to give to charities that save children at comparable cost.' Which view of ethics is Adi defending?
answer: Consequence ethics — Adi extends the pond-rescue logic across distance, holding aggregate child welfare per dollar binds him to give at the level the proximity case would have demanded.
choices: Consequence ethics — Adi extends the pond-rescue logic across distance, holding aggregate child welfare per dollar binds him to give at the level the proximity case would have demanded.
Rule ethics — Adi grounds the obligation in a universal duty to treat distant children as ends in themselves, treating the pond-rescue parallel as a less direct route to the same conclusion.
Care ethics — Adi treats his relationships with named donor recipients as concrete moral facts and rejects any abstract welfare-maximization frame for charity decisions in his own life.
Virtue ethics — Adi asks what kind of philanthropist character is cultivated by such giving and ranks the habit of regular sacrificial donation above the per-dollar welfare calculation.
context: Peter Singer's pond argument (Famine, Affluence, and Morality, 1972) is the modern stalking horse for impartialist consequentialism. Critics from care ethics (Held) and agent-relative views (Bernard Williams) press hard on whether distance is morally irrelevant in the way Singer requires.

question: A small-town doctor is offered a position at a major research hospital where she would save more lives in expectation. She declines: 'The people of this town have built their lives around having me here. That standing relationship isn't a sentimental detail — it's where my obligation begins.' On her terms, which principle takes priority?
answer: Care ethics — the doctor ranks the moral weight of her standing ties with the townspeople above the impartial expected-lives-saved calculation, treating concrete attachment as load-bearing.
choices: Care ethics — the doctor ranks the moral weight of her standing ties with the townspeople above the impartial expected-lives-saved calculation, treating concrete attachment as load-bearing.
Consequence ethics — the doctor weighs expected lives saved at each post and concludes the research hospital dominates the small town under any reasonable aggregate welfare measure.
Rule ethics — the doctor grounds her choice in a universal duty owed equally to all patients as ends in themselves, with no special weight given to standing local ties in the analysis.
Virtue ethics — the doctor asks which choice best fits the physician virtues and lets character formation settle the question without weighting relationships above impartial duty.
context: Care ethics distinguishes itself from impartialist views precisely on cases like this. The standing relationship isn't a contingent preference to be corrected away; it's a morally significant fact about the doctor's actual situation, on the care-ethics view.

question: An impartialist argues a father owes equal moral concern to all children. The father replies: 'I owe my own son particular things — time, sacrifice, preference — I don't owe other children. That's not a failure of reasoning; it's where reasoning starts.' Which view is the father defending?
answer: Agent-relative partiality — parenthood and friendship generate real duties of preference impartial reasoning cannot dissolve; the father's bias is morally grounded, not a defect to correct.
choices: Agent-relative partiality — parenthood and friendship generate real duties of preference impartial reasoning cannot dissolve; the father's bias is morally grounded, not a defect to correct.
Impartialist consequentialism — each child has equal claim on every adult; the father's preference is sentiment he should weigh symmetrically against the welfare of any stranger's child.
Kantian universalism — the duty is owed to every child as a rational end; his concern for his son must answer to the universal duty owed equally to all children he could help.
Care ethics as relationship — the father's concern depends on the relational tie he has with his son; were the tie absent, the duty would be absent, with no agent-relative grounding.
context: John Cottingham (Partiality and the Virtues, 1998) defends agent-relative obligations against Godwin-style impartialism. Bernard Williams (Moral Luck, 1981) reinforced the view: constitutive attachments — your child, your spouse, your life-shaping projects — generate duties impartial reasoning cannot rationalize as bias.

question: Peter Singer argues distance is morally irrelevant: if you would wade into a pond to save a drowning child, the same logic binds you toward distant children. Bernard Williams replies that a man who deliberates whether to save his wife or a stranger has 'one thought too many.' Which view is Williams defending?
answer: Agent-relative ethics — a spouse and a child are constitutive attachments; impartial calculation about them is itself defective moral psychology, since the extra thought corrodes the bond.
choices: Agent-relative ethics — a spouse and a child are constitutive attachments; impartial calculation about them is itself defective moral psychology, since the extra thought corrodes the bond.
Strong impartialism — Singer's pond logic is sound and Williams's complaint is sentimental cover for ignoring duties owed equally to strangers; impartial reason dissolves the husband's bias.
Rule-utilitarianism — the right principle is the one whose general adoption maximizes welfare; Williams objects only that some such rules permit limited partiality as a useful policy.
Care ethics as sentiment — Williams treats the husband's feeling as a weighty emotion Singer's reasoning underweights; what's at stake is the place of caring feelings in moral theory.
context: Williams's 'one thought too many' (Moral Luck, 1981) is the canonical reply to impartialist ethics: a husband who pauses to weigh whether saving his wife is justified on impartial grounds has already misunderstood what marriage IS. Constitutive attachments aren't biases to defeat — they're where moral agency lives.

question: Christina Hoff Sommers argues care ethics took a gendered moral sentiment — caring response common in women's experience — and elevated it to philosophical conclusion without scrutinizing the elevation itself. Which view is Sommers defending?
answer: Equity feminism — fair treatment of individuals requires substantive philosophical scrutiny of any moral sentiment before elevating it to theory; sentiment is data, not yet conclusion.
choices: Equity feminism — fair treatment of individuals requires substantive philosophical scrutiny of any moral sentiment before elevating it to theory; sentiment is data, not yet conclusion.
Gender feminism — gendered patterns of response are morally authoritative; women's caring style is the standard against which justice frames must be revised, and Sommers restates that line.
Strict rationalism — moral sentiment of any kind is irrelevant to philosophy; the objection is that care theorists took feelings seriously at all, not that they failed to scrutinize them.
Postmodern critique — philosophical scrutiny is itself a gendered move; Sommers's call for scrutiny reinscribes the masculine standard care ethics was supposed to displace from theory.
context: Christina Hoff Sommers (Who Stole Feminism?, 1994) distinguishes equity feminism — fair treatment of individuals on their merits — from gender feminism, which treats any difference as oppression. Her critique of care ethics is methodological: elevating sentiment without scrutiny is bad theory, not anti-care.

question: An economist argues against the welfare state's framing as scaled care: 'Centralized care assumes a planner can know what particular families need; that knowledge is dispersed across millions of local ties. Institutional care produces the dependency it was meant to relieve.' Which view is the economist defending?
answer: Hayekian classical liberalism — dispersed local knowledge cannot be assembled centrally; scaling care to institutions degrades it, and civil society outperforms top-down planning.
choices: Hayekian classical liberalism — dispersed local knowledge cannot be assembled centrally; scaling care to institutions degrades it, and civil society outperforms top-down planning.
Libertarian rights — the state has no authority to compel transfers whatever the effects, so the welfare debate is settled on rights grounds before any claim about dependency enters.
Marxist critique — welfare-state failures reflect capitalism's contradictions, not knowledge; central care fails because it sits inside a market system, not because of planning as such.
Communitarian conservatism — the welfare state crowds out family and church, weakening intermediate institutions; the critique is about culture, not knowledge problems.
context: F. A. Hayek (The Use of Knowledge in Society, 1945; The Constitution of Liberty, 1960) identified the knowledge problem: prices and local relations coordinate information no central planner can assemble. Scaled to care, institutional welfare destroys the very local knowledge that made care responsive.

question: A bioethicist on an organ-allocation panel argues: 'Some acts are wrong because of what they do to the agent's character, even when no third party is harmed.' A critic responds that wrongness without harm collapses into mere taste. Which framework most directly supports the bioethicist's claim?
answer: Virtue ethics — moral wrongness can attach to acts that corrupt the agent's character, since on this view the moral status of the agent's settled dispositions is itself a substantive moral concern.
choices: Virtue ethics — moral wrongness can attach to acts that corrupt the agent's character, since on this view the moral status of the agent's settled dispositions is itself a substantive moral concern.

Consequentialism — wrongness depends on identifiable welfare effects on persons; without harm to some party, the bioethicist's claim has no foothold unless 'damage to character' itself counts as harm done.

Deontology — wrongness turns on whether the act violates a universal rule binding on all rational agents, regardless of consequences and regardless of any effect on the agent's character traits over time.

Contractualism — wrongness turns on what principles could be justified to all affected parties; with no parties affected by the act, there is on this view no relational ground for a moral claim of wrongness.
context: Virtue ethics returned to prominence with Anscombe ('Modern Moral Philosophy,' 1958) and MacIntyre (After Virtue, 1981). Its signature move: acts can be wrong because of what they do to the agent, not only because of harm to others. The critic's 'imposing taste' challenge is real but answerable.

question: A research-ethics board argues that deceiving participants in a psychology study is wrong even when the deception is mild and the eventual gain to knowledge is large. 'Treating them as means to the experiment's ends is the violation, regardless of net welfare.' Which framework grounds the board's claim?
answer: Deontology — Kantian humanity-as-end forbids treating participants merely as instruments of the experiment; the wrongness lies in the manner of treatment, not in any downstream balance of welfare gained or lost.
choices: Deontology — Kantian humanity-as-end forbids treating participants merely as instruments of the experiment; the wrongness lies in the manner of treatment, not in any downstream balance of welfare gained or lost.

Consequentialism — the deception's wrongness would depend on whether net welfare improves or worsens; if the study's knowledge gain exceeds the participants' costs, the deception would on this view be permissible.

Virtue ethics — the issue is whether running deceptive studies cultivates dishonesty in the researchers; rules about consent matter only as proxies for the dispositions the practice over time forms in scientists.

Care ethics — wrongness depends on damage to the relational trust between researcher and participant; deception is wrong because it corrodes the particular relationships, not because of an abstract universal rule.
context: Kant's Groundwork (1785) gives the humanity-as-end formula: act so you treat humanity, in yourself or another, always as an end and never merely as a means. Modern research ethics (Belmont Report, 1979) operationalizes this through informed consent — the participant's standing as a rational agent.

question: A public-health ethicist defends a strict isolation rule during outbreaks: 'Yes, in this individual case the cost looks high and the benefit looks small. But we are choosing the rule we will follow across thousands of such cases.' Which framework most directly supports her reasoning?
answer: Rule consequentialism — rightness depends on the welfare effects of the rule applied across all such cases, not the welfare effects of breaking it in this particular instance where the local balance looks adverse.
choices: Rule consequentialism — rightness depends on the welfare effects of the rule applied across all such cases, not the welfare effects of breaking it in this particular instance where the local balance looks adverse.

Act consequentialism — rightness depends on the welfare effects of THIS act in THIS case; if the local balance favors breaking the rule, an act-consequentialist accepts the break and rejects the rule appeal.

Deontology — the isolation rule binds because it expresses a universal duty during contagion, regardless of any welfare calculation across cases; consequences play no role in establishing the rule's authority.

Virtue ethics — the question is what dispositions the rule fosters in public-health officials over time; rule appeals matter as character-formation, not as a calculation of aggregated welfare effects either way.
context: Brad Hooker's Ideal Code, Real World (2000) is the canonical contemporary defense of rule consequentialism. The view holds rightness derives from the welfare-best set of rules a society could internalize, even when act-by-act calculation would diverge. Critics: Mill's wavering on the act/rule distinction; Smart's challenge.

question: A philosopher panel debates whether parents acting on partiality toward their own children is morally justified. One panelist argues: 'The relationship itself generates obligations that strangers do not generate; moral reasoning starts from particular bonds, not from impartial principles.' Which framework grounds her position?
answer: Care ethics — moral obligations are generated by particular relationships of dependency and bond, so partiality toward one's own children is not a deviation from morality but constitutive of where moral reasoning starts.
choices: Care ethics — moral obligations are generated by particular relationships of dependency and bond, so partiality toward one's own children is not a deviation from morality but constitutive of where moral reasoning starts.

Impartialist consequentialism — moral reasoning weighs welfare from a view-from-nowhere, so partiality to one's own children is at best a useful disposition and at worst a moral failing the rigorous agent corrects.

Kantian deontology — duties hold universally between rational agents, and partiality is permitted only when it can be reconciled with universalizable maxims; the relationship itself does not on its own generate duty.

Contractualism — duties hold among parties under fair conditions; partiality is justified only when principles permitting it could not be reasonably rejected from a standpoint that abstracts from the existing relationships.
context: Nel Noddings (Caring, 1984) and Virginia Held (The Ethics of Care, 2006) argue that the impartialist tradition mistakes the starting point of moral reasoning. Particular relationships are not deviations from morality but the soil in which moral reasoning grows. Critics: how partial is too partial?

question: A bioethicist on an AI-standing panel argues: 'The question is not whether an AI feels but whether principles excluding AIs from moral consideration could be reasonably rejected by parties affected — including the AIs themselves, if they reach the relevant threshold.' Which framework grounds her test?
answer: Contractualism — Scanlon's standard makes wrongness depend on whether principles regulating conduct could be reasonably rejected by any affected party, extending standing to whoever meets the threshold for reasoned objection.
choices: Contractualism — Scanlon's standard makes wrongness depend on whether principles regulating conduct could be reasonably rejected by any affected party, extending standing to whoever meets the threshold for reasoned objection.

Sentience-based utilitarianism — moral standing depends on the capacity to suffer or have preferences, so the relevant question is whether AIs are conscious in the morally weighty sense, not whether principles are rejectable.

Virtue ethics — moral standing depends on what character the practice of excluding AIs would cultivate in the humans who adopt it; the relational test misses what really matters, which is the agent's habituated dispositions.

Kantian deontology — moral standing turns on rational agency: whether AIs are members of the kingdom of ends, not on what principles parties could agree to under fair reasoning conditions of the kind Scanlon proposes.
context: T.M. Scanlon's What We Owe to Each Other (1998) replaces a felicific calculus with a justifiability test: an act is wrong if a principle permitting it could not be justified to those affected. The framework expands naturally to nonhuman moral patients without first settling the consciousness question.

question: A military ethicist argues that destroying a munitions plant in war is permissible even when civilian deaths are foreseeable, provided the deaths are not intended and not the means to the military end. Critics call the foreseen/intended line untenable. Which framework grounds the ethicist's position?
answer: Natural law (double effect) — the doctrine of double effect distinguishes intended ends from foreseen but unintended side effects, permitting the strike on the munitions plant when civilian deaths are foreseen but not the means.
choices: Natural law (double effect) — the doctrine of double effect distinguishes intended ends from foreseen but unintended side effects, permitting the strike on the munitions plant when civilian deaths are foreseen but not the means.

Act consequentialism — what matters is the net welfare balance of the strike, not the agent's intentional structure; the strike is justified or not on the calculus alone, and double effect adds no moral content of its own.

Kantian deontology — using civilians as a means is forbidden whether intended or not, since the strike's structure treats them as instruments; the foreseen/intended line cannot rescue a violation of humanity-as-end here.

Virtue ethics — what matters is whether the practice cultivates the just-warrior dispositions over time; intentional structure matters only as it shapes character, not as a free-standing test of the act's permissibility now.
context: Aquinas (Summa II-II, q.64) developed the doctrine of double effect in discussing self-defense killing. John Finnis (Natural Law and Natural Rights, 1980) modernized the framework. Critics (Bennett, Foot) press hard on the intended/foreseen distinction. The line survives in international humanitarian law.

question: A philosopher writes that there are no exceptionless moral generalizations: 'A feature that makes one act worse can make another act better; whether honesty matters here depends on the rest of the case. Moral reasons are holistic, not contributory.' Which framework is the philosopher defending?
answer: Moral particularism — Dancy's holism about moral reasons holds that what counts as a reason in one case may count differently in another; the moral significance of any feature is settled by the rest of the case, not in advance.
choices: Moral particularism — Dancy's holism about moral reasons holds that what counts as a reason in one case may count differently in another; the moral significance of any feature is settled by the rest of the case, not in advance.

Rule deontology — moral reasoning relies on exceptionless general rules; any feature that matters morally carries the same weight wherever it appears, so a feature pulling one way here cannot pull the other way there.

Rule consequentialism — rightness derives from the welfare-best set of general rules; moral features keep stable weight across cases, and apparent reversals are at most disguised differences in some other rule-relevant fact.

Virtue ethics — the agent's settled dispositions track moral reality across cases; a virtuous person reads features the same way each time precisely because her character is stable, not because the case-by-case weighing varies.
context: Jonathan Dancy's Ethics Without Principles (2004) argues moral generalism is the legacy of trying to model ethics on logic. Holism: a feature is a reason here, but not there, or here a reason of opposite valence. Critics (McKeever, Ridge) reply that particularism overstates the case for context-dependence.

question: A bioethicist argues: 'Ordinarily it is impermissible to kill one innocent person to save five — the deontological constraint holds. But at very high stakes — to prevent the deaths of a million — the constraint gives way.' Which framework most directly captures her position?
answer: Threshold deontology — deontological constraints against killing the innocent hold up to a stakes threshold, beyond which catastrophic consequences override the constraint and permit the otherwise-forbidden killing in this case.
choices: Threshold deontology — deontological constraints against killing the innocent hold up to a stakes threshold, beyond which catastrophic consequences override the constraint and permit the otherwise-forbidden killing in this case.

Act consequentialism — there is no threshold; the calculus runs continuously, and one-for-five is forbidden only because the local balance disfavors it, not because a constraint applies up to a threshold then yields beyond it.

Strict deontology — the constraint against killing the innocent never yields, regardless of consequences; the bioethicist's threshold view abandons the constraint's distinctive force whenever the stakes get high enough.

Rule consequentialism — the right rule for cases of this shape would be selected by long-run welfare; any threshold reflects the welfare-best policy across cases, not a distinct moral structure of constraint plus override.
context: Threshold deontology (Moore, Alexander) is a hybrid: deontological constraints have real moral force but are not infinite. At catastrophic stakes the threshold is crossed and consequences take over. Critics on both sides — strict deontologists call it unprincipled; consequentialists call it ad hoc.

question: A philosopher argues: 'The neighbor who runs into the burning house to save the child does more than duty requires — the act is praiseworthy precisely because it is beyond what could have been demanded of her.' A critic replies the category itself is incoherent. Which framework defends the philosopher?
answer: Supererogationism — moral space includes acts that are praiseworthy yet not required; the neighbor's rescue is morally good without being morally demanded, which is precisely what makes the praise it earns appropriate.
choices: Supererogationism — moral space includes acts that are praiseworthy yet not required; the neighbor's rescue is morally good without being morally demanded, which is precisely what makes the praise it earns appropriate.

Act consequentialism — if the rescue produces the welfare-best outcome it is required, not optional; the praiseworthy-but-not-required category dissolves, since rightness on this view tracks the calculus continuously.

Rigorist Kantianism — what is required is what duty commands and what is forbidden is what duty forbids; the residual category of permissible-but-praiseworthy collapses into duty or indifference, with no space between.

Virtue ethics — the neighbor's act expresses courage and benevolence; praise tracks character, but the supererogation category in its standard form misdescribes what is happening, which is just the virtuous act done well.
context: J.O. Urmson's 'Saints and Heroes' (1958) is the canonical defense of supererogation as a distinct moral category. The critic's challenge (Kagan, in particular) is that maximizing consequentialism leaves no room for going beyond duty: whatever is best is what is required. The debate maps directly onto demandingness.

question: A bioethicist argues organ allocation should track 'what informed patients would themselves choose for themselves,' not raw life-years saved. A colleague insists welfare-maximization is the only defensible criterion. Which framework grounds the first bioethicist's view?
answer: Preference utilitarianism — the morally relevant magnitude is satisfaction of informed preferences rather than welfare, so allocation in this case tracks what patients would themselves choose given the relevant information.
choices: Preference utilitarianism — the morally relevant magnitude is satisfaction of informed preferences rather than welfare, so allocation in this case tracks what patients would themselves choose given the relevant information.

Welfare utilitarianism — the morally relevant magnitude is the actual well-being produced; preferences matter only as proxies for welfare, and allocation should track raw life-years saved rather than informed choice.

Contractualism — allocation principles must be justifiable to all parties under fair conditions; the relevant test is reasonable rejectability of the rule, not aggregation of preferences across the affected patients.

Capability theory — allocation should equalize basic capabilities rather than aggregate preferences or welfare; the morally relevant question is whether each patient can function across the central domains of human life.
context: Peter Singer (Practical Ethics, 1979) developed preference utilitarianism as an improvement on classical Benthamite welfare utilitarianism, addressing the problem of mistaken preferences with the 'informed' qualifier. Sumner's Welfare, Happiness, and Ethics (1996) is a careful comparison of the two.

question: A philosopher columnist argues: 'You are permitted to favor your own child even when, from a neutral standpoint, the same resources would produce more good directed at a stranger's child. The agent-relative permission is real.' Which framework most directly supports the columnist?
answer: Agent-relative deontology — each agent is permitted to weight her own projects, attachments, and children beyond what impartial calculation would license; the parent's partiality is a moral permission, not a failing.
choices: Agent-relative deontology — each agent is permitted to weight her own projects, attachments, and children beyond what impartial calculation would license; the parent's partiality is a moral permission, not a failing.

Strict impartialist consequentialism — what counts is the welfare-best distribution of resources from a view-from-nowhere; favoring one's own child when this reduces total welfare is at best a useful disposition.

Virtue ethics — the partiality of good parents reflects a settled disposition the virtuous parent has; the question is whether the disposition is virtuous, not whether agent-relative reasons license deviation.

Care ethics — the parent's obligations flow from the relationship of dependency itself, which generates the duties directly; the framework needs no separate notion of agent-relative permissions on top of that relational claim.
context: Samuel Scheffler's The Rejection of Consequentialism (1982) gives the canonical defense of agent-centered prerogatives: ethics can accommodate partiality without collapsing into self-indulgence. Bernard Williams's 'Persons, Character, and Morality' makes the closely related integrity-objection against utilitarianism.

question: An economist on a poverty-policy panel argues: 'The right benchmark is what principles parties would agree to from behind a veil that masks their actual position in society — their wealth, talents, and social standing.' Which framework grounds the economist's test?
answer: Rawlsian contractualism — the original-position device asks which principles parties would choose under a veil of ignorance about their own social position, so the panel's benchmark is what such parties would actually accept.
choices: Rawlsian contractualism — the original-position device asks which principles parties would choose under a veil of ignorance about their own social position, so the panel's benchmark is what such parties would actually accept.

Welfare utilitarianism — the benchmark is whichever policy maximizes aggregate well-being across the affected population, regardless of how gains and losses distribute; the veil-of-ignorance device plays no essential role.

Libertarian rights theory — the benchmark is whether the policy respects pre-political property rights and voluntary exchange; a hypothetical-agreement device misframes the question and obscures the rights at stake.

Capability theory — the benchmark is whether each person can function across the basic human capabilities; the test is direct evaluation of capability sets, not the hypothetical reasoning of contractors behind a veil.
context: John Rawls's A Theory of Justice (1971) develops the original position: parties choose principles knowing general facts about society but not their own positions in it. The device produces his two principles (equal basic liberties; the difference principle). Critics (Nozick, Sandel) press from rights and community.

question: A panelist defends a redistributive proposal. A critic responds: 'Taxation of legitimately earned income for transfer to others is on a moral par with forced labor — you cannot just override property in service of preferred patterns of distribution.' Which framework grounds the critic's position?
answer: Libertarian rights theory — Nozick's entitlement theory grounds property in just acquisition and transfer, so the proposal violates pre-political rights by treating legitimately earned holdings as instruments of pattern-fitting.
choices: Libertarian rights theory — Nozick's entitlement theory grounds property in just acquisition and transfer, so the proposal violates pre-political rights by treating legitimately earned holdings as instruments of pattern-fitting.

Rawlsian contractualism — the right tax structure is whatever parties behind a veil of ignorance would accept; the difference principle permits inequalities only when they benefit the worst-off, so pre-political claims misframe.

Welfare utilitarianism — the right tax structure is whichever schedule produces maximum aggregate welfare; the moral status of pre-tax holdings is at most an empirical fact about incentives, not a free-standing moral constraint.

Capability theory — the right tax structure is whichever lets each person reach the basic capability threshold; framing in terms of pre-political rights misses the fundamental issue, which is each person's functional flourishing.
context: Robert Nozick's Anarchy, State, and Utopia (1974) gives the entitlement theory of justice: just holdings depend on just acquisition and transfer, not on any preferred pattern of distribution. The 'taxation = forced labor' claim appears in chapter 7. Direct critique of Rawls's patterned principles is the book's spine.

question: An ethicist argues: 'There is a real moral difference between killing someone and letting them die — even when the outcome is identical, the doing/allowing distinction does moral work that no impartial calculation captures.' Critics deny the distinction has weight. Which framework supports the ethicist?
answer: Constraint-based deontology — the doing/allowing distinction marks a genuine moral difference, so the constraint against killing binds more stringently than any duty to rescue, even when outcomes look identical from outside.
choices: Constraint-based deontology — the doing/allowing distinction marks a genuine moral difference, so the constraint against killing binds more stringently than any duty to rescue, even when outcomes look identical from outside.

Act consequentialism — outcomes are what matter morally, so the doing/allowing distinction collapses; if killing and letting die produce identical outcomes, the two are on this view morally equivalent without remainder.

Virtue ethics — the relevant moral question is what character the practice of distinguishing killing from letting die cultivates in the agent; the deontological constraint is at most a proxy for stable virtuous dispositions.

Care ethics — what matters is the structure of relationships in which the act occurs, not an abstract doing/allowing line; the framework rejects the ethicist's principle in favor of attention to relational particulars of the case.
context: Philippa Foot's 'The Problem of Abortion and the Doctrine of the Double Effect' (1967) introduced trolley cases to test the doing/allowing distinction. Bennett (The Act Itself, 1995) attacks it. Frances Kamm (Morality, Mortality, 1993-96) defends a sophisticated version with constraints having genuine moral weight.

question: A panel debates whether a judge should let an innocent person be convicted to prevent a riot that would kill many. One judge says: 'No defensible legal system permits this; the rule against false conviction is what makes the system itself trustworthy.' Which framework defends her position?
answer: Rule consequentialism — the rule against convicting the innocent is justified by its welfare effects when applied across all such cases, even when this case favors breaking it; rule-following itself produces the welfare gain.
choices: Rule consequentialism — the rule against convicting the innocent is justified by its welfare effects when applied across all such cases, even when this case favors breaking it; rule-following itself produces the welfare gain.

Act consequentialism — the calculation in this case favors the conviction since the riot deaths outweigh the one wrongful conviction's harm; rule appeals here just substitute for the local welfare calculation the view demands.

Constraint-based deontology — false conviction is forbidden whatever its welfare effects, since the violation of the innocent person's status as an end-in-itself cannot be redeemed by any aggregate welfare gain in the case.

Virtue ethics — the question is what dispositions the practice cultivates in judges over time; the rule appeal is at most a proxy for the just-judge character the framework treats as the real ground of legal practice.
context: The case is McCloskey's (1957), designed against utilitarianism. Brad Hooker (Ideal Code, Real World, 2000) develops rule consequentialism precisely to handle such cases without collapsing into act consequentialism's counterintuitive verdicts. The act/rule divide remains contested within the family.

question: A philosopher argues that virtues cannot be specified apart from particular practices and traditions: 'There is no abstract honesty independent of the practice of inquiry in which honesty figures; the virtues are practice-internal goods.' Which framework grounds her position?
answer: MacIntyrean virtue ethics — virtues are constituted by their roles in practices and traditions, so honesty can be specified only through the practice of inquiry in which it figures, not as an abstract trait standing apart.
choices: MacIntyrean virtue ethics — virtues are constituted by their roles in practices and traditions, so honesty can be specified only through the practice of inquiry in which it figures, not as an abstract trait standing apart.

Kantian deontology — virtues are dispositions to act on universal maxims that hold for all rational agents; the practice-internal framing confuses the social embeddedness of moral education with the universal ground of duty.

Aristotelian virtue ethics — virtues are stable dispositions oriented toward eudaimonia (flourishing); MacIntyre adds practice-internality as a sociological claim, but the Aristotelian core does not require it as constitutive.

Rule consequentialism — virtues are useful dispositions for following welfare-promoting rules; their content is fixed by the rules' effects on aggregate welfare, not by the practices in which the dispositions are exercised.
context: Alasdair MacIntyre's After Virtue (1981) gives the practice-internal account: virtues are constituted by the roles they play in coherent practices oriented to internal goods. The view distinguishes itself from Aristotelian virtue ethics by its sociological claims about tradition and narrative unity of a life.

question: An ethicist on a development panel argues: 'The right measure of how well a society treats people is neither aggregate welfare nor primary goods but what each person can actually do and be — the capabilities they have to function across central domains of human life.' Which framework is she defending?
answer: Capability approach — what matters morally is each person's capability set across central human functionings, so the panel's measure tracks what people can actually do and be rather than aggregate welfare or resource shares.
choices: Capability approach — what matters morally is each person's capability set across central human functionings, so the panel's measure tracks what people can actually do and be rather than aggregate welfare or resource shares.

Welfare utilitarianism — what matters morally is aggregate well-being across the population; the capability framing is at most a useful proxy for welfare and adds no morally fundamental content beyond what aggregation captures.

Rawlsian contractualism — what matters is the distribution of primary goods, chosen by contractors behind a veil of ignorance; the capability framework rephrases the issue, but the contractual test does the underlying work.

Libertarian rights theory — what matters morally is whether holdings result from just acquisition and transfer; the capability framework imposes a theory of the good life that the rights view places outside the state's scope.
context: Amartya Sen (Commodities and Capabilities, 1985) and Martha Nussbaum (Women and Human Development, 2000) developed the capability approach as an alternative to welfarism and Rawlsian primary goods. Nussbaum's version specifies ten central capabilities; Sen leaves the list more open. UN Human Development Index draws on it.

question: A philosopher argues that modern ethics has inherited a vocabulary — 'moral obligation,' 'moral ought' — that originally belonged to a divine-command framework now abandoned, and the words have lost their content. 'We should drop them and return to talk of virtues and the human good.' Which framework grounds her view?
answer: Anscombean virtue ethics — the modern 'moral ought' vocabulary is a vestige of an abandoned divine-command framework, and the prescription is to return moral discourse to talk of virtues and the human good directly.
choices: Anscombean virtue ethics — the modern 'moral ought' vocabulary is a vestige of an abandoned divine-command framework, and the prescription is to return moral discourse to talk of virtues and the human good directly.

Kantian deontology — the 'moral ought' has a non-religious foundation in pure practical reason; the diagnosis misreads its source, since the categorical imperative grounds moral obligation in rational agency, not divine command.

Act consequentialism — the 'moral ought' just tracks welfare-maximization; the vocabulary's history is irrelevant to its current use, and the prescription discards a perfectly functional contemporary moral framework.

Contractualism — the 'moral ought' has its foundation in what principles parties could justify to one another; the diagnosis trades on a contested historical claim, but the contemporary framework supplies its own grounding.
context: G.E.M. Anscombe's 'Modern Moral Philosophy' (1958) made the case that 'moral ought' is a survival from divine-command theory and should be retired in favor of virtue discourse. The essay launched the Anglophone virtue-ethics revival continued by Foot, MacIntyre, Hursthouse, and others over the next half-century.

question: An applied ethicist argues: 'If you would wade into a shallow pond to save a drowning child at small cost to your shoes, distance and nationality cannot make a moral difference; the same reasoning obligates comparable rescue at any distance.' Which framework grounds the ethicist's reasoning?
answer: Impartialist utilitarianism — moral weight does not vary by spatial or national distance, so the reasoning extends pond-rescue obligations to comparable rescue at any distance, since welfare counts equally wherever parties are.
choices: Impartialist utilitarianism — moral weight does not vary by spatial or national distance, so the reasoning extends pond-rescue obligations to comparable rescue at any distance, since welfare counts equally wherever parties are.

Care ethics — moral obligations are generated by particular relationships of dependency and proximity, so the pond rescue is not a template for distant rescue; distance and absence of relationship do morally relevant work.

Agent-relative deontology — agents have permissions to favor their own projects and near others, so the pond argument's denial of distance-sensitivity overstates what impartial reasoning actually demands of an agent.

Threshold deontology — there is a constraint against demanding heroic sacrifice, holding until stakes are catastrophic; the reasoning here crosses no such threshold and so generates no obligation beyond the local rescue.
context: Peter Singer's 'Famine, Affluence, and Morality' (1972) gives the canonical pond argument: distance and national affiliation are not morally relevant, so substantial obligations of global aid follow. The argument has been refined for fifty years; central critics include Murphy, Cullity, and a long line of agent-relative theorists.

question: A philosopher argues that the human good is not pleasure, not preference satisfaction, and not the favored distribution of resources, but a kind of activity of soul over a whole life — flourishing in accordance with virtue. Which framework most directly grounds her position?
answer: Aristotelian virtue ethics — eudaimonia (flourishing as activity of soul in accordance with virtue over a life) is the human good, so the philosopher rules out pleasure, preference satisfaction, and resource shares as substitutes.
choices: Aristotelian virtue ethics — eudaimonia (flourishing as activity of soul in accordance with virtue over a life) is the human good, so the philosopher rules out pleasure, preference satisfaction, and resource shares as substitutes.

Hedonistic utilitarianism — the human good just is pleasure or the absence of suffering, so the philosopher discards the fundamental moral category in favor of an activity-of-soul notion adding no welfare-relevant content.

Preference utilitarianism — the human good is satisfaction of informed preferences, so the philosopher's view misreads the fundamental category; whatever activity of soul matters here is just one route to preference satisfaction.

Rawlsian contractualism — the human good is bracketed in favor of principles parties would choose under the veil; the philosopher's substantive theory of flourishing is the wrong kind of question for political ethics to settle.
context: Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics gives the canonical eudaimonist account: the human good is activity of the rational soul in accordance with virtue, over a complete life. Modern revivers (Hursthouse, On Virtue Ethics 1999; Annas, Intelligent Virtue 2011) defend versions of the framework against rival theories.

question: A philosopher argues that parents are morally obligated to favor their own children over strangers — that this preference is not a bias for impartial reason to correct but a duty grounded in what parents ARE. The view stands against William Godwin's claim that, between saving Fenelon and saving a relative, impartial reason commands saving Fenelon. Which view is being defended?
answer: Agent-relative partiality — constitutive attachments (parenthood, friendship, ground projects) generate duties of preference impartial reasoning cannot dissolve; they aren't biases but the soil moral agency grows from.
choices: Agent-relative partiality — constitutive attachments (parenthood, friendship, ground projects) generate duties of preference impartial reasoning cannot dissolve; they aren't biases but the soil moral agency grows from.
Godwinian impartialism — moral reasoning weighs all rational beings symmetrically; the parent's preference for their own child is the sentiment philosophy should expose as bias, not ratify as duty.

Care ethics as relational — duties arise from the ongoing relationships parents have with their children; were the relation absent, the duty would be absent, so obligation rests on the tie, not on parenthood as such.

Strict consequentialism — parental partiality is justified only where it tracks welfare; preferring one's own children is a general policy that produces good outcomes, with no agent-relative standing.
context: John Cottingham (Partiality and the Virtues, 1998) and Bernard Williams (Moral Luck, 1981) defend agent-relative duties against the Godwinian impartialism running from Political Justice (1793) through Singer's Famine, Affluence, and Morality (1972). Constitutive attachments aren't biases to dissolve — they're constituent of being a moral agent.

question: A Kantian objects to care ethics: 'Care's central move — respond to the particular face before you — cannot universalize. It describes what some people sometimes do but cannot ground obligation AS SUCH, since obligation requires a law that binds every rational agent in like cases.' Which view is the Kantian defending?
answer: Universalizability as requirement of duty — genuine moral obligation must be statable as a law binding every rational agent in like cases; particularist 'respond to this face' moves register moral facts but cannot ground duty.
choices: Universalizability as requirement of duty — genuine moral obligation must be statable as a law binding every rational agent in like cases; particularist 'respond to this face' moves register moral facts but cannot ground duty.

Rule-consequentialism — the right theory is the one whose general adoption maximizes welfare; the objection is really that care fails a welfare test, not a logical test of universalizability as a structural requirement.

Strict particularism — moral reasons are exhausted by their particular instances; the objection misunderstands that universalizability is itself defective, and care rightly rejects the demand for universal laws in like cases.

Communitarianism — moral reasoning is grounded in shared tradition rather than formal universal laws; the Kantian mistakes the structure of practical reason and ignores that obligations are always thick and community-embedded.
context: Kant (Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals, 1785) grounded duty in the categorical imperative — act only on maxims you could will as universal law. The Kantian critique of care ethics is structural: caring response can be morally good without grounding obligation, because obligation requires the universality particularism refuses.

question: Alasdair MacIntyre argues care ethics' grounding in concrete relationships makes it incapable of generating moral claims that cross communities. What looks like universality in care talk, he says, is borrowed from traditions — chiefly Aristotelian and Christian — that care theorists themselves have rejected. Which view is MacIntyre defending?
answer: Tradition-grounded virtue ethics — moral universality is real but issues from particular traditions of practice (Aristotelian, Thomistic) rather than from relational intuitions; care borrows it while sawing off the branch.
choices: Tradition-grounded virtue ethics — moral universality is real but issues from particular traditions of practice (Aristotelian, Thomistic) rather than from relational intuitions; care borrows it while sawing off the branch.

Liberal universalism — claims that cross communities rest on abstract rights of rational persons; MacIntyre misidentifies the source and lands on his own tradition-bound parochialism that cannot reach cross-community claims.

Nietzschean genealogy — all talk of universal morality is an expression of particular wills to power; MacIntyre's complaint reaches a universality he cannot supply, and the right response is to abandon universality altogether.

Postmodern critique — moral universality is a discredited Enlightenment ambition; care is right to ground morality in concrete relations, and the call for tradition substitutes one parochialism for another without delivering it.
context: Alasdair MacIntyre (After Virtue, 1981; Whose Justice? Which Rationality?, 1988) argues moral universality is real but issues from tradition-grounded practices, not from abstract principles or relational intuitions. Care ethics' moral force depends on background traditions (largely Christian-Aristotelian) its founders disavow.

question: Joan Tronto argues care must be politicized — institutionalized through the welfare state — to generalize beyond the personal. A Hayekian responds: 'Politicizing care institutionalizes it; institutional care reliably produces dependency without addressing root causes, because the knowledge that made care responsive cannot be assembled at scale.' Which view is the Hayekian defending?
answer: Hayekian institutional critique — care's responsiveness depends on local knowledge no planner can assemble; scaling care through the state degrades it and produces dependency as predictable failure; the objection is structural.
choices: Hayekian institutional critique — care's responsiveness depends on local knowledge no planner can assemble; scaling care through the state degrades it and produces dependency as predictable failure; the objection is structural.

Communitarian conservatism — politicizing care crowds out family and church, weakening intermediate institutions that traditionally carried care; the objection is about cultural displacement, not information problems.
Libertarian rights — the state has no authority to compel redistributive care whatever the effects, so the debate is settled on rights before any empirical claim about dependency or knowledge enters.

Post hoc — treating one thing as the cause of another simply because it happened to come earlier in time than it.
Hasty generalization — drawing a sweeping rule from a small handful of examples that are too few to ground the larger claim.
Slippery slope — claiming one small step must somehow trigger a chain of much worse outcomes without showing each link.
context: False cause errors treat two things that happen together as cause-and-effect. Rainy days keep customers indoors regardless of price; the prices and the slow sales just coincided.

question: Around the watchfire at the old keep, Jasper insists the cellar is haunted. Asked for any evidence, he shrugs: 'Nobody in this fortress has ever proven that it ISN'T, so it must be real.' Jasper's reasoning commits which logical fallacy?
answer: Appeal to ignorance — Jasper treats the lack of any disproof about the basement as positive proof it actually is haunted.
choices: Appeal to ignorance — Jasper treats the lack of any disproof about the basement as positive proof it actually is haunted.
Burden of proof — demanding that critics disprove a claim instead of giving evidence that supports the claim in the first place.
Circular reasoning — smuggling the conclusion into the premise so the argument quietly loops back on itself without support.
Hasty generalization — drawing a sweeping rule from a small handful of examples that are too few to ground the larger claim.
context: Appeal to ignorance moves from 'no one has shown X is false' to 'X is therefore true.' The mistake is treating absence of evidence as if it were positive evidence for the claim.

question: Dad promised Kai a new bike if he raised his math grade to a B. Kai pulled it up to a solid B. Dad now says: 'Wait — I actually meant a B PLUS, and also in science, before any bike happens.' Dad's response commits which logical fallacy?
answer: Moving the goalposts — Dad raises the bike standard above the math-B Kai already met, after the original test was passed.
choices: Moving the goalposts — Dad raises the bike standard above the math-B Kai already met, after the original test was passed.
Straw man — twisting an opponent's claim into a wilder version so the easier-to-mock version can be knocked down.
Special pleading — exempting yourself from a rule you apply to others without giving any real reason for the exception.
Red herring — changing the subject to dodge the actual question being asked, dragging in something unrelated to it.
context: Moving the goalposts changes the success criterion after a test has been passed, redefining 'success' so the original outcome no longer counts. The promise becomes permanently unwinnable.

question: Sara insists: 'Real fans of her band love every single album, no exceptions.' Pointed to her brother, a fan since middle school who hates the latest record, she says: 'Then he's not actually a real fan.' Sara's reply commits which logical fallacy?
answer: No true Scotsman — Sara redefines 'real fan' to exclude her brother just because his middle-school fandom doesn't fit her claim.
choices: No true Scotsman — Sara redefines 'real fan' to exclude her brother just because his middle-school fandom doesn't fit her claim.
Circular reasoning — smuggling the conclusion into the premise so the argument quietly loops back on itself without support.
Special pleading — exempting yourself from a rule you apply to others without giving any real reason for the exception.
Equivocation — shifting the meaning of a key word mid-argument so the conclusion only seems to follow from premises.
context: Antony Flew named this fallacy (Thinking About Thinking, 1975). The qualifier is added retroactively to preserve a sweeping claim against any counterexample that turns up against it.

question: Asked how she's doing in social studies, Naomi tells her parents: 'I got A's on three quizzes this month — I'm crushing it!' She leaves out the four C's and one F. Naomi's defense commits which logical fallacy?
answer: Cherry picking — Naomi reports only the three A's while leaving out the C's and the F that would change her parents' picture.
choices: Cherry picking — Naomi reports only the three A's while leaving out the C's and the F that would change her parents' picture.
Hasty generalization — drawing a sweeping rule from a small handful of examples that are too few to ground the larger claim.
Straw man — twisting an opponent's claim into a wilder version so the easier-to-mock version can be knocked down.
Burden of proof — demanding that critics disprove a claim instead of giving evidence that supports the claim in the first place.
context: Cherry picking covers selection bias in evidence — quietly choosing only the supporting cases while leaving counterexamples out. The story stays technically true but seriously misleading.

question: In a class debate over phones at lunch, Logan argues: 'Banning phones at lunch is exactly like banning students from talking — both restrict communication.' Logan's argument commits which logical fallacy?
answer: False equivalence — Logan treats a lunch phone-ban and a talking-ban as comparable when the two restrict very different things.
choices: False equivalence — Logan treats a lunch phone-ban and a talking-ban as comparable when the two restrict very different things.
Straw man — twisting an opponent's claim into a wilder version so the easier-to-mock version can be knocked down.
Slippery slope — claiming one small step must somehow trigger a chain of much worse outcomes without showing each link.
Appeal to emotion — using strong feelings (fear, pity, anger) to push a conclusion that the actual evidence does not support.
context: False equivalence treats two unequal cases as if they were the same kind of thing. A phone policy and a speech ban differ in scope, alternatives, and stakes — comparing them flattens all that.

question: Trying to push back her bedtime, Riya tells her mom in a wobbly voice: 'If you really loved me you'd let me stay up — you're going to make me cry myself to sleep.' Riya's argument commits which logical fallacy?
answer: Appeal to emotion — Riya leans on guilt and predicted tears about bedtime instead of giving reasons it should change.
choices: Appeal to emotion — Riya leans on guilt and predicted tears about bedtime instead of giving reasons it should change.
False dilemma — pretending only two choices exist when several other real options are present in the actual situation.
Loaded question — asking a question that hides an unproven assumption so any direct answer concedes what wasn't argued.
Special pleading — exempting yourself from a rule you apply to others without giving any real reason for the exception.
context: Appeal to emotion (argumentum ad passiones) uses strong feelings — fear, pity, anger — to push a conclusion the evidence doesn't support. Spotting it isn't anti-feeling; it's anti-substitution.

question: Ana corners her brother Ben at the breakfast table and asks, very calmly: 'So when did you stop being honest with me about the cookies missing from the jar?' Ana's question commits which logical fallacy?
answer: Loaded question — Ana's cookie-jar question hides the unproven assumption that Ben was already dishonest with her, baking it in.
choices: Loaded question — Ana's cookie-jar question hides the unproven assumption that Ben was already dishonest with her, baking it in.
Burden of proof — demanding that critics disprove a claim instead of giving evidence that supports the claim in the first place.
Straw man — twisting an opponent's claim into a wilder version so the easier-to-mock version can be knocked down.
Appeal to ignorance — treating the absence of any disproof as if it were positive proof that the claim being made is true.
context: Loaded questions hide an unproven assumption inside a question, so that any direct answer concedes the assumption. The classic example: 'Have you stopped lying to your friends?'

question: Maddie argues in debate club: 'Everyone has the right to free speech, so it's WRONG that the cafe charges money for coffee — coffee should be free!' She slides between two senses of 'free.' Maddie's argument commits which logical fallacy?
answer: Equivocation — Maddie shifts 'free' from speech-freedom to cost-free coffee mid-argument so her conclusion only seems to follow.
choices: Equivocation — Maddie shifts 'free' from speech-freedom to cost-free coffee mid-argument so her conclusion only seems to follow.
Straw man — twisting an opponent's claim into a wilder version so the easier-to-mock version can be knocked down.
False equivalence — treating two unequal claims or cases as if they were comparable, smuggling a contested comparison in.
Burden of proof — demanding that critics disprove a claim instead of giving evidence that supports the claim in the first place.
context: Equivocation slides between two meanings of a single word mid-argument. The form looks valid but the conclusion rides on a meaning swap. Spot it by asking: same word, same sense, throughout?

question: By sealed letter, Wesley drops a wild claim to his fellow squires: 'There's a secret tunnel under the citadel.' When they ask for any evidence at all, he fires back: 'Prove there ISN'T — that's on you, not me.' Wesley's reply commits which logical fallacy?
answer: Burden of proof — Wesley pushes the work of proving the citadel tunnel onto skeptics instead of supporting his own claim.
choices: Burden of proof — Wesley pushes the work of proving the citadel tunnel onto skeptics instead of supporting his own claim.
Appeal to ignorance — treating the absence of any disproof as if it were positive proof that the claim being made is true.
Tu quoque — deflecting criticism back at the critic by accusing them of the same fault they originally pointed out.
Red herring — changing the subject to dodge the actual question being asked, dragging in something unrelated to it.
context: The person making a claim carries the burden of proof; skeptics aren't obligated to disprove every wild assertion. Otherwise any unsupported claim wins by default just by being announced.

question: The family rule is no screens an hour before bed. Caught scrolling, Lila explains: 'My screens are different because I'm using them for something important right now, so the rule shouldn't count.' Lila's argument commits which logical fallacy?
answer: Special pleading — Lila exempts herself from the family screen rule without giving any real reason her case actually differs.
choices: Special pleading — Lila exempts herself from the family screen rule without giving any real reason her case actually differs.
Moving the goalposts — changing what counts as success once the original standard has already been met by the other person.
Circular reasoning — smuggling the conclusion into the premise so the argument quietly loops back on itself without support.
Tu quoque — deflecting criticism back at the critic by accusing them of the same fault they originally pointed out.
context: Special pleading invents a self-serving exception to a rule one was happy applying to others. The test is whether the carve-out tracks a real difference or just protects the pleader's case.

question: Voting on the harvest-fair sweets, Eli pushes for honey-only sweeteners. His argument: 'Honey is natural, and refined sugar is processed, so honey treats are obviously healthier for fair-goers.' Eli's argument commits which logical fallacy?
answer: Appeal to nature — Eli takes honey's natural label as proof his bake-sale sweeteners are healthier than processed sugar.
choices: Appeal to nature — Eli takes honey's natural label as proof his bake-sale sweeteners are healthier than processed sugar.
Hasty generalization — drawing a sweeping rule from a small handful of examples that are too few to ground the larger claim.
False equivalence — treating two unequal claims or cases as if they were comparable, smuggling a contested comparison in.
Bandwagon — treating popularity or how many people agree as if it were evidence that the claim must actually be true.
context: 'Natural' isn't a synonym for 'good': hemlock is natural, vaccines aren't. The appeal to nature substitutes a label for an actual analysis of whether the thing helps or harms.

question: Caught skipping his chores, Felix glares at his mom and snaps: 'Dad skipped HIS chores all weekend and didn't get yelled at — that means I shouldn't have to do mine either.' Felix's argument commits which logical fallacy?
answer: Two wrongs make a right — Felix defends his own skipped chores by pointing at Dad's weekend chore-skipping as if that excused his.
choices: Two wrongs make a right — Felix defends his own skipped chores by pointing at Dad's weekend chore-skipping as if that excused his.
Tu quoque — deflecting criticism back at the critic by accusing them of the same fault they originally pointed out.
Red herring — changing the subject to dodge the actual question being asked, dragging in something unrelated to it.
Ad hominem — attacking the person making the argument instead of engaging the actual content of the argument itself.
context: Two wrongs make a right is close kin to tu quoque but distinct: tu quoque deflects to dodge criticism; two wrongs claims one wrong actually justifies another. Both leave the original wrong intact.

question: Trying one bite from a new tavern in the realm, Theo declares to his household by messenger: 'This whole tavern is awful — NONE of their food is worth eating, ever, by anyone.' Theo's claim commits which logical fallacy?
answer: Hasty generalization — Theo jumps from a single bite to a sweeping verdict about every dish on the whole tavern's spread.
choices: Hasty generalization — Theo jumps from a single bite to a sweeping verdict about every dish on the whole tavern's spread.
False dilemma — pretending only two choices exist when several other real options are present in the actual situation.
Bandwagon — treating popularity or how many people agree as if it were evidence that the claim must actually be true.
Appeal to emotion — using strong feelings (fear, pity, anger) to push a conclusion that the actual evidence does not support.
context: Hasty generalizations come from samples too small to support the claim. One dish can't tell you about an entire menu; one bad day can't tell you about a friend or a year.

question: On a school forum, Priya posts careful reasons the lunch menu is unbalanced. Another student's reply is just: 'Lol nobody asked, weirdo — go bother someone else.' The reply commits which logical fallacy?
answer: Ad hominem — the forum reply insults Priya personally instead of engaging the lunch-menu reasons she actually posted.
choices: Ad hominem — the forum reply insults Priya personally instead of engaging the lunch-menu reasons she actually posted.
Genetic fallacy — judging an argument by where it came from or who said it rather than by what the argument actually says.
Red herring — changing the subject to dodge the actual question being asked, dragging in something unrelated to it.
Straw man — twisting an opponent's claim into a wilder version so the easier-to-mock version can be knocked down.
context: Online comment threads make ad hominem easy because there's no face-to-face cost. Spotting it is the first step in not being talked out of a real position by a confident-sounding insult.

question: In a council debate, Mara proposes trimming the noon-rest by five minutes to leave longer for the midday meal. Her opponent responds: 'So you want to eliminate noon-rest entirely and ruin our days?' The opponent's reply commits which logical fallacy?
answer: Straw man — the opponent reshapes Mara's five-minute recess trim into an eliminate-recess-entirely demand she didn't make.
choices: Straw man — the opponent reshapes Mara's five-minute recess trim into an eliminate-recess-entirely demand she didn't make.
False dilemma — pretending only two choices exist when several other real options are present in the actual situation.
Appeal to emotion — using strong feelings (fear, pity, anger) to push a conclusion that the actual evidence does not support.
Slippery slope — claiming one small step must somehow trigger a chain of much worse outcomes without showing each link.
context: Straw man fallacies are tempting because the distorted version really is easier to argue against. The honest move is to engage the actual proposal — five minutes — not a worse cousin.

question: Caleb's mom won't let him use the family laptop an extra fifteen minutes past curfew. She insists: 'If I add fifteen tonight, in three months you'll be on the laptop until 3 AM every single night.' Mom's argument commits which logical fallacy?
answer: Slippery slope — Mom treats Caleb's fifteen extra laptop minutes as if it must chain into nightly 3 AM laptop sessions.
choices: Slippery slope — Mom treats Caleb's fifteen extra laptop minutes as if it must chain into nightly 3 AM laptop sessions.
False dilemma — pretending only two choices exist when several other real options are present in the actual situation.
Appeal to authority — treating a famous or impressive name's say-so as proof that whatever they backed must therefore be true.
Hasty generalization — drawing a sweeping rule from a small handful of examples that are too few to ground the larger claim.
context: Slippery slopes can be real (some chains of consequence do play out), but the argument only works if each link is actually shown, not just asserted. Otherwise it's just a scare story.

question: In a class debate on honesty, Dana argues students shouldn't lie on assignments. Her opponent fires back: 'You told a fib last week about your missing homework, so you can't really argue this.' The opponent's reply commits which logical fallacy?
answer: Tu quoque — the opponent deflects Dana's honesty argument by pointing at her own missing-homework fib instead of answering.
choices: Tu quoque — the opponent deflects Dana's honesty argument by pointing at her own missing-homework fib instead of answering.
Ad hominem — attacking the person making the argument instead of engaging the actual content of the argument itself.
Genetic fallacy — judging an argument by where it came from or who said it rather than by what the argument actually says.
Red herring — changing the subject to dodge the actual question being asked, dragging in something unrelated to it.
context: Tu quoque (Latin: 'you also') is the 'you do it too' defense. Even if Dana herself once fudged about homework, that doesn't change whether her honesty argument is right or wrong.

question: Asked about a thoughtful idea for the company's market fund, Jordan sneers in his sealed reply: 'That idea came from the squire who never even joined our company last year, so we should just ignore it.' Jordan's response commits which logical fallacy?
answer: Genetic fallacy — Jordan rejects the market-fund idea by its source (a squire who skipped last year) instead of its merits.
choices: Genetic fallacy — Jordan rejects the market-fund idea by its source (a squire who skipped last year) instead of its merits.
Ad hominem — attacking the person making the argument instead of engaging the actual content of the argument itself.
Bandwagon — treating popularity or how many people agree as if it were evidence that the claim must actually be true.
Hasty generalization — drawing a sweeping rule from a small handful of examples that are too few to ground the larger claim.
context: Genetic fallacy and ad hominem overlap. Genetic fallacy is judging the CLAIM by its source; ad hominem attacks the source as a way to win the argument. Here Jordan judges the idea by its origin.

question: Asked why she believes a wild rumor about another teacher, Reese explains earnestly: 'My older cousin told me, and she's already in high school — so she would just know things like this.' Reese's argument commits which logical fallacy?
answer: Appeal to authority — Reese takes her older cousin's high-school say-so as proof of a wild rumor about that teacher.
choices: Appeal to authority — Reese takes her older cousin's high-school say-so as proof of a wild rumor about that teacher.
Genetic fallacy — judging an argument by where it came from or who said it rather than by what the argument actually says.
Bandwagon — treating popularity or how many people agree as if it were evidence that the claim must actually be true.
Hasty generalization — drawing a sweeping rule from a small handful of examples that are too few to ground the larger claim.
context: Being older or higher up in school isn't the same as having evidence. An appeal to authority only carries real weight when the cited authority actually knows the relevant facts.

question: A YouTuber with 5 million followers promises her new exercise routine will get viewers 'shredded in 30 days.' Asked for evidence the routine actually works, she replies: 'Look at my channel — millions of views, thousands of testimonials.' Her defense commits which logical fallacy?
answer: Appeal to popularity — the YouTuber treats viewership and testimonials as evidence her exercise routine itself actually produces the shredded results promised.
choices: Appeal to popularity — the YouTuber treats viewership and testimonials as evidence her exercise routine itself actually produces the shredded results promised.
Genetic fallacy — judging an argument by where it came from or who said it rather than by what the actual content of the argument says about the issue.
Straw man — distorting an opponent's argument into a weaker or wilder version so the easier-to-attack distortion can be knocked down in its place.
Begging the question — assuming the very point in dispute as a premise, so the conclusion is presupposed instead of being independently established.
context: Appeal to popularity (argumentum ad populum) is common online, where engagement metrics get treated as evidence of correctness. Five million followers measures interest or marketing — not whether the underlying claim about results is actually true.

question: A peer-reviewer flags a submitted study: the authors recruited participants from their own fan newsletter, and 'success' meant any weight lost during 30 days. The reviewer writes that the result was guaranteed before data collection began. What fallacy does the study's design commit?
answer: Cherry picking — the sample (self-selected fans) and the metric (any loss at all) were chosen in ways that practically guaranteed a confirming result.
choices: Cherry picking — the sample (self-selected fans) and the metric (any loss at all) were chosen in ways that practically guaranteed a confirming result.
Appeal to authority — treating a famous name's endorsement as proof the claim is true, even when the named source lacks the relevant subject expertise.
False equivalence — treating two unequal cases as if they were comparable, smuggling a contested comparison into the framing without arguing for it directly.
Moving the goalposts — changing the success criterion after the original standard has been met, so the original outcome no longer counts as success at all.
context: Cherry picking covers both selection bias in sampling and outcome cherry-picking in metric definition. Peer review exists to catch these design choices BEFORE the study enters the literature, where its 87% number would otherwise be cited as solid evidence.

question: On a debate panel, a commentator insists: 'All serious economists agree the policy is harmful.' Challenged with named economists holding the opposite view, he replies: 'Well, no SERIOUS economist holds that view.' His move commits which logical fallacy?
answer: No true Scotsman — the commentator tightens 'serious' on the spot to exclude any economist whose existence would falsify his sweeping claim about agreement.
choices: No true Scotsman — the commentator tightens 'serious' on the spot to exclude any economist whose existence would falsify his sweeping claim about agreement.
