choices: No true Scotsman — the pundit retroactively narrows 'serious economist' to exclude the named PhDs who endorse the tariff, preserving his sweeping claim by stipulation rather than evidence.
Appeal to authority — leaning on the credentials or reputation of a source rather than engaging the substance of the dispute, as if institutional standing settled what the argument has to establish.
Cherry picking — selecting only the supporting cases, intervals, or metrics from a larger body of evidence while suppressing the contrary cases that would force a revision of the claim.
Genetic fallacy — dismissing or accepting an argument based on its origin, the motives of its source, or its funding, rather than evaluating the content of the argument on its own evidentiary terms.
context: Antony Flew named the No True Scotsman fallacy in Thinking About Thinking (1975): a sweeping claim survives a counterexample only because the category is redefined retroactively. The move looks like a clarification but functions as immunization against any disconfirming case.

question: A columnist writes that 'modern technology is destroying childhood' — citing teen depression data and demanding sweeping platform bans. Challenged, she retreats: 'I only meant smartphones have downsides for some kids.' Once unchallenged, she resumes the destruction-of-childhood framing. Diagnose the rhetorical maneuver.
answer: Motte-and-bailey — the columnist alternates between the modest defensible claim (smartphones have downsides for some kids) and the bold controversial claim (destruction of childhood) as she defends or asserts.
choices: Motte-and-bailey — the columnist alternates between the modest defensible claim (smartphones have downsides for some kids) and the bold controversial claim (destruction of childhood) as she defends or asserts.
Equivocation — shifting the meaning of a key term between premises so the argument's apparent validity rides on a hidden change of sense rather than on a stable inference.

Moving the goalposts — redefining the success criterion after a prediction has been met or disconfirmed, so the original test no longer counts and the position remains permanently unfalsifiable in practice.
Straw man — distorting an opponent's position into a wilder or weaker version that is easier to refute, then attacking the distortion as if the original argument had been engaged.
context: Nicholas Shackel coined the motte-and-bailey label (2005), drawing on medieval castle architecture: the bailey is the productive land you actually want, the motte the small fortified keep you retreat to under attack. The argumentative version trades on conflating the two claims as if they were one.

question: On a podcast, a commentator dismisses a peer-reviewed study contradicting his preferred policy: 'Replicate it ten times with pre-registration before I take it seriously.' Asked about a study supporting that same policy with methodology no stronger, he simply cites it as proven. Diagnose the rhetorical maneuver.
answer: Isolated demand for rigor — the commentator applies a near-impossible evidentiary standard to the contradicting study while granting the supporting study a free pass on the same methodology.
choices: Isolated demand for rigor — the commentator applies a near-impossible evidentiary standard to the contradicting study while granting the supporting study a free pass on the same methodology.
Cherry picking — selecting only the supporting cases, intervals, or metrics from a larger body of evidence while suppressing the contrary cases that would force a revision of the claim.

Moving the goalposts — redefining the success criterion after a prediction has been met or disconfirmed, so the original test no longer counts and the position remains permanently unfalsifiable in practice.
Genetic fallacy — dismissing or accepting an argument based on its origin, the motives of its source, or its funding, rather than evaluating the content of the argument on its own evidentiary terms.
context: Scott Alexander gave the move its current name in 'The Isolated Demand for Rigor' (2014). The tell is asymmetry: the same study design that disqualifies inconvenient findings is silently accepted when it produces convenient ones. Rigor is selectively, not consistently, applied.

question: In a televised debate, one candidate rattles off seventeen distinct dubious claims in ninety seconds — selective statistics, mangled quotes, dropped citations. The other candidate, with two minutes total, can only address three. Pundits afterward declare the second 'unable to rebut.' Diagnose the first candidate's rhetorical maneuver.
answer: Gish gallop — the candidate buries the opponent under more dubious claims than can be refuted in the available time, so partial rebuttal of seventeen claims is misread by pundits as concession.
choices: Gish gallop — the candidate buries the opponent under more dubious claims than can be refuted in the available time, so partial rebuttal of seventeen claims is misread by pundits as concession.
Red herring — dropping an irrelevant but provocative point into the discussion so attention shifts off the original question and the substantive issue quietly goes unanswered in the diversion.
Burden-shifting — demanding the critic disprove a claim rather than the claim's defender support it, inverting the usual rule that the party asserting a positive thesis carries the case for it.
Straw man — distorting an opponent's position into a wilder or weaker version that is easier to refute, then attacking the distortion as if the original argument had been engaged.
context: Named for creationist Duane Gish, who deployed the technique routinely in 1970s-80s evolution debates. Eugenie Scott of the National Center for Science Education popularized the label. The asymmetry between production and refutation cost is what makes the maneuver work rhetorically.

question: An op-ed argues: 'Freedom requires limits — without traffic laws, no one is free to drive safely. Therefore restrictions on speech online actually expand freedom, just as traffic laws do.' The argument turns on the word 'freedom' carrying very different senses in its two halves. Diagnose the rhetorical maneuver.
answer: Equivocation — the word 'freedom' shifts between coordination-against-collisions (traffic laws) and political-liberty-from-state-action (speech) so the inference rides on a hidden change of sense.
choices: Equivocation — the word 'freedom' shifts between coordination-against-collisions (traffic laws) and political-liberty-from-state-action (speech) so the inference rides on a hidden change of sense.
False equivalence — treating two cases as morally or evidentially comparable when their relevant features differ in magnitude, kind, or causal role in ways the framing quietly suppresses.

Composition fallacy — inferring that what is true of the parts must be true of the whole, treating individually-true facts as if they automatically aggregated into a true claim about the system they compose.
Straw man — distorting an opponent's position into a wilder or weaker version that is easier to refute, then attacking the distortion as if the original argument had been engaged.
context: Equivocation has been catalogued since Aristotle (Sophistical Refutations). The move can be deliberate or accidental; what matters is that the apparent validity of the argument depends on a stable meaning for the key term, and the term is not stable. Naming the senses is the fix.

question: A wire-service report on a vaccine controversy reads: 'Critics and supporters disagree, with supporters citing fifteen large randomized trials and critics citing a documentary featuring two personal anecdotes.' The piece presents both as substantive sides of an open scientific debate. Diagnose the journalistic framing's rhetorical maneuver.
answer: False equivalence — the report treats fifteen large trials and a documentary of two anecdotes as comparable evidence simply because both exist, suppressing the gulf in their actual evidentiary weight.
choices: False equivalence — the report treats fifteen large trials and a documentary of two anecdotes as comparable evidence simply because both exist, suppressing the gulf in their actual evidentiary weight.
Appeal to popularity — treating widespread agreement, viewership, or follower counts as evidence the underlying claim is true, as if popular acceptance measured anything beyond popular acceptance.

Anecdotal evidence — treating a vivid individual case as if it overrode the systematic statistical pattern, as if one striking story outweighed the aggregate evidence the story is being used to dismiss.
Appeal to authority — leaning on the credentials or reputation of a source rather than engaging the substance of the dispute, as if institutional standing settled what the argument has to establish.
context: False equivalence (or false balance) is a recognized failure mode of both-sides journalism, documented across coverage of evolution, climate, and vaccines. The cost is hidden: by presenting asymmetric evidence as symmetric, the framing conveys uncertainty that the actual evidence does not.

question: Asked about credible reports of mass detentions in his country, an official responds: 'And what about the prisons in YOUR country? You have police shootings every week. How dare you lecture us.' He does not address whether the detentions occurred or were lawful. Diagnose the official's rhetorical maneuver.
answer: Whataboutism — the official deflects the detention question by pivoting to alleged wrongs of the questioner's country, leaving the original charge about mass detentions entirely unanswered.
choices: Whataboutism — the official deflects the detention question by pivoting to alleged wrongs of the questioner's country, leaving the original charge about mass detentions entirely unanswered.
Tu quoque — deflecting a charge by alleging the critic is guilty of the same or worse conduct, as if symmetrical imperfection answered the substantive point at issue.
Red herring — dropping an irrelevant but provocative point into the discussion so attention shifts off the original question and the substantive issue quietly goes unanswered in the diversion.
Ad hominem — attacking the character, motives, or identity of the arguer in place of engaging the substance of the argument, as if a fault in the speaker disqualified what they actually said.
context: Whataboutism is the Cold-War-era English label for a Soviet press tactic: any criticism met with 'and you lynch Negroes.' It is closely related to tu quoque but distinguished by being deployed by states or institutions rather than between individuals, and by its purely deflective function.

question: A market guru promotes his service by highlighting twelve trades that produced spectacular gains over the past three years. He omits the ninety-three trades over that span that broke even or lost money. The chosen twelve become the 'predicted-it-all-along' track record. Diagnose the guru's rhetorical maneuver.
answer: Texas sharpshooter — the guru draws the analytic target (his 'track record') around the twelve winning trades after the fact, presenting a cluster carved out of the data as if it had been predicted.
choices: Texas sharpshooter — the guru draws the analytic target (his 'track record') around the twelve winning trades after the fact, presenting a cluster carved out of the data as if it had been predicted.
Cherry picking — selecting only the supporting cases, intervals, or metrics from a larger body of evidence while suppressing the contrary cases that would force a revision of the claim.
Hindsight bias — treating an outcome as having been predictable from prior evidence only after the outcome is known, smuggling later knowledge into a reconstruction of what could have been foreseen.

Anecdotal evidence — treating a vivid individual case as if it overrode the systematic statistical pattern, as if one striking story outweighed the aggregate evidence the story is being used to dismiss.
context: The Texas sharpshooter fallacy is named for a marksman who fires at a barn first and then paints the target around the bullet holes. It differs from straightforward cherry picking by emphasizing the post-hoc target-drawing, common in epidemiology, finance, and parapsychology claims.

question: After a market crash, an analyst writes: 'The warning signs were obvious all along — anyone paying attention should have seen it coming.' He cites indicators that, before the crash, his own newsletter had dismissed as noise, and that pointed in conflicting directions at the time. Diagnose the analyst's rhetorical maneuver.
answer: Hindsight bias — the analyst reconstructs the pre-crash signals as 'obvious all along,' smuggling knowledge of the outcome into a tidy story about indicators he himself read differently at the time.
choices: Hindsight bias — the analyst reconstructs the pre-crash signals as 'obvious all along,' smuggling knowledge of the outcome into a tidy story about indicators he himself read differently at the time.
Texas sharpshooter — drawing the analytic target around the clusters in already-collected data so a pattern that was carved out after the fact is presented as if it had been predicted in advance.
Cherry picking — selecting only the supporting cases, intervals, or metrics from a larger body of evidence while suppressing the contrary cases that would force a revision of the claim.
Post hoc — treating sequence as proof of causation: because B followed A, A must have caused B, with no account of confounders, base rates, or whether the link is mechanistic at all.
context: Baruch Fischhoff documented the hindsight bias experimentally in the 1970s, showing subjects consistently overestimate what they would have predicted before knowing the outcome. The bias is stable, robust, and especially common in financial and political post-mortems.

question: A self-help guru defends his unfulfilled prediction that his readers would 'all be millionaires by thirty': 'First, most of you didn't follow the program. Second, the program never promised that. Third, the ones who did follow it actually are millionaires — just not yet in cash terms.' Diagnose the rhetorical maneuver in this stacked defense.
answer: Kettle logic — the guru's three excuses (readers didn't follow, the program never promised, those who followed succeeded) undercut each other; the second contradicts the third, the first contradicts the second.
choices: Kettle logic — the guru's three excuses (readers didn't follow, the program never promised, those who followed succeeded) undercut each other; the second contradicts the third, the first contradicts the second.

Moving the goalposts — redefining the success criterion after a prediction has been met or disconfirmed, so the original test no longer counts and the position remains permanently unfalsifiable in practice.
Equivocation — shifting the meaning of a key term between premises so the argument's apparent validity rides on a hidden change of sense rather than on a stable inference.
Motte-and-bailey — switching between a defensible modest claim (the motte) and a controversial bold claim (the bailey) depending on whether one is asserting or defending the position.
context: Freud illustrated kettle logic with a man accused of returning a borrowed kettle damaged: 'I never borrowed it; it was already broken when I borrowed it; it was undamaged when I returned it.' Each defense if true refutes the others. Stacking them reveals motivated rather than truth-tracking reasoning.

question: A nutrition-influencer press release: 'Our study shows participants lost an average of fifteen pounds.' Buried details: participants were self-selected from the influencer's own paid program, had to complete all six months to count, and ninety-three percent of enrollees dropped out. Diagnose the rhetorical maneuver embedded in the press release.
answer: Cherry picking — the press release reports only the seven percent of paid program participants who completed all six months, treating that survivorship-selected slice as if it represented the program's typical effect.
choices: Cherry picking — the press release reports only the seven percent of paid program participants who completed all six months, treating that survivorship-selected slice as if it represented the program's typical effect.
Hasty generalization — drawing a sweeping rule from a sample too small, too unrepresentative, or too self-selected to support the size of the claim being made about the general population.
Texas sharpshooter — drawing the analytic target around the clusters in already-collected data so a pattern that was carved out after the fact is presented as if it had been predicted in advance.

context: Cherry picking is a class of selection bias formally studied in clinical trial methodology and epidemiology; survivorship bias is its commonest form in commercial program evaluation. The fix is intention-to-treat analysis (counting everyone who started, not only those who finished).

question: Pressed on whether her wellness regimen actually works, an influencer with eleven million followers replies: 'If it didn't work, would I have eleven million followers? Would brands pay me what they pay me? The audience itself proves the regimen delivers.' Diagnose the influencer's rhetorical maneuver.
answer: Appeal to popularity — the influencer treats eleven million followers and brand-deal volume as evidence that her wellness regimen produces results, conflating audience size with substantive efficacy.
choices: Appeal to popularity — the influencer treats eleven million followers and brand-deal volume as evidence that her wellness regimen produces results, conflating audience size with substantive efficacy.
Appeal to authority — leaning on the credentials or reputation of a source rather than engaging the substance of the dispute, as if institutional standing settled what the argument has to establish.
Genetic fallacy — dismissing or accepting an argument based on its origin, the motives of its source, or its funding, rather than evaluating the content of the argument on its own evidentiary terms.

Circular reasoning — smuggling the conclusion into the premises so the argument restates rather than supports its claim, with the result that whoever already accepts the conclusion is the only audience persuaded.
context: Appeal to popularity (ad populum) becomes especially dangerous in attention-economy contexts where audience metrics are themselves heavily engineered by platform algorithms tuned to engagement, not truthfulness. Follower counts measure something — just not what they are being asked to measure.

question: In 2018 a guru predicted civilization would collapse 'within five years.' In 2023 challenged to explain why this hadn't happened, he replies: 'Collapse is a process, not an event. We're in early collapse right now. The five-year window referred to onset, not completion.' Diagnose the guru's rhetorical maneuver.
answer: Moving the goalposts — the guru redefines the original five-year collapse prediction after it failed, reinterpreting 'collapse' as 'early-stage onset' so no future state could ever falsify the claim.
choices: Moving the goalposts — the guru redefines the original five-year collapse prediction after it failed, reinterpreting 'collapse' as 'early-stage onset' so no future state could ever falsify the claim.

Burden-shifting — demanding the critic disprove a claim rather than the claim's defender support it, inverting the usual rule that the party asserting a positive thesis carries the case for it.
context: Moving the goalposts is closely related to motte-and-bailey but operates across time: a failed prediction is rescued by redescription rather than retracted. Karl Popper identified this pattern of unfalsifiability as the demarcation problem for science versus pseudo-science.

question: A populist politician claims a particular sweetener causes cancer, his evidence being three lab-mouse studies at exposure levels four hundred times realistic human intake. The studies' authors note this explicitly. Suppose for argument the sweetener does cause some harm at realistic doses. What fallacy does the ARGUMENT itself commit?
answer: Hasty generalization — the politician leaps from three lab-mouse studies at four hundred times human intake to a sweeping conclusion about realistic human exposure, whether or not the conclusion happens to hold.
choices: Hasty generalization — the politician leaps from three lab-mouse studies at four hundred times human intake to a sweeping conclusion about realistic human exposure, whether or not the conclusion happens to hold.
False equivalence — treating two cases as morally or evidentially comparable when their relevant features differ in magnitude, kind, or causal role in ways the framing quietly suppresses.
Appeal to authority — leaning on the credentials or reputation of a source rather than engaging the substance of the dispute, as if institutional standing settled what the argument has to establish.
Cherry picking — selecting only the supporting cases, intervals, or metrics from a larger body of evidence while suppressing the contrary cases that would force a revision of the claim.
context: The Even-if-correct pattern teaches the form-vs-conclusion distinction: a conclusion can be true for reasons other than the ones the argument supplies. A bad argument for a true claim is still a bad argument, and identifying its flaw is the analytic task — not adjudicating the underlying claim.

question: Asked about a study showing his preferred policy produced no measurable effect, a thinktank fellow responds: 'That study was funded by the opposing foundation — of course it found nothing.' He makes no engagement with the study's methodology, sample, or analysis. Diagnose the fellow's rhetorical maneuver.
answer: Genetic fallacy — the fellow dismisses the inconvenient study based on its funding origin rather than engaging the methodology, sample, or analysis that actually determine whether its conclusions hold.
choices: Genetic fallacy — the fellow dismisses the inconvenient study based on its funding origin rather than engaging the methodology, sample, or analysis that actually determine whether its conclusions hold.
Ad hominem — attacking the character, motives, or identity of the arguer in place of engaging the substance of the argument, as if a fault in the speaker disqualified what they actually said.
Burden-shifting — demanding the critic disprove a claim rather than the claim's defender support it, inverting the usual rule that the party asserting a positive thesis carries the case for it.
Cherry picking — selecting only the supporting cases, intervals, or metrics from a larger body of evidence while suppressing the contrary cases that would force a revision of the claim.
context: Funding sources are legitimately relevant to assessing potential conflicts of interest, but they are not substitutes for engagement with the evidence itself. The genetic fallacy is treating origin as if it settled content, when origin should at most prompt closer scrutiny of substantive claims.

question: A scholar argues municipalities should pilot small-scale congestion pricing in a single neighborhood before scaling citywide. A pundit responds: 'So she wants to charge poor people for the right to exist in their own city, with no escape. The cruelty is the point.' Diagnose the pundit's rhetorical maneuver.
answer: Straw man — the pundit reshapes the scholar's narrow pilot-proposal into a citywide cruelty-engine, attacking the distortion rather than addressing the actual congestion-pricing pilot under discussion.
choices: Straw man — the pundit reshapes the scholar's narrow pilot-proposal into a citywide cruelty-engine, attacking the distortion rather than addressing the actual congestion-pricing pilot under discussion.
Ad hominem — attacking the character, motives, or identity of the arguer in place of engaging the substance of the argument, as if a fault in the speaker disqualified what they actually said.
False dilemma — framing a decision as a binary between two options when the actual space of choices is wider, forcing an unfavorable conclusion by suppressing the unmentioned alternatives.
Slippery slope — treating one modest step as if it must trigger a chain of much worse consequences, without establishing why each link in the predicted cascade actually has to follow.
context: Straw man is among the most common adversarial argument moves in op-ed culture. The pedagogical test: rewrite the original claim in the strongest version its author would endorse (the steel-manning rule), then check whether the response engages that version. If not, a straw man is in play.

question: An economist testifies on the projected effects of a tariff package. Without engaging her data or model, a hostile senator says: 'You receive consulting fees from companies that benefit from this tariff. We don't need to hear your testimony — you're paid to say what you said.' Diagnose the senator's rhetorical maneuver.
answer: Ad hominem (circumstantial) — the senator dismisses the economist's tariff testimony by citing her consulting fees, treating financial interest as if it settled whether her data and model actually hold up.
choices: Ad hominem (circumstantial) — the senator dismisses the economist's tariff testimony by citing her consulting fees, treating financial interest as if it settled whether her data and model actually hold up.
Genetic fallacy — dismissing or accepting an argument based on its origin, the motives of its source, or its funding, rather than evaluating the content of the argument on its own evidentiary terms.
Ad hominem — attacking the character, motives, or identity of the arguer in place of engaging the substance of the argument, as if a fault in the speaker disqualified what they actually said.
Burden-shifting — demanding the critic disprove a claim rather than the claim's defender support it, inverting the usual rule that the party asserting a positive thesis carries the case for it.
context: The circumstantial variant of ad hominem alleges the speaker has a stake in the conclusion. Such interests legitimately warrant scrutiny but do not substitute for engagement with what was said. The fix is not to dismiss interested testimony but to examine it more carefully, not less.

question: Confronted with three consecutive missed recession calls, a financial forecaster on a panel responds: 'The other forecasters on this stage missed every recession of the last twenty years. Don't talk to me about being wrong.' He addresses neither the prior miss nor his current methodology. Diagnose the forecaster's rhetorical maneuver.
answer: Tu quoque — the forecaster deflects from his three missed recession calls by pointing at competitor forecasters' historical misses, leaving the substantive question about his own methodology untouched.
choices: Tu quoque — the forecaster deflects from his three missed recession calls by pointing at competitor forecasters' historical misses, leaving the substantive question about his own methodology untouched.
Whataboutism — deflecting a criticism by raising the wrongs of another party rather than addressing the original charge, treating tu-quoque parallels as if they answered the substantive point.
Red herring — dropping an irrelevant but provocative point into the discussion so attention shifts off the original question and the substantive issue quietly goes unanswered in the diversion.
Ad hominem — attacking the character, motives, or identity of the arguer in place of engaging the substance of the argument, as if a fault in the speaker disqualified what they actually said.
context: Tu quoque ('you also') becomes especially common in expert-panel formats where competitors' shared failure makes any individual failure feel less damaging. Symmetrical imperfection is not, in fact, an answer to the substantive question of whether the individual claim or method should be trusted.

question: A columnist warns: 'If we allow modest deposit-bottle deposits in this state, within a decade we will have a surveillance-state recycling apparatus monitoring every household trash receptacle.' She offers no intermediate steps connecting the deposit law to the surveillance regime. The columnist's argument relies on which logical fallacy?
answer: Slippery slope — the columnist asserts a chain from a modest deposit-bottle law to a household-monitoring surveillance state without supplying the intermediate steps that would establish why each link must follow.
choices: Slippery slope — the columnist asserts a chain from a modest deposit-bottle law to a household-monitoring surveillance state without supplying the intermediate steps that would establish why each link must follow.
False dilemma — framing a decision as a binary between two options when the actual space of choices is wider, forcing an unfavorable conclusion by suppressing the unmentioned alternatives.
Hasty generalization — drawing a sweeping rule from a sample too small, too unrepresentative, or too self-selected to support the size of the claim being made about the general population.
Appeal to ignorance — treating the absence of disproof as if it were positive evidence for a claim, as if no one having refuted X yet could substitute for someone actually establishing X.
context: Slippery-slope arguments are not always fallacious — some chains of policy consequence do unfold. The fallacy is asserting the cascade without supplying the connecting steps. A defensible version would identify the mechanism by which each link compels the next, not rely on alarming endpoint imagery.

question: A radio host promotes claims that ancient civilizations were taught technology by extraterrestrials. Asked for evidence, he replies: 'You can't disprove it. Until mainstream archaeologists rule it out definitively, my hypothesis stands.' He offers no positive evidence himself. The host's argument relies on which logical fallacy?
answer: Burden-shifting — the host treats his extraterrestrial-teachers claim as requiring no positive evidence, shifting the case onto mainstream archaeologists to disprove a hypothesis he himself has never positively supported.
choices: Burden-shifting — the host treats his extraterrestrial-teachers claim as requiring no positive evidence, shifting the case onto mainstream archaeologists to disprove a hypothesis he himself has never positively supported.

Circular reasoning — smuggling the conclusion into the premises so the argument restates rather than supports its claim, with the result that whoever already accepts the conclusion is the only audience persuaded.
Galileo gambit — treating being attacked, mocked, or rejected as itself evidence of being correct, as if persecution tracked truth rather than tracking how poorly an idea fared on the merits.
context: Burden-shifting is closely related to appeal-to-ignorance but distinct: appeal-to-ignorance is the inference itself ('no disproof → true'), burden-shifting is the prior rhetorical move that places the evidentiary case on the wrong party. The usual norm: whoever asserts a positive claim carries the case for it.

question: A finance commentator argues: 'Every responsible household balances its budget. Therefore the federal government, if it wishes to be responsible, must balance its budget too — what's true of households is true of nations.' The argument treats sovereign currency-issuing entities as if they were households. The argument relies on which logical fallacy?
answer: Composition fallacy — the commentator infers from balanced household budgets to a balanced federal budget, treating household-level facts as if they aggregated into a true claim about a sovereign currency-issuer.
choices: Composition fallacy — the commentator infers from balanced household budgets to a balanced federal budget, treating household-level facts as if they aggregated into a true claim about a sovereign currency-issuer.
False equivalence — treating two cases as morally or evidentially comparable when their relevant features differ in magnitude, kind, or causal role in ways the framing quietly suppresses.
Hasty generalization — drawing a sweeping rule from a sample too small, too unrepresentative, or too self-selected to support the size of the claim being made about the general population.
Equivocation — shifting the meaning of a key term between premises so the argument's apparent validity rides on a hidden change of sense rather than on a stable inference.
context: The composition fallacy (and its inverse, the division fallacy) was distinguished in medieval logic. What holds at one level of organization need not hold at another: a sovereign nation that issues its own currency operates under fundamentally different budget constraints than a household does.

question: A talk-show guest argues vaccines are dangerous: 'My nephew was developing typically, got the vaccine, and within three weeks the diagnosis came. You can show me whatever population-level studies you want — I know what I saw in my own family.' Vast aggregate trial data shows no causal link. Diagnose the guest's rhetorical maneuver.
answer: Anecdotal evidence — the guest treats one vivid family story about her nephew as if it overrode the population-level trial data, as if a single case outweighed the aggregate evidence she is using it to dismiss.
choices: Anecdotal evidence — the guest treats one vivid family story about her nephew as if it overrode the population-level trial data, as if a single case outweighed the aggregate evidence she is using it to dismiss.
Post hoc — treating sequence as proof of causation: because B followed A, A must have caused B, with no account of confounders, base rates, or whether the link is mechanistic at all.
Cherry picking — selecting only the supporting cases, intervals, or metrics from a larger body of evidence while suppressing the contrary cases that would force a revision of the claim.
Hasty generalization — drawing a sweeping rule from a sample too small, too unrepresentative, or too self-selected to support the size of the claim being made about the general population.
context: Personal experience is real and emotionally salient. It is also a sample of size one with no control, no blinding, and rich post-hoc rationalization. The aggregate-evidence reply is not dismissing the lived experience — it is asking what the lived experience can and cannot reliably show about causation.

question: A wellness coach blogs: 'Three of my clients adopted my morning ritual; within two weeks all three reported improved mood. The ritual is doing the work.' She does not consider regression to the mean, placebo response, the encouragement effect of paying for coaching, or seasonal variation. Diagnose the coach's rhetorical maneuver.
answer: Post hoc — the coach treats two-week mood improvement in three paying clients after adopting her ritual as proof the ritual caused the improvement, with no account of placebo, regression to mean, or coaching effects.
choices: Post hoc — the coach treats two-week mood improvement in three paying clients after adopting her ritual as proof the ritual caused the improvement, with no account of placebo, regression to mean, or coaching effects.

Texas sharpshooter — drawing the analytic target around the clusters in already-collected data so a pattern that was carved out after the fact is presented as if it had been predicted in advance.
Cherry picking — selecting only the supporting cases, intervals, or metrics from a larger body of evidence while suppressing the contrary cases that would force a revision of the claim.
context: Post hoc ergo propter hoc ('after this, therefore because of this') is the canonical confusion of sequence with causation. Causal inference from observational data requires controlling for plausible alternative explanations — placebo, selection, regression, secular trends — none of which the blog post addresses.

question: An apologist argues: 'We can trust scripture because it is divinely inspired. We know it is divinely inspired because scripture itself says so.' Asked to support the second claim independently, he redirects to passages within scripture. The argument never references anything outside the text. The argument relies on which logical fallacy?
answer: Circular reasoning — the apologist supports scripture's reliability by citing scripture's claim of divine inspiration, smuggling the conclusion (trustworthy scripture) into the premise (scripture says so) without external support.
choices: Circular reasoning — the apologist supports scripture's reliability by citing scripture's claim of divine inspiration, smuggling the conclusion (trustworthy scripture) into the premise (scripture says so) without external support.
Appeal to authority — leaning on the credentials or reputation of a source rather than engaging the substance of the dispute, as if institutional standing settled what the argument has to establish.
Burden-shifting — demanding the critic disprove a claim rather than the claim's defender support it, inverting the usual rule that the party asserting a positive thesis carries the case for it.
Appeal to ignorance — treating the absence of disproof as if it were positive evidence for a claim, as if no one having refuted X yet could substitute for someone actually establishing X.
context: Circular reasoning (begging the question, petitio principii) is a structural rather than rhetorical flaw: the argument's conclusion appears, in some form, among its premises. The reasoner is convinced by what already requires being convinced. The fix is supplying support that doesn't presuppose the conclusion.

question: A nutrition theorist whose claims have been repeatedly refuted by clinical trials writes: 'Of course the establishment mocks me. They mocked Galileo too. The fact that my views are dismissed by mainstream researchers IS the evidence that I am ahead of them.' Diagnose the rhetorical maneuver.
answer: Galileo gambit — the theorist treats establishment mockery of his refuted nutrition claims as itself evidence that he is correct, conflating being attacked or rejected with being ahead of his time.
choices: Galileo gambit — the theorist treats establishment mockery of his refuted nutrition claims as itself evidence that he is correct, conflating being attacked or rejected with being ahead of his time.
Genetic fallacy — dismissing or accepting an argument based on its origin, the motives of its source, or its funding, rather than evaluating the content of the argument on its own evidentiary terms.

context: Carl Sagan put the point sharply in The Demon-Haunted World (1995): they laughed at Galileo, but they also laughed at Bozo the Clown. Being mocked is necessary but not sufficient for being correct; the relevant difference is whether the substantive case for the claim holds up to scrutiny.

question: Pressed on her vote against a popular bill, a senator responds: 'You know what we should really be talking about? The price of eggs. Working families are hurting. That's the real issue.' She does not address why she voted as she did on the bill in question. Diagnose the senator's rhetorical maneuver.
answer: Red herring — the senator drops in eggs-and-working-families framing to shift attention off her actual vote on the bill, leaving the substantive question about why she voted as she did entirely unanswered.
choices: Red herring — the senator drops in eggs-and-working-families framing to shift attention off her actual vote on the bill, leaving the substantive question about why she voted as she did entirely unanswered.
Whataboutism — deflecting a criticism by raising the wrongs of another party rather than addressing the original charge, treating tu-quoque parallels as if they answered the substantive point.
Straw man — distorting an opponent's position into a wilder or weaker version that is easier to refute, then attacking the distortion as if the original argument had been engaged.
Burden-shifting — demanding the critic disprove a claim rather than the claim's defender support it, inverting the usual rule that the party asserting a positive thesis carries the case for it.
context: Red herring is the umbrella for diversion-style fallacies. Whataboutism (raising the questioner's wrongs) and tu quoque (alleging symmetrical fault) are specific subtypes. The pure red herring just introduces a more emotionally compelling topic without claiming the diversion answers the original question.

question: A cable host announces: 'Our exclusive panel of fourteen swing-state voters — a true cross-section of America — overwhelmingly favors the challenger.' He treats fourteen self-selected panel volunteers as a basis for claims about national electoral sentiment. Diagnose the cable host's rhetorical maneuver.
answer: Hasty generalization — the host treats fourteen self-selected swing-state volunteers as a 'true cross-section' of America, drawing a national-electorate conclusion from a sample too small and unrepresentative to support it.
choices: Hasty generalization — the host treats fourteen self-selected swing-state volunteers as a 'true cross-section' of America, drawing a national-electorate conclusion from a sample too small and unrepresentative to support it.
Cherry picking — selecting only the supporting cases, intervals, or metrics from a larger body of evidence while suppressing the contrary cases that would force a revision of the claim.

Anecdotal evidence — treating a vivid individual case as if it overrode the systematic statistical pattern, as if one striking story outweighed the aggregate evidence the story is being used to dismiss.
Appeal to popularity — treating widespread agreement, viewership, or follower counts as evidence the underlying claim is true, as if popular acceptance measured anything beyond popular acceptance.
context: Polling methodology has been formalized for nearly a century: random sampling, weighting against known demographics, sample-size requirements for stated margins of error. None of those apply to a panel of fourteen volunteers. Calling such a panel 'a true cross-section' is a category error dressed as analysis.

question: A talk radio host invokes a Nobel laureate physicist's strongly stated views on economic policy as settling a contested fiscal debate. The physicist has no formal training in economics, no published economic research, and the field's working economists disagree sharply with his position. Diagnose the host's rhetorical maneuver.
answer: Appeal to authority — the host leans on the Nobel-laureate physicist's name to settle a fiscal-policy debate that lies entirely outside the physicist's actual expertise, where the field's working economists in fact disagree.
choices: Appeal to authority — the host leans on the Nobel-laureate physicist's name to settle a fiscal-policy debate that lies entirely outside the physicist's actual expertise, where the field's working economists in fact disagree.
Genetic fallacy — dismissing or accepting an argument based on its origin, the motives of its source, or its funding, rather than evaluating the content of the argument on its own evidentiary terms.
Appeal to popularity — treating widespread agreement, viewership, or follower counts as evidence the underlying claim is true, as if popular acceptance measured anything beyond popular acceptance.
Cherry picking — selecting only the supporting cases, intervals, or metrics from a larger body of evidence while suppressing the contrary cases that would force a revision of the claim.
context: Appeal to authority becomes fallacious when (a) the cited authority is outside her area of competence, (b) genuine experts in the relevant field disagree, or (c) the appeal substitutes for engagement with the evidence. A Nobel in one field does not transfer competence to another, however distinguished the holder.

question: A talk-show host frames the curriculum debate: 'Either we teach our nation's full history including its darker chapters, or we wave the flag and lie to children. Pick one. There is no third option.' Educators in practice routinely combine honest treatment of difficult history with patriotic civic instruction. Diagnose the host's rhetorical framing maneuver.
answer: False dilemma — the host compresses the curriculum debate into two stark options (darker-chapters vs. flag-waving-lies), suppressing the middle ground where educators combine honest history with civic instruction.
choices: False dilemma — the host compresses the curriculum debate into two stark options (darker-chapters vs. flag-waving-lies), suppressing the middle ground where educators combine honest history with civic instruction.
Straw man — distorting an opponent's position into a wilder or weaker version that is easier to refute, then attacking the distortion as if the original argument had been engaged.
Slippery slope — treating one modest step as if it must trigger a chain of much worse consequences, without establishing why each link in the predicted cascade actually has to follow.

context: False dilemma (also: bifurcation, false dichotomy) is a framing fallacy: the choice space is presented as binary when in fact it is wider. The diagnostic move is to enumerate the suppressed alternatives and check whether they are genuinely available — often they are widely practiced, just unmentioned.

question: A paranormal-investigations host concludes a haunted-asylum episode: 'In three nights of investigation, we could not definitively rule out the presence of spirits. That, in our view, is as close to confirmation as the question allows.' He offers no positive evidence the asylum is haunted. Diagnose the host's rhetorical maneuver.
answer: Appeal to ignorance — the host treats his three-night failure to rule out asylum spirits as itself confirmation of their presence, substituting absence of disproof for the positive evidence the claim actually requires.
choices: Appeal to ignorance — the host treats his three-night failure to rule out asylum spirits as itself confirmation of their presence, substituting absence of disproof for the positive evidence the claim actually requires.
Burden-shifting — demanding the critic disprove a claim rather than the claim's defender support it, inverting the usual rule that the party asserting a positive thesis carries the case for it.

Circular reasoning — smuggling the conclusion into the premises so the argument restates rather than supports its claim, with the result that whoever already accepts the conclusion is the only audience persuaded.
Galileo gambit — treating being attacked, mocked, or rejected as itself evidence of being correct, as if persecution tracked truth rather than tracking how poorly an idea fared on the merits.
context: Appeal to ignorance (ad ignorantiam) inverts the basic evidentiary norm: that the case for X must be made, not the case against. The trap is rhetorical, because a three-night investigation 'unable to rule out' anything sounds like dispassionate inquiry while functioning as a license to assert.

question: Theo's sister flips through baby photos and tells him, 'That's still YOU at one year old — you can't remember it, but the memories link forward through every later year of you.' Which view of identity is she defending?
answer: Memory continuity — you're the same person if an unbroken chain of memory connects past and present selves.
choices: Memory continuity — you're the same person if an unbroken chain of memory connects past and present selves.

context: The puzzle is named for Jean Buridan (14th century), though he never wrote the donkey version — Spinoza and Leibniz used it later to debate the Principle of Sufficient Reason. The 'just pick one' reply treats action as not requiring a reason for every detail.

question: David Hume watched ball A strike ball B. B rolled away. Hume asked: what do you actually SEE that lets you say A CAUSED B to move? You see contact, then motion — but where is the 'causing'? Which view of causation is Hume pressing?
answer: Pattern view — 'causation' is just the pattern of strikes followed by motion; we never see a force, only the pairing.
choices: Pattern view — 'causation' is just the pattern of strikes followed by motion; we never see a force, only the pairing.
Hidden-power view — causes contain real pushing forces inside; the force can't be seen, but must be there since motion follows.
What-if view — A caused B means that without the strike, B would have stayed still; causation is about what would have happened.
Mind-habit view — causation is a brain-habit pairing strike with motion; nothing in the world itself matches the habit.
context: Hume's Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding (1748) used billiard balls to argue that 'causation' as a perceived force is nowhere in experience — only the pattern of constant conjunction is. Modern counterfactual and powers views are later replies.

question: A school newspaper editor writes: 'You step into the same river twice. The water is different each time, but the river itself is the same — what makes a river is its course and its flow, not the molecules passing through.' Which view of identity is she defending?
answer: Form identity — what makes a thing itself is its persistent structure and continuing role, not the particular matter that fills it.
choices: Form identity — what makes a thing itself is its persistent structure and continuing role, not the particular matter that fills it.
Material identity — same matter equals same thing; change every molecule and the result is a different thing wearing the old name.
Convention identity — there is no real fact of sameness; calling it 'the same river' is just a useful habit of speech, not a deep truth.
Process identity — rivers are events rather than things; what we call 'the river' is an ongoing flow without a fixed identity at any time.
context: Heraclitus (~500 BC) used the river to argue for material flux. The form-identity reply (running through Aristotle's substantial form to modern structural accounts) says rivers are individuated by course and flow — what they ARE structurally — not by which molecules occupy them right now.

question: A YouTuber tells viewers: 'A wooden sailboat had every plank, mast, and rope slowly replaced over twenty years. None of the original wood is left. The sailboat at the dock today is a DIFFERENT boat from the one launched two decades ago.' Which view of identity is he defending?
answer: Material identity — same matter equals same thing; once every original part has been replaced, the resulting object is no longer the same.
choices: Material identity — same matter equals same thing; once every original part has been replaced, the resulting object is no longer the same.
Form identity — what makes a thing itself is its persistent structure and continuing role, regardless of which matter happens to fill it.
Convention identity — sameness is a useful habit of speech; the boat counts as 'the same' as long as people keep applying the same name.
Process identity — boats are ongoing events of being-sailed, not fixed objects, so the question of sameness across years is not a real one.
context: The ship of Theseus puzzle (Plutarch, Life of Theseus) traces back to ancient debate about whether matter, structure, or naming carries identity. Material identity bites the bullet: same matter required, no exceptions.

question: A museum guide explains: 'This painting has been restored so many times that almost every pigment on the canvas today was applied by a restorer in the last hundred years. But the painting itself, with its composition and figures, is the same work.' Which view does she defend?
answer: Form identity — what makes the painting itself is the composition and design that persist through restoration, not the original pigment.
choices: Form identity — what makes the painting itself is the composition and design that persist through restoration, not the original pigment.
Material identity — the painting is its original paint; if almost none of that paint remains, what hangs in the gallery is a careful copy now.
Convention identity — calling it 'the original' is a useful museum habit; whether it really is the original is not a question with a true answer.
Origin identity — what something is depends on where it came from; since the canvas itself comes from the artist's studio, it remains his work.
context: Restoration debates surface a core question: is a work its physical pigment or its compositional structure? The form-identity reply emphasizes design and intent persisting through material replacement — a view shared by most modern conservation practice.

question: A music teacher tells her class: 'When two different orchestras play Beethoven's Fifth, they're playing the SAME piece of music, even though every note is produced by different instruments at different times in different cities.' Which view of identity is she defending?
answer: Form identity — what makes the symphony itself is its score and structure, which can be instantiated by many different performances at once.
choices: Form identity — what makes the symphony itself is its score and structure, which can be instantiated by many different performances at once.
Material identity — the piece is the actual sound waves on a particular night; two performances produce two strictly different musical objects.
Convention identity — saying 'the same piece' is just a useful habit; there is no deeper fact about whether two performances are really one work.
Bundle identity — the symphony is just a bundle of properties; since each performance bundles different properties, each is its own symphony.
context: Musical works raise a 'type-token' question: the score (type) is one thing; each performance (token) is another. Form identity says works are types — structures that can be instantiated repeatedly without losing themselves.

question: A school newspaper editor argues: 'A car brand announces it has redesigned every component — engine, frame, electronics, seats. The result is sold under the same model name, but it is a fundamentally NEW car, not the previous one.' Which view of identity is she defending?
answer: Material identity — once every component has been replaced, the result is a new thing; reusing a name does not preserve the underlying object.
choices: Material identity — once every component has been replaced, the result is a new thing; reusing a name does not preserve the underlying object.
Form identity — what makes the car itself is the role it plays and the structural pattern, which a redesigned version still continues.
Convention identity — what counts as the 'same car' is fixed by what carmakers and buyers agree to call it, not by which parts are inside.
Process identity — a car-line is an ongoing event of being-manufactured; asking whether it's the same car at different years is not a real question.
context: Component-replacement cases (cars, ships, computers) sharpen the material-identity intuition. Critics reply that we routinely treat sports teams, corporations, and orchestras as 'the same' across complete personnel turnover.

question: A YouTuber explains to viewers: 'A small company hires new employees every year for fifty years until none of the original staff remains. The office moves three times. But the COMPANY persists as one company — its mission and roles continue.' Which view does she defend?
answer: Form identity — what makes the company itself is its persistent structure and mission, not which particular employees happen to fill the roles.
choices: Form identity — what makes the company itself is its persistent structure and mission, not which particular employees happen to fill the roles.
Material identity — once every original employee has left and every office has moved, the result is a successor organization, not the same one.
Convention identity — whether it's 'the same company' is a matter of legal habit and naming, not of any deep fact about the organization itself.
Bundle identity — the company is just the bundle of people and properties present at any moment, so each year produces a strictly new company.
context: Corporations are a paradigm form-identity case: the law treats a company as the same entity across total turnover. The persistence is in roles, mission, and structural continuity — what philosophers since Aristotle have called the 'substantial form' of an organized thing.

question: A school sports columnist writes: 'The varsity basketball team that won the championship in 2010 had not one player in common with this year's team. But it is the SAME team — same name, same school, same league.' Which view of identity is he defending?
answer: Form identity — what makes a team itself is its persistent role and structure within an institution, not the particular players who fill it.
choices: Form identity — what makes a team itself is its persistent role and structure within an institution, not the particular players who fill it.
Material identity — the team is its members; once every player has left, the result is a different team that happens to share an old name.
Convention identity — calling it 'the same team' is a useful habit of speech, but there's no deeper truth about whether they are really one.
Process identity — a team is an ongoing event of playing-together; asking whether the 2010 team and the 2026 team are the same isn't a real question.
context: Sports teams, like corporations, persist as institutional structures while every individual changes. The form-identity reply emphasizes roles, league membership, and continuity of institutional rules over personnel.

question: A philosophy YouTuber tells his viewers: 'Asking whether the rebuilt ship counts as one and the same ship is a pseudo-question. There's no deep fact — we just have rules about when to apply a name, and those rules are useful but not true or false.' Which view does he defend?
answer: Convention identity — there is no deep fact of sameness; calling something 'the same' tracks our habits of naming, not any underlying truth.
choices: Convention identity — there is no deep fact of sameness; calling something 'the same' tracks our habits of naming, not any underlying truth.
Material identity — the question DOES have a deep fact; same matter is same thing, different matter is different thing, regardless of any naming habit.
Form identity — there IS a deep fact about sameness, and it tracks persistent structure rather than matter; deflating it loses what we are tracking.
Origin identity — there IS a fact of sameness, and it depends on what something came from; calling it 'just a habit' overlooks where it began.
context: Conventionalism about identity (associated with Carnap and some moves in Wittgenstein) treats persistence claims as governed by useful rules of speech rather than deep facts. Critics reply that some persistence judgments seem to track real differences we don't get to redefine away by changing habits.

question: A philosophy student argues: 'A river is not a thing that has a flow; it IS a flow — a process. Asking whether two snapshots show the same river treats it as a static object when really there's just an ongoing event.' Which view of identity is she defending?
answer: Process identity — rivers are events rather than things; the question of static sameness across moments dissolves once we see what is going on.
choices: Process identity — rivers are events rather than things; the question of static sameness across moments dissolves once we see what is going on.
Form identity — rivers are things with a persistent structure; calling them events misdescribes what makes them count as one river over time.
Material identity — rivers are collections of matter at a moment; different matter gives different rivers, but each snapshot remains a real thing.
Convention identity — neither 'thing' nor 'process' is the right label; whether to call a river one or many is settled by speech habits, not facts.
context: Process philosophy (Whitehead, Process and Reality, 1929) re-categorizes rivers, organisms, even persons as ongoing events rather than fixed objects. On this view, the puzzles of identity-through-change look less like genuine puzzles and more like signs we were using the wrong category from the start.

question: A philosophy class debates: a sailboat has every original plank slowly replaced (call this Boat A). A collector saves the discarded planks and reassembles them into a complete sailboat (Boat B). Which feature of the original boat settles which successor inherits its identity?
answer: Continuity of structure and use favors Boat A; continuity of original matter favors Boat B; the case forces a choice between these criteria.
choices: Continuity of structure and use favors Boat A; continuity of original matter favors Boat B; the case forces a choice between these criteria.
Boat A is obviously the original because it has never stopped being used as a sailboat; physical use is what makes an object the same boat.
Boat B is obviously the original because the planks themselves are the original material; matter is what makes an object the same boat.
Neither boat is the original; once any plank was replaced, the original ceased to exist, and naming either one 'the original' would be wrong.
context: The split version of the ship of Theseus (Hobbes, De Corpore) is what makes the puzzle bite: form identity says A; material identity says B. The puzzle exposes that there isn't one criterion of identity — different cases pick out different criteria, and our intuitions don't line up under pressure.

question: A museum receives two paintings claiming to be Vermeer originals. Painting A is the heavily restored canvas from the artist's studio. Painting B is a perfect replica made from analysis of A. Which feature settles which painting IS the Vermeer original?
answer: Continuity of the original canvas favors A; perfect compositional match favors B; the case forces a choice between origin and exact resemblance.
choices: Continuity of the original canvas favors A; perfect compositional match favors B; the case forces a choice between origin and exact resemblance.
Painting A is obviously the original because Vermeer himself touched its canvas; physical contact with the artist is what fixes which work is real.
Painting B is obviously the original because it best matches what Vermeer intended; faithful compositional match is what fixes which work is real.
Neither painting is the original; once the canvas was restored the original ceased to exist, and the replica was never the original to begin with.
context: Art-world cases sharpen origin identity vs. form identity. Curators usually side with A (the worked-over original canvas); some philosophers of art note that origin claims rely on a chain of contact that, in extreme restoration cases, can become thin enough to question.

question: A music student writes for her school paper: 'Two recordings of Beethoven's Fifth, made in different cities by different orchestras, are the SAME piece of music. What makes them the same is shared structure, not shared sound or shared performers.' Which view does she defend?
answer: Form identity — what makes the symphony itself is the structure and score that persist across many different sound-instantiations and performances.
choices: Form identity — what makes the symphony itself is the structure and score that persist across many different sound-instantiations and performances.
Material identity — the piece is the actual sound on the night; two recordings produce two strictly different musical objects, however similar.
Bundle identity — the symphony is just a bundle of properties at a time; each performance bundles different properties, so each is its own piece.
Convention identity — calling two performances 'the same piece' is a useful habit of music vocabulary, not a fact about underlying sameness.
context: Musical works are a paradigm 'abstract object' case for philosophy of art: the work is a structure (type) repeatedly instantiated in performances (tokens). Form identity tracks this well; material and bundle views struggle with the everyday fact that we treat performances as the same piece.

question: A school newspaper columnist argues: 'A cloud is just a bundle of water droplets, motion, temperature, and shape at a moment. There's no extra 'cloud' beyond the bundle. Two moments give two strictly different bundles, hence two clouds.' Which view does he defend?
answer: Bundle identity — a thing just is its collection of properties at a time; different bundles at different times are strictly different things.
choices: Bundle identity — a thing just is its collection of properties at a time; different bundles at different times are strictly different things.
Form identity — a thing is a persistent structure that holds different bundles of properties together over time, not the bundles themselves.
Material identity — a thing is its underlying matter; clouds and other groupings of matter remain the same as long as the matter persists.
Process identity — a thing is an ongoing event, not a bundle of properties; treating clouds as bundles misses that they are flowing happenings.
context: Bundle theory (Hume, Treatise I.4.6, 1739) treats objects as mere collections of properties with nothing extra holding them together. The approach faces classic difficulties with re-identification across time, but it remains philosophically live as a deflationary alternative.

question: A YouTuber making a video about her old chess club writes: 'Every member who founded the club has graduated. The club meets in a new room. But it is the SAME club — same name, same purpose, same place in the school's list of activities.' Which view does she defend?
answer: Form identity — what makes the club itself is its persistent role and structure within the school, not the particular members or meeting room.
choices: Form identity — what makes the club itself is its persistent role and structure within the school, not the particular members or meeting room.
Material identity — the club is its members; once every founder has left, the result is a successor club that happens to share an older name.
Convention identity — saying it's 'the same club' is a useful habit of school speech; there's no deeper fact about whether they really are.
Bundle identity — the club is just the bundle of members and properties at each moment; each year's bundle yields a different club from the last.
context: Clubs, sports teams, and corporations are paradigm form-identity cases for institutions. Their persistence is in role, charter, and structural continuity within a larger context — the matter (members) is replaceable while the form (function, mission) carries through.

question: A school newspaper book reviewer writes: 'A Russian novel translated into English remains the SAME novel — every word has changed, but the story, characters, and themes carry through. The novel is its narrative structure, not its particular wording.' Which view does she defend?
answer: Form identity — what makes a novel itself is its narrative structure and content, which can be carried by different words in different languages.
choices: Form identity — what makes a novel itself is its narrative structure and content, which can be carried by different words in different languages.
Material identity — a novel is its actual words; once every word has been replaced by a translation, the result is a strictly different work.
Convention identity — calling a translation 'the same novel' is a useful publishing habit; there's no deeper fact about whether they are one work.
Bundle identity — the novel is just a bundle of words and marks at a time; each translation creates a strictly distinct bundle and so a new work.
context: Literary works, like musical ones, raise type-token questions. Form identity treats the novel as a structure (plot, characters, themes) that survives language change. Material views struggle with the everyday fact that we discuss 'War and Peace' as one work across many translations.

question: A cooking YouTuber tells viewers: 'A grandmother's soup recipe, cooked fifty years later in a different kitchen with different brands of ingredients, remains the SAME recipe — what makes a recipe is the method, not the ingredients.' Which view does she defend?
answer: Form identity — what makes the recipe itself is its method and structure of preparation, which can be carried across kitchens and ingredients.
choices: Form identity — what makes the recipe itself is its method and structure of preparation, which can be carried across kitchens and ingredients.
Material identity — a recipe is its actual ingredients; once every brand and source has changed, the result is a strictly different recipe.
Convention identity — calling them 'the same recipe' is a useful family habit; whether the two soups are really one recipe is not a real question.
Bundle identity — a recipe is just a bundle of ingredients and steps at a time; different bundles in different kitchens are strictly different recipes.
context: Recipes work like musical scores: they are structures (methods) that can be instantiated by many different ingredient-sets across time. Form identity captures everyday practice; material identity would have to say each pot of soup is its own recipe, which loses the family transmission cases.

question: A YouTuber covers a company that split into two: Company A kept the name and the headquarters; Company B kept the original founders and most of the engineering staff. Which feature of the original company settles which successor IS the original?
answer: Continuity of name and place favors A; continuity of founders and people favors B; the case forces a choice between structural and personal continuity.
choices: Continuity of name and place favors A; continuity of founders and people favors B; the case forces a choice between structural and personal continuity.
Company A is obviously the original because it kept the official name and headquarters; legal continuity is what makes a company the same company.
Company B is obviously the original because the original people went with it; personal continuity is what makes a company the same company over time.
Neither is the original; once a company splits, the original ceases to exist, and calling either successor 'the original' would be an error.
context: Corporate splits are an If-A-and-B-which case in real law and ethics: which successor inherits obligations? Form identity (structure, name) and personal identity (founders, staff) can pull apart, forcing a choice. The case shows identity criteria don't always converge.

question: A philosophy teacher in front of her class points to a candle flame and says: 'A fire is not a thing that burns; it IS a burning — an ongoing event. Asking whether the flame at 8:00 and the flame at 8:01 are the same flame treats an event as if it were an object.' Which view?
answer: Process identity — fires are events rather than things; the question of strict sameness across moments dissolves once we see them as ongoing burnings.
choices: Process identity — fires are events rather than things; the question of strict sameness across moments dissolves once we see them as ongoing burnings.
Form identity — fires are things with a persistent flame structure; calling them events misdescribes what makes them count as one fire over time.
Material identity — a fire is the matter currently burning; since the matter constantly changes, each moment gives a strictly different fire altogether.
Bundle identity — a fire is just a bundle of heat, light, and smoke at a time; each moment bundles different properties, hence each fire is its own.
context: Process metaphysics (Whitehead, Process and Reality, 1929; Rescher) re-categorizes fires, weather systems, organisms as events not objects. On this view, certain identity puzzles are signs we were using the wrong category — once events are admitted, the puzzles look different.

question: A school newspaper editor writes for her hundredth-anniversary issue: 'No student or teacher from a century ago is still here. The buildings have all been rebuilt. But the SCHOOL is the same school — its name, its place in the town, its mission continue.' Which view does she defend?
answer: Form identity — what makes the school itself is its persistent role and mission in the town, not which particular students or buildings fill it.
choices: Form identity — what makes the school itself is its persistent role and mission in the town, not which particular students or buildings fill it.
Material identity — the school is its actual people and buildings; once both have completely turned over, the result is a different institution.
Convention identity — calling it 'the same school' is a useful habit of local speech; there is no deeper fact about whether they really are one.
Bundle identity — the school is just the bundle of people and buildings at each time; each year's bundle gives a strictly distinct school from the rest.
context: Schools, like corporations and sports teams, are paradigm institutional form-identity cases. Their continuity is in role, mission, and structural place within a community, even as every particular matter (people, buildings) gets replaced over the century.

question: The Statue and the Lump puzzle: a sculptor presses a lump of clay into a horse. Statue and lump fill the same space and share every particle, yet squashing destroys the statue while the lump persists. A student says: 'Two objects share one matter.' Which view is she defending?
answer: Constitution view — the statue is CONSTITUTED BY the lump but isn't identical to it; they coincide yet differ in persistence, so two objects share one place.
choices: Constitution view — the statue is CONSTITUTED BY the lump but isn't identical to it; they coincide yet differ in persistence, so two objects share one place.
Strict-identity view — same matter at the same place means one object; calling them 'two' just confuses different ways of describing a single thing.
Eliminativist view — neither statue nor lump exists; only particles arranged horse-wise are real, and 'statues' and 'lumps' are convenient labels.
Convention view — whether they are one or two depends on which name we apply; nothing in the world settles distinctness beyond our talk.
context: The Statue and the Lump puzzle (Allan Gibbard, 'Contingent Identity,' 1975; Lynne Rudder Baker) tests whether coincident objects can be distinct. The constitution view defends 'two objects, one matter'; identity-theorists insist two distinct objects can't share all the same matter at the same time.

question: Black's two iron spheres: a universe holds nothing but two perfect iron spheres — identical in every property, no observers, no marks. They are clearly TWO yet share every property. A student says: 'Then identity can't just be sameness of properties.' Which principle is she rejecting?
answer: Identity of indiscernibles — Leibniz's principle that things sharing every property must be one; Black's spheres are a counter-case showing the principle fails.
choices: Identity of indiscernibles — Leibniz's principle that things sharing every property must be one; Black's spheres are a counter-case showing the principle fails.
Indiscernibility of identicals — the principle that one thing has all its own properties; this is untouched, since the case involves two distinct spheres.
Bundle theory of objects — the view that objects ARE bundles of properties; Black's case actually supports it by showing properties exhaust what objects can be.
Relational identity view — the view that what distinguishes things is their spatial relations; the spheres differ in relations, and so the case dissolves.
context: Max Black's 'The Identity of Indiscernibles' (Mind, 1952) presented the two-spheres counter-example to Leibniz's principle. Defenders of the principle reply by counting spatial position or 'haecceity' (thisness) as a property. The debate is alive in current metaphysics of properties and identity.

question: The paradox of the bald man, a Sorites variant: a man with 100,000 hairs isn't bald; losing one hair never turns non-bald into bald; yet zero hairs IS bald. A logic teacher says: 'Some predicates have no sharp boundary.' Which view of vague predicates is she defending?
answer: Vague-predicate view — words like 'bald' admit borderline cases where the term neither clearly applies nor fails; vagueness lives in the predicate itself.
choices: Vague-predicate view — words like 'bald' admit borderline cases where the term neither clearly applies nor fails; vagueness lives in the predicate itself.
Hidden-cutoff view — there IS a precise hair-count that turns non-bald into bald, but knowers cannot detect which one; the sharpness is hidden, not absent.
Nihilist view — vague predicates fail to refer; since 'bald' has no fixed extension, the predicate names nothing real and should be replaced by hair counts.
Speaker-relative view — vagueness exists only in human classification, not in the world; speakers create each borderline by choosing where to apply the term.
context: The paradox of the bald man (Greek 'phalakros') is the canonical Sorites variant. The vagueness-in-the-predicate reading runs from Frege through Russell and Dummett. The hidden-cutoff view (Sorensen 1988; Williamson 1994) defends sharp boundaries we cannot know. Both remain seriously defended.

question: On a philosophy podcast, the host says: 'Yesterday is real in exactly the way today is real. It just happens to be located earlier in time, the way another city is located elsewhere in space. Calling it past doesn't make it less real.' Which view of time is the host defending?
answer: Eternalism — all moments past, present, and future are equally real; 'now' marks a particular position in time the way 'here' marks a position in space, not a privileged ontological status.
choices: Eternalism — all moments past, present, and future are equally real; 'now' marks a particular position in time the way 'here' marks a position in space, not a privileged ontological status.
Presentism — only the present moment is genuinely real; the past once existed but no longer does, and the future does not yet exist, so 'real' applies to right-now alone.
Growing-block view — past and present are real and time grows incrementally; the future is not yet real because new moments are added to the block of reality as time passes.
Time-illusion view — the apparent passage of time is a feature of conscious perception, not an objective property of reality; on this view neither past nor present is robustly real.
context: Eternalism (sometimes 'block universe view') is associated with McTaggart's B-series, with Einstein's relativistic spacetime, and with contemporary philosophers like Smart and Mellor. The standard contrast is with presentism, defended by Prior and Bigelow.

question: An op-ed columnist writes: 'The dinosaurs aren't real anymore, and your great-grandchildren aren't real yet. Only right now is real. Anything else is just a useful way of talking — history is records, the future is plans.' Which view of time does the columnist defend?
answer: Presentism — only the present moment is genuinely real; the past has been but no longer exists, and the future has not yet come to be, so reality is exhausted by what is now.
