choices: Presentism — only the present moment is genuinely real; the past has been but no longer exists, and the future has not yet come to be, so reality is exhausted by what is now.
Eternalism — all moments are equally real; 'now' is just a position in time the way 'here' is a position in space, so dinosaurs and great-grandchildren are real at their times.
Growing-block view — past and present are real but the future is not yet real; reality grows as new moments are added, so dinosaurs persist but unborn descendants do not.
Modal realism — every possible moment, past, present, future, and merely possible, exists as a concrete reality; what we call 'now' is just the moment we happen to inhabit.
context: Presentism (defended by A.N. Prior, John Bigelow, Dean Zimmerman) is the natural-language default and faces challenges from relativistic physics. Cross-temporal claims ('Caesar crossed the Rubicon') require careful treatment when only the present exists at all.

question: A philosophy seminar debates time. One student argues: 'The past is real — what happened happened, and that fact never goes away. But the future is open. New moments come into being as the present moves forward.' Which view of time does this student defend?
answer: Growing-block view — past and present are both real, but the future does not yet exist; reality literally grows over time as each new present becomes part of the fixed block of the past.
choices: Growing-block view — past and present are both real, but the future does not yet exist; reality literally grows over time as each new present becomes part of the fixed block of the past.
Presentism — only the present is real; the past once existed but no longer does, so the student's appeal to a still-real past mistakes records of happenings for the happenings themselves.
Eternalism — all moments past, present, and future are equally real; the future is no less existent than the past, and the apparent 'openness' of the future is an artifact of ignorance.
Tense-realism — what is true depends ineliminably on when it is said; past and future tense are basic features of reality, but the question of which moments exist does not arise at all here.
context: The growing-block view (C.D. Broad in Scientific Thought, 1923; defended recently by Michael Tooley, Peter Forrest) is the intuitive middle position: the past is closed, the future open. It faces the 'how do we know we're at the edge?' epistemic challenge.

question: On a panel on personal identity, a guest argues: 'I'm the same person I was at age six because I remember being him. The body has changed entirely, but an unbroken chain of memory connects me to that child.' Which view of personal identity is the guest defending?
answer: Memory continuity — the same person persists across time if and only if an unbroken chain of memory connects past and present selves; bodily persistence is not what makes the identity.
choices: Memory continuity — the same person persists across time if and only if an unbroken chain of memory connects past and present selves; bodily persistence is not what makes the identity.
Bodily continuity — the same person persists across time if and only if one physical body has persisted through all the changes; memory is one feature the body carries, not its identity.
Soul theory — the same person persists across time if and only if one immaterial soul has carried through every outer and inner change; memory and body are merely the soul's vehicles.
No-self view — there is no enduring same person from one moment to the next; each moment's self is a fresh bundle of experiences, and felt continuity is a useful illusion of memory.
context: John Locke's Essay Concerning Human Understanding (Book II, ch. 27, 1689) located personal identity in continuity of consciousness — particularly memory. Critics from Reid onward have pressed on memory loss, brave-officer cases, and the partly reconstructed nature of memory.

question: On a podcast on Alzheimer's, a daughter says of her late father: 'Even when he could no longer remember any of us, even his own name, he was still my father. The same body, the same person. Memory just is not what makes someone who they are.' Which view of personal identity is the daughter defending?
answer: Bodily continuity — a person is the same person across time if and only if one physical body (or biological organism) has persisted; memory is something the body has, not what the person IS.
choices: Bodily continuity — a person is the same person across time if and only if one physical body (or biological organism) has persisted; memory is something the body has, not what the person IS.
Memory continuity — the same person persists across time if and only if an unbroken chain of memory connects past and present selves; absence of memory dissolves personal identity here.
Soul theory — the same person persists across time if and only if one immaterial soul has persisted; neither memory nor body settles identity, since both are merely the soul's vehicles.
Narrative identity — the same person persists only if a coherent self-told story connects past and present; identity dissolves where the narrative-telling capacity itself dissolves.
context: Animalism (Eric Olson, The Human Animal, 1997; Paul Snowdon) holds that we are essentially biological organisms, and personal identity is just organismal identity. Bernard Williams's 'The Self and the Future' (1970) pressed memory-transfer cases to defend a bodily criterion.

question: An op-ed describes a teleporter: it scans every atom of the traveler, destroys the original, and assembles an identical copy at the other end. The copy has all the traveler's memories. A philosopher writes: 'The original is dead — what arrives is a perfect duplicate, not the traveler.' Which view of identity is being defended?
answer: Bodily continuity — the same person persists across time if and only if one continuous physical body has persisted; the teleporter breaks that thread, so the copy is a different person.
choices: Bodily continuity — the same person persists across time if and only if one continuous physical body has persisted; the teleporter breaks that thread, so the copy is a different person.
Memory continuity — the same person persists across time if and only if an unbroken chain of memory connects past and present selves; the copy has those memories, so it IS the traveler.
Psychological continuity — the same person persists across time if and only if a strong chain of overlapping mental states persists; the copy inherits all such states from the scan.
Mereological essentialism — the same person persists only if exactly the same parts persist; ordinary aging dissolves identity, so the teleporter is no worse off than any sleep would be.
context: Derek Parfit's Reasons and Persons (1984) made the teleporter and branching-fission cases central to personal identity. Parfit ultimately argued that strict identity is not what matters in survival — psychological continuity is — but the bodily-continuity intuition remains powerful.

question: On a philosophy class debate, a student argues: 'There is no single 'self' that persists through your life. There is just a stream of momentary experiences, each one new, that memory and habit stitch together into a story. The persisting self is a useful fiction.' Which view of personal identity does the student defend?
answer: No-self / bundle view — there is no enduring self that persists across moments; each moment is a fresh bundle of experiences, and felt continuity is a construction memory imposes.
choices: No-self / bundle view — there is no enduring self that persists across moments; each moment is a fresh bundle of experiences, and felt continuity is a construction memory imposes.
Memory continuity — the same person persists across time if and only if an unbroken chain of memory connects past and present selves; the bundles ARE the same person via that thread.
Soul theory — the same person persists across time if and only if one immaterial soul has persisted; felt impermanence is just the outer surface beneath which the soul stands unchanged.
Bodily continuity — the same person persists across time if and only if one biological organism has persisted; the experience stream is what the organism does, not what the person IS.
context: Hume's 'bundle' theory of the self (Treatise of Human Nature, 1739) anticipates the no-self view defended in classical Buddhist philosophy (anatta) and by contemporary philosophers like Mark Siderits. The view dissolves persistence puzzles by denying the persisting subject.

question: A philosophy class debates Theseus's ship: planks are replaced one by one until none of the original wood remains. A student argues: 'It's still the same ship. What makes a ship a ship is its design and function, not the particular wood. Replace one plank or all of them — same ship.' Which principle of identity does the student defend?
answer: Form / functional identity — a thing persists across time if and only if its structure and function persist; the particular matter it is made of is replaceable without disrupting identity.
choices: Form / functional identity — a thing persists across time if and only if its structure and function persist; the particular matter it is made of is replaceable without disrupting identity.
Mereological essentialism — a thing persists across time if and only if exactly the same parts persist; on this view every plank-replacement strictly produces a numerically different ship.
Material identity — a thing persists across time if and only if the same matter persists; the gradual replacement strictly produces a sequence of distinct ships sharing only a name.
Conventional identity — there is no deep fact about sameness; calling the repaired ship 'the same' is a habit of speech with no metaphysical weight one way or the other in this case.
context: Plutarch reports Theseus's ship in Life of Theseus (~75 AD). Hobbes added the reassembled-from-discarded-planks twist in De Corpore (1655) to sharpen the dilemma. Aristotle's distinction between substantial form and matter informs the form-based reply.

question: A metaphysics blog post argues: 'A persisting object is really a four-dimensional whole extended in time the way ordinary objects are extended in space. The 'object now' is just one temporal slice of a longer worm-shaped whole. Time is another dimension the object occupies.' Which view of persistence does this defend?
answer: Four-dimensionalism / perdurance — a persisting object is a four-dimensional whole spread across time; what we encounter at any moment is a temporal part of that whole, like a spatial slice.
choices: Four-dimensionalism / perdurance — a persisting object is a four-dimensional whole spread across time; what we encounter at any moment is a temporal part of that whole, like a spatial slice.
Three-dimensionalism / endurance — a persisting object is wholly present at every moment it exists; there are no 'temporal parts' to objects, only the same object existing again across time.
Stage theory — persisting objects are momentary stages connected by counterpart relations rather than identity; what we call 'the object' is strictly a present stage with a history at hand.
Mereological essentialism — a persisting object is identical across time only if its exact parts persist; gradual change produces a sequence of numerically distinct objects throughout.
context: Four-dimensionalism (David Lewis, On the Plurality of Worlds 1986; Theodore Sider, Four-Dimensionalism 2001) treats persisting objects as 'spacetime worms.' The standard rival is three-dimensionalism or endurantism (Sally Haslanger, E.J. Lowe).

question: On a metaphysics panel, a philosopher pushes back: 'A persisting thing isn't a long four-dimensional worm with a slice for each moment. It's the very same thing, wholly present whenever it exists. The cup on my desk at noon and the cup on my desk at one is the same cup — not two slices of one worm.' Which view does she defend?
answer: Three-dimensionalism / endurance — a persisting object is wholly present at every moment of its existence; there are no temporal parts, only the same object existing at successive times.
choices: Three-dimensionalism / endurance — a persisting object is wholly present at every moment of its existence; there are no temporal parts, only the same object existing at successive times.
Four-dimensionalism / perdurance — a persisting object is a four-dimensional whole; what is at the desk at noon is one temporal part; what is there at one o'clock is a distinct part.
Stage theory — persisting objects are momentary stages connected by counterpart relations rather than identity; the noon-cup and one-o'clock-cup are distinct stages, counterpart-linked.
Bundle theory of objects — an object is a co-located bundle of properties at a time; the noon-cup and one-o'clock-cup are distinct bundles linked by the conventional cup-name applied.
context: Three-dimensionalism / endurantism (E.J. Lowe, A Survey of Metaphysics 2002; Sally Haslanger) holds the common-sense view: persisting things are wholly present at each moment, the way you yourself are wholly here now rather than partly here and partly past.

question: A philosophy of language seminar discusses possible worlds. One participant argues: 'When we say something is possible, we mean it really happens — somewhere. Other possible worlds exist concretely, just like ours. They aren't here, but they are real in the same way our world is real.' Which view of modality is being defended?
answer: Modal realism — possible worlds are concrete realities of the same kind as the actual world; 'possibly P' is true if P is true at some genuinely existing possible world distinct from ours.
choices: Modal realism — possible worlds are concrete realities of the same kind as the actual world; 'possibly P' is true if P is true at some genuinely existing possible world distinct from ours.
Ersatz modal realism — possible worlds are abstract representations (sets of propositions, maximal states of affairs); 'possibly P' is true if some such abstract representation says P at it.
Actualism — only the actual world genuinely exists; possible-world talk is paraphrased as talk about properties of THIS world ('there could have been P' = our world has a P-possibility).
Conventionalism about modality — claims about possibility have no truth-makers in the world; they express the speaker's commitments about what frames of description are intelligible to her.
context: David Lewis's On the Plurality of Worlds (1986) defends extreme modal realism: possible worlds are concrete, with their own inhabitants. The 'incredulous stare' Lewis received from peers is itself part of the literature. Ersatzists (Plantinga, Adams) take worlds as abstract.

question: On a podcast on metaphysics, a philosopher argues: 'There are no other worlds — just THIS world. When we say something is possible, we are saying our actual world has a certain feature: it could have gone differently in the relevant respect. Possibility is a property of how the actual world is.' Which view does she defend?
answer: Actualism — only the actual world genuinely exists; modal talk is paraphrased into claims about properties of the actual world, so 'possibly P' is grounded in something true of THIS world.
choices: Actualism — only the actual world genuinely exists; modal talk is paraphrased into claims about properties of the actual world, so 'possibly P' is grounded in something true of THIS world.
Modal realism — possible worlds are concrete realities of the same kind as the actual world; 'possibly P' is true because P is genuinely the case at some other concretely existing world.
Ersatz modal realism — possible worlds are abstract entities (sets of propositions); they exist as abstracta even though they aren't concrete, and 'possibly P' picks one such abstract world.
Conventionalism about modality — modal claims have no truth-makers in the world; they should be replaced by talk of descriptions and inferential roles, since no fact grounds them.
context: Actualism (Alvin Plantinga, The Nature of Necessity 1974; Robert Stalnaker) is the majority view among contemporary metaphysicians. It typically uses abstract possible worlds as a representational tool while denying that other concrete worlds exist.

question: On a metaphysics seminar, a presenter argues: 'An apple is nothing over and above its redness, its roundness, its sweetness, and so on. There is no underlying 'thing' carrying the properties — the apple just IS the co-located bundle of those properties together at that location.' Which view of objects is the presenter defending?
answer: Bundle theory of objects — an object is nothing but a co-located bundle of properties; there is no underlying substance carrying them, so the apple just IS the bundle of its features.
choices: Bundle theory of objects — an object is nothing but a co-located bundle of properties; there is no underlying substance carrying them, so the apple just IS the bundle of its features.
Substance theory — an object is an underlying substance that BEARS properties; the apple is a thing distinct from its redness, roundness, and sweetness, though those features inhere in it.
Bare-particular theory — an object is a bare propertyless substratum that takes on properties; the apple's redness and roundness are added to a featureless substrate grounding their unity.
Trope theory — properties are themselves particular non-shareable things; the apple is a bundle of such tropes, but unity comes from the tropes' mutual compresence in a single location.
context: Bundle theory has roots in Hume (Treatise 1739) and is defended in contemporary form by L.A. Paul ('Logical Parts,' 2002) and others. The standard rival is substance theory (Lowe). The competing 'bare particular' view tries to keep substance without properties.

question: On a philosophy panel, a guest argues: 'An apple isn't just a collection of properties hanging together. There's a THING there — the apple itself — that HAS those properties. Strip away the redness and the roundness, and the apple loses qualities, but the apple is what was carrying them.' Which view does the guest defend?
answer: Substance theory — an object is an underlying substance that BEARS properties; the apple is a thing distinct from its properties, though it cannot exist without having some properties.
choices: Substance theory — an object is an underlying substance that BEARS properties; the apple is a thing distinct from its properties, though it cannot exist without having some properties.
Bundle theory of objects — an object IS nothing but a co-located bundle of properties; there is no underlying substance to bear them, so the apple just is the collection of its features.
Trope theory — properties are non-shareable particulars and the object is a bundle of property-particulars; there is no substance behind the bundle, just tropes held together by compresence.
Process theory of objects — an object is a temporally extended process rather than a substance; the apple is what is HAPPENING at that location, not a thing distinct from the properties.
context: Substance theory has Aristotelian roots (Categories) and is defended in contemporary form by E.J. Lowe (A Survey of Metaphysics 2002) and Michael Loux. The contrast with bundle theory has been a fixture of metaphysics since Hume pressed the bundle side.

question: On a metaphysics podcast, a guest argues: 'When two apples are both red, they share something — the very same property, redness itself. That shared something is real. Without admitting such shared universals, we cannot explain what the two apples have in common.' Which view about universals is the guest defending?
answer: Realism about universals — properties shared between objects are real entities, repeatable across instances; the redness in one apple is literally the same universal as in the other apple.
choices: Realism about universals — properties shared between objects are real entities, repeatable across instances; the redness in one apple is literally the same universal as in the other apple.
Nominalism — only particulars exist; the two apples share no extra entity, and 'they are both red' just records a similarity relation, or our convention of grouping particulars in language.
Trope theory — each apple has its own non-shareable redness; the two rednesses resemble each other closely but are numerically distinct tropes, not a single shared universal at all.
Conceptualism — shared properties exist only in the mind as concepts; the two apples share nothing in the world, and their 'common redness' is just a concept we have formed of them both.
context: Realism about universals goes back to Plato (Forms) and Aristotle (in re universals). Contemporary defenders include David Armstrong (Universals and Scientific Realism 1978). Nominalists (Quine, Goodman) reject universals; trope theorists (D.C. Williams, Keith Campbell) split the difference.

question: An art critic writes: 'When the sculptor molds a lump of clay into a statue, the statue and the lump exist in the same place at the same time. Smash the statue and you still have the lump. So the statue and the lump must be two different objects, even though they share their matter.' Which metaphysical view is the critic defending?
answer: Constitution view — a statue and the lump that constitutes it are distinct objects sharing matter; they differ in persistence (the lump survives smashing, the statue does not).
choices: Constitution view — a statue and the lump that constitutes it are distinct objects sharing matter; they differ in persistence (the lump survives smashing, the statue does not).
Identity view — the statue just IS the lump arranged statue-wise; they are one object that we describe under two different sortal terms, with no real numerical distinction between the two.
Mereological essentialism — an object is identical across time only if its exact parts persist; the lump and statue have the same parts now, so they are strictly the same object.
Mereological nihilism — neither 'statue' nor 'lump' picks out a genuine object; what exists are only fundamental particles arranged statue-wise, and ordinary-object talk is a useful fiction.
context: The statue/lump puzzle (Lynne Rudder Baker, Persons and Bodies 2000; Kit Fine 2003) presses the question: can two objects share all their matter? Constitution theorists say yes; identity-theorists insist on one object; eliminativists deny there are statues or lumps at all.

question: A philosophy class reads Parfit. One student summarizes his view: 'What matters across time isn't strict identity. It's psychological continuity — overlapping memories, intentions, beliefs, traits, even if the underlying substrate keeps changing. If those carry over, that's what survival comes to.' Which view of personal identity is this?
answer: Psychological continuity — the same person persists across time (or what matters for survival) if there is a strong chain of overlapping mental states; substrate-continuity is not required.
choices: Psychological continuity — the same person persists across time (or what matters for survival) if there is a strong chain of overlapping mental states; substrate-continuity is not required.
Memory continuity (strict Lockean) — identity holds if and only if direct memory connects past and present selves; intentions and beliefs without memory of the source do not preserve it.
Bodily continuity — the same person persists across time if and only if one physical body or biological organism has persisted; mental overlap is irrelevant if the body doesn't continue.
No-self / bundle view — there is no enduring 'same person'; each moment is a fresh bundle of experiences and felt continuity is a useful fiction, so 'what survives' is the wrong question.
context: Derek Parfit (Reasons and Persons, 1984) generalized Locke's memory criterion to a broader 'psychological continuity' — overlapping chains of memories, intentions, personality traits. Parfit's twist: identity itself is not what matters; continuity does.

question: On a philosophy podcast, a guest argues: 'Rivers, fires, and storms aren't really things at all — they are events, processes. We call them objects because language is built for objects, but a river is something that HAPPENS rather than something that IS.' Which view of persistence is the guest defending?
answer: Process metaphysics — what we call 'objects' are really ongoing processes or events; a river is something that happens at a place over time, not a thing that endures at it as stable object.
choices: Process metaphysics — what we call 'objects' are really ongoing processes or events; a river is something that happens at a place over time, not a thing that endures at it as stable object.
Three-dimensionalism / endurance — a persisting object is wholly present at each moment of its existence; the river is a single object that exists fully at each time, not a series of events.
Four-dimensionalism / perdurance — a persisting object is a four-dimensional whole; the river is one extended worm in spacetime, but the worm itself is a thing rather than a process.
Mereological essentialism — a thing persists across time if and only if exactly the same parts persist; rivers strictly fail this and are not persistent objects in the strict sense.
context: Process metaphysics has roots in Heraclitus (~500 BC) and Whitehead (Process and Reality, 1929); contemporary defenders include Johanna Seibt and Nicholas Rescher. The view challenges substance metaphysics by making process basic and object-talk derivative.

question: On a podcast on identity over time, a guest argues: 'What makes me the same person across decades is not memory and not body — both can change drastically. It is the persistence of an immaterial self, distinct from the body, that carries through every outer and inner change.' Which view of personal identity does the guest defend?
answer: Soul theory / substance dualism — the same person persists across time if and only if one immaterial soul has persisted; neither memory nor body settles identity, since both are vehicles.
choices: Soul theory / substance dualism — the same person persists across time if and only if one immaterial soul has persisted; neither memory nor body settles identity, since both are vehicles.
Memory continuity — the same person persists across time if and only if an unbroken chain of memory connects past and present selves; body and any putative soul are inessential to identity.
Bodily continuity — the same person persists across time if and only if one physical body has persisted; appeals to an immaterial self introduce an entity with no worldly evidence at all.
No-self / bundle view — there is no enduring self across moments; each moment is a fresh bundle of experiences, so the postulated immaterial substance is a useful fiction memory imposes.
context: Substance dualism / soul theory (Plato's Phaedo; Descartes's Meditations VI, 1641; Richard Swinburne, The Evolution of the Soul 1986) holds that the person is an immaterial substance. The view is in the minority among contemporary philosophers but remains defended.

question: Newcomb's paradox: Box A holds $1,000 (visible). Box B is opaque. A near-infallible predictor has put $1,000,000 in B if she predicted you'd take only B, or nothing if she predicted you'd take both. A friend insists: 'Take just B — one-boxers leave rich.' Which view is she defending?
answer: Evidential decision theory — the rational choice gives best EVIDENCE of a good outcome; one-boxing correlates with the million, so the rational chooser one-boxes despite causal independence.
choices: Evidential decision theory — the rational choice gives best EVIDENCE of a good outcome; one-boxing correlates with the million, so the rational chooser one-boxes despite causal independence.
Causal decision theory — the rational choice CAUSES the best outcome; since the prediction is already made, two-boxing strictly dominates and is rational however reliable the predictor.
Plain expected-value view — the rational choice has the highest payoff weighted by probability; the answer depends entirely on what reliability the predictor is taken to have.
Deflationist view — the case is incoherent because a near-infallible predictor of a free choice cannot exist; decision theory does not apply to impossible scenarios at all.
context: Newcomb's problem was devised by physicist William Newcomb and made famous by Robert Nozick ('Newcomb's Problem and Two Principles of Choice,' 1969). Evidential vs. causal decision theory (Jeffrey, Lewis, Joyce) split sharply here, with most contemporary causal theorists two-boxing and most one-boxers leaning evidential.

question: A Frankfurt case: Jones decides on his own to vote X. Unknown to him, a brain chip would have FORCED that vote if he'd tried otherwise — but Jones never wavered, so the chip never fired. A philosopher concludes: 'Jones is fully responsible, though he could not have voted differently.' Which view does this defend?
answer: Source-of-action view — responsibility tracks whether the act flows from the agent's own deliberation, not whether alternatives existed; the chip never fired, so the act was Jones's.
choices: Source-of-action view — responsibility tracks whether the act flows from the agent's own deliberation, not whether alternatives existed; the chip never fired, so the act was Jones's.
Alternate-possibilities view — responsibility requires a genuine ability to do otherwise, so Jones is NOT responsible; the chip's presence removes that ability even unfired.
Hard determinism — no one is ever responsible since no one could ever have done otherwise; the chip just dramatizes what holds of every action, so Jones is unremarkable.
Libertarian view — responsibility requires causally undetermined choice, which the chip's existence cancels; Jones cannot be responsible since a sufficient cause was in place.
context: Harry Frankfurt's 'Alternate Possibilities and Moral Responsibility' (Journal of Philosophy, 1969) introduced the case to attack the Principle of Alternate Possibilities (PAP). Critics (Widerker, Kane) defend PAP by arguing Frankfurt cases either smuggle in alternatives or fail to track real deliberation. The case restructured free-will debate.

question: Hume's billiard-balls case dramatized a still-live question: when ball A strikes ball B and B moves, what makes it TRUE that A caused B to move? A contemporary philosopher argues: 'The truth-maker is a counterfactual fact — had A not struck, B would not have moved.' Which theory of causation is the philosopher defending?
answer: Counterfactual theory — 'A caused B' is true because in the closest possible world where A did not occur, B did not occur; causation reduces to counterfactual dependence.
choices: Counterfactual theory — 'A caused B' is true because in the closest possible world where A did not occur, B did not occur; causation reduces to counterfactual dependence.
Regularity theory — 'A caused B' is true because of an exceptionless pattern of A-type events being followed by B-type events; no other worlds are needed beyond the actual.
Powers theory — 'A caused B' is true because of a real causal power in A that produces B; the power is a genuine feature of objects, irreducible to patterns or counterfactuals.
Process theory — 'A caused B' is true because a continuous spatiotemporal process transmits a conserved quantity from A to B; both regularities and counterfactuals are downstream.
context: David Lewis's 'Causation' (Journal of Philosophy, 1973) launched the counterfactual program, now refined by interventionism (Pearl, Woodward). The regularity tradition runs from Hume through J.L. Mackie. Powers theories (Cartwright, Mumford) and process theory (Salmon, Dowe) are the major alternatives. The billiard-ball scenario is still the field's reference case.

question: A wooden ship is repaired over many years by replacing planks one at a time, until no original plank remains. Meanwhile, a craftsman has collected each discarded plank and reassembled them into a second, complete ship. Both have a claim to being the original. The puzzle exposes a tension between two competing principles of identity.
answer: Continuity-of-form vs. continuity-of-matter — the case forces a choice between identity through persisting shape and function (the repaired ship) and identity through original physical stuff (the reassembled ship).
choices: Continuity-of-form vs. continuity-of-matter — the case forces a choice between identity through persisting shape and function (the repaired ship) and identity through original physical stuff (the reassembled ship).

Numerical identity vs. qualitative similarity — the two ships only look alike but cannot both BE the original since identity is one-to-one; the puzzle is a confusion about 'the same' that dissolves once clarified.

Persistence vs. impermanence — the case forces a choice between things genuinely persisting through time and the Buddhist thesis that all apparent persistence is finally illusion, with neither ship really persisting.

Particular vs. universal — the puzzle is really about whether 'a ship' names a particular or a kind; once that ambiguity is stipulated the identity question dissolves and no principle of identity is at stake.
context: Plutarch reports the puzzle in Life of Theseus (~75 AD). Hobbes added the reassembled-ship twist in De Corpore (1655) to sharpen the tension. Modern variants — Parfit's branching-teleporter cases (Reasons and Persons, 1984), Lewis on perdurance — keep the form/matter dilemma alive.

question: A philosopher argues: 'Just as your body extends through space and has spatial parts (hands, feet), it extends through time and has temporal parts (your-yesterday-self, your-today-self). The whole person is the four-dimensional sum of these temporal parts.' Which view of persistence does the philosopher defend?
answer: Perdurantism — Lewis's view that objects have temporal parts and persist by being four-dimensional sums, with the whole spread across time the way a road is spread across space, never wholly present at any one moment.
choices: Perdurantism — Lewis's view that objects have temporal parts and persist by being four-dimensional sums, with the whole spread across time the way a road is spread across space, never wholly present at any one moment.

Endurantism — the rival view that objects are wholly present at each moment they exist, with the same whole persisting through time rather than being composed of temporal stages; the case explicitly rejects this picture.

Presentism — the view that only the present moment exists, so there are no past or future objects to be temporal parts of anything; persistence reduces to identity across the strictly present and tensed grammar.

Stage theory — Sider's refinement on which the object IS the momentary stage, with persistence via counterpart relations across stages; the philosopher speaks of four-dimensional sums, not stages, so the views differ.
context: David Lewis's On the Plurality of Worlds (1986) defends perdurantism. Ted Sider's Four-Dimensionalism (2001) is the modern textbook. Endurantism (E.J. Lowe, Trenton Merricks) holds the rival view. Stage theory (Sider, Hawley) is a perdurantist refinement taking the stage as primary.

question: A teleporter scans you on Earth, transmits the data, and reconstructs an exact duplicate on Mars — but a malfunction also leaves the Earth-original intact. Both duplicates have your memories and physical structure. A philosopher concludes: 'Personal identity is not what matters in survival.' Which view does this defend?
answer: Psychological reductionism (Parfit) — personal identity reduces to psychological continuity, and since continuity branches in fission, what matters in survival is the continuity itself rather than strict identity.
choices: Psychological reductionism (Parfit) — personal identity reduces to psychological continuity, and since continuity branches in fission, what matters in survival is the continuity itself rather than strict identity.

Soul theory (Reid, Swinburne) — personal identity is grounded in a non-physical soul that cannot branch; at most one duplicate has the original's soul, and the other is merely a copy without genuine personhood.

Animalism (Olson) — personal identity is identity of the human animal; the question turns on which biological organism continues, so the Earth-body is you and the Mars-duplicate is merely a psychological copy.

Constitution view (Baker) — persons are constituted by but not identical to bodies, so the case fails until we determine which body stands in the right constituting relation to the original first-person perspective.
context: Derek Parfit's Reasons and Persons (1984) develops the teleporter-fission argument: branching psychological continuity shows identity and what-matters-in-survival are separable. Critics (Olson, The Human Animal, 1997; Baker, Persons and Bodies, 2000) reject the reduction. The debate is unresolved.

question: A metaphysician argues: 'When I say it is possible I could have been a banker, what makes the claim true is a concrete other world — every bit as real as this one — in which a counterpart of me is a banker. Possible worlds are not abstractions; they are existing places.' Which view does she defend?
answer: Modal realism — Lewis's view that possible worlds are concrete maximally-connected wholes existing on a par with the actual world, with 'actual' being merely indexical (this world here, from our standpoint).
choices: Modal realism — Lewis's view that possible worlds are concrete maximally-connected wholes existing on a par with the actual world, with 'actual' being merely indexical (this world here, from our standpoint).

Linguistic ersatzism — Carnap's view that possible worlds are maximal consistent sets of sentences, with modal claims made true by relations among such sets; the metaphysician explicitly rejects this deflationary route.

Combinatorial ersatzism — Armstrong's view that possible worlds are recombinations of actual-world elements, with no need for concrete other places; the metaphysician insists on concrete worlds, not recombinations.

Modal fictionalism — Rosen's view that 'in world w, p' is shorthand for 'according to the modal-realist fiction, p'; the metaphysician disclaims fiction and insists the other worlds are existing places.
context: David Lewis's On the Plurality of Worlds (1986) defends modal realism. The 'incredulous stare' Lewis describes is the standard reaction. Ersatzist alternatives (Plantinga's abstract worlds, Stalnaker's properties, Armstrong's combinations, Rosen's fictionalism) try to keep modal talk without the cost.

question: Two metaphysicians debate the trout-turkey: a putative object composed of the front half of a trout and the back half of a turkey. The first holds it genuinely exists. The second holds only particles exist and 'the trout-turkey' refers to nothing. The puzzle exposes a tension between two competing principles.
answer: Mereological universalism vs. mereological nihilism — universalism (Lewis) says any collection composes an object; nihilism (van Inwagen, almost) says only simples exist and ordinary-object talk paraphrases away.
choices: Mereological universalism vs. mereological nihilism — universalism (Lewis) says any collection composes an object; nihilism (van Inwagen, almost) says only simples exist and ordinary-object talk paraphrases away.

Composition as identity vs. composition as distinctness — whether composed objects are identical to their parts taken collectively; this concerns the composition relation's nature, not whether arbitrary collections compose.

Endurantism vs. perdurantism — whether composed objects persist by being wholly present or by having temporal parts; this concerns persistence rather than the prior question of whether the trout-turkey composes at all.

Realism vs. nominalism about properties — whether universals exist independently of instances; this concerns properties rather than when collections of particulars compose further particulars, the actual issue here.
context: David Lewis (Parts of Classes, 1991) defends universalism: any plurality has a fusion. Peter van Inwagen's Material Beings (1990) defends near-nihilism: only lives compose. Trenton Merricks (Objects and Persons, 2001) defends a fuller nihilist line. The 'special composition question' is van Inwagen's framing.

question: A sculptor shapes a lump of clay into a statue. They share every spatial part at every moment of joint existence. Yet the lump existed before the sculpting and would survive squashing; the statue would not. A metaphysician argues: 'They are distinct objects sharing matter without sharing identity.' Which view does this defend?
answer: Constitution view (Baker, Wiggins) — the statue is constituted by but not identical to the lump, so two distinct objects share matter without sharing identity, since their modal properties differ by Leibniz's law.
choices: Constitution view (Baker, Wiggins) — the statue is constituted by but not identical to the lump, so two distinct objects share matter without sharing identity, since their modal properties differ by Leibniz's law.

Mereological essentialism (Chisholm) — strict identity requires sameness of parts at all times, so the lump existing before the statue means the lump cannot be the statue; one shared object merely gets renamed.

Stage-theoretic identity (Sider) — statue and lump are momentary stages with shared parts, and modal claims are made true by counterpart relations to different stages; modal difference doesn't require distinct present things.

Substance monism (Spinoza) — statue and lump are modes of one underlying substance, so they are not distinct objects but features of a single reality; the distinctness claim mistakes the level of analysis at which objects appear.
context: Lynne Rudder Baker's Persons and Bodies (2000) defends constitution. David Wiggins's Sameness and Substance Renewed (2001) is the classic statement that statue and lump differ in sortal but share matter. Nihilists (Merricks) deny the statue exists; monists handle modal difference without two-thing ontology.

question: A physicist colleague says: 'In relativity, simultaneity is frame-relative — what's present for one observer is past for another. So all moments must be equally real; there is no privileged Now. The universe is a four-dimensional block.' A metaphysician adopts this reasoning. Which view of time does she defend?
answer: Eternalism — all moments are equally real, with 'now' being indexical the way 'here' is indexical for space; time is a fourth dimension and the universe a four-dimensional block, with past and future on a par with the present.
choices: Eternalism — all moments are equally real, with 'now' being indexical the way 'here' is indexical for space; time is a fourth dimension and the universe a four-dimensional block, with past and future on a par with the present.

Presentism — only the present is real; the past has been but no longer exists, the future has not yet come; relativity is a description of measurement rather than ontology, and the block reading overreaches the physics.

Growing-block theory (Broad) — past and present are real but the future is not; reality grows as time passes, with new slices added at the leading edge; the metaphysician treats past and future symmetrically instead.

Time-illusion view (McTaggart's C-series) — temporal becoming is illusory and events form a non-temporal order; the metaphysician retains an ordering of moments as temporal, which McTaggart's stronger conclusion rejects.
context: J.J.C. Smart's 'The River of Time' (1949) connects eternalism to relativity. Arthur Prior (Past, Present, and Future, 1967) is the seminal modern presentist. C.D. Broad (Scientific Thought, 1923) defends growing-block. McTaggart's 1908 paper splits the A-series and B-series of time.

question: Suppose the soul of a prince enters the body of a cobbler, carrying with it the prince's memories and consciousness, while leaving behind the cobbler's body's previous psychological states. A philosopher concludes: 'The resulting person is the prince, not the cobbler — though to neighbors he is the cobbler.' Which view?
answer: Memory continuity (Locke) — personal identity is constituted by continuity of consciousness and memory, so wherever the prince's memories go, the prince goes; body matters for re-identification but not for the metaphysics.
choices: Memory continuity (Locke) — personal identity is constituted by continuity of consciousness and memory, so wherever the prince's memories go, the prince goes; body matters for re-identification but not for the metaphysics.

Animalism (Olson) — personal identity is identity of the human animal, so the person in the cobbler's body is the cobbler; the prince's memories have transferred but the person has not, since persons are organisms.

Soul theory (Reid) — identity is carried by the soul, which the case stipulates transferred; the verdict is right but for the wrong reason, since memory is evidence of soul-transfer, not what constitutes identity.

No-self view (Buddhist anatta) — there is no enduring self to be either prince or cobbler; both appearances are aggregates of impermanent psychological events, so the question rests on a false presupposition.
context: John Locke's Essay Concerning Human Understanding (Book II, ch. 27, 1689) introduces the prince-cobbler case. Reid insists on substance; Parfit replaces identity with continuity. Olson's animalism (The Human Animal, 1997) revives the body-side view. The debate is one of the deepest in personal identity.

question: A philosopher argues: 'Suppose it is indeterminate whether a is identical to b. Then a has the property of being-indeterminately-identical-to-b. But b does not (it is determinately identical to itself). By Leibniz's law, a is not b after all.' This argument targets which metaphysical thesis?
answer: Ontic vagueness about identity — the thesis that identity itself can be genuinely indeterminate, with no fact whether a equals b; Evans concludes this thesis is incoherent, since indeterminate identity violates Leibniz's law.
choices: Ontic vagueness about identity — the thesis that identity itself can be genuinely indeterminate, with no fact whether a equals b; Evans concludes this thesis is incoherent, since indeterminate identity violates Leibniz's law.

Semantic vagueness about identity — the thesis that vagueness lies in language, with 'a is identical to b' indeterminate because our terms are imprecise; Evans does not target this, which keeps determinate identity in reality.

Mereological essentialism — the view that objects have all parts essentially, so identity is determinate once parts are fixed; Evans asks whether identity CAN be vague, not which part-whole story grounds determinate identity.

Counterpart theory (Lewis) — the view that modal claims about an object are about counterparts in other worlds; this is separate from the Evans-Salmon debate about whether actual-world identity admits indeterminacy.
context: Gareth Evans's 'Can There Be Vague Objects?' (1978) — a one-page paper — gives the classical argument against ontic vagueness of identity. Defenders (Parsons, van Inwagen, Akiba) reply by challenging Leibniz's law for indeterminate properties. Nathan Salmon's version (1981) is also widely cited.

question: A philosopher writes: 'I am not literally in any other possible world. When we say I could have been a banker, what is true is that in some other world a counterpart of me — someone resembling me in the relevant respects — is a banker. The actual I am here only.' Which view does this defend?
answer: Counterpart theory (Lewis) — modal claims about an individual are made true by counterparts in other possible worlds rather than by that individual existing in them, with counterpart fixed by relevant resemblance to context.
choices: Counterpart theory (Lewis) — modal claims about an individual are made true by counterparts in other possible worlds rather than by that individual existing in them, with counterpart fixed by relevant resemblance to context.

Trans-world identity (Kripke, Plantinga) — the rival view that individuals can exist in multiple possible worlds, so I myself am a banker in some other world; this is what counterpart theory was developed to reject.

Modal fictionalism (Rosen) — the view that 'in world w, p' is shorthand for 'according to the modal-realist story, p'; this denies the literal existence of other worlds rather than addressing individual re-appearance.

Haecceitism — the view that worlds can differ purely about which individual is which, with no qualitative difference; counterpart theory is anti-haecceitist, while trans-world identity allows haecceitism.
context: David Lewis's 'Counterpart Theory and Quantified Modal Logic' (1968) develops counterpart theory. Saul Kripke's Naming and Necessity (1980) defends trans-world identity with rigid designators. Plantinga's The Nature of Necessity (1974) defends transworld identity within actualism. The choice remains a fundamental fork.

question: A philosopher argues: 'Queen Elizabeth could not have had different biological parents than she in fact had — someone produced from different parents would not be her, however similar in personality and appearance. The origin of an individual is essential to that individual's identity across worlds.' Which view?
answer: Origin essentialism (Kripke) — biological origin is essential to identity, so no being from different parents could be the same individual; this constrains trans-world identity by ruling out different-origin candidates.
choices: Origin essentialism (Kripke) — biological origin is essential to identity, so no being from different parents could be the same individual; this constrains trans-world identity by ruling out different-origin candidates.

Sortal essentialism (Wiggins) — an individual essentially falls under a sortal kind (human, oak, ship) and could not have been of a different kind; this concerns kind-membership across worlds rather than origin-individuation.

Haecceitism — individuals have non-qualitative 'thisness' grounding identity across worlds; this can accept or reject origin essentialism depending on whether thisness is origin-constrained, so it cuts coarser than the case.

Counterpart theory (Lewis) — modal claims involve counterparts rather than identity across worlds; this is compatible with various counterpart relations and treats the claim as a constraint on counterpart relation form.
context: Saul Kripke's Naming and Necessity (1980, Lecture III) gives the origin essentialism argument. Critics (Salmon, Reference and Essence, 1981) press the four-worlds argument: gradual variation in origin can chain a thing to a starkly-different-origin counterpart, threatening transitivity. Defenders restrict the chaining.

question: A neurosurgeon transplants your cerebrum (the seat of psychological continuity) into another body. The recipient body's previous brainstem keeps the original organism alive. A philosopher argues: 'You stay with the body whose brainstem persists, even though your psychology travels.' Which view?
answer: Animalism (Olson) — personal identity is identity of the human animal, with the animal's biological life continuous through the brainstem; psychology can detach without the person detaching, so you go where the animal goes.
choices: Animalism (Olson) — personal identity is identity of the human animal, with the animal's biological life continuous through the brainstem; psychology can detach without the person detaching, so you go where the animal goes.
Psychological continuity (Locke, Parfit) — personal identity is constituted by continuous psychology, so you go with the cerebrum to the other body; the verdict is precisely the one this view denies.

Constitution view (Baker) — persons are constituted by but not identical to organisms, so the question is where the first-person perspective is constituted; the verdict needs additional argument separate from animalism.

Soul theory (Swinburne) — personal identity is grounded in a non-physical soul, which neither transplant nor brainstem-continuity directly tracks; the verdict needs a substantive claim about where the soul follows.
context: Eric Olson's The Human Animal (1997) and What Are We? (2007) defend animalism. The 'too many thinkers' problem (if persons are distinct from animals, both think the same thoughts) is the standard motivation. Critics (Baker, Shoemaker, Parfit) press psychological-continuity intuitions on the case.

question: A metaphysician argues: 'There is no underlying substratum that has properties — to be an object just IS to be the bundle of co-instantiated properties (this red, this round, this hard, all together). Take away every property and nothing is left, not a bare bearer.' Which view does she defend?
answer: Bundle theory (Hume, Russell) — an object is nothing over and above its bundle of co-instantiated properties, with no underlying substratum to bear them; object-identity reduces to identity of property bundles.
choices: Bundle theory (Hume, Russell) — an object is nothing over and above its bundle of co-instantiated properties, with no underlying substratum to bear them; object-identity reduces to identity of property bundles.

Substratum theory (Locke) — properties are borne by an underlying 'something I know not what,' a bare particular distinct from any quality; this is precisely what the metaphysician rejects when she denies a property-less bearer.

Trope theory (Williams, Campbell) — properties themselves are particular (this red here), not universals, and objects are bundles of tropes; this is a bundle theory but adds a particularity thesis bundle theory alone leaves open.

Hylomorphism (Aristotle) — objects are composites of matter and form, with matter as substrate and form as organizing principle; this is a third option distinct from both bundle and bare-substratum theories.
context: Bertrand Russell (Inquiry into Meaning and Truth, 1940) defends a bundle theory of particulars. Hume (Treatise, 1739) gives the classical bundle account. Locke's 'something I know not what' (Essay, II.xxiii) is the canonical statement of substratum theory. Trope theory (D.C. Williams, 1953; Campbell, 1990) is the leading variant.

question: Replace one atom of a statue with a qualitatively identical atom from elsewhere. The statue remains. Repeat 10^25 times. After each step the result is the same statue; after the whole sequence, no original atom remains. A metaphysician says: 'Either no replacement preserves identity, or all do.' The puzzle exposes a tension between two principles.
answer: Identity-preservation under small change vs. identity-preservation under total change — the case forces a choice between accepting each tiny step (which iterates to total replacement) and denying it from the start.
choices: Identity-preservation under small change vs. identity-preservation under total change — the case forces a choice between accepting each tiny step (which iterates to total replacement) and denying it from the start.

Mereological essentialism vs. its negation — whether objects have all parts essentially; this concerns a single thesis about essential parts, not the structural problem of iterated identity-preserving steps that aggregate.

Universalism vs. nihilism about composition — whether arbitrary collections compose at all; this concerns whether the statue exists in the first place rather than whether identity persists through replacement.

Endurantism vs. perdurantism — whether the statue persists by being wholly present or by having temporal parts; both face the puzzle equally, since the question is about qualitative replacement, not temporal structure.
context: The puzzle generalizes the Theseus problem and connects to the sorites paradox (Eubulides, ~4th century BC). Peter Unger ('The Problem of the Many,' 1980) and Roderick Chisholm (Person and Object, 1976, on 'loose and popular' identity) develop modern responses. The structural form is now called a sorites of identity.

question: A philosopher argues: 'When you point at the table, what you literally pick out is a momentary stage — the table-at-this-instant. The four-dimensional whole the table belongs to is not what the demonstrative refers to. Persistence is a relation between stages, not identity of a sum.' Which view does this defend?
answer: Stage theory (Sider, Hawley) — ordinary objects are momentary stages, with persistence explained by a temporal-counterpart relation across stages; this is perdurantist-adjacent but takes the stage as primary.
choices: Stage theory (Sider, Hawley) — ordinary objects are momentary stages, with persistence explained by a temporal-counterpart relation across stages; this is perdurantist-adjacent but takes the stage as primary.

Standard perdurantism (Lewis) — ordinary objects are four-dimensional sums of temporal parts, with the whole sum being what 'the table' picks out; the philosopher rejects this for the stage-as-referent alternative.

Endurantism — ordinary objects are wholly present at each moment, with no temporal parts at all; the commitment to stages and counterpart relations is inconsistent with whole-present persistence at each time.

Eternalism about time — all moments are equally real; this is a thesis about times rather than about what the demonstrative picks out, and both stage theory and perdurantism are eternalist, so this is independent.
context: Ted Sider's Four-Dimensionalism (2001) develops stage theory as a perdurantist refinement. Katherine Hawley's How Things Persist (2001) is the other foundational stage-theoretic work. Standard perdurantism (Lewis, On the Plurality of Worlds, 1986) has the four-dimensional whole as referent. Stage theory shifts it.

question: A metaphysician argues: 'A whole composed of parts is not a further entity over and above the parts taken together — to count the parts and then also the whole is to double-count. The whole IS the parts, taken collectively. Composition is a special kind of identity.' Which view does she defend?
answer: Composition as identity (Baxter, Lewis) — a composite object is literally identical to its parts taken collectively, so counting parts plus whole double-counts; composition just IS the many-one identity relation.
choices: Composition as identity (Baxter, Lewis) — a composite object is literally identical to its parts taken collectively, so counting parts plus whole double-counts; composition just IS the many-one identity relation.

Composition as distinct (van Inwagen) — wholes are entities distinct from their parts, so 'the chair' picks out something further than 'the chair-particles'; this is what the metaphysician explicitly rejects in the argument.

Mereological nihilism (Merricks) — strictly speaking there are no composite objects at all, only simples; this also says no further entity exists, but because the whole doesn't exist rather than by identity to parts.

Mereological universalism (Lewis) — any plurality of objects composes a further object; this is the thesis that composition always occurs, separate from whether the resulting whole is identical to its parts.
context: Donald Baxter ('Identity in the Loose and Popular Sense,' 1988; 'Many-One Identity,' 1988) introduces composition as identity. David Lewis (Parts of Classes, 1991) defends an 'almost' version. Critics (Sider, Yi) press the counting problem: how can many parts and one whole be 'the same'?

question: A philosopher argues: 'When you are bent and then straight, you are not the bent-stage plus the straight-stage. You are wholly bent at t1 and wholly straight at t2 — the very same you. Properties are had AT TIMES, not had simpliciter, and persistence is identity through such changes.' Which view?
answer: Endurantism with time-indexed properties — objects are wholly present at each time and persist by being numerically identical across times, with properties had at times to handle change without temporal parts.
choices: Endurantism with time-indexed properties — objects are wholly present at each time and persist by being numerically identical across times, with properties had at times to handle change without temporal parts.

Endurantism with relations-to-times (Mellor) — the rival endurantist gambit on which properties are fundamentally relations between objects and times rather than had at times; the phrasing is closer to indexing than to relating.

Perdurantism (Lewis) — objects have temporal parts and persistence is mereological rather than identity; the philosopher explicitly rejects the temporal-parts framing by insisting on wholly-present-at-each-time.

Stage theory (Sider) — ordinary objects are momentary stages with counterpart relations across times; the philosopher rejects this when she insists on numerical identity rather than mere counterpart relations.
context: Lewis's problem of temporary intrinsics (On the Plurality of Worlds, 1986) is the canonical challenge for endurantism: how can the same thing be both bent and straight without temporal parts? Time-indexing (van Inwagen, Lowe) is one main reply; relations-to-times (Mellor, Real Time II, 1998) is another.

question: A metaphysician argues: 'There are no other concrete worlds. When we talk about what is possible, we are talking about properties — maximal consistent properties the actual world might have had or could have. These are abstract entities, not concrete places. Only one concrete world is real.' Which view?
answer: Actualism with abstract worlds (Plantinga, Stalnaker) — only the actual world is concrete and possible worlds are abstract entities (properties, propositions) the actual world might have instantiated; modal claims rest on these.
choices: Actualism with abstract worlds (Plantinga, Stalnaker) — only the actual world is concrete and possible worlds are abstract entities (properties, propositions) the actual world might have instantiated; modal claims rest on these.

Modal realism (Lewis) — possible worlds are concrete maximally-connected wholes existing on a par with the actual world; the metaphysician explicitly rejects this when she denies any other concrete worlds at all.

Modal fictionalism (Rosen) — modal claims are made true by what holds according to the modal-realist fiction; the metaphysician takes the abstract worlds as literally existing rather than as features of a fiction.

Combinatorial actualism (Armstrong) — possible worlds are recombinations of actual elements; the metaphysician takes them as abstract entities rather than recombinations, so the abstracta and combinatorial routes diverge.
context: Alvin Plantinga's The Nature of Necessity (1974) defends abstract-worlds actualism. Robert Stalnaker's Inquiry (1984) defends a properties-as-worlds version. The competitor programs are Lewis's concrete modal realism, Armstrong's combinatorialism (1989), and Rosen's fictionalism (1990). All remain active.

question: A contemporary metaphysician argues: 'A statue is not just clay — it is clay arranged statue-wise, with form (the organizing structure) as a real metaphysical component alongside the matter. Neither form alone nor matter alone is the object; the object is the composite.' Which view does she defend?
answer: Hylomorphism (Aristotle, Fine, Koslicki) — ordinary objects are composites of matter and form, with form as a real metaphysical component organizing the matter; the object is the structured combination of both.
choices: Hylomorphism (Aristotle, Fine, Koslicki) — ordinary objects are composites of matter and form, with form as a real metaphysical component organizing the matter; the object is the structured combination of both.

Constitution view (Baker) — the statue is constituted by but not identical to the lump of clay, with statue and lump as distinct objects sharing matter; this differs from hylomorphism by not treating form as a real component.

Mereological universalism (Lewis) — any collection composes an object, so the atoms automatically compose the statue; this is silent on whether the statue has form as a component, so it lives at a different layer of metaphysics.

Bundle theory (Russell) — an object is a bundle of co-instantiated properties; this rejects any underlying matter-substrate, while hylomorphism keeps matter as a real component alongside form, so the views diverge.
context: Aristotle (Metaphysics, Z) develops the original hylomorphic doctrine: substances are matter-form composites. The Neo-Aristotelian revival is led by Kit Fine ('Things and Their Parts,' 1999), Kathrin Koslicki (The Structure of Objects, 2008), and Mark Johnston. The view re-emerged as metaphysicians sought alternatives to bare-substratum and bundle theories.

question: The Cartesian demon is usually read as an EPISTEMIC challenge: maybe a deceiver makes you wrong about everything. A contemporary metaphysician reframes it as a METAPHYSICAL question: is an external world necessary, contingent, or built into the conditions of thought itself? Which view of the world's modal status is she investigating?
answer: Contingent-world view — externality is a contingent feature of our world; a coherent demon-scenario is genuinely possible even if not actual, so externality is not metaphysically necessary.
choices: Contingent-world view — externality is a contingent feature of our world; a coherent demon-scenario is genuinely possible even if not actual, so externality is not metaphysically necessary.

Transcendental-necessity view — externality is a necessary condition of any thinking subject's experience; the demon-scenario is incoherent because doubt itself presupposes the world it tried to fake.
Semantic-externalism view — Putnam-style, the content of 'doubt' depends on real-world reference; the demon hypothesis cannot even be formulated by a thinker located inside that very scenario.
Modal-fictionalism view — talk of demon-worlds is shorthand for a useful fiction with no metaphysical commitment; the question of whether the world is necessary or contingent simply does not arise.
context: Descartes (Meditations, 1641) framed the demon epistemically. The metaphysical reframing — what modal status does externality have? — was sharpened by Kant (Refutation of Idealism, 1787), Putnam (Brains in a Vat, 1981), and modern modal metaphysics (Stalnaker, Chalmers). Each view assigns the demon hypothesis a different modal status: live, impossible, or empty.

question: Nozick's experience machine offers lifelong indistinguishable simulation of any experiences you'd most want — friendship, love, mastery — with no awareness you are plugged in. A philosopher argues: 'Most reflective people refuse, though felt quality inside and outside is identical. The refusal reveals what we VALUE.' Which view of well-being does it support?
answer: Objective-list view — well-being is constituted by goods beyond felt experience (real relationships, real achievement, contact with reality); the refusal shows pleasant experience alone does not exhaust the good life.
choices: Objective-list view — well-being is constituted by goods beyond felt experience (real relationships, real achievement, contact with reality); the refusal shows pleasant experience alone does not exhaust the good life.

Refined hedonism — well-being is still pleasant experience, but the refusal is itself an experiential preference for autonomy and reality; once those count as experiences, hedonism survives the case intact.

Desire-satisfaction view — well-being consists in having one's desires fulfilled; the refusal reflects desires for real-world objects the machine cannot satisfy, but the underlying theory stays experience-relative.

Eliminativist response — the thought experiment is malformed because perfectly indistinguishable simulation is metaphysically impossible; no conclusion about value follows from a scenario that could never be realized.
context: Robert Nozick, Anarchy, State, and Utopia (1974), used the machine to argue against hedonism — the view that pleasant experience is the only intrinsic good. Hedonist replies (Crisp, Feldman) redescribe the refusal as itself experiential. Desire-satisfaction theories (Brandt, Griffin) take a different route. Objective-list views (Parfit, Finnis) accept the refusal at face value.

question: The Ship of Theseus can be read as a Sorites variant: each plank-replacement seems to leave the ship the same, yet a complete series produces a different ship. A philosopher of language argues: 'The puzzle is best resolved by abandoning bivalence — at some plank-counts there is no determinate fact whether the ship is the original.' Which theory of vague identity is she defending?
answer: Degree theory — identity statements take values between fully true and fully false; as planks accumulate, 'this is the original ship' shifts continuously in truth-value rather than flipping at a hidden cutoff.
choices: Degree theory — identity statements take values between fully true and fully false; as planks accumulate, 'this is the original ship' shifts continuously in truth-value rather than flipping at a hidden cutoff.

Supervaluationism — statements are super-true if true on every admissible precise reading and super-false if false on every reading; borderline cases are neither, but bivalence is retained at each precise reading separately.

Epistemicism — bivalence holds throughout and there IS a precise plank-count at which identity flips; the vagueness lies in our knowledge of the cutoff, not in the predicate or in the identity relation itself.

Ship-eliminativism — there are no ships, only planks arranged ship-wise; the identity question presupposes objects the fundamental ontology rejects, so the puzzle dissolves once composition is correctly understood.
context: Reading Theseus as a Sorites variant (Unger, 1979; Williamson, 1994) links identity puzzles to the wider vagueness literature. Degree theory (Smith, Edgington) abandons bivalence; supervaluationism (Fine, 1975) saves it at precisifications; epistemicism (Sorensen, Williamson) saves it absolutely. Eliminativist mereologies (Van Inwagen, Sider) dissolve the puzzle.

question: Hungry after school, Mia decides to make a sandwich. Her brother asks, 'What part of you actually decided?' Mia says, 'ME — my brain and body work as one. The whole me decided.' Which view of mind is Mia defending?
answer: Whole-person view — brain and body work together as one agent; the decision belongs to YOU, not one organ.
choices: Whole-person view — brain and body work together as one agent; the decision belongs to YOU, not one organ.
Brain-only view — every choice you make is just neurons firing; your brain alone does the deciding for you.
Soul view — an immaterial soul makes your choices and uses the brain and body to carry them out.
No-mind view — 'deciding' is just a folk story; chemistry runs the action and we narrate it after the fact.
context: Whole-person agency runs from Aristotle through modern philosophy of action. The intuition: choices belong to the unified person, not a part. Brain-only and no-mind views push back; soul view goes the other direction.

question: Sam stubs his toe and yells. His dad asks, 'Where was the pain?' Sam shrugs: 'In my brain. Pain is just what the brain does when nerves fire — nothing else is needed.' Which view of mind is Sam defending?
answer: Brain-only view — every thought and feeling is just brain activity; nothing else is needed to explain pain.
choices: Brain-only view — every thought and feeling is just brain activity; nothing else is needed to explain pain.
Whole-person view — pain belongs to the whole person; brain, nerves, and body together register the hurt.
Soul view — pain is felt by an immaterial soul; the brain only relays signals from the body to the soul.
Mystery view — pain feels like something real, but how brain activity produces that feeling is still unsolved.
context: Brain-only views (the identity theory, modern physicalism) say mental states ARE brain states — same thing, two names. Rivals object that this leaves out what pain FEELS like, not just the firing pattern behind it.

question: A Sunday school teacher tells the class, 'Your thinking and feeling come from your soul. The brain is the tool the soul uses, like a hand uses a pencil.' Which view of mind is the teacher defending?
answer: Soul view — an immaterial soul does the thinking and feeling; the brain is the tool the soul works through.
choices: Soul view — an immaterial soul does the thinking and feeling; the brain is the tool the soul works through.
Brain-only view — thoughts and feelings are just brain activity; there is no separate immaterial soul at work.
Whole-person view — thinking and feeling belong to the whole person; brain and body act together as one.
No-mind view — talk of 'thinking and feeling' is folk talk; only chemistry and behavior are really happening.
context: Soul views (Plato, Descartes, much of religious tradition) hold mind and body as distinct kinds of thing. The pencil image captures dualism's intuition: the soul USES the body but isn't identical to it.

question: A coach tells Lina, 'I can't see your feelings inside — I just see what you DO. If you act brave on the field, you ARE brave. Bravery isn't some hidden thing.' Which view of mind is the coach defending?
answer: Behaviorism — mind is what you DO; talk of hidden inner states is empty unless it cashes out in behavior.
choices: Behaviorism — mind is what you DO; talk of hidden inner states is empty unless it cashes out in behavior.
Soul view — bravery lives in the soul; what you do on the field is the soul's choice working through the body.
Brain-only view — bravery is a brain pattern; what we see on the field is the outward sign of that pattern.
Whole-person view — bravery belongs to the whole person; brain, body, and action are one in being brave.
context: Behaviorism (Ryle's 'ghost in the machine' critique, Skinner in psychology) treated talk of hidden inner states with suspicion. The cost: it has trouble making room for PAIN — which feels like more than wincing.

question: Watching a chatbot reply, Theo's older brother says, 'There's no MIND in there — just patterns and outputs. Even your own 'mind' is just chemistry; the word is a story.' Which view of mind is his brother defending?
answer: No-mind view — talk of 'mind' is folk story; only chemistry and outputs are really happening underneath.
choices: No-mind view — talk of 'mind' is folk story; only chemistry and outputs are really happening underneath.
Brain-only view — minds ARE brains; chemistry is real, and 'mind' just renames what brain activity is.
Mystery view — minds feel real but how chemistry makes feelings is unsolved; the puzzle is open.
Soul view — chatbots have no soul, so no mind, but humans have souls that do the real thinking.
context: Eliminativism (Churchland) holds folk-psychology terms like 'belief' and 'mind' don't pick out real things — future science may replace them entirely. Most philosophers disagree, but it remains a live view.

question: Uncle Joe tells Nora, 'I know your nose sends signals to your brain when Grandma bakes cookies — but how those signals turn into the SMELL you love is still a real puzzle.' Which view of mind is Uncle Joe defending?
answer: Mystery view — feelings and smells are real, but how the brain produces them from signals is still unsolved.
choices: Mystery view — feelings and smells are real, but how the brain produces them from signals is still unsolved.
Brain-only view — the smell IS the brain activity; there is no further puzzle once you know the brain state.
Soul view — the smell is felt by an immaterial soul; the brain only delivers signals for the soul to enjoy.
Behaviorism — what we call 'smelling' is just sniffing and reacting; there is no inner smell to explain.
context: The 'hard problem of consciousness' (Chalmers, 1995) names exactly Uncle Joe's puzzle: even a complete story of nerves and brain activity wouldn't, on its own, explain why anything is FELT at all.

question: A robot toy droops and whines. Ada's cousin says, 'If it ACTS sad — droops, slows down — then it IS sad. There's nothing more to being sad than behaving sadly.' Which view of mind is her cousin defending?
answer: Behaviorism — being sad just IS acting sad; nothing extra inside needs adding to the outward behavior.
choices: Behaviorism — being sad just IS acting sad; nothing extra inside needs adding to the outward behavior.
Soul view — only beings with souls can really be sad; the robot is acting, with no soul behind the act.
Brain-only view — sadness is a brain state; without a brain producing it, the robot can mimic, not feel.
Mystery view — whether the robot is sad turns on whether anything is FELT, and that question is open.
context: Behaviorism's challenge from robots: if a thing perfectly mimics sad behavior, the behaviorist must call it sad. Critics use this against the view — perfect mimicry without inner life still seems to fall short.

question: A parrot copies sentences perfectly. Grandma tells Ravi, 'It TALKS but doesn't UNDERSTAND — only beings with a soul really mean what they say. The parrot has no soul.' Which view of mind is Grandma defending?
answer: Soul view — real understanding takes an immaterial soul; without one, copied sentences carry no meaning.
choices: Soul view — real understanding takes an immaterial soul; without one, copied sentences carry no meaning.
Brain-only view — understanding is brain activity; the parrot's brain isn't built to process meaning that way.
Behaviorism — understanding just IS using sentences correctly; the parrot copies, but can't use them right.
No-mind view — talk of 'understanding' is folk story; only sound-making and reactions are happening here.
context: Soul-based views often draw the human/animal line at understanding, not just behavior. Critics ask: how would you tell, from the outside, whether something has a soul? The view stays alive in religious philosophy.

question: Asked where dreams happen, Maya's older sister says, 'In the brain. Dreams are just brain activity during sleep — there's nowhere else for them to be.' Which view of mind is Maya's sister defending?
answer: Brain-only view — every mental event, including dreams, is just brain activity; no other place is needed.
choices: Brain-only view — every mental event, including dreams, is just brain activity; no other place is needed.
Soul view — dreams happen to an immaterial soul; the brain only sets the stage during sleep, not the dream.
Whole-person view — dreams happen to the whole sleeping person; brain, body, and rest combine to make them.
Mystery view — dreams are clearly real, but how the brain makes the FELT experience of one is still open.
context: The brain-only answer is the standard scientific picture. Rivals push back not by denying brain activity but by asking whether brain activity alone EXPLAINS what dreaming feels like from the inside.

question: After Kai says 'I freely chose chocolate,' his older friend says, 'Choice is a story. Atoms moved; you narrate. There's no inner 'chooser' apart from chemistry.' Which view of mind is the friend defending?
answer: No-mind view — talk of an inner 'chooser' is folk story; only chemistry runs, and the chooser is added later.
choices: No-mind view — talk of an inner 'chooser' is folk story; only chemistry runs, and the chooser is added later.
