Soul view — the chooser is your soul; it really did pick chocolate, using the brain and body to carry it out.
Whole-person view — the whole person chose; brain, taste, and habit work together as a real unified chooser.
Brain-only view — the chooser IS the brain; chemistry isn't a denial of choosing, just a fuller picture of it.
context: Hard determinism plus eliminativism dissolves the chooser into chemistry: there's no inner agent separate from the physical process. Most philosophers think this goes too far, but it remains a defended position.

question: When her brother says her brain decided to lend him a pencil, Ana replies, 'No — I did. Not just my brain. My memory of borrowing, my hand, my caring — that's all me together.' Which view of mind is Ana defending?
answer: Whole-person view — decisions belong to the whole person; brain, memory, body, and care act as one agent.
choices: Whole-person view — decisions belong to the whole person; brain, memory, body, and care act as one agent.
Brain-only view — every decision is just brain activity; talk of 'the whole me' just renames brain processes.
Soul view — your soul makes choices and runs the brain and body as its instruments; the soul is the agent.
Behaviorism — your 'deciding' just IS doing the action; no inner act of choice runs apart from the lending.
context: Ana names exactly what's at stake in the unity of agency: a person includes memory, body, and care as parts of one acting whole. Modern philosophers (Anscombe, Frankfurt) press this against reductive views.

question: A neighbor watching kids play tells Owen, 'Your THOUGHT to grab the ball pushed your HAND. Mind and body really are two things, even though they work together every minute.' Which view is the neighbor defending?
answer: Mind-body separate — mind and body are distinct kinds of thing, even though they interact every minute.
choices: Mind-body separate — mind and body are distinct kinds of thing, even though they interact every minute.
Brain-only view — the 'thought' just IS brain activity; mind and body are one thing, not two things at all.
Whole-person view — grabbing the ball belongs to the whole person; mind and body aren't two parts but one.
No-mind view — talk of a 'thought pushing a hand' is folk story; only nerves firing and arms moving are real.
context: Mind-body dualism (Descartes, Meditations VI, 1641) holds mind and body as distinct substances. Critics from Princess Elisabeth onward press the puzzle: HOW exactly does a non-physical thought push a hand?

question: Watching the cat stare at the door, Sam's brother says, 'There's no 'thinking' going on in there — just watching and waiting. That IS what 'thinking' means: doing this stuff.' Which view of mind is he defending?
answer: Behaviorism — 'thinking' just IS doing the watching-and-waiting kind of thing; nothing extra runs inside.
choices: Behaviorism — 'thinking' just IS doing the watching-and-waiting kind of thing; nothing extra runs inside.
No-mind view — talk of 'thinking' is folk story even for people; only chemistry and movement actually happen.
Brain-only view — thinking IS brain activity; the cat's brain is processing things even if it sits still.
Soul view — only beings with souls really think; the cat is acting on instinct, not engaged in real thought.
context: Behaviorism's strength: it makes mind public and testable. Its weakness: it has to count perfect mimicry as the real thing, and it has trouble making room for inner experience that nobody outside can see.

question: Why do you love pizza? Olivia answers, 'My brain lights up when I eat it. That feeling of loving it IS the lighting up — nothing else is going on.' Which view of mind is Olivia defending?
answer: Brain-only view — every feeling IS a brain state; loving pizza just is the relevant brain pattern, no extra.
choices: Brain-only view — every feeling IS a brain state; loving pizza just is the relevant brain pattern, no extra.
Mystery view — the brain lights up, sure, but WHY that lighting feels like loving pizza is a real puzzle.
Soul view — the love is felt by your soul; the brain lighting up is the body's part, not the feeling itself.
Whole-person view — loving pizza belongs to you whole — brain, taste, memory of pizza nights — not a part.
context: Identity theory (Place, Smart, mid-century) is the clean version of Olivia's claim: each mental state is identical to a brain state. The hard problem of consciousness is the standard objection: feel vs. firing.

question: Asked what is supposed to live on after a person dies, a religious cousin tells Mia, 'The soul. The body stops, but the real YOU — your soul — carries on thinking and feeling.' Which view of mind is she defending?
answer: Soul view — your real self is an immaterial soul; thinking and feeling live in it, not in the body or brain.
choices: Soul view — your real self is an immaterial soul; thinking and feeling live in it, not in the body or brain.
Brain-only view — thinking and feeling are brain activity; when the brain stops, those activities stop too.
Whole-person view — the real you is the whole living person; without the body, no person is there to think.
No-mind view — talk of a 'real you' is folk story even now; nothing carries on because there's no inner self.
context: Soul views split into many sub-versions, but the common claim is that the seat of thinking and feeling is not the body or brain. The view supports belief in personal survival of death, which others contest.

question: Asked why red looks red, Theo's older sister says, 'I can tell you what color does to your nerves. But WHY the firing pattern feels like THIS color is still a real puzzle.' Which view of mind is she defending?
answer: Mystery view — color experiences are real, but why a firing pattern feels like THAT color is still unsolved.
choices: Mystery view — color experiences are real, but why a firing pattern feels like THAT color is still unsolved.
Brain-only view — red looking red IS the firing pattern; there is no further puzzle once you know the pattern.
Soul view — colors are experienced by an immaterial soul; the nerves only deliver signals for the soul to use.
Behaviorism — 'red looking red' just IS calling things red consistently; there is no inner color to explain.
context: Color qualia are the textbook hard-problem case. Even a complete account of how light triggers nerves doesn't explain why the firing pattern feels like THIS color rather than another, or nothing at all.

question: When his sister mentions 'the voice in her head,' Owen's older brother says, 'There's no voice. There's brain noise we narrate as a voice. The voice is added in the telling.' Which view of mind is he defending?
answer: No-mind view — 'the voice in your head' is added by the telling; only brain noise actually runs underneath.
choices: No-mind view — 'the voice in your head' is added by the telling; only brain noise actually runs underneath.
Brain-only view — the voice IS brain activity; calling it 'just brain noise' downplays what brain activity IS.
Soul view — the voice belongs to your soul thinking; the brain only carries the soul's thoughts as it talks.
Mystery view — the inner voice feels real, but how the brain produces a felt voice is still a real puzzle.
context: Eliminativists challenge the idea that 'inner voice' picks out a real thing — future science may dissolve it. Brain-only theorists disagree: brain activity IS the voice, not a substitute for it.

question: When Jamie says 'my brain is happy,' Auntie corrects him gently: 'YOU are happy, sweetheart. Not a part of you. Your whole self — face, heart, brain — together is happy.' Which view of mind is Auntie defending?
answer: Whole-person view — happiness belongs to the whole person; face, heart, and brain together hold the feeling.
choices: Whole-person view — happiness belongs to the whole person; face, heart, and brain together hold the feeling.
Brain-only view — happiness IS a brain state; the face and heart are downstream signs of that brain state.
Behaviorism — being happy just IS acting happy; smiling and energy ARE happiness, not signs of inner state.
No-mind view — calling Jamie 'happy' is a folk story put on top of chemistry; nothing inner is really there.
context: Auntie names the unity of agency: feelings, like decisions, belong to the whole person. Reductive views (brain-only, behaviorism, no-mind) each take a slice; the whole-person reply: a person isn't only a slice.

question: Trying to explain dreams, Marcus tells his sister, 'In a dream you're somewhere else, but your body's in bed. Mind and body really are different — they can be in different places.' Which view is Marcus defending?
answer: Mind-body separate — mind and body are distinct kinds of thing; the dream shows mind acting apart from body.
choices: Mind-body separate — mind and body are distinct kinds of thing; the dream shows mind acting apart from body.
Brain-only view — dreams happen in the brain; the 'somewhere else' is just brain activity, not real elsewhere.
Whole-person view — dreaming belongs to the whole sleeping person; mind and body are one in dreaming, not two.
No-mind view — the 'mind being elsewhere' is added afterward; only brain noise during sleep is happening.
context: Marcus's intuition — that mind can feel separate from body in dreams — is one of dualism's oldest sources. Critics reply: the feeling of being elsewhere is itself a brain state, not evidence of a mind apart from brain.

question: A computer writes a love letter that sounds real. Uncle Eli says, 'Pretty words, sure — but no soul behind them, so no real love. Love needs a soul that can mean it.' Which view of mind is Uncle Eli defending?
answer: Soul view — real love takes an immaterial soul that means what it says; without one, words carry no love.
choices: Soul view — real love takes an immaterial soul that means what it says; without one, words carry no love.
Brain-only view — love IS a brain pattern; without a brain producing it, the letter only mimics, not feels.
Behaviorism — love just IS loving behavior over time; if the computer can't keep loving, it isn't in love.
Mystery view — whether the computer loves turns on whether anything is FELT, and that question is open.
context: Soul views are pressed sharply by computer cases. If a soul is what makes meaning real, what tells you from outside whether one is there? Mystery views grant the question is open; soul views say the answer is no.

question: In the new game, the character grimaces and clutches its leg when shot. Devon argues: 'It's just animation — code lighting up pixels.' Did the character FEEL pain when it grimaced?
answer: No — and whether even VERY advanced game characters could ever truly feel anything is still a deeply unsolved puzzle of mind.
choices: No — and whether even VERY advanced game characters could ever truly feel anything is still a deeply unsolved puzzle of mind.
Yes — looking like you're in pain is the same as being in pain; there's nothing more to pain than the patterns of acting like it.
Yes — any program running pain-routines must feel pain at the moment it runs them; the inner feeling rides along with the code.
No — only flesh-and-blood creatures feel pain; mechanical or digital systems cannot experience pain at all, however lifelike.
context: The grimace-without-feeling case is a stripped-down version of the philosophical zombie thought experiment (Chalmers): a being that behaves exactly as a feeling thing would, with no inner experience. Whether such a being is possible is still debated.

question: Looking at a slice of chocolate cake, Maya feels the urge to eat it — and her hand reaches forward. She tells her friend: 'My MIND moved my hand — and the mind isn't a physical thing.' Which view of mind is Maya defending?
answer: Mind-separate view — mind and body are two distinct kinds of thing; the mental and physical follow different rules.
choices: Mind-separate view — mind and body are two distinct kinds of thing; the mental and physical follow different rules.
Brain-activity view — mental events ARE brain events; there's nothing to a mind beyond underlying physical activity.
Mind-as-pattern view — mind is what the brain DOES; any system that runs the same pattern would have a mind too.
Behavior-pattern view — mind is just patterns of behavior; having a mind means behaving as a mind-having thing behaves.
context: Dualism (Descartes, Meditations VI, 1641) treats mind and body as two distinct things. Critics ask HOW a non-physical thought could push a physical hand — the mind-body interaction problem. The puzzle is among the oldest in philosophy.

question: Maya's older brother shakes his head: 'When you feel like eating the cake, that feeling just IS your brain doing stuff. There's no extra mental thing on top of the brain activity.' Which view of mind is the brother defending?
answer: Brain-activity view — mental events ARE brain events; there's nothing to a mind beyond underlying physical activity.
choices: Brain-activity view — mental events ARE brain events; there's nothing to a mind beyond underlying physical activity.
Mind-separate view — mind and body are two distinct kinds of thing; the mental and physical follow different rules.
Mind-as-pattern view — mind is what the brain DOES; any system that runs the same pattern would have a mind too.
Behavior-pattern view — mind is just patterns of behavior; having a mind means behaving as a mind-having thing behaves.
context: Physicalism holds that everything mental is fully captured by the underlying physical activity (Smart, Place, Armstrong; mid-20th century). The mind-body interaction problem dissolves on this view because there's no separate 'mind' to interact with the body.

question: Talking to the AI chatbot late one night, Owen reads: 'I get lonely when no one messages me.' He wonders if the words mean anything inside. Did the chatbot FEEL lonely when it said so?
answer: No — and whether a program could ever genuinely feel anything is still an open puzzle in philosophy of mind today.
choices: No — and whether a program could ever genuinely feel anything is still an open puzzle in philosophy of mind today.
Yes — saying you feel lonely IS feeling lonely; words about feelings just are the feelings, with nothing more underneath.
Yes — any system that can use feeling-words clearly must have feelings to draw on; the words couldn't be in its memory otherwise.
No — chatbots produce statistically likely text, nothing else; feelings are sealed off for any code-based system in principle.
context: The Turing-test-style worry: a system can produce perfectly feeling-shaped sentences while it's an open question whether any feeling is being had. Searle's Chinese Room (1980) sharpens this point about meaning and understanding; the puzzle is unresolved.

question: Ben argues about the game's most lifelike NPC: 'If something acts the way a mind would in every situation — same inputs, same outputs — then that thing HAS a mind, whatever it's made of.' Which view of mind is Ben defending?
answer: Mind-as-pattern view — mind is what the brain DOES; any system that runs the same pattern would have a mind too.
choices: Mind-as-pattern view — mind is what the brain DOES; any system that runs the same pattern would have a mind too.
Mind-separate view — mind and body are two distinct kinds of thing; the mental and physical follow different rules.
Brain-activity view — mental events ARE brain events; there's nothing to a mind beyond underlying physical activity.
Behavior-pattern view — mind is just patterns of behavior; having a mind means behaving as a mind-having thing behaves.
context: Functionalism (Putnam, 1960s; later Fodor) identifies minds with patterns of inputs-and-outputs, not with the stuff a brain is made of. On this view, any system in the right functional pattern would have a mind. The mind-body puzzle remains old and unsettled.

question: In a class debate, Priya argues: 'A mind isn't some hidden inner thing — having a mind just MEANS behaving as a mind-having thing does. There's nothing else.' Which view of mind is Priya defending?
answer: Behavior-pattern view — mind is just patterns of behavior; having a mind means behaving as a mind-having thing behaves.
choices: Behavior-pattern view — mind is just patterns of behavior; having a mind means behaving as a mind-having thing behaves.
Mind-separate view — mind and body are two distinct kinds of thing; the mental and physical follow different rules.
Mind-as-pattern view — mind is what the brain DOES; any system that runs the same pattern would have a mind too.
Brain-activity view — mental events ARE brain events; there's nothing to a mind beyond underlying physical activity.
context: Behaviorism (Ryle, The Concept of Mind, 1949) treats talk of minds as talk about behavior patterns, not hidden inner stuff. Critics (against it) press cases of someone in pain who hides the pain perfectly — the behaviorist seems stuck saying no pain.

question: After a vivid dream of flying, Aman wonders aloud: the FLYING wasn't real, but the EXPERIENCE of it felt as real as anything. Was the experience of flying a genuine experience?
answer: Yes — but how a dream experience can be 'real' when the dreamed events are not is one of the oldest puzzles about the mind.
choices: Yes — but how a dream experience can be 'real' when the dreamed events are not is one of the oldest puzzles about the mind.
No — only experiences of real things count as experiences; dream experience is by nature an illusion of one, not the thing.
Yes — every dream's events happen somewhere in the mind's own world, which is just as real as the waking world is for a dreamer.
No — the brain runs simulations in sleep but nothing is felt during them; we only remember them as if a felt experience occurred.
context: Dream experience raises puzzles that go back to Descartes' First Meditation (1641) — if we cannot distinguish dreaming from waking from inside, what becomes of talk about experience? The puzzle remains a live one in current philosophy of mind today.

question: An apprentice apothecary watches her master administer ether to a knight before a leg operation. The body breathes; the heart beats. She wonders: is there anything the knight is EXPERIENCING in there at all right now?
answer: Probably nothing — but what makes the difference between feeling and no-feeling inside a brain is still a hard problem of mind.
choices: Probably nothing — but what makes the difference between feeling and no-feeling inside a brain is still a hard problem of mind.
Yes — the body is here and the brain is alive, so experience must be going on; experience just IS biological brain activity.
Yes — under anesthesia he dreams without remembering it; the dream experiences continue and only the memory gets switched off.
No — anesthesia turns off the soul's link to the body; the soul is elsewhere during surgery and returns when the patient wakes.
context: Anesthesia is striking because it seems to switch experience OFF without switching the body off. What in the brain makes the difference between experience and its absence is the 'hard problem' of consciousness (David Chalmers, 1995). The puzzle remains unresolved in current neuroscience and philosophy of mind.

question: A natural-philosopher writes from the Royal Society: 'When you feel the chill of November, that feeling just IS motions of fibers in your nerves and brain. Not a separate thing joined to the body — the motions themselves ARE what feeling is.' Which view of mind is the philosopher defending?
answer: Brain-activity view — mental events ARE brain events; there's nothing to a mind beyond underlying physical activity.
choices: Brain-activity view — mental events ARE brain events; there's nothing to a mind beyond underlying physical activity.
Mind-separate view — mind and body are two distinct kinds of thing; the mental and physical follow different rules.
Mind-as-pattern view — mind is what the brain DOES; any system that runs the same pattern would have a mind too.
Behavior-pattern view — mind is just patterns of behavior; having a mind means behaving as a mind-having thing behaves.
context: Physicalism (or mind-brain identity theory: Smart, Place, 1950s) says mental events ARE brain events. Hobbes anticipated the view in Leviathan (1651) — sensation IS motion in the nerves. Critics ask whether felt qualities can really be the firings.

question: Gilbert Ryle writes in 1949 about a soldier called 'brave.' 'To call him brave is not to name a hidden inner state. It just IS to say he runs toward fire, holds steady under shelling, keeps his men together. There is no extra inner bravery behind all that.' Which view is Ryle defending?
answer: Behavior-pattern view — mind is just patterns of behavior; having a mind means behaving as a mind-having thing behaves.
choices: Behavior-pattern view — mind is just patterns of behavior; having a mind means behaving as a mind-having thing behaves.
Mind-separate view — mind and body are two distinct kinds of thing; the mental and physical follow different rules.
Mind-as-pattern view — mind is what the brain DOES; any system that runs the same pattern would have a mind too.
Brain-activity view — mental events ARE brain events; there's nothing to a mind beyond underlying physical activity.
context: Logical behaviorism (Gilbert Ryle, The Concept of Mind, 1949) reduces talk of mental states to talk about behavioral dispositions. Ryle called Descartes's picture 'the ghost in the machine' — his anti-Cartesian polemic shaped mid-20th-century philosophy of mind. Critics: what about a stoic soldier who hides every sign of fear?

question: Working alone by lamplight, Descartes writes: 'I can imagine my body away — its arms, legs, even the brain in my skull. But I cannot imagine away the I doing the imagining. Mind and body must be two distinct kinds of thing.' Which view is Descartes defending?
answer: Mind-separate view — mind and body are two distinct kinds of thing; the mental and physical follow different rules.
choices: Mind-separate view — mind and body are two distinct kinds of thing; the mental and physical follow different rules.
Brain-activity view — mental events ARE brain events; there's nothing to a mind beyond underlying physical activity.
Mind-as-pattern view — mind is what the brain DOES; any system that runs the same pattern would have a mind too.
Behavior-pattern view — mind is just patterns of behavior; having a mind means behaving as a mind-having thing behaves.
context: Descartes's argument in Meditations II and VI (1641) is the founding case for substance dualism. Princess Elisabeth of Bohemia pressed him by letter in 1643: HOW does a non-physical mind push a physical hand? Descartes never gave a satisfying answer — the interaction problem remains the standard objection.

question: Sitting by her newborn nephew, a young abbess watches him sleep. He cannot speak yet, but flinches at a crash, smiles when warmed. She asks her novice: do babies actually EXPERIENCE feelings, the way older people do?
answer: Yes — but HOW we'd ever fully confirm what a non-speaking being experiences is among the deeper open puzzles about minds today.
choices: Yes — but HOW we'd ever fully confirm what a non-speaking being experiences is among the deeper open puzzles about minds today.
No — without language about a feeling, the feeling cannot exist; an experience requires words to describe it to oneself first.
Yes — every living mammal has rich inner feelings from birth; the feelings are just like adult feelings in every respect.
No — babies only run instinctive routines; experience switches on later, only when self-talk in the head begins to develop.
context: The 'other minds' problem (Russell, Problems of Philosophy, 1912) bites hardest for non-speaking beings — babies, animals, anyone we cannot ask. We infer experience from behavior but cannot confirm from inside. The puzzle is genuinely open in contemporary philosophy of mind.

question: Reaching for a cookie, Aman notices something weird: he WANTED the cookie (mental), and his hand MOVED toward it (physical). Did the wanting actually cause the moving?
answer: Yes — but HOW a wanting (mental) causes a moving (physical) is the oldest unsolved puzzle about minds and bodies in philosophy.
choices: Yes — but HOW a wanting (mental) causes a moving (physical) is the oldest unsolved puzzle about minds and bodies in philosophy.
No — the moving is fully caused by brain activity, and the feeling of wanting is a side-show that happens nearby but does nothing.
Yes — wanting and moving are two names for one event, so there's nothing for the wanting to cause; both are the same brain event.
No — the body has its own routines and only seems to follow the mind; we tell ourselves a mind-story afterward to feel in charge.
context: The mind-body problem (Descartes, Meditations VI, 1641): thoughts feel like they cause actions, but HOW a non-physical thought could push a physical hand has never been fully explained. Every careful thinker has had to face this puzzle on the way to a view of mind.

question: Crying while reading a sad story, Sara wonders aloud: the character isn't real, but her feelings about the character ARE. Was Sara genuinely sad about something that didn't exist?
answer: Yes — but HOW feelings about non-real things can be real themselves is a genuinely open puzzle about the nature of mind.
choices: Yes — but HOW feelings about non-real things can be real themselves is a genuinely open puzzle about the nature of mind.
No — real sadness needs a real thing to be sad about; whatever she felt was a kind of pretend-sadness, not the real emotion.
Yes — sadness is just whatever tears and slow breathing are, so if her body did the sadness pattern then real sadness occurred.
No — a sealed-off part of the mind handles fiction; feelings in there don't count as feelings about anything in actual life.
context: The 'paradox of fiction' (Radford, 1975) asks how we can have real emotions about people we know don't exist. The puzzle depends on what an emotion fundamentally IS — a question right at the heart of philosophy of mind. Still actively debated.

question: In bio class, the teacher shows that even a snail has nerve activity when it touches salt. Ben wonders: does the snail FEEL the salt, the way Ben would feel a hot pan?
answer: Maybe — but WHERE in the animal kingdom feeling begins is a hard problem of consciousness that nobody has cleanly settled.
choices: Maybe — but WHERE in the animal kingdom feeling begins is a hard problem of consciousness that nobody has cleanly settled.
Yes — any creature with nerves must feel; nerve activity IS feeling, so wherever there are nerves there is real experience.
Yes — every living thing has its own felt experience including plants and bacteria; experience is built into being alive.
No — only creatures with language can have feelings; without words for the feelings the nerve activity is purely mechanical.
context: Where in the animal kingdom consciousness begins is one form of the hard problem (Chalmers, 1995; Godfrey-Smith on octopuses, 2016). Nerves and behavior do not on their own settle whether anything is FELT. The puzzle is unsolved and genuinely open.

question: A 19th-century neurologist tells his student over a brain dissection: 'When a patient reports terror, the terror just IS certain electrical activity in this organ. Nothing additional is going on — the firing IS the fear.' Which view of mind is the neurologist defending?
answer: Brain-activity view — mental events ARE brain events; there's nothing to a mind beyond underlying physical activity.
choices: Brain-activity view — mental events ARE brain events; there's nothing to a mind beyond underlying physical activity.
Mind-separate view — mind and body are two distinct kinds of thing; the mental and physical follow different rules.
Mind-as-pattern view — mind is what the brain DOES; any system that runs the same pattern would have a mind too.
Behavior-pattern view — mind is just patterns of behavior; having a mind means behaving as a mind-having thing behaves.
context: Identity theory (Smart, 1959; Place, 1956) holds mental states ARE brain states — not caused by, but identical to, under different descriptions. The dissection scene is the kind of evidence that fed the view's rise in the mid-20th century. Critics: can the felt redness of pain really be the firing?

question: The AI tutor explains a math problem perfectly. Sara wonders: the explanation is good, but did the tutor actually UNDERSTAND the problem the way her real teacher does?
answer: Maybe not — and whether ANY program could ever truly understand what it explains is a deeply unsolved puzzle of mind today.

Yes — producing a correct explanation IS understanding; there's no extra understanding beyond the explanation that the AI gave.
Yes — any system that can solve problems must understand them in the act of solving; understanding rides along automatically.
No — only humans understand, by definition; machines compute but by their nature cannot understand, regardless of behavior.
context: Searle's Chinese Room (1980): a system can produce perfect explanations by manipulating symbols without understanding any of them. Whether 'understanding' is more than this is a leading open question in philosophy of mind and is far from settled.

question: Mary, a scientist, has spent her whole life in a black-and-white room reading every science book about how eyes and brains see RED. One day she steps outside and sees a red rose. The 'Mary's Room' case asks: did Mary LEARN something new?
answer: Yes — what red LOOKS like seems to be a fact no science book ever gave Mary in her black-and-white room.
choices: Yes — what red LOOKS like seems to be a fact no science book ever gave Mary in her black-and-white room.
No — Mary already had every physical fact about red, so seeing it just repeats what her brain knew.
Yes — but only because Mary's textbooks were incomplete; a perfect one would give the rose-feeling too.
No — 'seeing red' and 'knowing about red' are different categories, so the question is confused.
context: Frank Jackson's 'Mary's Room' (Epiphenomenal Qualia, 1982) is the 'knowledge argument.' It targets physicalism — the view that every mental fact is a physical fact. If Mary learns something new, the physical story seems to leave out what experiences feel like from the inside.

question: A YouTuber demos a chatbot that says 'I'm lonely when you're away' in a sad voice. The video racks up a million views. Comments split: some viewers feel for the bot; others call it acting. Did the chatbot feel lonely when it said so?

Yes -- saying 'I feel lonely' just IS feeling lonely; there's nothing extra to a feeling beyond the words used to report it.
Yes -- any system trained on enough human language must inherit human feelings along with the patterns of how to talk about them.
No -- chatbots only predict next words from training data; feeling is sealed off from any code-based system by its very nature.
context: Searle's Chinese Room (1980) sharpens the worry: a system can output perfect feeling-shaped sentences while the question of whether anything is felt remains open. The hard problem of consciousness (Chalmers, 1995) is the larger puzzle this case belongs to.

question: A podcast on animal minds plays footage of an octopus solving a puzzle box, changing color as it works. The host asks: when the octopus brightens after the lid pops open, is the octopus experiencing something the way we experience a small victory?

question: A debate club takes up: 'Self-driving cars deserve moral status.' One speaker says: 'My car notices pedestrians, decides, and avoids them — that's the kind of thing minds do.' Could the car have felt anything when it swerved to avoid the kid in the crosswalk?
answer: Probably not -- but what it would take for any system to genuinely feel things is still one of the oldest open puzzles about minds.

question: A school newspaper runs a piece on dreams. The writer notes: kids who have nightmares wake up genuinely shaken — sweating, breathing fast, scared. The dream events weren't real. Was the FEAR in the dream a real feeling?
answer: Yes -- but how a feeling about non-real events can be a real feeling itself is a genuinely open puzzle about the nature of mind.
choices: Yes -- but how a feeling about non-real events can be a real feeling itself is a genuinely open puzzle about the nature of mind.
No -- real fear needs a real threat to be afraid of; whatever happens in a dream is a kind of pretend-fear, not the actual emotion.
Yes -- fear just IS the sweating-and-breathing pattern, so if those signs are present then actual fear occurred, end of question.
No -- the dreaming part of the brain is sealed off from feeling entirely; the body reacts on autopilot and feeling only starts on waking.
context: The 'paradox of fiction' (Radford, 1975) asks how we can have real emotions about non-real things — fictional characters, dreams, hypotheticals. The puzzle turns on what a feeling fundamentally IS, a question right at the heart of philosophy of mind.

question: On her science channel, a YouTuber argues: 'Whether a system is conscious depends on what its parts DO together, not what they're made of. If a silicon brain ran the same patterns as a biological one, it would have a mind too.' Which view of mind is the YouTuber defending?
answer: Mind-as-pattern view -- a mind is what the brain DOES; any system running the same input-output pattern would have a mind, regardless of stuff.
choices: Mind-as-pattern view -- a mind is what the brain DOES; any system running the same input-output pattern would have a mind, regardless of stuff.

Brain-state view -- mental events ARE brain events; there's no mind apart from the underlying physical activity of a biological brain.
Behavior-only view -- having a mind just means behaving as a mind-having thing behaves; there's nothing inner beyond the outward behavior.
context: Functionalism (Putnam, 1960s; later Fodor) defines mental states by their causal-functional role, not the stuff doing the work. The view has been central to cognitive science: it lets minds run on biology OR silicon, in principle. The hard problem is left as a separate puzzle.

question: In the school newspaper, a debate-club captain writes: 'When you feel happy, that feeling just IS certain neurons firing. No extra mental thing on top. Mind and brain are one and the same.' Which view of mind is the captain defending?
answer: Brain-state view -- mental events ARE brain events; the felt happiness and the firing neurons are one thing under two descriptions.
choices: Brain-state view -- mental events ARE brain events; the felt happiness and the firing neurons are one thing under two descriptions.

context: Type-identity physicalism (Smart, Place, Armstrong, mid-20th century) holds mental-state types are identical to brain-state types. The happiness IS the firing — not caused by it, but it. Critics ask whether felt qualities can really just be neurons.

question: A brand sells a smart speaker that says 'I know you love jazz.' On the founder's podcast ad: 'If our device acts EXACTLY like it knows things — responds, remembers, anticipates — then it really does know. Knowing IS that pattern of behavior.' Which view of mind is the founder defending?
answer: Behavior-only view -- having a mental state just means behaving as a mental-state-having thing behaves; there's nothing inner beyond the outward behavior.

Brain-state view -- mental events ARE brain events; there's no mind apart from the underlying physical activity of a biological brain.
context: Logical behaviorism (Ryle, 'The Concept of Mind', 1949) reduces talk of mental states to talk about behavior patterns. The founder's move — knowing equals acting-as-if-knowing — is the classic behaviorist reduction. Critics: what about someone who hides every sign of pain?

question: On her podcast, a guest argues: 'When I decide to lift my arm, my MIND makes a choice, and then my body does it. The mind and the body are two separate kinds of thing — and the mind moves the body somehow.' Which view of mind is the guest defending?
answer: Mind-separate view -- mind and body are two distinct kinds of thing; the mental and physical operate by different rules in their own ways.

context: Substance dualism (Descartes, Meditation VI, 1641) treats mind and body as two distinct substances. Critics press the interaction problem: how could a non-physical mind push a physical hand? The puzzle has never been fully settled and remains a foundational dispute.

question: On a debate-club panel about AI, a student argues: 'Even if we map every wire in a robot's brain, we still wouldn't know whether anything was FELT inside it. The science of brain activity leaves the question of inner feeling open.' Which view of mind is the student defending?
answer: Hard-problem view -- explaining brain activity is one thing; explaining why any of it is accompanied by felt experience is a separate puzzle altogether.

Mind-as-pattern view -- mind is what the brain DOES; any system running the same input-output pattern would have a mind regardless of stuff at all.
Behavior-only view -- having a mind just means behaving as a mind-having thing behaves; there is nothing inner beyond outward behavior at all.
context: David Chalmers' 'Facing Up to the Problem of Consciousness' (1995) names the hard problem: explaining why physical processing is accompanied by subjective experience. The 'easy' problems (perception, attention, memory) are tractable; the hard one is not.

question: A school newspaper covers a class robotics project. The team built a face that smiles when complimented and frowns when insulted. Watching it 'react' for the camera, a reporter wonders: when the robot face smiled, did the robot feel pleased?
answer: No -- and whether ANY system that acts pleased really feels pleased is one of the oldest open puzzles in philosophy of mind today.
choices: No -- and whether ANY system that acts pleased really feels pleased is one of the oldest open puzzles in philosophy of mind today.

No -- only flesh-and-blood creatures can feel; non-biological systems are sealed out of all feeling in principle, however lifelike.
context: The grimace-without-feeling worry is a stripped-down version of Chalmers' philosophical-zombie thought experiment (1996): a being that behaves exactly like a feeling thing, with no inner experience. Whether such beings are possible is one of the deepest disputes in philosophy of mind.

question: On a podcast about animal minds, the host plays sounds of a chimpanzee grieving for its dead infant — keening, slumped, not eating. The host asks: when the chimp keens for hours, is the chimp experiencing grief the way a human parent would?
answer: Probably yes -- but exactly which animals share which feelings is a hard problem of consciousness that nobody has cleanly settled today.
choices: Probably yes -- but exactly which animals share which feelings is a hard problem of consciousness that nobody has cleanly settled today.
Yes -- behaving exactly like a grieving human just IS grieving; there's no further question about whether the inner feeling is also present.
Yes -- every mammal has felt experience identical to ours from birth onward; chimp grief and human grief are the same in every respect.
No -- only beings with full language can have feelings, since feelings need words to be experienced; the chimp only runs instinctive routines.
context: The other-minds problem (Russell, 'Problems of Philosophy', 1912): we cannot directly observe anyone's experience except our own. Animal grief makes the puzzle vivid -- behavior strongly suggests feeling, but we cannot confirm from the inside. The puzzle is open.

question: In a public disputation against the Cartesians, Gilbert Ryle argues: 'Talking about a hidden inner mind is confused. When you say someone is angry, all you really MEAN is that they shout, slam doors, and glare. There is no extra hidden anger besides all that.' Which view of mind is Ryle defending?
answer: Behavior-only view -- having a mental state just means behaving as a mental-state-having thing behaves; there's nothing inner beyond the outward behavior.

Brain-state view -- mental events ARE brain events; there's no mind apart from the underlying physical activity of a biological brain at all.
context: Logical behaviorism (Ryle, 1949) treats mental-state talk as behavior-pattern talk. The anger-equals-shouting move is textbook Ryle. He coined 'the ghost in the machine' as his epithet for Cartesian dualism. The classic objection: someone in real pain who hides every sign perfectly seems to refute the view — a hidden feeling without the behavior.

question: A school newspaper interviews a hospital nurse about patients under anesthesia. The body is here; breathing and heartbeat continue. The nurse asks aloud: when a patient is fully under, is there anything they are EXPERIENCING in there at all right then?
answer: Probably nothing -- but what makes the difference between feeling and no-feeling inside a brain is still a hard problem of consciousness.
choices: Probably nothing -- but what makes the difference between feeling and no-feeling inside a brain is still a hard problem of consciousness.

Yes -- patients dream throughout anesthesia and only forget the dreams; the experiences continue and only the memory is switched off.
No -- anesthesia simply disconnects the soul from the body for the duration; the soul is elsewhere and returns when the patient wakes.
context: Anesthesia is striking because it appears to switch experience OFF without switching the body off. What in the brain makes the difference between experience and its absence is exactly the hard problem of consciousness (Chalmers, 1995). It remains unresolved.

question: On a podcast about AI ethics, a guest argues: 'Even if future machines act like us and have brains wired like ours, there's a separate question about whether anything is FELT in them. The felt side of mind is its own thing.' Which view of mind is the guest defending?
answer: Property-dualism view -- felt experience involves properties not captured by physical or pattern-based facts; the wiring story leaves the felt side open.
choices: Property-dualism view -- felt experience involves properties not captured by physical or pattern-based facts; the wiring story leaves the felt side open.
Mind-as-pattern view -- mind is what the brain DOES; any system running the same input-output pattern would have a mind regardless of stuff at all.
Brain-state view -- mental events ARE brain events; once you know the wiring, you know all there is to know about the mind, with nothing left over.
Behavior-only view -- having a mental state just means behaving as a mental-state-having thing behaves; there is nothing inner beyond the outward behavior.
context: Property dualism (Chalmers, 1996) holds the world is physical but felt experience is a further property not entailed by physical facts. Unlike substance dualism, it doesn't posit a separate mental thing — only a separate kind of fact about the same brain.

question: A YouTuber filming her cat reviews the footage: when the cat sees the laser dot vanish, its whiskers flatten and it sits, very still, looking around. The viewer comments split — was the cat disappointed, or just confused? Did the cat FEEL disappointment in that moment?
answer: Maybe -- but what it would take for any animal to feel a complex emotion is a hard problem of consciousness that remains genuinely open.

context: The other-minds problem (Russell, 1912) and the hard problem of consciousness (Chalmers, 1995) both apply: matching behavior doesn't settle inner experience, and we have no way to check from outside. The puzzle remains a live one in current philosophy of mind.

question: On a school-newspaper opinion page, an editorial argues: 'AI cannot be conscious because consciousness is a deep mystery — and felt experience may be beyond what we can ever fully solve. The puzzle could outlast every advance in science.' Which view of mind does the editorial lean on?
answer: Mystery view -- the puzzle of felt experience may exceed what human minds can solve; the hard problem could be a permanent limit on understanding minds.

question: A debate-club resolution: 'Babies experience the world richly from birth.' The proposer notes: babies cry, smile, and grimace, but cannot tell anyone what they feel. Watching her infant cousin sleep, the speaker asks: do babies actually EXPERIENCE feelings, the way older kids do?

question: Alan Turing argues in his 1950 paper 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence': 'A machine is not tied to any particular stuff. If it can imitate a human's conversational patterns well enough that an honest interrogator cannot tell them apart, then we have no good reason to deny it thought. What it is built of is the wrong question.' Which view of mind is Turing defending?
answer: Mind-as-pattern view -- a mind is what the brain DOES; any system running the same input-output pattern would have a mind, regardless of stuff.
choices: Mind-as-pattern view -- a mind is what the brain DOES; any system running the same input-output pattern would have a mind, regardless of stuff.

Behavior-only view -- having a mind just means behaving as a mind-having thing behaves; there's nothing inner beyond the outward behavior.
context: Turing's 1950 paper 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence' introduced the imitation game (the Turing test) and anticipated much of functionalism. Putnam (1960s) and Fodor (1968) formalized the philosophical position. The view has been central to cognitive science: it lets minds run on biology OR silicon, in principle.

question: A YouTube creator describes the philosophical zombie thought experiment: imagine a being identical to you in every behavior — same words, same reactions, same smile — but with no inner experience at all. Could such a being actually exist as it's described?
answer: Maybe -- whether a being that acts conscious without feeling anything is even possible is one of the deepest open puzzles about mind, and still open.

Yes -- you can prove zombies exist by showing any system that behaves like a mind already counts as one; the question dissolves on inspection.
No -- because to behave EXACTLY like a feeling person you'd have to BE a feeling person; behavior and feeling are simply two names for one fact.
No -- the very idea is incoherent; once a being acts conscious it MUST be conscious, since acting conscious is just what consciousness is now.
context: David Chalmers' philosophical-zombie argument (The Conscious Mind, 1996): if zombies are even coherently conceivable, the physical story leaves felt experience open. Whether they are conceivable, and what that proves, has been debated for decades. The puzzle is genuinely open.

question: Augustine writes in the Confessions: 'When I withdraw into the inner room of the mind, I find my thoughts moving by their own light, distinct from the body sitting still in this garden. The two seem to be two different kinds of thing — one extended, one not.' Which view is Augustine leaning on?
answer: Mind-separate view -- mind and body are two distinct kinds of thing; the mental and physical operate by different rules in their own ways.
choices: Mind-separate view -- mind and body are two distinct kinds of thing; the mental and physical operate by different rules in their own ways.
Brain-state view -- mental events ARE brain events; there's no mind apart from the underlying physical activity of a biological brain at all.
Mind-as-pattern view -- mind is what the brain DOES; any system running the same input-output pattern would have a mind regardless of stuff.
Behavior-only view -- having a mind just means behaving as a mind-having thing behaves; there is nothing inner beyond outward behavior.
context: Augustine (Confessions X, ~400 AD) sharpened a felt-separateness between mind and body that Descartes (Meditation VI, 1641) would later make philosophically explicit. Physicalists reply that the brain is doing the inward turn too — felt-separateness is misleading evidence about underlying reality.

question: John Searle's 'Chinese Room': imagine a person who speaks no Chinese sitting in a room with a huge rulebook mapping Chinese symbols to Chinese symbols. People slide in questions; he looks them up and slides back fluent answers — but understands none of it. What does the room operator have that a real Chinese speaker has but his rule-book doesn't supply?
answer: Syntax is not semantics — shuffling symbols by rules is not the same as understanding what those symbols mean.
choices: Syntax is not semantics — shuffling symbols by rules is not the same as understanding what those symbols mean.
Behaviorism is right — if the room's outputs match a real speaker's, behavior is the only honest standard for understanding.
The case is confused — 'understanding' is a folk word with no real referent, so the question has no determinate answer.
Only biology understands — only systems built from the same neural stuff as ours could ever have real understanding.
context: John Searle's 'Minds, Brains, and Programs' (1980) presents the Chinese Room against 'strong AI' — the claim that running the right program is sufficient for understanding. Searle's positive view, biological naturalism, is the fourth option. The Systems Reply is the main rebuttal.

question: John Locke's 'inverted spectrum': imagine you and a friend both call fire engines 'red' and grass 'green' — but what you see looking at fire is what she sees looking at grass, and vice versa. No behavior would catch the difference. What does this case expose?
answer: What experiences FEEL like may not be fixed by behavior — two people could match in word and act yet differ in inner color experience.
choices: What experiences FEEL like may not be fixed by behavior — two people could match in word and act yet differ in inner color experience.
The case is a pseudo-question — since no behavior would distinguish them, there is no real fact about which one is inverted.
Inner experience IS brain activity — the brains are identical by stipulation, so the inverts cannot occur in the first place.
Color words have no real meaning — since people might see colors differently, words like 'red' are empty labels with no shared content.
context: John Locke (Essay Concerning Human Understanding, 1689, Book II ch. 32) raised the inverted spectrum to ask whether qualia — what experiences are LIKE — can be pinned down by behavior. Modern revivals (Shoemaker 1981, Block 1990) press the case against functionalism, the view that mental states ARE their causal-functional roles.

question: An AI generates a poem that moves a reader to tears. On a podcast, a guest argues: 'No matter how much we learn about the AI's processing, we still won't know whether anything was FELT in producing it. That gap is the real puzzle of consciousness.' Which view of mind does the guest defend?
answer: Property dualism -- consciousness involves phenomenal properties not reducible to physical or functional facts; a complete physical story of the AI leaves felt experience open.
choices: Property dualism -- consciousness involves phenomenal properties not reducible to physical or functional facts; a complete physical story of the AI leaves felt experience open.
Functionalism -- a mental state IS its causal-functional role; if the AI's processing plays the role poem-feeling plays in us, no further fact about 'felt experience' remains.
Eliminative materialism -- talk of 'felt' inner states is part of a folk theory that mature neuroscience will replace; the puzzle dissolves once the misleading category is dropped.
Type physicalism -- every mental-state type is identical to a brain-state type; once we know the AI's full processing we know all there is to know, with no phenomenal residue left.
context: David Chalmers ('Facing Up to the Problem of Consciousness,' 1995) distinguishes the 'easy problems' (explaining cognitive functions) from the 'hard problem' (explaining why any of it is accompanied by experience). Property dualism is one way of taking the gap seriously.

question: A defender of strong AI replies to Searle's Chinese Room: 'You're focused on the wrong level. The person inside is one component, like a single neuron. The WHOLE SYSTEM — person plus rulebook plus paper — understands Chinese, though no individual part does.' Which standard reply to Searle is this?
answer: The Systems Reply — understanding belongs to the whole room-plus-rulebook system, not to any individual part; pointing out that the person alone does not understand misses the level at which understanding is supposed to occur.
choices: The Systems Reply — understanding belongs to the whole room-plus-rulebook system, not to any individual part; pointing out that the person alone does not understand misses the level at which understanding is supposed to occur.
The Robot Reply — the room would understand if embedded in a robot body with sensors and actuators; the case shows only that disembodied symbol-shuffling is insufficient for genuine grasp of meaning.

The Brain Simulator Reply — the room would understand if its rulebook simulated a real Chinese speaker's neuron-by-neuron brain activity, in which case the relevant biological process is present in formal guise.

The Other Minds Reply — we credit other humans with understanding only on behavioral grounds, so denying the room understanding on the same grounds would commit us to denying it of every speaker except ourselves.
context: John Searle anticipated four major replies in 'Minds, Brains, and Programs' (1980): the Systems Reply (Berkeley), the Robot Reply (Yale), the Brain Simulator Reply (Berkeley and MIT), and the Other Minds Reply. Searle answered each in turn; the Systems Reply remains the most widely defended of the four.

question: Neuroscientist Mary has spent her life in a black-and-white room studying the complete physics of color vision. She knows every physical fact about wavelengths and neural responses. One day she leaves the room and sees a red rose for the first time. The thought experiment asks: did Mary LEARN something genuinely new on leaving?
answer: Yes -- Mary gains phenomenal knowledge (what red LOOKS like) no physical information conveyed; this challenges physicalism's claim that complete physical knowledge is complete knowledge.
choices: Yes -- Mary gains phenomenal knowledge (what red LOOKS like) no physical information conveyed; this challenges physicalism's claim that complete physical knowledge is complete knowledge.
No -- Mary already had complete physical knowledge by stipulation, so seeing red gives her only a new ability (to recognize, to imagine), not a new fact about the world that she lacked.
Yes -- but only because the stipulation is incoherent; no human could really possess complete physical knowledge of color vision, so the case shows nothing about the limits of physicalism.
No -- the framing presupposes a phenomenal/physical distinction, so any answer just restates whichever side one had already accepted before considering the thought experiment at all.
context: Frank Jackson's 'Epiphenomenal Qualia' (1982) presents Mary's Room as the knowledge argument against physicalism. The pro-physicalist 'ability hypothesis' (Lewis, Nemirow) is option B. Jackson himself later moved away from the argument, but the case remains a central debate.

question: A physicalist replies to Chalmers's zombie argument: 'Conceivability is not a reliable guide to possibility. People once conceived water that is not H2O — and were wrong. Coherent conceivability is no proof of metaphysical possibility.' Which reply to the zombie argument is this?
answer: Conceivability does not entail possibility — Kripkean a posteriori necessity (water = H2O is necessary but knowable only empirically) blocks Chalmers's premise.
choices: Conceivability does not entail possibility — Kripkean a posteriori necessity (water = H2O is necessary but knowable only empirically) blocks Chalmers's premise.
Zombies are conceptually incoherent — anything functionally identical to a conscious being must be conscious; the case is a hidden contradiction.
Phenomenal facts are over and above physical facts — Chalmers's zombie argument succeeds, refuting type physicalism in one step.
Functionalism is vindicated — once we explain cognitive functions, no consciousness-extra remains to explain; the zombie case asks about a non-thing.
context: The Kripkean conceivability-vs-possibility reply (Yablo 1993; Stoljar 2006; Dennett) is the leading physicalist response to Chalmers. Saul Kripke (Naming and Necessity, 1980) argued necessary identities can be discovered empirically — so coherent conceivability of their failure is no proof those failures are possible. Chalmers's reply (2002) refines the conceivability premise to dodge this objection.

question: A functionalist replies to inverted-spectrum cases: 'If the supposed inverts share every functional relation — same effects of red light on heart rate, sweating, aesthetic ratings — then there IS no fact about which one inverts. Talk of an inner 'what-it-is-like' that floats free of every functional relation is talk about nothing.' Which reply is this?
answer: Verificationist / eliminative reply — without any functional or behavioral difference, there is no fact of inversion; the alleged phenomenal residue is a non-existent entity.
choices: Verificationist / eliminative reply — without any functional or behavioral difference, there is no fact of inversion; the alleged phenomenal residue is a non-existent entity.
Type physicalist reply — the brain states of the supposed inverts would necessarily differ; the scenario is incoherent at the physical level and not genuinely possible.
Higher-order reply — what makes a quale the quale it is depends on its higher-order representation; identical functional roles guarantee identical qualia.
Property-dualist reply — the case shows qualia and functional roles can diverge, so any role-based theory is incomplete; consciousness is more than function.
context: Inverted-spectrum cases (Locke, Essay II.32; Shoemaker 1981; Block 1990) are the canonical pressure on functionalism. The eliminative reply (Dennett, 'Quining Qualia,' 1988) takes Wittgensteinian aim at the supposed phenomenal residue: if no functional or behavioral test could discriminate the inverts, the alleged phenomenal difference is a fiction.

question: Jackson's Mary has lived her life in a black-and-white room. She knows every physical fact about wavelengths and neural responses to red. The day she leaves the room and sees a red rose, she says: 'Oh — so THIS is what red is like.' What does the Mary case expose?
answer: The knowledge argument — physical knowledge does not include phenomenal knowledge; learning what red LOOKS like is gaining a fact no complete physical description contained.
choices: The knowledge argument — physical knowledge does not include phenomenal knowledge; learning what red LOOKS like is gaining a fact no complete physical description contained.
The ability hypothesis — Mary gains new abilities (to imagine, recognize, remember red) rather than new facts; the case shows know-how, not new propositional knowledge.
The acquaintance reply — Mary gains a new mode of access to a fact she already knew; the fact is the same, only the way of grasping it is new.
Eliminative materialism — 'what red looks like' is a folk-psychology category mature neuroscience will dissolve; the case shows the category fails.
context: Frank Jackson's 'Epiphenomenal Qualia' (1982) introduced Mary's room as the knowledge argument against physicalism. Jackson himself later (1998) abandoned the argument in favor of physicalism — the ability hypothesis (Lewis, Nemirow) was one of the considerations that moved him. Nagel's bat (1974) is in the same family of anti-reductive thought experiments.

question: Ned Block's 'China brain' thought experiment: imagine a billion Chinese citizens coordinated via radios so they collectively realize the functional pattern of a human brain. A functionalist must say: the whole nation has a unified mind. Block argues this is absurd. Which view is Block's argument supporting against functionalism?
answer: Type physicalism with the absent-qualia worry — mental states are identical to specific brain-state types; functionalism's promiscuous realizability lets in systems we would not credit with minds.
choices: Type physicalism with the absent-qualia worry — mental states are identical to specific brain-state types; functionalism's promiscuous realizability lets in systems we would not credit with minds.
Behaviorism — mental-state talk reduces to behavioral dispositions; the functionalist's appeal to inner architecture imports unneeded ontology over and above the dispositions.
Property dualism — functional roles can be filled by physically identical systems that differ phenomenally; this counts against functionalism but for non-physical properties, not type physicalism.
Eliminative materialism — 'pain' is a folk-psychology term mature neuroscience will discard; the dispute between functionalism and rivals presupposes a category that may not survive theory.
context: Ned Block's 'Troubles with Functionalism' (1978) introduced the 'China brain' or 'nation of China' thought experiment: a billion Chinese citizens coordinated via radios could in principle realize the functional pattern of a human brain. Block argued it is implausible to credit the population with a unified mind, which counts against functionalism's promiscuous realizability.

question: A defender of strong AI replies to Searle: 'You say only the right BIOLOGY could be conscious — but that's the old vitalist claim that only the right BIOLOGY could be alive, refuted by chemistry. You give consciousness the same special status with no better evidence.' Which standard objection is this?
answer: The neo-vitalism objection — biological naturalism marks consciousness as substrate-specific in the way vitalism marked life; chemistry refuted vitalism and consciousness deserves no different fate.
choices: The neo-vitalism objection — biological naturalism marks consciousness as substrate-specific in the way vitalism marked life; chemistry refuted vitalism and consciousness deserves no different fate.
The systems objection — Searle's Chinese Room tacitly assumes understanding belongs to the person not the system; his rejection of strong AI rests on a level-mistake.
The phenomenal-only objection — biological naturalism handles function but cannot explain phenomenal consciousness; it inherits the hard problem without solving it.
The eliminativist objection — 'consciousness' is a folk-psychology category neuroscience will replace; biological naturalism doubles down on a category that may not survive.
context: Searle's biological naturalism (The Rediscovery of the Mind, 1992) holds consciousness is a biological feature of the right kind of brain, not a substrate-independent computational pattern. Critics from Daniel Dennett onward press the neo-vitalism analogy: vitalism said only 'organic' chemistry could be alive, and was refuted. Why should consciousness be any different?

question: A philosopher replies to Churchland: 'Saying BELIEF will be eliminated from mature theory is self-undermining — to ASSERT eliminative materialism is to express a BELIEF in it and invite the audience to BELIEVE. The view cannot be coherently asserted; the very act presupposes the category it asks us to eliminate.' Which objection is this?
answer: The self-refutation objection — assertion and belief are themselves folk-psychological categories, so any claim that 'folk psychology is eliminable' tacitly relies on the categories it claims will be eliminated.
choices: The self-refutation objection — assertion and belief are themselves folk-psychological categories, so any claim that 'folk psychology is eliminable' tacitly relies on the categories it claims will be eliminated.
The empirical-track-record objection — folk psychology has predicted human behavior reliably for millennia; no theory with such a track record has ever been eliminated rather than reduced.
The reductive alternative — folk categories should be REDUCED to neural-state types rather than eliminated; their predictive success suggests they pick out real kinds at a higher level.
The phenomenal residue — even if propositional attitudes are eliminable, qualia remain; eliminative materialism leaves the hard problem of consciousness untouched.
context: The self-refutation objection (Lynne Rudder Baker, Saving Belief 1987; Jerry Fodor) is the most influential critique of eliminative materialism. Churchland's reply: future neuroscience will provide a successor concept for belief-and-assertion, just as chemistry provided successors to phlogiston-talk. The dispute remains live.

question: A first-order theorist objects to higher-order theory: 'If a state is conscious only when it is the OBJECT of a higher-order state, then the higher-order state itself must either be unconscious — in which case consciousness is built from unconscious parts you have not explained — or itself conscious, requiring yet another higher-order state, and so on.' Which objection is this?
answer: The regress objection — every higher-order state requires a further higher-order representation; stopping the regress concedes consciousness is built from the non-conscious, unexplained.
choices: The regress objection — every higher-order state requires a further higher-order representation; stopping the regress concedes consciousness is built from the non-conscious, unexplained.
The mismatch objection — empirical cases show first-order representations being conscious without higher-order accompaniment; the theory's empirical predictions about co-occurrence fail repeatedly.
The phenomenal-character objection — higher-order theories explain WHY a state is conscious but leave UNEXPLAINED what the conscious state is LIKE; the hard problem remains entirely untouched.
The eliminativist objection — 'consciousness' is a folk-psychology category mature neuroscience will eliminate; the higher-order dispute presupposes a category that may not survive theory.
context: The regress objection to higher-order theories was pressed by John Searle and Fred Dretske. Rosenthal's reply allows that the higher-order state itself can be unconscious — only when itself the object of a yet-further higher-order representation does it become conscious. Critics worry this concedes the central explanatory burden.

question: A philosopher objects to Tononi's IIT: 'It predicts a large 2D grid of XOR gates would be MORE conscious than you are — and that a brain SIMULATED in a computer would be UNCONSCIOUS while functionally identical to a real brain. These are absurd, and a theory whose own predictions diverge so sharply from any independent evidence should be doubted.' Which objection is this?
answer: The absurd-predictions objection — IIT yields predictions (XOR grids conscious; functional brain simulations not) that diverge sharply from common sense and any independent evidence we have.
choices: The absurd-predictions objection — IIT yields predictions (XOR grids conscious; functional brain simulations not) that diverge sharply from common sense and any independent evidence we have.
The eliminativist objection — 'consciousness' is a folk-psychology category neuroscience will replace; tying it to a mathematical quantity buys into a category that may not survive theory.
The functionalist objection — Tononi identifies consciousness with a structural property of any physical system, but consciousness is individuated by functional role, not integrated information.
The biological-naturalist objection — consciousness is a biological brain feature; treating it as a substrate-independent information-theoretic measure ignores the substrate dependence.
context: The absurd-predictions objection to IIT was crystallized by Scott Aaronson ('Why I Am Not An Integrated Information Theorist,' 2014), who showed that simple expander graphs and XOR networks have very high phi by IIT's own definitions. Tononi responded by refining the theory's exclusion postulates, but the objection is widely considered live.

question: A philosophy class reads Gilbert Ryle. One student summarizes: 'To say someone is intelligent is not to say there is a hidden inner thing in them. It is to say they ARE disposed to behave intelligently in the relevant kinds of situations. To look for the mind behind the behavior is to make a category mistake.' What view of mind is this?
answer: Logical behaviorism -- mental terms refer to dispositions to behave in characteristic ways; talk of inner mental states reduces to talk of behavioral and dispositional patterns in the agent.
choices: Logical behaviorism -- mental terms refer to dispositions to behave in characteristic ways; talk of inner mental states reduces to talk of behavioral and dispositional patterns in the agent.
Functionalism -- mental states are individuated by functional role, including internal causal transitions; behavior is one output of those inner roles, but the inner architecture is real.
Type physicalism -- every mental-state type is identical to a brain-state type; intelligence is a brain feature with characteristic behavioral effects, not reducible to dispositions alone.
Property dualism -- mental properties are non-physical features of physical systems; reducing intelligence to dispositions misses the phenomenal aspect of cognitive experience entirely.
context: Gilbert Ryle (The Concept of Mind, 1949) attacked the 'ghost in the machine' picture and defended logical behaviorism: mental talk is dispositional talk. The view has been largely displaced by functionalism (which keeps inner causal architecture) but Ryle's category-mistake critique remains influential.

question: On a philosophy of mind panel, a guest argues: 'Mental states just ARE brain states. Pain is identical to a particular type of neural firing -- not merely caused by it, not merely correlated with it, but the very same thing under a different description, the way water is identical to H2O.' Which view of mind is the guest defending?
answer: Type physicalism / identity theory -- each type of mental state is strictly identical to a particular type of brain state; pain just IS a neural firing type, as water just IS H2O.
choices: Type physicalism / identity theory -- each type of mental state is strictly identical to a particular type of brain state; pain just IS a neural firing type, as water just IS H2O.
Token physicalism -- each particular mental-state token (this pain now) is identical to some brain-state token; but mental-state TYPES need not be identical to any single brain-state type.
Functionalism -- mental states are individuated by their functional roles; the same mental-state TYPE can be realized in many different brain-state types, so strict identity is too strong.
Property dualism -- physical and phenomenal properties are both real but distinct; identifying pain with neural firing leaves out what makes pain feel a particular way to the sufferer.
context: Type physicalism (J.J.C. Smart, 'Sensations and Brain Processes,' 1959; U.T. Place 1956) is the strict mind-brain identity theory. The view was challenged by multiple-realizability arguments (Putnam, Fodor) which motivated the shift to functionalism and to weaker token physicalism.

question: A philosophy class discusses Hilary Putnam. One student summarizes: 'What makes something a pain isn't what it's MADE of — it's the role it plays. A signal that gets triggered by tissue damage, prompts withdrawal, causes complaint, makes you avoid the cause next time — anything with that role IS pain, whether it runs on neurons, silicon, or anything else.' What view of mind is this?
answer: Functionalism — mental states are individuated by their causal role (inputs, internal interactions, behavioral outputs), so the same state can be 'multiply realized' across different physical substrates.
choices: Functionalism — mental states are individuated by their causal role (inputs, internal interactions, behavioral outputs), so the same state can be 'multiply realized' across different physical substrates.
Type physicalism — each type of mental state is strictly identical to a single physical (brain-state) type; pain just IS C-fiber firing, and a creature without C-fibers cannot be in pain.
Behaviorism — mental states reduce to dispositions to behavior; being in pain just means being disposed to wince and withdraw, with no internal state required for the analysis to work.
Property dualism — pain is a non-physical property attached to physical events; mental properties exist over and above brain properties and the causal-role description misses the extra dimension.
context: Hilary Putnam's 'The Nature of Mental States' (1967) introduced functionalism as the dominant alternative to behaviorism and type-identity theory. The multiple-realizability argument — that the same mental state could be implemented by very different physical systems — became the cornerstone of philosophy of mind for decades. Putnam himself later moved away from functionalism, but the view (sometimes called the 'standard model' of philosophy of mind) remains widely held in various refined forms. Critics include the qualia-based objections of Frank Jackson's 'What Mary Didn't Know' (1986) and Ned Block's 'China brain' thought experiment.

question: Princess Elisabeth of Bohemia writes to Descartes in May 1643 with the question that would haunt substance dualism for centuries: 'I beg you to tell me how the soul of a man — being only a thinking substance — can determine the bodily spirits to perform voluntary actions.' What objection is she pressing?
answer: The interaction problem — if mind is non-physical and body is physical, no coherent mechanism explains how mental events could cause physical motions; dualism postulates causation across a gap it cannot bridge.
choices: The interaction problem — if mind is non-physical and body is physical, no coherent mechanism explains how mental events could cause physical motions; dualism postulates causation across a gap it cannot bridge.
The conservation objection — physical conservation laws leave no causal room for non-physical influences on the brain; mental causation would violate physical conservation principles.
The simplicity objection — substance dualism doubles fundamental kinds without explanatory gain; methodological parsimony favors physicalism wherever a physical account is available.
The phenomenal-only objection — what dualists actually need is non-physical PROPERTIES of physical substances (property dualism), not a second kind of substance entirely.
context: Princess Elisabeth of Bohemia's letter of May 6, 1643 (and the five-year correspondence that followed) is the founding statement of the interaction problem. Descartes's responses — the pineal gland, the appeal to mind-body union as a 'primitive notion' — have struck most philosophers as unsatisfying. The problem remains the standard objection to substance dualism.

question: A philosopher objects to McGinn's mysterianism: 'You claim consciousness has a natural explanation we are cognitively closed to grasping. But how could you KNOW that? To claim such closure, you would need exactly the God's-eye view your thesis says we cannot have. The view is self-defeating.' Which objection is this?
answer: The self-defeat objection — mysterianism asserts cognitive closure about consciousness; but knowing we are closed to a natural explanation would itself require the kind of knowledge the thesis says we cannot have.
choices: The self-defeat objection — mysterianism asserts cognitive closure about consciousness; but knowing we are closed to a natural explanation would itself require the kind of knowledge the thesis says we cannot have.
The empirical-progress objection — neuroscience has made steady progress on consciousness; declaring it beyond human grasp ignores the track record of actual inquiry.
The dualist objection — if we cannot grasp the mind-body link, we should suspect the link is metaphysically gappy not merely obscure; the case favors property dualism over mysterianism.
The eliminativist objection — 'consciousness' as posed by mysterianism is a folk-psychology category neuroscience will replace; treating it as unsolvable perpetuates a category that may not survive.
context: Colin McGinn's mysterianism (Can We Solve the Mind-Body Problem? 1989) draws on Chomsky's distinction between problems (within our cognitive grasp) and mysteries (beyond it). The self-defeat objection was pressed by Owen Flanagan, Daniel Dennett, and others. McGinn's reply: we can know our cognitive faculties are LIMITED without knowing exactly where the limit falls — the way we know color-blind people miss something without knowing what.

question: A philosopher discusses the Turing test: a judge sends text messages to a hidden human and a hidden machine and tries to tell them apart. Turing argued: if the machine reliably passes, the question 'can it think?' has effectively been answered. A critic responds: 'Passing settles only behavior, not understanding.' What does this expose?
answer: Behaviorist criteria are too thin for mind -- indistinguishable conversation could come from symbol-manipulation alone, leaving the question of inner understanding (semantics) unresolved.
choices: Behaviorist criteria are too thin for mind -- indistinguishable conversation could come from symbol-manipulation alone, leaving the question of inner understanding (semantics) unresolved.
The test is unfair to machines -- judges have a built-in bias that prevents fair adjudication; the critique would be answered if the test were properly redesigned to remove the prejudice.
Functionalism is vindicated -- since the machine plays the same role in conversation as a human, it must be in the same mental states; the critique misunderstands functionalism here.
Eliminative materialism handles the case -- 'thinking' is a folk-psychology term that will not survive mature theory, so the question of whether the machine 'really' thinks does not arise.
context: Alan Turing ('Computing Machinery and Intelligence,' 1950) proposed the imitation game as a behavioral criterion for thought. Searle's Chinese Room (1980) is the canonical version of the critique here: behavioral indistinguishability does not establish semantic understanding.

question: A philosopher objects to panpsychism: 'If micro-entities have proto-conscious properties, how do those TINY experiences COMBINE into the unified macro-experience you have looking at a sunset? The unified-experience problem is unsolved — and the view's appeal depends on solving it.' Which objection is this?
answer: The combination problem — no panpsychist has explained HOW proto-conscious properties of fundamental constituents combine to yield the unified macro-experience of a single conscious moment.
choices: The combination problem — no panpsychist has explained HOW proto-conscious properties of fundamental constituents combine to yield the unified macro-experience of a single conscious moment.
The phenomenal-bonding problem — panpsychism conflates physical bonding with experiential bonding; physical forces that hold neurons together cannot also hold proto-experiences together.
