The eliminativist objection — 'experience' is a folk-psychology category neuroscience will eliminate; extending it to fundamental matter doubles down on a fragile category.
The biological-naturalist objection — consciousness is a feature of brains specifically; locating it at fundamental physics ignores substrate dependence.
context: The combination problem was pressed against William James in 1890 by Stumpf, and given modern form by Sam Coleman ('The Combination Problem,' 2014). Galen Strawson, Philip Goff, and Hedda Hassel Morch have proposed solutions (constitutive panpsychism, cosmopsychism, phenomenal bonding) — none yet universally accepted. The problem remains the central challenge for the panpsychist revival.

question: A philosophy of mind seminar discusses intentionality. The professor explains: 'Mental states are ABOUT things in a way physical states do not seem to be. A rock is not about anything. A belief is about its object -- a person, an event, even a nonexistent thing like a unicorn. This aboutness is the mark of the mental.' Which view is this?
answer: Brentano's intentionality thesis -- intentionality (the 'aboutness' or directedness of mental states toward objects) is the distinctive feature of the mental, marking mind from the physical.
choices: Brentano's intentionality thesis -- intentionality (the 'aboutness' or directedness of mental states toward objects) is the distinctive feature of the mental, marking mind from the physical.
Eliminative materialism -- 'aboutness' is a folk-psychology category mature neuroscience will replace; treating intentionality as the mark of the mental presupposes a doomed category.
Functionalism -- mental states are individuated by causal-functional role; aboutness is one role among many but does not pick out a fundamental distinction between mental and physical kinds.
Type physicalism -- mental states are identical to brain-state types; 'aboutness' is a high-level description of neural processing with no irreducible philosophical significance of its own.
context: Franz Brentano (Psychology from an Empirical Standpoint, 1874) revived the medieval term 'intentionality' to capture the directedness of mental states toward objects. Naturalizing intentionality (Fodor, Dretske, Millikan) is one of the central projects in contemporary philosophy of mind.

question: A philosopher objects to epiphenomenalism: 'On your view, mental states do no causal work. But then how could BELIEF in epiphenomenalism — itself a mental state — have produced the very book you wrote arguing for it? If your theory is true, your theory could not have caused you to publish it.' Which objection is this?
answer: The self-stultification objection — if mental states have no causal power, no belief (including in epiphenomenalism) could have caused the speech-acts asserting it; the view undermines its assertion-conditions.
choices: The self-stultification objection — if mental states have no causal power, no belief (including in epiphenomenalism) could have caused the speech-acts asserting it; the view undermines its assertion-conditions.

The evolutionary objection — consciousness has been selected for across evolutionary time; this would be impossible if it conferred no causal benefit, so a causally-inert feature could not be entrenched.
The phenomenal-only objection — what dualists need is non-physical properties WITH causal influence; epiphenomenalism withholds that influence and so undermines what made dualism appealing.
The eliminativist objection — 'mental states' as posed by epiphenomenalism is a folk-psychology category neuroscience will eliminate; treating them as real-but-inert keeps a fragile category.
context: The self-stultification objection has been pressed against epiphenomenalism since William James (Principles of Psychology, 1890). Frank Jackson, who defended epiphenomenalism in his Mary's-room paper (1982), later abandoned it partly on these grounds. The evolutionary objection (Popper, Eccles) is the second major worry — consciousness's pervasive presence across species would be inexplicable if it did no causal work.

question: Donald Davidson's 'deviant causal chain': a climber holding a partner on a rope WANTS to drop her to save himself and BELIEVES letting go would do it. The very thought makes him so nervous his hand trembles and accidentally releases the rope. The desire and belief 'caused' the release — but did he genuinely ACT?
answer: No — action requires the right KIND of causal path from intention to movement; the climber's tremor was caused by his intention but did not execute it.
choices: No — action requires the right KIND of causal path from intention to movement; the climber's tremor was caused by his intention but did not execute it.
Yes — since the belief and desire produced the movement that fulfilled them, the causal theory of action counts this as a genuine action.
Yes — the climber wanted her to fall and she did, so morally he did the act; the inner pathway from thought to motion is a scientific detail.
No — no bodily movement is ever truly an action; 'action' is folk-psychology talk that mature science will replace with muscle and neural firing.
context: Donald Davidson ('Actions, Reasons, and Causes,' 1963; 'Freedom to Act,' 1973) developed the causal theory of action: actions are bodily movements caused IN THE RIGHT WAY by beliefs and desires. Deviant causal chains (climber, nervous assassin) show that 'caused by' is not enough; specifying the 'right way' has resisted clean solution.

question: In Sperry and Gazzaniga's 'split-brain' studies, patients whose two brain halves had been surgically separated could VERBALLY report only what the left hemisphere saw, while the left HAND (driven by the right hemisphere) reached correctly for objects the patient claimed not to see. What does it mean that the right hemisphere acts on visual information the patient denies seeing?
answer: Unity of consciousness is not guaranteed by having one body — the patient may host two streams of awareness, straining the picture of a single unified self.
choices: Unity of consciousness is not guaranteed by having one body — the patient may host two streams of awareness, straining the picture of a single unified self.
Personal identity reduces to body — the patient is plainly one person because one body persists, so the experimental quirks add nothing to identity.
There is no self at all — the case proves the everyday notion of personal identity is empty, since careful experiments dissolve any single thinking subject.
Consciousness is non-physical — since two streams cannot share one body, the case proves the mind is a substance separate from the brain entirely.
context: Roger Sperry's split-brain research (Nobel Prize 1981) on patients whose corpus callosum was severed to treat epilepsy revealed two streams of processing operating independently. Michael Gazzaniga ('The Bisected Brain,' 1970) developed the philosophical implications. The case is a linchpin in modern debates about personal identity and unity of mind.

question: In a philosophy seminar on AI consciousness, a panelist argues: 'Even a complete neural map of the network's processing would still leave one question open — whether anything was FELT during the generation. The gap between physical description and phenomenal character is not engineering, it is metaphysics.' Which view of mind is the panelist defending?
answer: Property dualism — mental properties (notably phenomenal character) are not reducible to physical or functional properties; the complete physical story leaves felt experience open.
choices: Property dualism — mental properties (notably phenomenal character) are not reducible to physical or functional properties; the complete physical story leaves felt experience open.
Functionalism — a mental state IS its causal-functional role; if the system plays the role pain or felt-experience plays in us, no extra phenomenal residue is needed.
Eliminative materialism — 'felt experience' is a folk-psychological category that mature neuroscience will replace; the supposed gap dissolves once the bad category is dropped.
Type physicalism — every mental-state type is identical to a brain-state type; the panelist is double-counting the same fact under two descriptions.
context: David Chalmers ('Facing Up to the Problem of Consciousness,' 1995) sharpens the gap between 'easy problems' (cognitive function) and the 'hard problem' (why function is accompanied by experience). Property dualism is one principled way of taking that gap seriously without collapsing into Cartesian substance dualism.

question: Mary, a neuroscientist, has spent her entire life in a black-and-white room studying the science of color. She knows every physical fact about wavelengths, cone activation, and cortical processing. Stepping outside, she sees a red rose for the first time. The thought experiment asks: did Mary LEARN something genuinely new on stepping outside?
answer: Yes — Mary gains phenomenal knowledge (what red is LIKE) that no physical description conveyed; this challenges physicalism (the view that complete physical knowledge is complete knowledge).
choices: Yes — Mary gains phenomenal knowledge (what red is LIKE) that no physical description conveyed; this challenges physicalism (the view that complete physical knowledge is complete knowledge).
No — Mary had every physical fact by stipulation, and seeing red gives only a new ability (to recognize, to imagine), not a new fact about the world she previously lacked.
Yes — but only because the stipulation is incoherent; no human could really possess complete physical knowledge, so the case proves nothing about the limits of physicalism.
The question is malformed — 'experience' and 'knowledge' are distinct categories, and asking whether one yields the other commits a category mistake from the outset.
context: Frank Jackson's 'Epiphenomenal Qualia' (1982) is the canonical version. The pro-physicalist 'ability hypothesis' (Lewis, Nemirow) is choice B; Jackson himself later moved toward it. The knowledge argument remains a central test case for any reductive theory of mind.

question: A philosophy seminar reads Searle's Chinese Room: a person who speaks no Chinese sits in a room with an enormous rulebook mapping Chinese symbols to Chinese symbols. From outside, the answers look fluent. Searle concludes: 'The room passes the test but understands nothing.' What does the Chinese Room case expose?
answer: Functionalism faces a syntax/semantics gap — the room's behavior matches a Chinese speaker's, yet symbol-shuffling alone does not constitute understanding the meaning of the symbols.
choices: Functionalism faces a syntax/semantics gap — the room's behavior matches a Chinese speaker's, yet symbol-shuffling alone does not constitute understanding the meaning of the symbols.
Behaviorism is vindicated — since the room's outputs are indistinguishable from understanding, behavior is the only honest standard for crediting any system with comprehension.
Eliminative materialism is supported — 'understanding' is a folk-psychology term with no real referent, so the question of whether the room understands has no determinate answer.
Type physicalism is too narrow — only systems made of the same neural-state types as ours could understand, and the room's physical implementation is plainly the wrong stuff.
context: John Searle, 'Minds, Brains, and Programs' (1980), argues that syntax (formal symbol manipulation) is not sufficient for semantics (meaning). Searle's positive view is biological naturalism: only the right biology yields semantic content. The Systems Reply and Robot Reply contest the conclusion.

question: On a panel on integrated theories of consciousness, a guest describes the philosophical zombie: a being physically identical to you down to the last neuron, behaving exactly as you do, yet with no inner experience whatsoever. She argues: 'Even if no such creature could exist, it is coherently CONCEIVABLE, and that alone says something important.' What does the zombie case expose?
answer: Phenomenal facts are not entailed by physical facts — if zombies are coherently conceivable, the physical story leaves consciousness undetermined, counting against type physicalism.
choices: Phenomenal facts are not entailed by physical facts — if zombies are coherently conceivable, the physical story leaves consciousness undetermined, counting against type physicalism.
Conceivability tracks possibility unreliably — we can conceive impossibilities (water not H2O), so zombie-conceivability does not show consciousness is metaphysically extra at all.
Eliminative materialism is the natural conclusion — once 'phenomenal experience' allows such bizarre cases, we should suspect the category is incoherent and drop it from theory.
Functionalism is vindicated — since the zombie functions exactly as you do, it must be in the same mental states, so 'no inner experience' is a contradiction in terms here.
context: David Chalmers (The Conscious Mind, 1996) deploys the zombie argument: conceivability implies possibility, possibility entails non-entailment, and non-entailment refutes physicalism. The standard reply (Dennett, Yablo) is choice B — conceivability is a weak guide to metaphysical possibility.

question: A philosophy of mind workshop discusses inverted spectrum: two people raised identically, both calling fire engines 'red' and grass 'green,' yet one inwardly experiences what the other would call green when looking at fire, and vice versa. No behavioral test would distinguish them. What does the inverted spectrum case expose?
answer: Functional role does not fully fix phenomenal character — two systems can be functionally identical yet differ in what their experiences are LIKE; this counts against functionalism.
choices: Functional role does not fully fix phenomenal character — two systems can be functionally identical yet differ in what their experiences are LIKE; this counts against functionalism.
Behaviorism is vindicated — since no behavior would distinguish the two, there is no genuine fact about which inverts, and the case dissolves as a pseudo-question entirely.
Type physicalism handles the case — the brain states are identical by stipulation, so the inverts are impossible, and the conceivability of inversion is confused intuition.
Eliminative materialism is supported — 'what experience is like' relies on a folk category with no scientific anchor, so the case shows the category should be abandoned.
context: Inverted spectrum cases (Locke, Essay II.32; Sydney Shoemaker 1981; Ned Block 1990) press the gap between functional role and phenomenal quale. The case is designed to show that two systems can share all functional and behavioral properties yet differ phenomenally — a problem for any role-based theory of mind.

question: On a podcast on the limits of objective science, a philosopher summarizes Thomas Nagel: 'Bats navigate by sonar, a modality we lack. We can describe their neurology completely and STILL not know what their experience is like from the inside. The subjective is missed by the objective story.' The thought experiment asks: what does the bat case expose?
answer: Irreducibility of the subjective — phenomenal character (the 'what-it-is-likeness') is a property not captured by any third-person physical description of the system.
choices: Irreducibility of the subjective — phenomenal character (the 'what-it-is-likeness') is a property not captured by any third-person physical description of the system.
Higher-order theory — consciousness is a state's being the object of a higher-order representation; the bat is unknowable because we lack higher-order access to its states.
Functionalism vindicated — mental states are individuated by functional roles, so simulating the bat's functional architecture would give us full access to its experience.
Eliminative materialism — 'what it is like' relies on folk-psychological intuition mature neuroscience will discard; the bat case poses no problem once the category is dropped.
context: Thomas Nagel, 'What Is It Like to Be a Bat?' (1974), argues that the subjective character of experience cannot be captured by any objective, third-person account. The paper is an ancestor of Chalmers's hard problem and a foundational text for property dualism and related anti-reductive views.

question: A cognitive scientist on a podcast argues: 'Pain is not just a particular brain state. An octopus, a human, and a hypothetical silicon-based alien could all be in pain — what makes a state pain is what it DOES, the role it plays in the creature's life, not what it is made of.' Which view of mind is the cognitive scientist defending?
answer: Functionalism — mental states are individuated by causal-functional role (inputs, outputs, internal transitions); the same role can be realized in many different physical substrates.
choices: Functionalism — mental states are individuated by causal-functional role (inputs, outputs, internal transitions); the same role can be realized in many different physical substrates.
Type physicalism — every mental-state type is identical to a particular brain-state type; pain in octopus and human cannot be 'the same' state if their brain types differ.
Behaviorism — mental-state talk reduces to talk of behavioral dispositions; pain is just the disposition to wince and avoid, with no inner functional architecture doing extra work.
Biological naturalism — only certain biological systems (specifically, brains of the right sort) can have mental states; silicon-based aliens could not be in pain on this view.
context: Functionalism (Hilary Putnam, 'The Nature of Mental States,' 1967; Jerry Fodor, 1968) was motivated by multiple realizability: the same psychological state can be realized in different physical systems. The view dominated philosophy of mind for decades; Searle, Block, and Chalmers press it from different directions.

question: On a panel critiquing strong AI, a philosopher summarizes Searle: 'Consciousness is a biological phenomenon, like digestion or photosynthesis. Real brains made of real neurons cause it. A computer running the same program would not literally be conscious, any more than a simulation of a storm is a real storm.' Which view of mind is being summarized?
answer: Biological naturalism — consciousness is a biological feature of certain physical systems (brains) and cannot be replicated by a system merely implementing the same program in different substrate.
choices: Biological naturalism — consciousness is a biological feature of certain physical systems (brains) and cannot be replicated by a system merely implementing the same program in different substrate.
Functionalism — mental states are fixed by functional role, not physical substrate; any system implementing the right program will share the relevant mental states by stipulation.
Property dualism — consciousness is a non-physical property arising wherever certain physical conditions hold; substrate is irrelevant so long as the right functional conditions hold.
Eliminative materialism — 'consciousness' is a folk-psychology category mature neuroscience will replace; substrate-dependence presupposes a category that will not survive theory.
context: John Searle (The Rediscovery of the Mind, 1992) defends biological naturalism: consciousness is caused by and realized in brain processes, not by 'computation' per se. The view rejects both substance dualism and any form of functionalism that allows substrate-independence — a delicate balance to maintain.

question: In a philosophy of mind seminar, a student summarizes Paul Churchland: 'Beliefs, desires, hopes, fears — these are categories of folk psychology, an old theory we use to predict each other. As neuroscience matures, those categories will be replaced by brain-level ones, much as caloric and phlogiston were dropped.' Which view of mind is being defended?
answer: Eliminative materialism — folk-psychological categories (belief, desire, feeling) form a defective theory mature neuroscience will replace; the categories will be eliminated, not reduced.
choices: Eliminative materialism — folk-psychological categories (belief, desire, feeling) form a defective theory mature neuroscience will replace; the categories will be eliminated, not reduced.
Reductive type physicalism — folk-psychological categories are real but identical to brain-state types; mature neuroscience will REDUCE belief and desire to neural states, not eliminate.
Instrumentalism about belief — belief talk is a useful predictive stance toward systems but lacks deep metaphysical reality; categories are kept for utility, not dropped from theory.
Functionalism — mental states are individuated by causal-functional role; folk psychology captures real functional kinds and survives neuroscience as a higher-level psychological theory.
context: Paul Churchland, 'Eliminative Materialism and the Propositional Attitudes' (1981), argues that folk psychology is itself a theory, and a poor one. The standard rivals are reductive physicalism (which reduces rather than eliminates) and instrumentalism (Dennett's 'intentional stance').

question: On a podcast on theories of consciousness, a guest argues: 'A mental state is conscious not because of anything intrinsic to the state itself, but because it is the object of another, higher-order state that REPRESENTS it. When you become aware of your headache, what makes the pain conscious is your awareness of having it.' Which view of consciousness is this?
answer: Higher-order theory — a mental state is conscious when, and only when, suitably represented by a distinct higher-order state (a thought about, or perception of, the lower-order state).
choices: Higher-order theory — a mental state is conscious when, and only when, suitably represented by a distinct higher-order state (a thought about, or perception of, the lower-order state).
First-order intrinsicalism — a state is conscious in virtue of intrinsic features of the state itself; nothing more is needed beyond the state's own phenomenal character to make it conscious.
Functionalism (broad) — a state is conscious in virtue of its overall functional role in cognition; higher-order representation is one role among several, not the constitutive feature.
Eliminative materialism — 'conscious' is a folk-psychology term future neuroscience will discard; explaining what makes a state conscious presupposes a category that will not survive theory.
context: Higher-order theories (David Rosenthal, 'Two Concepts of Consciousness,' 1986; Peter Carruthers 2000) hold that a state is conscious iff it is represented by a higher-order state. First-order theorists (Dretske, Tye) deny this: consciousness is intrinsic to the right first-order state.

question: On a neuroscience panel, a researcher describes Giulio Tononi's view: 'Consciousness IS integrated information — the quantity called phi. A system is conscious to the extent that its parts together carry more information than the parts considered separately. On this view, even a thermostat has a tiny flicker of consciousness.' Which view of mind is this?
answer: Integrated Information Theory — consciousness IS integrated information (phi); any physical system with positive phi is conscious to that degree, so consciousness comes in degrees.
choices: Integrated Information Theory — consciousness IS integrated information (phi); any physical system with positive phi is conscious to that degree, so consciousness comes in degrees.
Functionalism — consciousness consists in the functional roles a system's states play; a thermostat lacks the rich functional architecture associated with mind, so it is unconscious.
Biological naturalism — consciousness is a feature of biological systems and cannot arise in non-biological devices like thermostats, regardless of any information-theoretic measure.
Higher-order theory — a state is conscious iff suitably represented by a higher-order state; a thermostat has no higher-order representations, so it lacks consciousness entirely.
context: Giulio Tononi's Integrated Information Theory (Phi, 2012; revisions through 2020s) identifies consciousness with integrated information. The view's panpsychist tendency — positive phi anywhere implies some degree of consciousness — is one of its most controversial features.

question: A cognitive scientist on a podcast argues: 'Consciousness is what gets BROADCAST. Most processing in the brain runs in parallel, unconscious. A narrow stream of information wins competition and is globally distributed to memory, planning, and report systems — and THAT is the moment of conscious access.' Which view of consciousness is the scientist defending?
answer: Global Workspace Theory — consciousness arises when information is broadcast widely across cognitive subsystems via a 'workspace'; access by many consumers IS the conscious state.
choices: Global Workspace Theory — consciousness arises when information is broadcast widely across cognitive subsystems via a 'workspace'; access by many consumers IS the conscious state.
Higher-order theory — a state is conscious iff suitably represented by a distinct higher-order state; broadcast across subsystems is incidental and not what constitutes consciousness.
Property dualism — consciousness is a non-physical property over and above any neural or functional architecture; describing broadcast leaves what consciousness IS untouched.
Integrated Information Theory — consciousness IS integrated information (phi); broadcast describes the dynamics but mislocates the constitutive property to access rather than integration.
context: Bernard Baars (A Cognitive Theory of Consciousness, 1988) introduced the global workspace metaphor; Stanislas Dehaene (Consciousness and the Brain, 2014) developed the neuronal version. Access consciousness is identified with broadcast; phenomenal consciousness, on critics, may not reduce to it.

question: On a philosophy of mind podcast, a guest argues: 'Consciousness does not come from nothing. Either it emerges magically at some threshold of complexity, or it is present, in tiny degrees, in the basic constituents of matter. The second is less mysterious — consciousness is fundamental and ubiquitous, like mass.' Which view of mind is the guest defending?
answer: Panpsychism — consciousness is a fundamental and ubiquitous feature of physical reality; complex consciousness in brains is built from the proto-conscious properties of basic constituents.
choices: Panpsychism — consciousness is a fundamental and ubiquitous feature of physical reality; complex consciousness in brains is built from the proto-conscious properties of basic constituents.
Property dualism with strong emergence — consciousness appears at certain levels of physical organization, not predictable from lower-level facts; basic matter has no proto-conscious side.
Eliminative materialism — 'consciousness' is a folk-psychology category future science will replace; treating it as ubiquitous extends a defective category rather than dissolving it.
Functionalism — mental states are functional roles realized by complex architectures; consciousness is not in basic matter but only in systems sophisticated enough to play the right roles.
context: Panpsychism (William James; Bertrand Russell; recently revived by Galen Strawson 2006, Philip Goff, Hedda Hassel Mørch) takes consciousness as fundamental. The view faces the 'combination problem': how do micro-experiences combine into the unified macro-experience you actually have?

question: On a podcast critiquing common-sense psychology, a philosopher argues: 'Consciousness is real and non-physical, but it does no causal work. Your decision to lift your arm FELT like it caused the lift, but the real causation ran through the brain. Mental experience is like steam from a train — real, but not what is pulling the cars.' Which view of mind is this?
answer: Epiphenomenalism — mental states are real non-physical effects of brain states but exert no causal influence on the physical world; felt 'because of my decision' is a phenomenal byproduct.
choices: Epiphenomenalism — mental states are real non-physical effects of brain states but exert no causal influence on the physical world; felt 'because of my decision' is a phenomenal byproduct.
Property dualism with mental causation — mental properties are non-physical and DO cause physical effects; denying mental causation would make experience pointless, which this view resists.
Eliminative materialism — mental states do not exist as a distinct kind; saying they exist but lack causal power keeps a category future science will discard, which the view rejects.
Functionalism — mental states are causal-functional roles by definition; calling them real but inert is a contradiction in terms, since 'mental state' just IS being part of a causal architecture.
context: Epiphenomenalism (T.H. Huxley, 1874; Frank Jackson, 1982, before his later reversal) holds that mental events are caused by physical events but cause nothing themselves. The 'self-stultification' worry: if mental states do no work, how could belief IN epiphenomenalism have produced this very sentence?

question: On a podcast on the limits of human inquiry, a guest argues: 'Consciousness IS produced by the brain. But we may be cognitively closed to understanding HOW. Human minds may be the wrong shape to grasp the mind-body link, the way a dog cannot grasp calculus. There is a real answer; we just cannot know it.' Which view of mind is the guest defending?
answer: Mysterianism — consciousness has a natural explanation that human minds are cognitively closed to grasping; the hard problem is real but reflects our limits, not a metaphysical gap.
choices: Mysterianism — consciousness has a natural explanation that human minds are cognitively closed to grasping; the hard problem is real but reflects our limits, not a metaphysical gap.
Eliminative materialism — 'consciousness' is a folk-psychology category future science will discard; appealing to cognitive closure assumes a category that may not survive mature theory.
Property dualism — the gap between physical and phenomenal facts is metaphysical, not epistemic; the puzzle reflects a real feature of reality, not just a limit on human comprehension.
Functionalism — consciousness is fully captured by functional architecture, and once we map that architecture there is no further puzzle; the cognitive-closure move is needlessly mysterian.
context: Colin McGinn ('Can We Solve the Mind-Body Problem?,' 1989; The Problem of Consciousness, 1991) argues for 'transcendental naturalism' or 'new mysterianism': consciousness is natural, but our minds are not equipped to understand it. The view tries to be a third option between physicalism and dualism.

question: A philosophy of mind seminar reads Donald Davidson. A student summarizes: 'Every particular mental event is some particular physical event — there is no extra ghostly stuff. But there are no strict laws linking mental TYPES (belief, desire) to physical types. Mind is physical token-by-token, yet no mental type reduces.' Which view of mind is this?
answer: Anomalous monism — each particular mental event is identical to some particular physical event, but no lawful type-type bridges link mental kinds to physical kinds (mental is anomalous).
choices: Anomalous monism — each particular mental event is identical to some particular physical event, but no lawful type-type bridges link mental kinds to physical kinds (mental is anomalous).
Type physicalism — each type of mental state is strictly identical to a brain-state type; belief and desire reduce to specific neural-state types under a complete neuroscience of mind.
Property dualism — physical events have both physical and irreducible mental properties; mental properties are real features over and above the physical, with no token-token identity.
Eliminative materialism — mental categories like belief and desire form a defective folk theory and will be eliminated; token-token or type-type reduction does not even arise here.
context: Donald Davidson's 'Mental Events' (1970) presents anomalous monism: token physicalism without psychophysical laws. The view tries to combine physicalism with the irreducibility (the 'anomalousness') of the mental as a domain of explanation — a delicate balance Kim and others press on.

question: On a panel responding to the Mary's Room argument, a physicalist replies: 'Mary gains a new CONCEPT of red, not a new FACT. Physical and phenomenal concepts refer to the same property under different cognitive modes — like "Hesperus" and "Phosphorus" both naming Venus. The gap is epistemic, not metaphysical.' Which physicalist move is the panelist defending?
answer: Phenomenal concepts strategy — physical and phenomenal concepts pick out the same underlying property; Mary acquires a new concept of an already-known property, so no new metaphysical fact is gained.
choices: Phenomenal concepts strategy — physical and phenomenal concepts pick out the same underlying property; Mary acquires a new concept of an already-known property, so no new metaphysical fact is gained.
Eliminative materialism — 'phenomenal' is a folk-psychology category mature neuroscience will discard; Mary's apparent learning is the surface of a confused concept, not new knowledge.
Property dualism — Mary really does learn a new non-physical property of experience; conceding that physicalism handles the case would give up the irreducibility of phenomenal character.
Functionalism — mental states are functional roles, so Mary already had every fact about red-experience that mattered; even the 'new concept' description misdescribes what occurs.
context: Brian Loar ('Phenomenal States,' 1990; 1997) and David Papineau (Thinking about Consciousness, 2002) developed the phenomenal concepts strategy: physicalism is true; the appearance of an explanatory gap is generated by the special cognitive mode of phenomenal concepts, not by extra properties.

question: On a philosophy of mind podcast, a guest argues: 'The mind and the body are two distinct substances. The mind is non-physical, indivisible, and capable of existing without the body. The body is physical, extended in space, and divisible. They interact, but they are not the same kind of thing.' Which view of mind is the guest defending?
answer: Substance dualism — the mind is a non-physical substance distinct from the body; mental and physical are two basic kinds of stuff, capable in principle of existing apart from one another.
choices: Substance dualism — the mind is a non-physical substance distinct from the body; mental and physical are two basic kinds of stuff, capable in principle of existing apart from one another.
Property dualism — mental and physical properties are distinct, but one kind of substance (physical) bears both; mental properties do not exist apart from a physical bearer on this view.
Type physicalism — mental states ARE brain states under a different description; appeal to a non-physical substance smuggles in an entity for which no evidence has been produced at all.
Functionalism — mental states are functional roles realizable in many substrates; treating mind as a special substance confuses high-level functional architecture with basic stuff entirely.
context: René Descartes (Meditations on First Philosophy, 1641) defends substance dualism: res cogitans (thinking substance) and res extensa (extended substance) are distinct kinds. Princess Elisabeth's interaction objection (1643) and contemporary physicalist arguments make the view a minority position today.

question: A philosophy of mind seminar discusses multiple realizability. A guest argues: 'Each particular instance of pain — this pain now, in this creature — IS a particular physical event. But pain as a TYPE need not be identical to any one brain-state type, because octopus pain and human pain are realized differently.' Which view of mind is the guest defending?
answer: Token physicalism — each particular mental-state token (this pain now) is identical to some physical-state token; but mental-state TYPES need not be identical to any single brain-state type.
choices: Token physicalism — each particular mental-state token (this pain now) is identical to some physical-state token; but mental-state TYPES need not be identical to any single brain-state type.
Type physicalism — each type of mental state is strictly identical to a particular brain-state type; pain just IS a neural firing type, as water just IS H2O across instances.
Property dualism — physical and phenomenal properties are both real but distinct; identifying any token pain with a neural event leaves out the phenomenal character of pain entirely.
Eliminative materialism — 'pain' is a folk-psychological category that will not survive mature neuroscience; token or type identity claims presuppose a category that will be discarded.
context: Token physicalism, sustained by multiple-realizability arguments (Putnam, Fodor), preserves materialism while granting that mental kinds need not carve nature at the same joints as physical kinds. Davidson's anomalous monism is one variety; non-reductive functionalism is another.

question: On a philosophy of mind seminar, a guest sharpens the case against type physicalism: 'Even granted that pain is correlated with C-fiber firing, WHY is C-fiber firing accompanied by anything felt at all? A complete physical story explains structure and function, but not why any of it is LIT UP from the inside.' What does the guest's argument expose?
answer: The explanatory gap — physical descriptions explain structure and function but leave unexplained why any of it is accompanied by phenomenal experience, which counts against type physicalism.
choices: The explanatory gap — physical descriptions explain structure and function but leave unexplained why any of it is accompanied by phenomenal experience, which counts against type physicalism.
Conceivability tracks possibility unreliably — we can conceive impossibilities, so the felt-gap intuition does not show consciousness is metaphysically extra; reductive theories survive.
Eliminative materialism is the proper response — 'lit up from the inside' relies on a folk category mature neuroscience will discard; the gap is generated by bad concepts, not reality.
Functionalism is vindicated — once we specify the functional role of pain, no further question about felt-ness remains; the explanatory gap is a confusion about what pain IS at the start.
context: Joseph Levine ('Materialism and Qualia: The Explanatory Gap,' 1983) coined the phrase; Chalmers (1995) sharpened it into the 'hard problem.' Type physicalists reply that all explanation has to bottom out somewhere; phenomenal-concepts theorists locate the gap in cognition, not metaphysics.

question: On a podcast on cognitive science, Andy Clark argues: 'Otto carries a notebook everywhere; he relies on it as Inga relies on biological memory. When Otto consults the notebook, his BELIEF that the museum is on 53rd Street is partly constituted by the notebook itself. Mind isn't bounded by skull and skin.' Which view of mind is Clark defending?
answer: Extended mind thesis — cognitive processes can extend beyond the biological body into reliably-coupled external resources (notebooks, phones, tools) that play the same functional role.
choices: Extended mind thesis — cognitive processes can extend beyond the biological body into reliably-coupled external resources (notebooks, phones, tools) that play the same functional role.
Type physicalism — every mental-state type is identical to a brain-state type; calling a notebook part of Otto's mind confuses an external prop with an internal cognitive state.
Property dualism — mental properties are non-physical features over and above neural ones; extending mind to notebooks confuses functional dependence with constitutive identity.
Eliminative materialism — 'belief' is a folk-psychology category mature neuroscience will discard; the extended-mind move just extends a defective category outside the skull entirely.
context: Andy Clark and David Chalmers, 'The Extended Mind' (Analysis, 1998), argue for the parity principle: if a process going on outside the head plays the same role as one inside, both are part of cognition. Critics (Adams & Aizawa, Rupert) deny the parity and insist on the 'mark of the cognitive.'

question: Hilary Putnam's 'brain in a vat': imagine a brain floating in nutrient fluid, wired to a supercomputer that feeds it the experiences of a normal life. Putnam argues — surprisingly — that such a brain could NOT truly think 'I am a brain in a vat,' because its words would refer to vat-fed images, not real brains and vats. Which view of meaning does Putnam's reply require?
answer: Semantic externalism — the meanings of words are partly fixed by what they have causally tracked in the speaker's environment, so an envatted brain's 'brain' and 'vat' refer to its world, not ours.
choices: Semantic externalism — the meanings of words are partly fixed by what they have causally tracked in the speaker's environment, so an envatted brain's 'brain' and 'vat' refer to its world, not ours.
Semantic internalism — meanings are determined entirely by what's in the head of the speaker, so the envatted brain's words could refer to real brains and vats as long as its concepts match ours.
Eliminative materialism — 'meaning' is a folk-psychological category mature cognitive science will replace, so the question of what the envatted brain refers to does not require an answer.
Behaviorism about meaning — word meaning is fixed by patterns of speaker behavior alone, so the envatted brain's words mean whatever its dispositions would settle in actual exchanges with others.
context: Hilary Putnam (Reason, Truth and History, 1981) deploys semantic externalism — first defended in 'The Meaning of "Meaning"' (1975, the Twin Earth case) — to defuse radical skepticism. If meaning is fixed by causal contact with the environment, the skeptic's worry self-undermines: to formulate it requires standing outside the vat one is supposedly in.

question: John Locke's 'prince and the cobbler' case: imagine that the consciousness of a prince — with all his memories of palace life — moves overnight into the body of a cobbler, while the cobbler's body wakes the next morning thinking and remembering as the prince. Locke holds the resulting person IS the prince in a cobbler's body. Which view of personal identity does this support?
answer: Memory-continuity view — a person persists through time as long as memory and personality form an unbroken chain; the body that carries the consciousness is just the vehicle.
choices: Memory-continuity view — a person persists through time as long as memory and personality form an unbroken chain; the body that carries the consciousness is just the vehicle.
Bodily-continuity view — a person persists through time as the same organism; on this account the cobbler-bodied figure remains the cobbler, whatever memories he reports.
Soul view — a person persists as the same immaterial soul behind every change of body or memory; the case turns on which soul ended up where after the night.
No-self view — no person endures behind either body at all; the prince and the cobbler are each bundles of momentary experiences with no further fact about identity.
context: John Locke (Essay Concerning Human Understanding, 1689, Book II ch. 27) uses the prince-and-cobbler case to defend a memory-based account of personal identity: a person is whoever can extend consciousness back to earlier experiences. Derek Parfit (1984) later refined this into the broader psychological-continuity theory and pressed the branching cases.

question: Harry Frankfurt's 'unwilling addict' case: a drug addict desires heroin and uses it, but at a deeper level desires NOT to desire heroin — he wishes his cravings did not move him. Frankfurt contrasts this with a 'wanton' addict who simply has the craving and acts on it with no inner objection. What distinction does the case expose, on Frankfurt's view?
answer: First-order vs. higher-order desires — genuine agency requires desires ABOUT one's desires (wanting-not-to-want); the unwilling addict has them, the wanton lacks them, and that is the mark of a free will.
choices: First-order vs. higher-order desires — genuine agency requires desires ABOUT one's desires (wanting-not-to-want); the unwilling addict has them, the wanton lacks them, and that is the mark of a free will.

Reasons vs. causes — the addict is unfree because his action is caused, not reasoned; only desires backed by reasons constitute genuine agency, and any craving (higher-order or not) just disqualifies him.
Compatibilism vs. libertarianism — the case is meant to show that determinism is incompatible with freedom; the addict is unfree because his desires were caused by prior states he did not control.
Mental causation vs. epiphenomenalism — the addict's higher-order wish does no causal work in the world; the case shows that mental states are inert byproducts of brain events, not real causes.
context: Harry Frankfurt's 'Freedom of the Will and the Concept of a Person' (1971) introduces second-order desires — desires about which first-order desires move us. A 'person' is a creature who has, and acts from, second-order volitions. Critics (Watson, Wolf) press the question of what makes a higher-order desire AUTHORITATIVE without an infinite regress.

question: Your sister says the no-screens-at-dinner rule is fair because every member of the family agreed to it at the kitchen meeting. Which view of political authority is she defending?
answer: Consent theory — a rule binds those affected because they agreed to it; agreement is what makes it valid.
choices: Consent theory — a rule binds those affected because they agreed to it; agreement is what makes it valid.
Tradition theory — a rule binds because the group has always lived by it; custom is what confers it.
Strength theory — a rule binds because those in charge can enforce it; power is what makes it stand.
Anarchism — no household rule has real authority; obeying is always optional, even when you do agree.
context: Consent theory (Locke, Rousseau) holds that rules bind only those who agreed to them. Modern democracies trace their legitimacy to this idea: a vote turns power into authority.

question: Coach Reeves keeps the same pre-game huddle ritual. He says: 'Every team since 1962 has done it this way — it's part of what makes us this team.' Which view of authority is Coach defending?
answer: Tradition theory — a rule binds because the group has always lived by it; custom is what makes it valid.
choices: Tradition theory — a rule binds because the group has always lived by it; custom is what makes it valid.
Consent theory — a rule binds those affected because they agreed to it; agreement is what confers it.
Strength theory — a rule binds because those in charge can enforce it; power is what makes it stand.
Authority-by-merit — a rule binds because the wisest member designed it; expert judgment confers it.
context: Tradition theory (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, 1790) grounds authority in continuity. Long-standing practice carries knowledge that no single person could design from scratch.

question: On the playground, the biggest sixth-grader announces who gets the swings. He tells Ana: 'Rules are whatever I say they are — try to stop me.' Which view of authority is he defending?
answer: Strength theory — a rule binds because the powerful can enforce it; power itself is what makes it valid.
choices: Strength theory — a rule binds because the powerful can enforce it; power itself is what makes it valid.
Consent theory — a rule binds those affected because they agreed to it; agreement is what gives it force.
Tradition theory — a rule binds because the group has always lived by it; custom is what makes it stand.
Anarchism — no playground rule has real authority; obeying any rule is always a free personal choice.
context: Strength theory is the view Thrasymachus defends in Plato's Republic: 'justice is the advantage of the stronger.' Socrates rejects it — power can compel, but compulsion alone doesn't make rules just.

question: In chess club, captain Priya picks every opening for tournament practice. She tells the group: 'I'm the highest-rated player — that's why I make the call.' Which view of authority is she defending?
answer: Authority-by-merit — a rule binds because the best-qualified member is the one deciding for the group.
choices: Authority-by-merit — a rule binds because the best-qualified member is the one deciding for the group.
Consent theory — a rule binds those affected because they agreed to it; agreement is what confers it.
Tradition theory — a rule binds because the group has always lived by it; custom is what makes it stand.
Strength theory — a rule binds because the powerful can enforce it; power itself is what makes it valid.
context: Authority-by-merit traces to Plato's Republic: rulers should be those who know best (the 'philosopher kings'). Critics worry: who decides which knowledge counts? Modern democracies tend to balance expertise with consent.

question: At the library, Marco whispers to his friend: 'Quiet rule? Nobody really gets to tell me to be quiet — I just choose to be, because I want to.' Which view of authority is Marco defending?
answer: Anarchism — no rule has real authority over you; obeying any rule is always your personal free choice.
choices: Anarchism — no rule has real authority over you; obeying any rule is always your personal free choice.
Consent theory — a rule binds those affected because they agreed to it; agreement is what gives it force.
Tradition theory — a rule binds because the group has always lived by it; custom is what makes it stand.
Authority-by-merit — a rule binds because the best-qualified member is the one who is deciding here.
context: Anarchism (from Greek anarkhia, 'no ruler') denies that any institution has genuine authority over the individual. Thinkers like Bakunin and Tolstoy argued obedience is always a free choice, never a duty.

question: At scout troop, everyone votes on which lake to camp by. Leon says: 'Once we voted, the majority pick is binding — even on the kids who lost.' Which view of authority is Leon defending?
answer: Consent theory — a rule binds because the group ran a fair vote; the agreement to vote creates the duty.
choices: Consent theory — a rule binds because the group ran a fair vote; the agreement to vote creates the duty.
Tradition theory — a rule binds because the group has always lived by it; custom is what confers it.
Strength theory — a rule binds because those in charge can enforce it; power is what makes it stand.
Authority-by-merit — a rule binds because the best-qualified member is the one who is deciding for all.
context: Modern democratic theory builds on consent: even those who voted against a measure are bound, because they agreed in advance to abide by the process. Locke called this 'tacit consent' to the rules of the game.

question: The senior knight defends the morning-watch rotation: 'The company has kept it for seven generations — that is what binds us. Custom carries knowledge no captain could write in a manual.' Which view is the knight defending?
answer: Tradition theory — a rule binds because the group has always lived by it; custom is what makes it valid.
choices: Tradition theory — a rule binds because the group has always lived by it; custom is what makes it valid.
Consent theory — a rule binds those affected because they agreed to it; agreement is what confers it.
Strength theory — a rule binds because those in charge can enforce it; power is what makes it stand.
Anarchism — no rule has real authority; obeying is always optional, even when you choose it.
context: Tradition theory (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, 1790; Roger Scruton in our day) defends inherited custom as authority. Long-standing practice carries collective knowledge that no single person could design from scratch. Burke's reply to the Jacobins was exactly this argument.

question: Big brother Sam grabs the remote and announces: 'Whoever can take it gets to pick the show — that's the only rule that actually counts here.' Which view of authority is Sam defending?
answer: Strength theory — a rule binds only because the powerful can enforce it; force itself is what makes it valid.
choices: Strength theory — a rule binds only because the powerful can enforce it; force itself is what makes it valid.
Consent theory — a rule binds those affected because they agreed to it; agreement is what confers it.
Tradition theory — a rule binds because the family has always lived by it; custom is what gives it force.
Natural-rights view — a rule binds because it protects basic rights; rights are what give the rule its force.
context: Strength theory says might makes right. Hobbes took it seriously: without sovereign power, life would be 'nasty, brutish, and short.' But Hobbes also said the sovereign owes protection in return.

question: Ms. Park, the librarian, picks every book for fifth-grade reading group. She explains: 'I trained in children's literature — that training is why this is my call.' Which view of authority is she defending?
answer: Authority-by-merit — a rule binds because the most-trained person is the one making the call for the group.
choices: Authority-by-merit — a rule binds because the most-trained person is the one making the call for the group.
Consent theory — a rule binds those affected because they agreed to it; agreement is what confers it.
Tradition theory — a rule binds because the school has always lived by it; custom is what makes it stand.
Strength theory — a rule binds because those in charge can enforce it; power is what gives the rule force.
context: Authority-by-merit (Plato's philosopher-kings) defends expertise as a ground of rule. The doctor tells you what medicine to take; the pilot flies the plane. The challenge: how to choose the experts.

question: At the school uniform meeting, cousin Owen tells his parents: 'No school actually has the right to tell me what to wear — I just play along if I want.' Which view of authority is Owen defending?
answer: Anarchism — no school rule has real authority over you; following one is always your personal free choice.
choices: Anarchism — no school rule has real authority over you; following one is always your personal free choice.
Consent theory — a rule binds those affected because they agreed to it; agreement is what gives it force.
Tradition theory — a rule binds because the school has always lived by it; custom is what makes it stand.
Authority-by-merit — a rule binds because the best-trained adults are the ones deciding for the students.
context: Anarchist thinkers (Kropotkin, Emma Goldman) argued that genuine cooperation cannot be commanded; it has to be chosen. Owen's wording — 'I play along if I want' — captures the anarchist view exactly.

question: The neighborhood pool committee draws up rules after every family signs in to vote. Leticia says: 'Because we all signed and voted, the rules apply to us all.' Which view of authority is she defending?
answer: Consent theory — a rule binds those affected because they agreed to it; the act of signing creates the duty.
choices: Consent theory — a rule binds those affected because they agreed to it; the act of signing creates the duty.

question: Mr. Vance picks every debate-club topic himself. He tells the team: 'I've coached debate for twenty-two years — my judgment is the basis for these calls.' Which view of authority is he defending?

question: When the lunch monitor refuses lunch to a hungry kid who forgot his ticket, Theo objects: 'Some basic things just can't be taken away — feeding a hungry child is one.' Which view of authority is Theo defending?

question: When scout troop dues are due, Hugo refuses. He tells the troop leader: 'No troop really gets to demand money from me — I pay only if and when I personally choose to.' Which view of authority is Hugo defending?

question: Asked why she alone decides the pet-club rules, sixth-grader Greta says: 'I'm the only one who actually knows how each animal should be handled — that's why I decide.' Which view of authority is she defending?

question: On the council of squires, Maya defends a new market-fair rule: 'It binds us because every councilor voted for it together — the vote IS the authority.' Which view of political authority is Maya defending?

question: Asked why hall passes are required, Mr. Park answers: 'Every class at this school has used hall passes since the school opened — that long practice is what binds us now.' Which view of political authority is Mr. Park defending?

question: The class president pushes a rule limiting which clubs meet Fridays. Dani notes it unfairly targets her math team. The president shrugs: 'I won the election fair and square.' Why is 'I won the election' NOT the same as 'the rule is just'?

question: A YouTuber on civics argues: 'Free speech isn't a right because the constitution wrote it down. The constitution wrote it down because it's already a right — and if the constitution were repealed tomorrow, the right would still exist.' Which view of rights is she defending?

question: An online civics commentator says: 'Rights aren't discovered like elements on a periodic table, and they aren't decreed by lawmakers either. They're whatever the community treats as rights — useful agreements that hold while we honor them.' Which view of rights is she defending?

question: A debate-club captain argues: 'A right is legitimate when rational people, imagining they didn't know who they'd be in a society, would agree to grant it. Hypothetical fair agreement is the test that filters out unjust rules.' Which view of rights is she defending?

Natural rights — rights exist prior to any agreement; what rational agents would agree to is downstream of moral facts that ground their reasoning.
Legal positivism — rights exist only because law creates them; hypothetical agreements are interesting fiction but cannot generate any actual right.
Communitarianism — rights are grounded in the shared traditions of a community; abstracting away from concrete community erases what makes rights real.
context: Contractarianism / contractualism: rights and rules are justified by what people could agree to. Rawls (A Theory of Justice, 1971) uses the 'veil of ignorance' to specify the fair conditions; Scanlon (What We Owe to Each Other, 1998) varies the test.

question: A school newspaper editor pushes back on a peer's claim about universal rights: 'Rights make sense inside a community of shared practices. Strip away the tradition that gives them meaning and you have abstract slogans, not real rights.' Which view of rights is she defending?
answer: Communitarianism — rights derive meaning from shared communal traditions; abstract universal rights without a thick community to embed them lose grip.
choices: Communitarianism — rights derive meaning from shared communal traditions; abstract universal rights without a thick community to embed them lose grip.
Natural rights — rights belong to every human being regardless of community; universal grounding is what makes them rights and not local customs.
Legal positivism — rights exist only because law creates them; the appeal to communal tradition is irrelevant to whether a right is formally enacted.
Contract theory — rights are grounded in what rational agents could agree to abstractly; communal context is incidental to the agreement test.
context: Communitarianism (MacIntyre, After Virtue 1981; Sandel, Liberalism and the Limits of Justice 1982) argues liberal abstract-rights theories ignore that moral concepts draw meaning from concrete communal practices — Aristotelian roots.

question: A peer-review reader argues: 'A right means freedom from arbitrary power. You have a right to speak when no one can silence you at whim — even if the law happens to permit speech today, dependence on whim is the absence of a right.' Which view of rights is she defending?
answer: Civic republicanism — a right is freedom from arbitrary domination; what counts is that no one can silence you at whim, not merely that no one happens to.
choices: Civic republicanism — a right is freedom from arbitrary domination; what counts is that no one can silence you at whim, not merely that no one happens to.
Natural rights — rights exist prior to government and arbitrary power is wrong because it violates them; the right grounds the wrongness of domination.
Legal positivism — rights exist only when the legal code recognizes them; freedom from arbitrary power is a legal description, not a kind of right.
Classical liberalism — a right is a sphere of non-interference protected by law; the question is whether the state interferes, not whether anyone might.
context: Civic republicanism (Pettit, Republicanism 1997; Skinner) defines liberty as non-domination — protection from arbitrary power — and contrasts with liberal non-interference. Roman roots: a free citizen was one with no master, even a kind one.

question: A YouTuber explains why the state may collect taxes by force: 'It can only do this because the people governed have agreed — either explicitly or by accepting the benefits of citizenship — to be bound by the rules they helped make.' Which view of political authority is she defending?
answer: Consent theory — the state's right to use force comes from the agreement of the governed; without consent, coercion is just force without authority.
choices: Consent theory — the state's right to use force comes from the agreement of the governed; without consent, coercion is just force without authority.
Hobbesian absolutism — the state's right to use force comes from its ability to prevent war of all against all; consent is incidental compared to order.
Divine-right theory — the state's right to use force comes from authority granted by a higher power; the consent of the governed does not ground it.
Tradition theory — the state's right to use force comes from continuous practice; long-standing custom legitimates state action regardless of agreement.
context: Consent theory of authority (Locke, Two Treatises 1689; Rousseau, Social Contract 1762) grounds the state in agreement. Tacit consent (taking benefits, staying in the territory) extends it beyond explicit signatures, though this extension is contested.

question: A peer-review reader writes about a failed state: 'The first job of any state is to prevent the collapse into violence. A state that secures order against lawlessness has earned its authority, however imperfect the rules it enforces.' Which view of political authority is she defending?
answer: Hobbesian view — the state's authority comes from securing order against lawlessness; preventing war of all against all founds its legitimacy.
choices: Hobbesian view — the state's authority comes from securing order against lawlessness; preventing war of all against all founds its legitimacy.
Lockean consent view — the state's authority comes from agreement of the governed; preventing collapse is a reason to consent but not the source.
Communitarian view — the state's authority comes from the shared traditions of its community; security is incidental to that community-grounded basis.
Anarchist view — the state has no genuine authority at all; preventing collapse is a service some states perform but does not generate any right to rule.
context: Hobbes (Leviathan, 1651) argued the state's first job is to escape the 'state of nature' — a war of all against all. Almost any government beats that, so almost any state that prevents civil collapse has earned at least minimal legitimacy.

question: A debate-club captain argues: 'The state may use force only to prevent harm to others — never to make people better, healthier, or more devout. Beyond harm-prevention, the state stops being legitimate and starts being intrusive.' Which view of political authority is she defending?
answer: Classical liberalism — the state's legitimate force is limited to preventing harm; coercion to improve people beyond their consent oversteps that boundary.
choices: Classical liberalism — the state's legitimate force is limited to preventing harm; coercion to improve people beyond their consent oversteps that boundary.
Communitarianism — the state may legitimately promote shared communal goods; limiting force to harm-prevention treats people as separate when they are not.
Hobbesian view — the state may use force to prevent civil collapse; anything that secures order falls within authority, including paternalism.
Civic republicanism — the state may use force to secure non-domination; promoting civic virtue is part of preventing arbitrary power, not overreach.
context: Mill's 'harm principle' (On Liberty, 1859) is the canonical classical-liberal limit: 'The only purpose for which power can be rightfully exercised over any member of a civilized community, against his will, is to prevent harm to others.'

question: A debate-club captain argues: '51% of the student body voted to ban the chess club from using the library. The vote was clean and the rule was applied fairly.' A peer pushes back. Why is 'majority approved' not the same as 'justly decided'?
answer: Majority vote settles process — a clean count of preferences; justice asks whether the rule treats people rightly, a question prevalence cannot answer.
choices: Majority vote settles process — a clean count of preferences; justice asks whether the rule treats people rightly, a question prevalence cannot answer.
Majority vote tracks utility — what most people want maximizes aggregate good; the chess ban is utilitarian and just by that consequence-weighing standard.
Majority vote expresses tradition — long-standing communal practice; the chess vote ratifies whatever shared values the school's tradition has settled.
Majority vote secures order — agreement prevents civil collapse; whatever the majority decides counts as just because the alternative is contested chaos.
context: 'Tyranny of the majority' (Mill, On Liberty 1859; Tocqueville, Democracy in America 1835) names this danger. Majority approval is a procedural fact about preferences; justice is a substantive question about whether rules treat people rightly.

question: A school newspaper editor argues: 'The principal makes fair decisions case by case — but every case should still go through written rules first, even when a rule produces a worse outcome than his personal judgment.' Why is 'good decisions by good rulers' not the same as 'rule of law'?
answer: Rule of law constrains decisions in advance — public written rules everyone can see; case-by-case judgment yields outcomes but not the same constraint.
choices: Rule of law constrains decisions in advance — public written rules everyone can see; case-by-case judgment yields outcomes but not the same constraint.
Rule of law is whatever the ruler announces — published or not; the editor's distinction collapses once rulers can codify their preferences as rules.
Rule of law tracks majority will — whatever most people prefer becomes law; individual judgment by the principal is irrelevant to the procedural meaning.
Rule of law is identical to good rule — both produce just outcomes; the editor draws a distinction with no real moral weight beyond procedural appearance.
context: Rule of law (Dicey, Introduction to the Study of the Law of the Constitution 1885; Hayek, The Constitution of Liberty 1960) requires general, public, prospective rules that constrain officials. Even benevolent rulers acting case-by-case lack this constraint.

question: A peer-review reader notes that a school's new dress code was 'agreed to' by students who would have been suspended for refusing. He argues this does not count as genuine consent at all. Why is 'agreed under threat of penalty' not the same as 'consented to'?
answer: Consent requires real options — at least one acceptable alternative besides agreement; agreement under threat tracks compliance, not authority-giving consent.
choices: Consent requires real options — at least one acceptable alternative besides agreement; agreement under threat tracks compliance, not authority-giving consent.
Consent requires explicit signature — written approval on a formal document; the dress-code students did not sign, so the issue is paperwork, not coercion.
Consent requires majority support — at least 51% of those affected agreeing; the question is how many students approved, not whether penalties applied.
Consent requires good outcomes — agreement is genuine when results turn out well; the dress code's effects retroactively determine whether consent was real.
context: The 'highwayman objection' to tacit consent (Spooner, No Treason 1870; Hume, Of the Original Contract 1748): 'Your money or your life' produces compliance, not consent. Real consent requires meaningful alternatives — the option to refuse without penalty.

question: A school newspaper editor argues against a proposed governance reform: 'A tradition this old encodes hard-won lessons we'd discard at our peril. The burden is on the reformer, not on the practice that has survived for centuries.' Which view of political authority is she defending?
answer: Tradition theory — long-standing practice carries presumptive authority; surviving generations is evidence of accumulated wisdom reformers must overcome.
choices: Tradition theory — long-standing practice carries presumptive authority; surviving generations is evidence of accumulated wisdom reformers must overcome.
Consent theory — practice carries authority only by present agreement of the governed; the tradition argument confuses age of a rule with whether it binds.
Natural rights theory — practice carries authority only when it tracks pre-political rights; an old rule violating rights is not legitimated by antiquity.
Contract theory — practice carries authority only when rational agents could agree to it; the tradition argument substitutes longevity for justification.
context: Edmund Burke's defense of inherited institutions (Reflections on the Revolution in France, 1790) frames tradition as accumulated practical wisdom — the burden of proof falls on the reformer because surviving customs encode lessons we cannot fully see.

question: A YouTuber argues: 'Even a 90% vote shouldn't be able to strip the basic rights of the remaining 10%. That's why constitutions put some rights outside what any majority can change — democracy itself needs limits to keep being democracy.' Which view of political authority is she defending?
answer: Constitutionalism — some basic rights stand outside what any majority may change; the constitution constrains the majority, keeping democracy possible.
choices: Constitutionalism — some basic rights stand outside what any majority may change; the constitution constrains the majority, keeping democracy possible.
Pure majoritarianism — whatever a majority decides binds the minority; constitutional limits on the majority are themselves anti-democratic by this view.
Anarchism — no majority and no constitution has genuine authority over the individual; both vote and constitution are equally suspect grounds for force.
Hobbesian view — the sovereign's authority is whatever prevents collapse; constitutional limits on the sovereign undercut the security that grounds it.
context: Constitutionalism (Madison, Federalist 10 and 51, 1787-88) is the response to majority tyranny: put basic rights into a higher-law document the majority cannot rewrite by ordinary vote. Constraints on the majority preserve the conditions for democracy.

question: A school newspaper editor argues: 'A government has authority over us because we are members of a community with shared history, language, and obligations. Membership comes with duties no contract could ever fully capture.' Which view of political authority is she defending?
answer: Communitarian view — authority comes from membership in a community with shared identity; obligations of membership exceed what any contract spells out.
choices: Communitarian view — authority comes from membership in a community with shared identity; obligations of membership exceed what any contract spells out.
Consent theory — authority comes from agreement of the governed; shared history is one reason to consent but the consent itself is the actual source.
Natural rights theory — authority comes from securing pre-political rights; the community grounding is incidental to the rights that ground legitimacy.
Hobbesian view — authority comes from preventing the war of all against all; shared community matters only as it reduces the threat of civil collapse.
context: Communitarianism (Sandel, Liberalism and the Limits of Justice 1982; Taylor, Sources of the Self 1989) emphasizes that we are 'encumbered selves' embedded in communities with constitutive attachments — duties that contract theory misses.

question: A debate-club captain argues: 'Whatever a majority of the people want should become the law, full stop. The whole point of democracy is that the people rule — letting judges or constitutions overrule a majority undoes that.' Which view of political authority is she defending?
answer: Pure majoritarianism — the majority's will is the foundation of legitimate authority; judicial or constitutional limits on it subvert democracy itself.
choices: Pure majoritarianism — the majority's will is the foundation of legitimate authority; judicial or constitutional limits on it subvert democracy itself.
Constitutionalism — basic rights stand outside what the majority may change; limits on the majority preserve the conditions that make democracy worth having.
Civic republicanism — what counts is non-domination, not raw majority preference; a majority can dominate a minority as effectively as any single ruler can.
Tradition theory — long-standing practice carries authority, not present majorities; what the majority wants today must yield to what generations have set.
context: Pure majoritarianism reduces legitimacy to a head-count of present preferences. Rousseau's 'general will' (Social Contract, 1762) is sometimes read this way; Tocqueville (Democracy in America, 1835) warned against the 'tyranny of the majority.'

question: A peer-review reader notes a city's new ordinance fines anyone who feeds the homeless without a permit. The ordinance passed by ordinary procedure and the city enforces it consistently. He still calls it illegitimate. Why is 'lawfully enacted' not the same as 'legitimately binding'?
answer: Legitimacy adds a moral question — whether the rule treats people rightly; lawful enactment is procedural and can produce rules that fail the moral test.
choices: Legitimacy adds a moral question — whether the rule treats people rightly; lawful enactment is procedural and can produce rules that fail the moral test.
Legitimacy is just procedural correctness — whether the rule was enacted properly; the reader's complaint reduces to procedure, and the ordinance meets it.
Legitimacy tracks majority support — whether most citizens approved the rule; enactment by representatives is just an approximation of majority will here.
Legitimacy tracks effectiveness — whether the rule actually achieves its stated ends; lawful enactment is unrelated to whether the policy works as intended.
context: Legal positivism distinguishes what law IS (lawfully enacted) from what law OUGHT to be (morally legitimate). Even Hart (The Concept of Law, 1961), who defended this separation, agreed an unjust law remains genuinely law — but legitimacy is a further question.

question: An online civics commentator argues: 'When a state systematically violates basic human rights, citizens are not bound to obey unjust commands. State authority dissolves at exactly the point where it stops protecting rights.' Which view of political authority is she defending?
answer: Natural-rights view — state authority is conditional on protecting basic rights; systematic rights violation dissolves the state's claim to obedience.
choices: Natural-rights view — state authority is conditional on protecting basic rights; systematic rights violation dissolves the state's claim to obedience.
Legal positivism — state authority comes from valid law; whether the law is just is a separate moral question that does not affect the duty to obey commands.
Hobbesian view — state authority comes from preventing the war of all against all; any state that prevents collapse retains authority, however unjust its rules.
Tradition theory — state authority comes from long-standing practice; whether the state currently protects rights is incidental to its continuous claim.
context: The right of resistance traces back through Locke (Second Treatise, 1689; 'whenever the legislators endeavour to take away and destroy the property of the people'). Aquinas' natural-law tradition makes a similar move: unjust law fails to bind in conscience.

question: A YouTuber explains a tax policy debate: 'A distribution of resources is just if the rules of fair acquisition and voluntary transfer were followed all the way back. The final pattern doesn't matter — only the history of voluntary steps.' Which view of justice is she defending?
answer: Procedural justice — distributions are just if fair acquisition and voluntary transfer were followed throughout; the final pattern of holdings is irrelevant.
choices: Procedural justice — distributions are just if fair acquisition and voluntary transfer were followed throughout; the final pattern of holdings is irrelevant.
Distributive justice (Rawlsian) — distributions are just only if they benefit the least-advantaged; procedural history is a factor but does not settle justice.
Communitarian justice — distributions are just when they fit the shared values of the community; abstract procedural rules cannot replace communal judgment.
Utilitarian justice — distributions are just when they maximize aggregate good; the history of transfer matters only as it relates to total welfare.
context: Procedural / historical-entitlement justice (Nozick, Anarchy State and Utopia 1974) argues if acquisition and transfer were just, the resulting distribution is just whatever it looks like. Rawls (A Theory of Justice 1971) judges by patterns of outcomes.

question: A school newspaper editor argues: 'A person owns the work of his own hands. When he mixes his labor with land or material no one yet owns, he makes a rightful claim to the result — and that claim is a right the state finds, not invents.' Which view of property rights is she defending?
answer: Natural-rights labor view — property rights arise from mixing one's labor with unowned resources; the claim exists pre-politically and the state recognizes it.
choices: Natural-rights labor view — property rights arise from mixing one's labor with unowned resources; the claim exists pre-politically and the state recognizes it.
Legal positivism — property rights exist only because law creates them; appeals to mixing labor are useful descriptions but cannot generate any actual right.
Utilitarian justification — property rights are recognized because doing so produces better aggregate outcomes; mixing labor is a heuristic for sorting claims.
Communitarian view — property rights derive from the shared traditions of a community; what counts as ownership is whatever community practice recognizes.
