Lockean liberalism — the state is a creature of consent instrumental to protecting natural rights, so treating it as the substantive actualization of freedom inverts the relation of persons to institutions.

Marxism — the Hegelian picture inverts the real order; the state's apparent rationality masks its actual function as a committee for managing the common affairs of the bourgeoisie, as materialism exposes.

Anarcho-capitalism — the state is illegitimate because it monopolizes force and taxes without consent; ethical-life claims merely dress coercion in metaphysical drapery, leaving the rights premise untouched.
context: G.W.F. Hegel's Philosophy of Right (1821) sets out three moments of Sittlichkeit: family, civil society, the state. Freedom is not the bare absence of constraint but the substantive participation in institutions where rational will is realized. Marx's early critique (1843) inverts the Hegelian schema; Charles Taylor's Hegel (1975) is the canonical Anglophone reconstruction.

question: A policy analyst defends a tax-and-transfer scheme: 'Permitting an unequal distribution is justifiable only when the inequality actually benefits the least advantaged members of society — equality is the baseline against which deviations must be defended, not the other way around.' Which tradition most directly grounds this principle?
answer: Rawlsian liberalism — the difference principle (inequalities permitted only when they maximize the position of the least advantaged) makes equality the baseline and treats deviations as needing justification.
choices: Rawlsian liberalism — the difference principle (inequalities permitted only when they maximize the position of the least advantaged) makes equality the baseline and treats deviations as needing justification.

Entitlement libertarianism — the relevant test is whether holdings arose by just acquisition and transfer, not whether their pattern benefits the worst-off; treating equality as baseline begs the question.

Welfare utilitarianism — the right policy is whichever maximizes aggregate welfare regardless of distribution; privileging the worst-off is at most a proxy for welfare-maximization, not a deep commitment.

Capability approach — the test is whether each person reaches central capability thresholds; framing in terms of advantaged-vs-disadvantaged groups misses the focus on each person's functional life directly.
context: John Rawls's A Theory of Justice (1971) frames the difference principle as one of two principles chosen behind the veil of ignorance. Equality of basic liberties is lexically prior; economic inequalities are permitted only when they maximize the position of the worst-off. Nozick's Anarchy, State, and Utopia (1974) is the canonical libertarian reply.

question: A political theorist argues: 'Politics is not the application of pre-formed doctrines to situations but the pursuit of intimations within a tradition of behavior — the rationalist's attempt to start from abstract principles mistakes the kind of activity politics is.' Which tradition most directly grounds her view?
answer: Oakeshottian conservatism — Rationalism in Politics treats politics as the pursuit of intimations within a concrete tradition, so abstract-principle politics misdescribes the practice it claims to direct.
choices: Oakeshottian conservatism — Rationalism in Politics treats politics as the pursuit of intimations within a concrete tradition, so abstract-principle politics misdescribes the practice it claims to direct.

Rawlsian liberalism — political principles can be specified independently of any tradition through the original position; the rationalism critique mistakes a theoretical device for a recipe-book of rules.

Burkean conservatism — the closely allied view; Burke emphasizes prescription and accumulated wisdom, whereas Oakeshott's emphasis on pursuit of intimations places more weight on present tradition coherence.
Marxism — appeals to 'tradition' obscure the class function of inherited practice; the rationalism-vs-practice framing is the bourgeoisie's preferred way of insulating its arrangements from critique.
context: Michael Oakeshott's Rationalism in Politics (1962) gives the canonical attack on doctrinal politics. The kindred Burkean line emphasizes prescription; Oakeshott's distinctive contribution is the metaphor of tradition as a conversation whose 'intimations' political practice pursues. Aligned with the broader anti-rationalist tradition (Polanyi, Hayek, Berlin).

question: A constitutional scholar argues: 'When a government systematically violates the rights it was constituted to protect, those subject to it are released from their obligation to obey — they may resist, and may constitute a new government, because legitimacy was conditional on the protection it has now forfeited.' Which tradition most directly grounds this argument?
answer: Lockean liberalism — the Second Treatise grounds revolution in conditional consent: legitimacy rests on protection of natural rights, so systematic violation dissolves the obligation to obey the ruler.
choices: Lockean liberalism — the Second Treatise grounds revolution in conditional consent: legitimacy rests on protection of natural rights, so systematic violation dissolves the obligation to obey the ruler.

Hobbesian absolutism — the obligation to obey survives all but the absolute breakdown of the sovereign's capacity to maintain order; rights-violation grounds presuppose conditions only the sovereign sustains.

Burkean conservatism — change should be incremental and within established forms, since the abstract right of revolution invites disasters that destroy the institutional inheritance from which the rights came.

Marxism — talk of natural rights and constitutional violation abstracts from the underlying class question; revolution is the transformation of production, not the restoration of pre-political rights.
context: John Locke's Second Treatise of Government (1689) develops the right of revolution as conditional on the ruler's protection of natural rights. The framework is the philosophical backbone of the American Declaration of Independence (1776) and the early French revolutionary documents. Hobbes (Leviathan, 1651) is the contemporary opposite pole.

question: A historian writes: 'There is no single conservative ideology — there is a sensibility: prudence, attachment to the permanent things, suspicion of utopia, and respect for the variousness of human communities. To formalize the sensibility into doctrine would be to betray it.' Which tradition most directly grounds this picture?
answer: Kirkian conservatism — Russell Kirk's The Conservative Mind defines conservatism as a sensibility marked by prudence, attachment to permanent things, and respect for variousness, not as formal doctrine.
choices: Kirkian conservatism — Russell Kirk's The Conservative Mind defines conservatism as a sensibility marked by prudence, attachment to permanent things, and respect for variousness, not as formal doctrine.

Burkean conservatism — the closely allied view; Burke emphasizes prescription and inherited practice, whereas Kirk frames conservatism more explicitly as a sensibility across many parallel traditions.

Oakeshottian conservatism — the kindred critique of rationalism; Oakeshott emphasizes the pursuit of intimations within a single tradition, whereas Kirk's framing accommodates plural conservative traditions.

Communitarianism — substantive shared goods generate community-grounded obligations; the picture overlaps with the conservative sensibility but rests on a more explicit metaphysics of identity than Kirk needs.
context: Russell Kirk's The Conservative Mind (1953) traced the Anglo-American conservative tradition from Burke through John Adams, Coleridge, Disraeli, and Newman to T.S. Eliot. Kirk's six canons of conservatism are deliberately framed as a sensibility rather than a doctrine, distinguishing his framework from rationalist political theory.

question: Professor Halse argues corporations should be governed for stakeholders rather than shareholders, weighing workers, communities, and the environment. Critic Stenz replies: 'The question is who decides what counts as a stakeholder interest. Whoever holds that power will use it as such powers are always used. Predict from the incentives, not the rationale.' Which reasoning move is Stenz making?
choices: Public choice — those granted discretionary power are self-interested actors rather than neutral fiduciaries; predict outcomes from the incentives the arrangement creates, not the public-interest rationale.

Knowledge problem — information needed to weigh diverse stakeholder interests across millions of decisions is dispersed and tacit, so a centralized framework miscarries the coordination it aims to perform.
Regulatory capture — agencies created to regulate an industry come over time to serve that industry; stakeholder governance gets captured by the corporate boards it nominally constrains.

Dispersed costs — small organized stakeholder groups extract from large diffuse groups (shareholders, consumers) when the math is negative-sum, because organization asymmetry favors concentrated beneficiaries.
answer: Public choice — those granted discretionary power are self-interested actors rather than neutral fiduciaries; predict outcomes from the incentives the arrangement creates, not the public-interest rationale.
context: James Buchanan and Gordon Tullock's The Calculus of Consent (1962) launched public-choice analysis: predict outcomes from the incentives of those empowered, treating policymakers as self-interested actors rather than neutral guardians. Friedman's 'social responsibility of business' essay (NYT Magazine, 1970) anticipates Stenz's specific critique of stakeholder-as-mandate.

question: Iyer proposes a new agency to oversee a complex industry, citing public-interest expertise. Critic Vora replies: 'Agencies created to regulate an industry come to serve that industry — regulated firms supply the expertise, the revolving door routes personnel, the agency's survival comes to depend on a healthy industry. Predict from the structure.' Which reasoning move is Vora making?
choices: Regulatory capture — agencies come over time to serve the interests of the industry they regulate; predict outcomes from the structural relations (information asymmetry, revolving door) between them.
Public choice — policymakers are self-interested actors rather than neutral planners; the agency's outcome should be predicted from the incentives of legislators who created it, not its mandate.
Knowledge problem — dispersed information required to regulate a complex industry cannot be assembled by a centralized agency; the resulting failures are about information, not loyalty.
Dispersed costs — small organized industry groups extract from large diffuse consumer groups when the math is negative-sum, because organized beneficiaries out-mobilize unorganized payers.
answer: Regulatory capture — agencies come over time to serve the interests of the industry they regulate; predict outcomes from the structural relations (information asymmetry, revolving door) between them.
context: George Stigler's 'The Theory of Economic Regulation' (Bell Journal, 1971) gave the canonical formal treatment of regulatory capture, building on Bernstein. The move predicts outcomes from the structural relations (information asymmetry, revolving door, agency dependence on industry) rather than from formal mandates.

question: Renn proposes a universal basic income (UBI) to ensure a floor under poverty. Critic Pell replies: 'The interesting question is not whether the rationale is appealing but whether the policy delivers what it promises. The pilot data, second-order labor-market effects, inflation pass-through to recipients — these are the test, not the framing.' Which reasoning move is Pell making?
choices: Judge by results — a policy's standing depends on outcomes it actually produces (pilot data, labor-market and price effects), not on the moral framing when it was proposed.
Knowledge problem — information needed to set an optimal UBI level is dispersed across households and labor-market decisions, so any centrally-set figure miscarries the coordination it attempts.
Public choice — UBI designers are self-interested actors rather than neutral planners; predict outcomes from the incentives of those who set the level and the administrative apparatus.
Compared-to-what — every UBI proposal must be measured against realistic alternatives (negative income tax, earned-income credits, in-kind transfers), not against the imagined zero-poverty world.
answer: Judge by results — a policy's standing depends on outcomes it actually produces (pilot data, labor-market and price effects), not on the moral framing when it was proposed.
context: Milton Friedman's 'judge by results, not intentions' summarizes the move and applies cleanly to UBI: the empirical record is the test, not the rationale. The other three choices are real critiques applied to UBI elsewhere. Friedman himself proposed a negative income tax as the compared-to-what alternative.

question: Drew defends an equity mandate setting demographic targets for admissions and hiring. Critic Mara replies: 'The visible effect is the balanced demographic profile in the numbers. The harder-to-see effect is the signal that standards softened — it travels with the credential and reduces its value for everyone, including the supposed beneficiaries.' Which reasoning move is Mara making?
choices: Seen vs. unseen — the visible balanced demographic outcome must be weighed against harder-to-see signal effects (lost credential value, statistical discrimination against beneficiaries) the policy produces.

Compared-to-what — every equity policy must be measured against realistic alternatives (earlier-pipeline programs, mentorship, recruitment), not against the imagined frictionless world the framing invokes.

Public choice — administrators of equity mandates are self-interested actors rather than neutral planners; predict outcomes from their incentives, not the stated equity goals on which they were appointed.

Knowledge problem — information needed to set demographic targets across departments is dispersed and tacit, so a central mandate miscarries the coordination it aims to perform across heterogeneous units.
answer: Seen vs. unseen — the visible balanced demographic outcome must be weighed against harder-to-see signal effects (lost credential value, statistical discrimination against beneficiaries) the policy produces.
context: Bastiat's seen/unseen (1850) and its modern applications in signaling theory (Spence, 1973; Sowell on the signaling cost of preferences, e.g., Affirmative Action Around the World, 2004) together do the work: a policy can hit its visible target while quietly imposing an unseen cost on the very group it intends to help via degraded signal value.

question: A policy seminar defends a redistributive scheme: 'Social justice requires reallocation.' A Hayek-influenced critic replies: 'Social JUSTICE only makes sense where an agent acts unjustly. Market outcomes are no one's decision — they emerge from countless exchanges. Talking of injustice without an actor is a category error.' Which distinction is the critic drawing?
answer: Catallactic order vs designed order — Hayek's distinction between spontaneous outcomes (no actor, so 'injustice' misapplies) and designed outcomes (which can genuinely be unjust).
choices: Catallactic order vs designed order — Hayek's distinction between spontaneous outcomes (no actor, so 'injustice' misapplies) and designed outcomes (which can genuinely be unjust).
Just law vs legal plunder — Bastiat's distinction between law as a restraint on aggression and law used as an instrument for taking from one party to give the proceeds to another party.
Procedural legitimacy vs substantive justice — a procedurally regular vote can produce outcomes failing tests of substantive fairness; procedural legitimacy does not entail substantive justice.
Sovereign immunity vs ordinary moral reasoning — whether the state is subject to the same moral constraints individuals respect or operates under standards exempt from those constraints.
context: Hayek's The Mirage of Social Justice (Law, Legislation and Liberty Vol. 2, 1976) argues 'social justice' as applied to spontaneous market outcomes commits a category error — only agents can be just or unjust. Critics (Sen, Cohen, Nussbaum) reply that institutional choices that shape distributions ARE agent-acts. The bank flags the distinction; the verdict is open.

context: Counting believers across rival religions illustrates the limit of headcount arguments: Christianity, Islam, Hinduism each have hundreds of millions, but they make incompatible truth-claims about God. Popular numbers can't decide which is right.

question: After a guest speaker described his conversion, Talia tells her after-school friends: 'A direct experience of God that changes a person is real evidence — public, life-changing testimony.' Which view is Talia defending?
answer: Religious experience as evidence — first-person experience of God can give real grounds; testimony of it is a kind of public sign.
choices: Religious experience as evidence — first-person experience of God can give real grounds; testimony of it is a kind of public sign.
Strict evidentialism — only public, repeatable evidence supports belief; first-person reports of God don't meet that standard.
Pragmatism — what matters is the life-impact of the convert; whether the experience itself was a reason is a separate question.
Fideism — religious belief requires no reasons or experiences; whether the convert experienced God is beside the point of faith.
context: Alston's Perceiving God (1991) and the broader Reformed tradition argue that religious experience can ground belief similarly to sense perception. C.S. Lewis and many converts make this move in their testimonies. Critics worry about rival experiences.

question: At a sleepover, Sara asks: 'Why do you believe?' Her friend Anna answers: 'I just do. I don't think reasons are even the right way to talk about faith — faith is its own thing.' Which view of religious belief is Anna defending?
answer: Fideism — religious belief stands on faith without leaning on reasons; asking for reasons misses what faith really is here.
choices: Fideism — religious belief stands on faith without leaning on reasons; asking for reasons misses what faith really is here.
Reasonable faith — religious belief is rational on background reasons; even if not proven, ordinary trust can ground it.
Pragmatism — religious belief earns its place by what it does in life; faith is a tool not a stance about reasons or proofs.
Strict evidentialism — religious belief needs evidence; if you don't have it, the only fair move is to refrain from holding it.
context: Pure fideism (Tertullian's 'I believe because it is absurd'; Kierkegaard's leap of faith) treats reasons as outside faith's domain. Aquinas, Plantinga, and Swinburne all reject this: Christian theology has long offered reasons too.

question: After her aunt felt peaceful praying for the first time, she tells everyone: 'I felt peace, so God must be real.' Mara — kindly — challenges her. Why is 'I felt peace in prayer' NOT enough on its own to prove God exists?
answer: Other things give the same feeling — meditation, music, deep breaths produce peace; the experience can't pick its own source.
choices: Other things give the same feeling — meditation, music, deep breaths produce peace; the experience can't pick its own source.
Sincerity isn't truth — sincerely feeling something doesn't make a belief true; the feeling can be sincere yet still mistaken.
Tradition isn't truth — that prayer is an old practice doesn't make any one prayer connect with God; longevity is unrelated here.
Popularity isn't truth — that millions feel peace while praying settles nothing; head counts don't bear on which religion is true.
context: The 'argument from religious experience' has a parallel problem: peace, awe, and comfort can come from many sources. Religious-experience defenders (Alston) respond that pattern across many believers, not one feeling, is what matters.

question: Asked how she can believe in a God she's never seen, Esme tells the teacher: 'I believe in numbers like infinity nobody has ever seen either. Belief in real unseen things is normal for thoughtful people.' Which view is Esme defending?
answer: Reasonable faith — belief in unseen real things is rational on background reasons; religious belief fits that pattern too.
choices: Reasonable faith — belief in unseen real things is rational on background reasons; religious belief fits that pattern too.
Fideism — religious belief stands without reasons or analogies; the math comparison is the kind of move faith doesn't need.
Strict evidentialism — every claim needs evidence to be believed; if math facts lack it, mathematicians shouldn't believe either.
Pragmatism — religious belief earns its place by what it does; the comparison to math is helpful but isn't what justifies it.
context: The unseen-realities argument (used by C.S. Lewis, Mere Christianity, 1952, and Reformed epistemologists) parallels theism with abstract entities. Critics reply that mathematical objects are tested in proofs, not by direct observation — a disanalogy.

question: Talking through which religion is true, Felix tells his sister: 'You can't pick by sincerity or experience — too many people are sincere across religions. Only shareable evidence can pick out the right one.' Which view is Felix defending?
answer: Strict evidentialism — picking between religions requires shareable evidence; private experience won't do because rivals share it.
choices: Strict evidentialism — picking between religions requires shareable evidence; private experience won't do because rivals share it.
Reasonable faith — picking between religions can be rational on background reasons; strict proof isn't what is asked for here.
Religious experience as evidence — picking between religions can rest partly on experience; rival experiences don't simply cancel.
Fideism — picking between religions isn't an evidence question at all; faith isn't the kind of thing reasoned about that way.
context: The 'religious diversity' problem: sincere believers across religions can't all be right. Clifford's evidentialism takes this as a reason to demand shareable evidence. Plantinga and Alston reply that rival experiences may still leave room for warranted belief.

question: Asked why she believes, Carla shrugs: 'It's what my family always believed.' Her school friend Diego asks her to think about it. Why is 'my family always believed it' NOT enough to settle whether it's true?
answer: Family sets exposure, not truth — kids of rival religions inherit different ones; family background can't pick the true religion.
choices: Family sets exposure, not truth — kids of rival religions inherit different ones; family background can't pick the true religion.
Sincerity isn't truth — believing what parents believed sincerely doesn't make it so; sincerity does no work to verify a claim.
Popularity isn't truth — large religions have many family lines; wide hand-down doesn't settle which religion is the right one.
Tradition isn't truth — long practice can encode error; the age of a family religion is unrelated to whether it tracks reality.
context: The 'genetic-of-belief' worry: people in Riyadh raised Muslim, in Chennai raised Hindu, in Atlanta raised Baptist. Family of origin shapes who believes what but can't be the reason a religion is true — competing families can't all be right.

question: When her brother teases her for not being able to argue back, Greta says: 'I don't need a tight proof. My faith holds my life together — that's what matters about it, and that's why I keep it.' Which view of religious belief is Greta defending?
answer: Pragmatism — religious belief is held for what it does in a life; coherence of argument isn't what bears its weight in this view.
choices: Pragmatism — religious belief is held for what it does in a life; coherence of argument isn't what bears its weight in this view.
Fideism — religious belief stands beyond reasons; whether it 'holds your life together' is one effect, not what backs the trust.
Reasonable faith — religious belief is rational on background reasons; what it does for you is a side benefit, not the ground.
Strict evidentialism — religious belief needs evidence; what it does in your life can't substitute for the missing real proof.
context: Pragmatism in religion (James, 'Will to Believe,' 1896; Dewey's later work) centers what belief does — its 'cash value' for living. Christian thinkers raise the 'true even if costly' point: Paul's letters insist truth comes first, comfort second.

question: When something specific she prayed for happened, Theo's friend Selena says: 'That answered prayer is a real reason to believe — not a proof, but more than a coincidence I can ignore.' Which view of religious belief is Selena defending?
answer: Religious experience as evidence — answered prayer can count as a real ground for belief, not a stand-in for absolute proof.
choices: Religious experience as evidence — answered prayer can count as a real ground for belief, not a stand-in for absolute proof.
Strict evidentialism — only shareable, controlled evidence supports belief; a one-off matching outcome doesn't meet that standard.
Pragmatism — what matters is whether prayer helps you live well; whether this case 'worked' is beside that practical concern.
Fideism — religious belief rests on faith alone; whether prayers seem answered is unrelated to what really sustains real faith.
context: The 'answered prayer' move is a low-stakes religious-experience claim: the outcome plus the prayer pattern serves as a reason. Critics note confirmation bias — unanswered prayers are forgotten. Defenders reply that patterns matter, not single cases.

question: In a debate-club round, Mason quotes a religious text to settle whether the text is reliable. His opponent objects. Why is 'the book says it's true' NOT enough — in this kind of debate — to prove the book is true?
answer: Self-citation isn't proof — using the book to vouch for the book begs the question; outside reasons must do that job here.
choices: Self-citation isn't proof — using the book to vouch for the book begs the question; outside reasons must do that job here.
Sincerity isn't truth — Mason sincerely trusting the book doesn't establish it; what one earnestly cites can still be plain wrong.
Popularity isn't truth — many people quoting the same book settles nothing; headcounts of citers don't bear on whether it's true.
Experience isn't truth — feeling moved by the book settles nothing; emotions while reading don't supply a reliable reason at all.
context: Begging the question (Latin: petitio principii) when arguing for a text's reliability with the text itself is a familiar problem in debates between religious and non-religious thinkers. The reply: appeals must extend to shared ground.

question: A debate-club captain argues: 'Everything we see began to exist somewhere. But an infinite chain of causes can't itself explain why anything exists at all. Something outside the chain must ground it.' Which view of God's existence is she defending?
answer: Cosmological argument — contingent things need a first cause outside the chain, since an infinite regress cannot itself ground existence.
choices: Cosmological argument — contingent things need a first cause outside the chain, since an infinite regress cannot itself ground existence.
Design argument — the fine-tuning of physical constants for life points to an intelligent designer, since extreme precision is improbable on chance.
Moral argument — objective moral obligations require a transcendent lawgiver, since human convention alone cannot generate genuine binding force.
Ontological argument — the concept of a maximally great being entails its existence, since a being none greater than which can be conceived must exist.
context: The cosmological argument has several forms: Aquinas' Five Ways (Summa Theologiae, c. 1265) include the argument from contingency; Leibniz asks 'why is there something rather than nothing?' (1697). The Kalam version (al-Ghazali, revived by Craig) adds a beginning.

question: A YouTuber on apologetics argues: 'The physical constants of the universe sit in an incredibly narrow window that allows life. Change gravity by a hair and no stars form. That precise tuning points to a tuner.' Which view of God's existence is she defending?
answer: Design argument — the fine-tuning of physical constants for life points to an intelligent designer, since extreme precision is improbable on chance.
choices: Design argument — the fine-tuning of physical constants for life points to an intelligent designer, since extreme precision is improbable on chance.
Cosmological argument — contingent things need a first cause outside the chain, since an infinite regress cannot itself ground existence at all.
Moral argument — objective moral obligations require a transcendent lawgiver, since human convention alone cannot generate genuine binding force.
Ontological argument — the concept of a maximally great being entails its existence, since a being none greater than which can be conceived must exist.
context: Fine-tuning is a modern descendant of Paley's watchmaker (Natural Theology, 1802). Defenders include Robin Collins and John Polkinghorne. Critics propose the multiverse and anthropic selection as alternative explanations of the observed precision.

question: A school newspaper editor argues: 'If there's no God, moral wrongs are just personal dislikes. But torturing children for fun is really wrong — not just disliked. That kind of binding fact has to come from outside us.' Which view of God's existence is she defending?
answer: Moral argument — objective moral obligations require a transcendent lawgiver, since human convention alone cannot generate genuine binding force on us.
choices: Moral argument — objective moral obligations require a transcendent lawgiver, since human convention alone cannot generate genuine binding force on us.
Cosmological argument — contingent things need a first cause outside the chain, since an infinite regress cannot itself ground existence at all.
Design argument — the fine-tuning of physical constants for life points to an intelligent designer, since extreme precision is improbable on chance.
Ontological argument — the concept of a maximally great being entails its existence, since a being none greater than which can be conceived must exist.
context: The moral argument runs through Kant (Critique of Practical Reason, 1788) and in modern form C. S. Lewis (Mere Christianity, 1952). The core: objective moral obligation requires a personal ground; mere preference cannot capture cruelty's wrongness.

question: A friend asks a debate-club captain: 'If God is all-good and all-powerful, why let people do terrible things?' The captain replies that God values real freedom, and freedom must include the genuine possibility of doing wrong. Which response to the problem of evil is she defending?
answer: Free-will defense — God permits moral evil because removing wrong choice would also remove the genuine freedom that makes moral agency meaningful.
choices: Free-will defense — God permits moral evil because removing wrong choice would also remove the genuine freedom that makes moral agency meaningful.
Skeptical theism — humans lack the capacity to judge whether God has good reasons for permitting evils; absence of seen reason is not absence of reason.
Soul-making theodicy — suffering builds virtuous character; a world without challenge could not develop the moral souls a good God intends to form here.
Mystery move — divine reasons exceed our understanding entirely; the puzzle is beyond our ability to address and should be set aside rather than engaged.
context: The free-will defense was developed by Augustine and given modern form by Plantinga (God, Freedom, and Evil, 1974). It targets the logical problem of evil — the claim that God and evil are logically incompatible — and aims to show their joint possibility.

question: A friend says: 'Look at a child dying of cancer. Free will can't explain that. If God had a reason, we'd see it.' A peer-reviewer replies: 'Why expect to see all God's reasons? Our view of the whole picture is limited.' Which response to the problem of evil is the peer-reviewer defending?
answer: Skeptical theism — humans lack the capacity to judge whether God has good reasons for permitting evils; absence of seen reason is not absence of reason.
choices: Skeptical theism — humans lack the capacity to judge whether God has good reasons for permitting evils; absence of seen reason is not absence of reason.
Free-will defense — God permits moral evil because removing wrong choice would also remove the genuine freedom that makes moral agency meaningful.
Soul-making theodicy — suffering builds virtuous character; a world without challenge could not develop the moral souls a good God intends to form here.
Greater-goods defense — apparent evils may be permitted to serve unseen goods that could not otherwise be obtained; the evil is real but serves a real good.
context: Skeptical theism (Wykstra, Alston, Bergmann) targets the EVIDENTIAL problem of evil. The move: from 'I see no reason' it does not follow that 'there is no reason' — our cognitive position is much like a beginner's relative to a master in many domains.

question: A YouTuber on apologetics argues: 'Belief in God doesn't have to be inferred from evidence the way science is. It can be properly basic — grounded directly in experience, like belief in other minds or in yesterday's memories.' Which view of religious belief is she defending?
answer: Reformed epistemology — belief in God can be properly basic, grounded directly in experience rather than inferred from evidence, like belief in other minds.
choices: Reformed epistemology — belief in God can be properly basic, grounded directly in experience rather than inferred from evidence, like belief in other minds.
Evidentialism — every belief must be proportioned to evidence; properly basic belief in God smuggles in what the evidence standard would actually reject.
Fideism — religious belief is justified by faith alone without any rational warrant; it stands outside the standard evaluation of belief from the start.
Verificationism — only beliefs verifiable in principle by experience are meaningful; religious claims that resist empirical testing fail that standard.
context: Reformed epistemology (Plantinga, 'Reason and Belief in God' 1983; Warranted Christian Belief 2000; Alston, Perceiving God 1991) holds belief in God need not be inferred. Like belief in other minds, it can be a properly basic starting point of cognition.

question: A debate-club captain argues: 'A statement is meaningful only if some observation could in principle confirm or disconfirm it. "God loves us" makes no testable prediction — so the statement isn't really saying anything.' Which view of religious language is she defending?
answer: Verificationism — only statements verifiable in principle by observation are meaningful at all; untestable religious claims fail to meet that minimal bar.
choices: Verificationism — only statements verifiable in principle by observation are meaningful at all; untestable religious claims fail to meet that minimal bar.
Evidentialism — religious claims may be meaningful but must be proportioned to evidence; lack of evidence makes belief unjustified but the claim has content.
Reformed epistemology — belief in God can be properly basic, grounded directly in experience; verification by external test is not required for any warrant.
Religious pluralism — many traditions offer partial access to one transcendent reality; testability is the wrong category for the kind of claim religion makes.
context: Verificationism / the verification principle (A.J. Ayer, Language Truth and Logic, 1936) held religious and ethical statements were literally meaningless because untestable. Critics noted the principle itself fails its own test, and most philosophers abandoned it.

question: A school newspaper editor argues: 'Different traditions describe the same transcendent reality from different cultural angles. Each catches part of the truth without exhausting it — none is uniquely right or uniquely wrong.' Which view of religious diversity is she defending?
answer: Religious pluralism — different traditions offer partial access to one transcendent reality, each catching part of the truth without exhausting it.
choices: Religious pluralism — different traditions offer partial access to one transcendent reality, each catching part of the truth without exhausting it.
Exclusivism — one tradition is uniquely correct about the divine, and other traditions are mistaken where they conflict; truth admits no equal alternatives.
Inclusivism — one tradition has the fullest truth, but others contain partial truths and can mediate genuine grace; the relation is hierarchical, not equal.
Religious naturalism — religious experience is purely a feature of human psychology; no transcendent reality lies beneath the experience to be accessed.
context: Religious pluralism is associated with John Hick (An Interpretation of Religion, 1989), drawing on Kant's noumenon/phenomenon distinction. Different traditions are culturally-shaped responses to the same ultimate ('the Real'). Exclusivism and inclusivism rival it.

question: A peer-review reader replies to a classmate who says she believes in God because she felt peace during prayer: 'Lots of people feel peace for many reasons. The feeling can't settle whether the belief is true.' Why is 'I sincerely feel it' not enough, on this account, to justify belief?
answer: Evidentialism — sincere feelings don't track truth reliably enough; justifying any belief requires evidence beyond the feeling itself.
choices: Evidentialism — sincere feelings don't track truth reliably enough; justifying any belief requires evidence beyond the feeling itself.
Reformed epistemology — religious experience can ground belief directly without external evidence; the reader misapplies evidentialism to basic belief.
Fideism — religious belief is justified by faith and stands outside the demand for evidence; the reader assumes the wrong framework for the claim.
Religious pluralism — many traditions touch the same reality through experience; the feeling is meaningful even without pinning down which tradition.
context: Evidentialism (W.K. Clifford, 'The Ethics of Belief' 1877: 'It is wrong always, everywhere, and for anyone, to believe anything upon insufficient evidence.') sets a uniform evidence standard for any belief. Plantinga's reformed epistemology is the standard reply.

question: A YouTuber argues: 'Trying to prove God by argument misses what faith really is. Faith is a personal commitment that goes beyond what reason can settle — and that's not a weakness, it's what faith specifically means.' Which view of faith is she defending?
answer: Fideism — religious faith is justified by commitment beyond what reason can establish; demanding proof misunderstands what faith really means at its core.
choices: Fideism — religious faith is justified by commitment beyond what reason can establish; demanding proof misunderstands what faith really means at its core.
Reformed epistemology — religious belief can be properly basic, grounded directly in experience; reason and faith do not stand in opposition to one another.
Evidentialism — every belief requires evidence proportionate to its strength; faith without argument is unjustified belief however personally committed one is.
Natural theology — reason can establish core religious truths on its own; faith fills in what reason cannot reach, with each in its proper distinct domain.
context: Fideism has many forms — Tertullian ('credo quia absurdum'), Kierkegaard's 'leap of faith' (Fear and Trembling, 1843). Strong fideism holds reason is hostile to faith; weak fideism (Pascal) holds reason runs out somewhere short of full assent.

question: A peer-review reader writes about a natural disaster: 'The suffering is real. But we can imagine allowing it serves goods we don't fully see — the structure of a world where choices matter, character formed through hardship.' Which response to the problem of evil is she defending?
answer: Greater-goods defense — apparent evils may be permitted to serve unseen goods that could not otherwise be obtained; the evil is real but serves a real good.
choices: Greater-goods defense — apparent evils may be permitted to serve unseen goods that could not otherwise be obtained; the evil is real but serves a real good.
Free-will defense — God permits moral evil because removing wrong choice would also remove the genuine freedom that makes moral agency meaningful.
Skeptical theism — humans lack the capacity to judge whether God has good reasons for permitting evils; absence of seen reason is not absence of reason.
Deflection — the responsibility for evil lies entirely with human choosers; natural-disaster cases dissolve once all suffering is attributed to human agency.
context: The greater-goods defense (Augustine, Aquinas, classical theodicy) claims apparent evil may serve goods otherwise unobtainable. Critics (Mackie) note it must show the goods are actually unobtainable without the evil — a stronger claim than the bare possibility.

question: A debate-club captain argues: 'Even if we can't prove God exists, the stakes are asymmetric. If I believe and God exists, I gain everything. If I disbelieve and God exists, I lose everything. Belief is the rational bet.' Which view of religious belief is she defending?
answer: Pascalian decision theory — under uncertainty, infinite-stakes asymmetric payoffs make belief the rationally preferable choice without conclusive evidence.
choices: Pascalian decision theory — under uncertainty, infinite-stakes asymmetric payoffs make belief the rationally preferable choice without conclusive evidence.
Evidentialism — every belief must be proportioned to the available evidence; payoff asymmetry does not track truth, so it does not justify belief on its own.
Reformed epistemology — belief in God can be properly basic, grounded in experience; the decision-theoretic framing misses how religious belief is warranted.
Fideism — religious faith is justified by commitment beyond what reason settles; calculating expected value reduces faith to a wager and misses its character.
context: Pascal's Wager (Pensées, 1670) treats belief as a decision under uncertainty with asymmetric payoffs. Critics raise the 'many gods' objection (which God to bet on?) and worry that wager-style belief isn't genuine belief at all — a strategy isn't faith.

question: A school newspaper editor argues: 'Suffering isn't pointless if it produces virtue. A world without challenge produces no courage, no patience, no resilience. The hardships we face are the material moral character is built from.' Which response to the problem of evil is she defending?
answer: Soul-making theodicy — suffering and challenge produce virtuous character; a world without hardship cannot develop the moral souls a good God intends.
choices: Soul-making theodicy — suffering and challenge produce virtuous character; a world without hardship cannot develop the moral souls a good God intends.
Free-will defense — God permits moral evil because removing wrong choice would also remove the genuine freedom that makes moral agency meaningful.
Skeptical theism — humans lack the capacity to judge whether God has good reasons for permitting evils; absence of seen reason is not absence of reason.
Mystery move — divine reasons exceed all human understanding entirely; the puzzle should be set aside rather than addressed, since we cannot progress on it.
context: Soul-making theodicy is most associated with John Hick (Evil and the God of Love, 1966), drawing on Irenaeus rather than Augustine. The world is 'a vale of soul-making' (Keats): not a paradise but a workshop where moral character is genuinely formed.

question: A YouTuber explains a classical view: 'Some truths about God can be reached by reason — that God exists, that He is one, that creation depends on Him. Other truths require revelation. Reason and faith do not conflict; they cooperate.' Which view of faith and reason is she defending?
answer: Natural theology — reason can establish core truths about God on its own; revelation extends what reason reaches without contradicting any rational result.
choices: Natural theology — reason can establish core truths about God on its own; revelation extends what reason reaches without contradicting any rational result.
Fideism — religious truth is reached only by faith; demanding reasons misunderstands faith, and natural theology overestimates what reason accomplishes.
Verificationism — only empirically testable claims are meaningful at all; the natural-theology project and revelation both fail to deliver real religious truth.
Reformed epistemology — belief in God is properly basic, grounded in experience; neither natural theology nor pure revelation is required for warrant at all.
context: Aquinas (Summa Theologiae, c. 1265) distinguishes 'preambles of faith' reason can reach (God's existence, oneness) from 'articles of faith' requiring revelation (Trinity, Incarnation). Natural and revealed theology cooperate; faith presupposes reason where reason reaches.

question: A peer-review reader replies to a miracle claim at a healing service: 'Sincere reports, even from honest people, can't settle whether the cause was supernatural. Ordinary causes produce surprising recoveries too.' Why is 'sincere eyewitnesses reported it' not enough to establish a miracle?
answer: Humean evidentialism — extraordinary claims need evidence stronger than testimony usually provides; ordinary causes remain a live alternative for recoveries.
choices: Humean evidentialism — extraordinary claims need evidence stronger than testimony usually provides; ordinary causes remain a live alternative for recoveries.
Reformed epistemology — religious experience grounds belief directly without external evidence; the reader misapplies evidentialism to a properly basic belief.
Fideism — faith neither requires nor benefits from evidence; the reader assumes the wrong framework for assessing what kind of claim a miracle report is.
Verificationism — only statements verifiable in principle are meaningful; the reader's complaint is about meaning, not evidence, and misses what miracles do.
context: Hume's argument against miracles (Enquiry, X, 1748): 'No testimony is sufficient to establish a miracle unless its falsehood would be more miraculous than the fact it endeavours to establish.' Critics (Earman, Hume's Abject Failure 2000) dispute the probabilistic framing.

question: An online apologetics commentator argues: 'Religious experience works like sensory experience. People who experience God are in something like the position of people who experience trees — direct perception that counts as evidence.' Which view of religious experience is she defending?
answer: Perceptual model — religious experience is structurally like sense perception and carries the same prima facie evidential weight; both are doxastic practices.
choices: Perceptual model — religious experience is structurally like sense perception and carries the same prima facie evidential weight; both are doxastic practices.
Evidentialism — religious experience must meet the same evidence standard as any claim; the perceptual analogy fails because experience reports don't converge.
Reformed epistemology — religious belief is properly basic without being modeled on perception; the perceptual analogy is unnecessary scaffolding here.
Verificationism — only empirically testable claims are meaningful at all; religious experiences that resist external testing fail to deliver any content.
context: William Alston (Perceiving God, 1991) develops the perceptual model: 'Christian mystical practice' is a doxastic practice on a par with sense-perceptual practice. Both are circular if pressed for non-circular validation, so neither can fault the other.

question: A school newspaper editor argues: 'An action is right because God commands it. Without that grounding, morality reduces to preferences. The divine command itself is what makes a moral fact a fact.' Which view of God and morality is she defending?
answer: Divine command theory — moral facts are grounded in God's commands; without the command there is no moral fact, so morality stands or falls with the lawgiver.
choices: Divine command theory — moral facts are grounded in God's commands; without the command there is no moral fact, so morality stands or falls with the lawgiver.
Natural-law theory — moral facts are grounded in human nature as designed; God's commands track these facts but the facts derive from nature's design.
Moral realism — moral facts are objective features of reality independent of commands; God's role might be to reveal them but is not the ground of fact.
Moral relativism — moral facts depend on cultural and personal stance; both divine commands and natural-law claims overreach what morality could consist in.
context: Divine command theory faces the Euthyphro problem (Plato, Euthyphro): is an action right because God commands it, or does God command it because it is right? Adams' modified divine command theory (Finite and Infinite Goods, 1999) is a sophisticated modern response.

question: A school newspaper editor replies to a claim that God must exist because most cultures have religions: 'That many people across history believed in something doesn't settle whether what they believed in is real.' Why is 'most cultures have believed it' not enough to establish God exists?
answer: Individualist evidentialism — widespread belief doesn't track truth reliably; the question is what evidence the cultures had, not how many cultures believed.
choices: Individualist evidentialism — widespread belief doesn't track truth reliably; the question is what evidence the cultures had, not how many cultures believed.
Religious pluralism — different traditions touch one reality partially; the consensus across cultures supports a shared reality the editor's reply misreads.
Reformed epistemology — religious belief can be properly basic, grounded in experience; the consensus across cultures is then evidence of a shared faculty.
Fideism — religious belief is justified by personal faith not cultural counting; the editor rejects consensus rightly but for the wrong sort of reason here.
context: The 'common consent' argument (consensus gentium) appears in Cicero and lingers as background warrant. Critics note that wide belief tracks human cognitive tendency, not the truth of the object — many false beliefs have also been near-universal across cultures.

question: A debate-club captain explains a classical argument: 'God is by definition that than which nothing greater can be conceived. But a God who exists in reality is greater than one who exists only in the mind. So God must exist.' Which view of God's existence is she defending?
answer: Ontological argument — the concept of a maximally great being entails its existence, since a being none greater than which can be conceived must exist.
choices: Ontological argument — the concept of a maximally great being entails its existence, since a being none greater than which can be conceived must exist.
Cosmological argument — contingent things need a first cause outside the chain, since an infinite regress cannot itself ground existence at all.
Design argument — the fine-tuning of physical constants for life points to an intelligent designer, since extreme precision is improbable on chance.
Moral argument — objective moral obligations require a transcendent lawgiver, since human convention alone cannot generate genuine binding force on us.
context: Anselm's ontological argument (Proslogion, 1078) reasons from the concept of God to His existence. Gaunilo replied with the 'perfect island.' Kant objected that existence is not a real predicate. Modal versions (Plantinga, The Nature of Necessity 1974) renew the project.

question: A friend asks a youth-group leader: 'If God is all-good and all-powerful, why does evil exist?' The leader replies: 'You shouldn't ask that — it's disrespectful to question God's ways.' Which response actually engages the problem of evil rather than refusing it?
answer: Free-will defense — God permits moral evil because removing wrong choice would also remove the genuine freedom that makes moral agency meaningful.
choices: Free-will defense — God permits moral evil because removing wrong choice would also remove the genuine freedom that makes moral agency meaningful.
Suppression move — questioning is disrespectful, so the issue should not be raised at all; the puzzle dissolves once the questioner is told to stop asking.
Verdict move — God exists despite the evil, so any reasoning that troubles this conclusion must be mistaken; the puzzle is settled by conclusion not argument.
Motive impugning — atheists must want evil to keep happening, so the objection is self-defeating; the puzzle dissolves once motives are reframed badly.
context: The free-will defense engages the actual structure of the problem of evil — it accepts the question's premise (evil exists) and offers a candidate reason (free agency requires possibility of wrong). Refusing to ask or impugning motives does not engage it.

question: An op-ed columnist writes: 'If God is all-good and all-powerful, creatures who could only do good would still be possible - so why permit moral evil?' A theologian replies: 'A world with genuine moral agents requires the real possibility they choose wrongly; rigged goodness is not goodness.' Which response is the theologian giving?
answer: Free-will defense - moral evil is the cost of creating genuine moral agents, since rigged goodness in creatures who never went wrong would not be moral agency at all.
choices: Free-will defense - moral evil is the cost of creating genuine moral agents, since rigged goodness in creatures who never went wrong would not be moral agency at all.
Greater-goods defense - apparent evil is permitted only when it serves higher goods we cannot fully see, without denying the evil or weakening any divine moral attribute.
Sceptical theism - humans simply lack the cognitive capacity to judge whether God has good reasons for any specific permitted evil; agnosticism about divine reasons is the honest move.
Soul-making theodicy - evil is the necessary occasion for moral growth, since souls develop virtue only by working through suffering they could not face in a frictionless world.
context: Alvin Plantinga's God, Freedom, and Evil (1974) develops the free-will defense against Mackie's logical problem of evil. Plantinga shows it is logically possible that God could not actualize a world containing free creatures who never sin - blocking the Mackie inconsistency proof.

question: On a religion-and-philosophy podcast, host Camille presses: 'Surely we can SEE that some sufferings serve no greater good.' Theologian Dwight responds: 'A finite mind isn't well-placed to rule out reasons an infinite mind might have; not-seeing-a-reason isn't the same as seeing-no-reason.' Which response is Dwight giving?
answer: Sceptical theism - finite minds aren't well-placed to canvass an infinite mind's reasons, so 'we see no good' falls short of 'there is no good'; agnosticism about specifics is honest.
choices: Sceptical theism - finite minds aren't well-placed to canvass an infinite mind's reasons, so 'we see no good' falls short of 'there is no good'; agnosticism about specifics is honest.
Free-will defense - the suffering in question is the price of genuine moral agency, since a world in which wrong choices were impossible would not contain real moral agents at all.
Greater-goods defense - the suffering serves identifiable goods (moral growth, the stability of natural law, structures of meaningful choice) that justify permitting the evil in this case.
Soul-making theodicy - the suffering is the necessary occasion for character development, since souls grow into virtue only through facing trials they could not face in a frictionless world.
context: Sceptical theism (Stephen Wykstra, 1984; Michael Bergmann, 2001) blocks the evidential problem of evil at the inferential step: our failure to see God-justifying reasons for some evil doesn't license the inference that no such reasons exist. The position is logically modest and widely discussed in contemporary philosophy of religion.

question: Philosophy podcaster Bex summarizes an argument: 'Whatever begins to exist has a cause. The universe began to exist. Therefore the universe has a cause - and a cause that is itself uncaused, beyond time, and immensely powerful.' At its sharpest, what does this argument claim?
answer: Kalam cosmological argument - because the universe began to exist, it requires a cause; the argument concludes to a timeless, immensely powerful cause as the source of the universe.
choices: Kalam cosmological argument - because the universe began to exist, it requires a cause; the argument concludes to a timeless, immensely powerful cause as the source of the universe.
Thomistic First Way - every motion requires a prior mover, and the regress of movers must terminate in an unmoved mover; the argument turns on causal series here and now, not beginnings.
Ontological argument - the very concept of a maximally great being entails its existence, since a being that exists in reality is greater than one that exists in the mind alone here.
Fine-tuning design argument - the physical constants are calibrated so precisely for life that brute chance is a poor explanation; the conclusion is intelligent design, not first cause.
context: The kalam version (William Lane Craig, The Kalam Cosmological Argument, 1979) is distinguished by its reliance on the universe's temporal beginning - philosophical arguments against actual infinites plus cosmological evidence. Aquinas's cosmological arguments do not turn on a temporal beginning; they reason from causal dependence.

question: On a panel, theologian Aleksy presents an argument: 'In every chain of contingent beings, each one depends on another for existing right now. The whole chain of dependent existers cannot itself be the explanation; there must be a non-contingent ground.' At its sharpest, what does Aleksy's argument claim?
answer: Thomistic argument from contingency - dependent existers cannot collectively ground their own existing; an explanatorily ultimate non-contingent being is required as the ground of all.
choices: Thomistic argument from contingency - dependent existers cannot collectively ground their own existing; an explanatorily ultimate non-contingent being is required as the ground of all.
Kalam cosmological argument - whatever begins to exist has a cause; the universe began, so its cause is timeless and powerful; the argument turns on a temporal beginning of the cosmos.
Design argument - the fitting arrangement of natural things for ends presupposes an ordering intelligence; the argument turns on apparent purpose, not on dependent existence's ground.
Moral argument - objective moral obligations exist and are best explained by a moral lawgiver; the argument turns on the existence of binding ethical norms, not contingent existence.
context: Aquinas's Third Way (Summa Theologiae I.2.3) reasons from contingency: things that can fail to exist could not all be contingent, since then at some point nothing would have existed. Modern readers (Edward Feser, Five Proofs of the Existence of God, 2017) distinguish this Thomistic argument sharply from Craig's kalam, despite shared 'cosmological' label.

question: On a podcast on classical arguments, host Reza summarizes a medieval move: 'God is THAT than which no greater can be conceived. Such a being must exist in reality - because one existing only in the mind would be less great than one existing in fact.' At its sharpest, what does this argument claim?
answer: Ontological argument - existence is built into the concept of a maximally great being; the very coherence of the concept entails its instantiation, by analysis of the idea alone.
choices: Ontological argument - existence is built into the concept of a maximally great being; the very coherence of the concept entails its instantiation, by analysis of the idea alone.
Cosmological argument - contingent things require a non-contingent cause; the argument here moves from the actual world's dependence outward to its ground, rather than from any concept.
Design argument - the regularities and apparent purposes of nature presuppose an ordering intelligence; the argument moves from features of the world outward, rather than from any concept.
Moral argument - the binding character of objective moral obligations is best explained by a moral lawgiver; the argument moves from ethical features of reality, not from any concept.
context: Anselm's Proslogion (1078) is the classical ontological argument. Kant's standard objection holds that 'existence is not a predicate' the way 'great' is. Plantinga's modal ontological argument (1974) recasts it using modal logic: a maximally great being possibly exists, so necessarily exists. Critics dispute the possibility premise.

question: Science writer Pell summarizes the case for cosmic design: 'The physical constants are calibrated within tolerances so narrow that shifting any one slightly would forbid stars, chemistry, or life. Brute chance is a remarkably poor explanation; design is a better inference.' At its sharpest, what does this argument claim?
answer: Fine-tuning design argument - the precise calibration of physical constants for life is better explained by intelligent design than by chance, even with multiverse hypotheses in view.
choices: Fine-tuning design argument - the precise calibration of physical constants for life is better explained by intelligent design than by chance, even with multiverse hypotheses in view.
Paley's watchmaker argument - the integrated functional complexity of organisms presupposes a designer; the argument turns on biological adaptation, not on physical constants of the cosmos.
Kalam cosmological argument - whatever begins to exist has a cause; the universe began, so its cause is timeless and powerful; the argument here is about the cosmos beginning, not its laws.
Anthropic principle - we shouldn't be surprised to find ourselves in a life-permitting universe since only such universes contain observers; the move undercuts inference to design.
context: Modern fine-tuning arguments (Robin Collins, John Polkinghorne) build on physical-constants data developed since the 1970s. Paley's earlier watchmaker (Natural Theology, 1802) reasons from biological complexity. Hume's Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion (1779) anticipates objections, and the anthropic principle is the standard rebuttal.

question: On a campus debate, philosopher Renault argues: 'Objective moral obligations are real - the wrongness of torturing innocents isn't a feeling we have. But objective obligations need a ground, and natural facts do not deliver oughts. A moral lawgiver is the best explanation.' At its sharpest, what does this argument claim?
answer: Moral argument - the reality of objective moral obligations points to a transcendent moral lawgiver as their best explanation, since natural facts alone do not yield genuine oughts.
choices: Moral argument - the reality of objective moral obligations points to a transcendent moral lawgiver as their best explanation, since natural facts alone do not yield genuine oughts.
Ontological argument - the concept of a maximally great being entails its existence, since a being that exists in reality is greater than one that exists in the mind alone here.
Cosmological argument - the existence of contingent things requires a non-contingent cause; the argument moves from the actual world's dependence outward, not from binding moral norms.
Pragmatic Pascalian wager - given uncertain stakes about God's existence, the expected utility of belief outweighs unbelief; the argument here is decision-theoretic, not about morals.
context: The moral argument has classical roots (Kant treats God as a postulate of practical reason) and modern defenders (C. S. Lewis, Mere Christianity, 1952; William Lane Craig). Critics (J. L. Mackie, Ethics: Inventing Right and Wrong, 1977) accept the conditional but reject moral realism. Naturalist moral realism is a further rival.

question: Reporter Sina presses a philosopher: 'People report encounters with the divine, but feelings aren't evidence.' The philosopher answers: 'Perception generally confers prima facie warrant on experience-based belief. If religious experience is perception-like, the same default applies.' Which response engages the reporter's challenge?
answer: Religious experience as evidence - if such experience is genuinely perception-like, the standard epistemic default treating perception as prima facie warranting applies to it directly.
choices: Religious experience as evidence - if such experience is genuinely perception-like, the standard epistemic default treating perception as prima facie warranting applies to it directly.
Fideism - religious belief requires no evidence at all, since demanding evidence misunderstands what faith is; the appropriate posture is trust prior to and apart from any argument.
Reformed epistemology - belief in God can be properly basic, formed in basic conditions without inference from other beliefs; the response should bypass the evidence framing altogether.
Strict evidentialism - the reporter is right that feelings alone aren't evidence; serious religious belief requires shareable arguments and external evidence in the standard public sense.
context: William Alston (Perceiving God, 1991) develops religious experience as a doxastic practice on a par with sense perception. Richard Swinburne's principle of credulity (The Existence of God, 1979): in the absence of defeaters, experiences are evidence for what they seem to be experiences of. Critics dispute the perception-like claim.

question: An evidentialist insists: 'No belief is rational without a supporting argument; belief in God is no exception.' Philosopher Tess responds: 'Many basic beliefs - that there is a past, that other minds exist - have no supporting argument yet are perfectly rational; belief in God may sit among them.' Which response engages the challenge?
answer: Reformed epistemology - belief in God can be properly basic, formed in appropriate conditions without inference, like our basic beliefs about the past and about other minds.
choices: Reformed epistemology - belief in God can be properly basic, formed in appropriate conditions without inference, like our basic beliefs about the past and about other minds.
Religious experience as evidence - the warrant for belief in God comes from perception-like religious experience that confers prima facie warrant on its content under epistemic defaults.
Pragmatic Pascalian wager - the relevant warrant is decision-theoretic: under uncertainty about God's existence, the expected utility of belief outweighs that of unbelief on the stakes.
Strict evidentialism - the challenger is right; rational belief requires sufficient public argument, and any move to 'basic belief' is special pleading for one belief no other belief enjoys.
context: Alvin Plantinga's 'Reformed Objections to Natural Theology' (1980) and Warranted Christian Belief (2000) develop properly-basic theistic belief on the model of basic beliefs about the past, other minds, and the external world. The position rejects classical evidentialism (Clifford) at the level of foundational epistemology, not theology.

question: A blog post defends religion by Pascal's wager: 'Either God exists or doesn't. If you believe and He exists, you win infinitely; everything else is finite. So believe.' Theologian Aaron objects: 'A bet driven by payoff cannot deliver real faith - mere expected utility isn't belief.' Why is the wager not enough, on Aaron's view?
answer: Belief-from-utility objection - faith is a relational stance toward God, not a bet on expected utility; reasoning oneself into belief from payoff alone does not produce real belief.
choices: Belief-from-utility objection - faith is a relational stance toward God, not a bet on expected utility; reasoning oneself into belief from payoff alone does not produce real belief.
Many-gods objection - the wager assumes a binary choice, but rival religions offer rival infinite payoffs; without a way to choose between them the decision matrix does not yield a verdict.
Infinite-utility math objection - decision theory breaks down once any option has infinite expected utility, since any positive probability of belief yields the same infinity as any other.
Evidentialist objection - one shouldn't believe anything without sufficient evidence regardless of stakes; using prudential reasons to fix one's beliefs is a violation of intellectual duty.
context: Pascal's Pensees (1670) presents the wager as practical reasoning under uncertainty. Standard objections include the many-gods problem (William James), infinite-utility breakdown (Alan Hajek), and the belief-from-utility objection: utility doesn't produce belief, only intention to acquire belief, which is a different mental state.

question: Philosopher Mira presents a classic argument: 'An all-powerful, all-good being could and would prevent any evil. Evil exists. So an all-powerful, all-good being does not. The three claims are STRICTLY inconsistent.' At its sharpest, what does Mira's argument claim?
answer: Logical problem of evil - traditional divine attributes plus the existence of any evil at all are strictly logically inconsistent, so no being matching the description can exist.
choices: Logical problem of evil - traditional divine attributes plus the existence of any evil at all are strictly logically inconsistent, so no being matching the description can exist.
Evidential problem of evil - particular evils of certain types provide strong probabilistic evidence against God, even if the relevant claims are not strictly logically inconsistent here.
Hume's argument against miracles - reports of miraculous events should never be believed since the evidence for the regularity violated is always stronger than testimony for the violation.
Divine hiddenness argument - a perfectly loving God would not allow nonresistant nonbelief to occur; widespread nonresistant nonbelief therefore tells against the existence of such a being.
context: J. L. Mackie's 'Evil and Omnipotence' (Mind, 1955) is the canonical statement of the logical problem of evil. Plantinga's free-will defense (God, Freedom, and Evil, 1974) is widely taken to have shown the logical version unsuccessful: it is logically possible that God could not create free creatures who never sin. The debate then shifted.

question: Op-ed philosopher Drest writes: 'A fawn dies slowly after a forest fire, alone, with no human to learn from or be ennobled by it. Suffering of THIS kind - intense and apparently pointless - is EVIDENCE against the existence of an all-good, all-powerful God, even if not strict proof.' At its sharpest, what does Drest claim?
answer: Evidential problem of evil - particular instances of apparently pointless intense suffering are probabilistic evidence against traditional theism, even without strict logical inconsistency.
choices: Evidential problem of evil - particular instances of apparently pointless intense suffering are probabilistic evidence against traditional theism, even without strict logical inconsistency.
Logical problem of evil - traditional divine attributes plus the existence of any evil at all are strictly logically inconsistent, so no being matching the description can exist whatsoever.
Argument from divine hiddenness - a perfectly loving God would not allow nonresistant nonbelief, so widespread nonresistant nonbelief is evidence against the existence of such a being.
Argument from religious diversity - the deep disagreement of sincere people about religious matters tells against any one tradition's claims to deliver knowledge of the divine reliably.
context: William Rowe's 'The Problem of Evil and Some Varieties of Atheism' (American Philosophical Quarterly, 1979) introduced the fawn case and the evidential framing. Standard theistic replies (Wykstra's sceptical theism; Stump's soul-making theodicy) target the inference from 'no good we see' to 'no good there is.'

question: Op-ed columnist Inez argues: 'Real suffering exists, and appealing to mystery is intellectually weak.' Theologian Yara responds: 'Goods like genuine moral growth, meaningful choice, and stable natural law cannot be obtained without permitting some evils we see; the evils are not denied, only contextualized.' Which response is Yara giving?
answer: Greater-goods defense - apparent evil is permitted only when it serves identifiable greater goods (moral growth, meaningful choice, lawful nature); the evil is not denied, only situated.
choices: Greater-goods defense - apparent evil is permitted only when it serves identifiable greater goods (moral growth, meaningful choice, lawful nature); the evil is not denied, only situated.
Sceptical theism - finite minds aren't placed to canvass an infinite mind's reasons, so 'we see no good' falls short of 'there is no good'; agnosticism about specifics is the honest move.
Free-will defense - the evil at issue is the cost of creating genuine moral agents, since rigged goodness in creatures whose choices never went wrong would not be moral agency at all.
Soul-making theodicy - the evil at issue is the necessary occasion for soul-development, since souls grow toward virtue only by working through trials they could not face in a soft world.
context: The greater-goods defense has classical roots in Augustine (Confessions VII) and Aquinas (Summa Theologiae I.49), and is elaborated in modern theodicy (Richard Swinburne, Providence and the Problem of Evil, 1998). It is broader than the free-will defense and overlaps with John Hick's soul-making theodicy (Evil and the God of Love, 1966).

question: A pastor cites eyewitness testimony for a miracle. Sceptic Niall answers: 'A miracle would be a violation of a regularity confirmed by countless cases. Testimony, no matter how earnest, is supported by much weaker regularity than the law it would overturn. The rational man rejects testimony.' Which response is Niall giving?
answer: Humean argument against miracles - testimony for a miracle is always supported by weaker evidence than the regularity the alleged miracle would violate, so the rational stance is rejection.
choices: Humean argument against miracles - testimony for a miracle is always supported by weaker evidence than the regularity the alleged miracle would violate, so the rational stance is rejection.
Evidential problem of evil - apparent gratuitous suffering is probabilistic evidence against an all-good, all-powerful God; the argument here is against theism through evil, not testimony.
Logical problem of evil - the attributes of God are strictly logically inconsistent with the existence of any evil at all; the argument here proceeds through inconsistency, not testimony.
Argument from religious diversity - deep disagreement of sincere people about religion tells against a tradition's claim to divine knowledge; the move isn't specifically about miracles.
context: Hume's 'Of Miracles' (Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, 1748) argues that the evidence for the law violated is always stronger than the evidence of testimony for the violation. Modern Bayesian replies (John Earman, Hume's Abject Failure, 2000) press the case that strong, independent multiple testimony can in principle suffice.

question: Podcast guest Helga argues: 'If I sincerely believe my religion, that's all the warrant I need.' Philosopher Olen pushes back: 'Sincerity is consistent with believing anything; sincere people believe contradictory things. Whatever sincerity is, it cannot be what makes a religious claim true.' Why is sincerity not enough, on Olen's view?
answer: Evidentialism - sincerity is consistent with believing contradictory things, so sincerity alone cannot make a religious claim true; reasons external to the believer's stance are required.
choices: Evidentialism - sincerity is consistent with believing contradictory things, so sincerity alone cannot make a religious claim true; reasons external to the believer's stance are required.
Religious experience reply - sincerity isn't enough because the relevant warrant comes from genuine perception-like experience of the divine, not from the subjective feeling of sincerity.
Reformed epistemology - sincerity isn't enough; the property is being formed in appropriate basic conditions, which a properly working faculty might supply where mere sincerity does not.
Pragmatic objection - sincerity isn't enough because religious practice requires action under genuine commitment, which is shown by what one does rather than by inner subjective assurance.
context: W. K. Clifford's 'The Ethics of Belief' (1877) is the classical statement of evidentialism: 'It is wrong, always, everywhere, and for anyone, to believe anything upon insufficient evidence.' William James's 'The Will to Believe' (1896) and modern Reformed epistemology offer the leading replies to Clifford's strict standard.

question: An atheist columnist writes: 'Faith is belief without reasons; reasoned inquiry is its opposite.' Theologian Marlin replies: 'On the classical view, faith and reason address overlapping matters and ultimately cannot contradict, since the same God is the source of both natural light and revelation.' Which response is Marlin giving?
answer: Faith-and-reason concord (Thomistic) - faith and reason address overlapping subject matters and cannot ultimately contradict, since both natural inquiry and revelation have the same source.
choices: Faith-and-reason concord (Thomistic) - faith and reason address overlapping subject matters and cannot ultimately contradict, since both natural inquiry and revelation have the same source.
Fideism - faith and reason are separate domains; religious truth lies wholly outside the reach of reason, and demanding reasons misunderstands what faith requires of the believer.
Evidentialism - faith is rational only as it rests on sufficient public argument; absent such argument the columnist is right that faith is belief without reasons in the relevant sense.
Reformed epistemology - faith is rational because belief in God can be properly basic without argument, much as belief in other minds is properly basic; the columnist mistakes the model.
context: Aquinas (Summa Contra Gentiles I.7) holds that since truth cannot contradict truth, what is delivered by faith and what is delivered by reason cannot ultimately conflict. Vatican I (1869-70) and Fides et Ratio (John Paul II, 1998) reaffirm the concord. Tertullian's 'credo quia absurdum' is the fideist counter-tradition within Christianity.

question: Reader Phin worries: 'If God knows now what I'll choose tomorrow, my choice is fixed - so how is it free?' Philosopher Selene answers: 'God's knowledge isn't a forecast in advance.
