He sees all of time at once. Knowing what I freely choose doesn't make me unfree, any more than a friend's seeing it does.' Which response is Selene giving?
answer: Boethian eternalism - God knows time-bound events from outside time as a single eternal present, so foreknowledge isn't prior forecasting and doesn't compromise creaturely freedom.
choices: Boethian eternalism - God knows time-bound events from outside time as a single eternal present, so foreknowledge isn't prior forecasting and doesn't compromise creaturely freedom.
Open theism - the future of free choices isn't yet a fact, so even God doesn't know in advance what creatures will do; freedom is preserved by limiting the scope of divine foreknowledge.
Molinist middle knowledge - God knows what each possible free creature would choose in each possible circumstance, and uses that in providence without overriding the creature's choice.
Hard theological compatibilism - foreknowledge fixes future actions, but freedom is compatible with this since freedom means acting on one's own desires, not enjoying metaphysical openness.
context: Boethius's Consolation of Philosophy (524) offers the eternalist solution: God's knowledge is timeless rather than temporally prior, so the analogy to forecasting fails. Molinism (Luis de Molina, 1588) and open theism (Pinnock et al., 1994) are the two major rivals. The issue remains live in contemporary philosophical theology.

question: Philosopher Cale presses an argument: 'A loving God would not allow open-hearted seekers to remain without belief. But such seekers exist. So no such God exists.' Theologian Riva replies: 'Forming a loving relationship may require kinds of epistemic distance that overwhelming presence would foreclose.' Which response is Riva giving?
answer: Epistemic-distance reply to hiddenness - loving relationship may require cognitive openness that overwhelming divine presence would foreclose, making hiddenness consistent with divine love.
choices: Epistemic-distance reply to hiddenness - loving relationship may require cognitive openness that overwhelming divine presence would foreclose, making hiddenness consistent with divine love.
Sceptical theism - finite minds aren't placed to canvass the reasons an infinite mind might have for hiding from some seekers; agnosticism about the specific reasons in hiddenness is honest.
Free-will defense - the hiddenness in question is the cost of creating creatures whose belief is genuinely free; overwhelming evidence would coerce belief and undercut its freedom and merit.
Reformed epistemology - the hiddenness is illusory; seekers who appear blameless actually fail to form belief because the sensus divinitatis is damaged, not because evidence is lacking.
context: J. L. Schellenberg's Divine Hiddenness and Human Reason (1993) developed the modern hiddenness argument. The epistemic-distance reply traces to John Hick (Faith and Knowledge, 1957) - genuine love between persons requires a measure of non-coercive distance. Free-will and sceptical-theism replies are also live in the literature.

question: Columnist Reza writes: 'Given how many sincere people disagree about religion, no tradition can claim privileged knowledge.' Philosopher Tova replies: 'Sincere disagreement occurs in every contested domain, including ethics and politics. It doesn't show no tradition is right; only that the question is hard.' Which response is Tova giving?
answer: Exclusivist response to diversity - sincere disagreement occurs in every contested domain without showing no view is right, so religious diversity alone doesn't undercut a tradition's claim.
choices: Exclusivist response to diversity - sincere disagreement occurs in every contested domain without showing no view is right, so religious diversity alone doesn't undercut a tradition's claim.
Religious pluralism - all major traditions are independently valid responses to the same transcendent reality; the disagreement is real but compatible with each being a path to that reality.
Religious inclusivism - one tradition is uniquely true but salvation isn't restricted to its adherents; sincere followers of other paths participate in the truth without recognizing it.
Sceptical theism - finite minds aren't well-placed to judge whether God has reasons for permitting diversity; the disagreement of sincere people doesn't tell against any tradition's claim.
context: Religious pluralism (John Hick, An Interpretation of Religion, 1989) treats traditions as equally valid responses. Exclusivists (Alvin Plantinga, 'Pluralism: A Defense of Religious Exclusivism,' 1995) press that disagreement in contested domains is normal and does not undercut a particular view's claim to be the right answer.

question: On a panel, theologian Maren defends a theodicy: 'The world is a vale of soul-making. Virtues like courage and compassion only develop where there is danger and need; a frictionless paradise could not contain the creatures we are MEANT to become.' Which response is Maren giving?
answer: Soul-making theodicy - evil is the necessary occasion for moral and spiritual growth, since virtues like courage and compassion develop only by working through trials in a difficult world.
choices: Soul-making theodicy - evil is the necessary occasion for moral and spiritual growth, since virtues like courage and compassion develop only by working through trials in a difficult world.
Free-will defense - moral evil is the cost of creating genuine moral agents, since the real possibility of doing wrong is required for the real possibility of doing right under accounts.
Greater-goods defense - apparent evil is permitted only when it serves identifiable goods, including the stability of natural law and structures of meaningful choice that the world embeds.
Sceptical theism - humans simply lack the cognitive capacity to canvass an infinite mind's reasons for permitting any specific evil; agnosticism about divine reasons is the honest move here.
context: John Hick's Evil and the God of Love (1966) develops the soul-making theodicy from an Irenaean tradition (against the Augustinian perfect-and-then-fallen frame). Virtues that distinguish mature moral character are response-dependent on difficulty. Critics press that some sufferings are too severe for soul-making to plausibly explain.

question: A philosopher of religion argues on a seminar panel: 'If it is even possible that a maximally great being exists, then by the logic of necessity such a being exists in every possible world, including ours — the premise carries the conclusion once we grant the possibility.' Which argument is the philosopher defending?
answer: Modal ontological argument — Plantinga uses possible-worlds logic to argue that maximal greatness, if possibly instantiated, must be instantiated necessarily, so the conclusion follows.
choices: Modal ontological argument — Plantinga uses possible-worlds logic to argue that maximal greatness, if possibly instantiated, must be instantiated necessarily, so the conclusion follows.

Kalam cosmological argument — the universe began to exist; whatever begins to exist has a cause; so the universe has a cause, traditionally identified with God, but the move here uses causation rather than modality.

Anselmian classical argument — God is that than which nothing greater can be conceived; existence in reality is greater than existence in the mind alone, so God exists in reality, but Anselm's form predates modal logic.

Fine-tuning argument — the physical constants are improbably calibrated for life; design is the best explanation of the calibration, but the argument turns on probability and physical evidence rather than possibility-necessity.
context: Alvin Plantinga's modal ontological argument (The Nature of Necessity, 1974) reformulated Anselm's argument in modal logic: if a maximally great being (omnipotent, omniscient, morally perfect in every possible world) is possibly instantiated, then by S5 modal logic it is necessarily instantiated. Critics dispute the possibility premise itself.

question: A theologian on stage argues: 'Whatever begins to exist has a cause of its existence; the universe began to exist, as both philosophical arguments against actual infinities and contemporary cosmology support; therefore the universe has a cause that transcends it.' Which argument is the theologian advancing?
answer: Kalam cosmological argument — Craig (Reasonable Faith) revives the medieval kalam form, linking the causal premise with arguments against an actually infinite past plus Big Bang cosmology to infer a transcendent cause.
choices: Kalam cosmological argument — Craig (Reasonable Faith) revives the medieval kalam form, linking the causal premise with arguments against an actually infinite past plus Big Bang cosmology to infer a transcendent cause.

Thomistic contingency argument — the Five Ways third proof, Aquinas's argument from contingency to a necessary being, focuses on why anything exists rather than on the universe's having a beginning; the temporal premise is absent.

Leibnizian PSR argument — every fact requires a sufficient reason; the universe is a fact; so its reason lies outside it in a necessary being, but the route runs through sufficient reason rather than beginnings-and-causes.

Fine-tuning argument — the physical constants are calibrated for life within narrow margins; design is the best explanation, but the argument concerns the universe's character rather than the existence of a temporal first cause.
context: The kalam (Arabic: 'speech, theology') argument originated with medieval Islamic philosophers (al-Ghazali, Reasonable Faith) and was revived in modern philosophy of religion by William Lane Craig (The Kalam Cosmological Argument, 1979). The argument's distinctive feature is its conjunction of causal premise with the universe having a finite past.

question: A philosophy-of-religion seminar discusses an argument: 'Contingent beings — those that might not have existed — cannot account for their own being; if everything were contingent, nothing would exist at all; so a being whose existence is not contingent must ground the contingent ones.' Which classical argument is this?
answer: Thomistic contingency argument — Aquinas's Third Way (Summa I.2.3, ex possibili et necessario) infers from the existence of contingent beings to a necessary being whose existence is not borrowed from any other source.
choices: Thomistic contingency argument — Aquinas's Third Way (Summa I.2.3, ex possibili et necessario) infers from the existence of contingent beings to a necessary being whose existence is not borrowed from any other source.

Kalam cosmological argument — the universe began to exist; what begins to exist has a cause; so the universe has a cause, but the kalam works through the universe's temporal beginning rather than through contingency itself.

Modal ontological argument — possible-worlds logic: if maximal greatness is possibly instantiated, it is necessarily instantiated, but the route is purely modal and does not pass through contingency-and-explanation at all.

Teleological argument — natural processes exhibit ordered ends toward which they tend; ordered processes presuppose intelligence directing them, but the argument concerns directedness rather than necessary existence as such.
context: Thomas Aquinas's Summa Theologiae I.2.3 sets out the Five Ways (motion, efficient causation, contingency, gradation, governance). The Third Way (ex possibili et necessario) argues from the existence of contingent beings to a necessary being. Modern restatements include Norman Geisler and Edward Feser (Five Proofs, 2017); critics include Russell, Mackie, Sobel.

question: An atheist philosopher argues: 'An omnipotent and wholly good God could and would prevent all evil; evil exists; so the existence of such a God is logically impossible.' A theistic philosopher replies, offering a possibility-claim about why God might permit some evils. Which reply is the theistic philosopher giving?
answer: Free-will defense — Plantinga (God, Freedom, and Evil, 1974) argues that if creating genuinely free agents is possibly a great good, then God's permitting moral evil is logically compatible with omnipotence and goodness.
choices: Free-will defense — Plantinga (God, Freedom, and Evil, 1974) argues that if creating genuinely free agents is possibly a great good, then God's permitting moral evil is logically compatible with omnipotence and goodness.

Soul-making theodicy — Hick (Evil and the God of Love, 1966) argues evil is the necessary environment for moral and spiritual growth, but the move is a positive theodicy of why evil exists, not a possibility defense.

Skeptical theism — Bergmann argues humans lack the cognitive resources to judge whether God has good reasons for any specific evil, but the move sidesteps the logical problem rather than answering its compatibility claim.

Privation theory — Augustine treats evil as the absence or corruption of good rather than a positive thing in itself, but the metaphysics of evil-as-privation does not by itself settle the logical compatibility question.
context: J.L. Mackie's 'Evil and Omnipotence' (1955) formulated the logical problem of evil. Alvin Plantinga's God, Freedom, and Evil (1974) developed the free-will defense, arguing it is possible that God could not actualize a world with morally significant freedom and no moral evil. Most philosophers treat the logical problem as defused; the evidential problem remains live.

question: A theologian on stage argues: 'Evil and suffering, distressing as they are, can be the necessary environment for the development of moral and spiritual qualities — courage, compassion, mature love — that could not be formed in a frictionless paradise.' Which theodicy is the theologian advancing?
answer: Soul-making theodicy — Hick argues God permits evil because the world is a vale of soul-making where moral and spiritual character is forged, not a hedonic paradise of frictionless ease.
choices: Soul-making theodicy — Hick argues God permits evil because the world is a vale of soul-making where moral and spiritual character is forged, not a hedonic paradise of frictionless ease.

Free-will defense — Plantinga argues that if creating free agents is possibly a great good, God's permitting moral evil is logically compatible with goodness, but the move is a possibility defense, not a positive account.

Skeptical theism — Bergmann argues humans lack the cognitive resources to judge whether God has good reasons for specific evils; the position grants the puzzle but counsels agnosticism rather than offering a positive theodicy.

Augustinian privation theory — evil is the absence of good rather than a positive thing in itself; the metaphysics describes what evil is, not the divine purpose for permitting the suffering people actually experience.
context: John Hick's Evil and the God of Love (1966) develops the soul-making (Irenaean) theodicy, drawing on the second-century theologian Irenaeus rather than Augustine. The Augustinian theodicy attributes evil to the Fall; the Irenaean treats this world as an environment designed for moral-spiritual development. Critics: Rowe, Plantinga (different routes).

question: An evidentialist atheist argues: 'Some particular evils — the slow death of an animal in the forest from untreated injury — appear gratuitous; no good we can identify justifies them; so they probably are gratuitous, and gratuitous evil counts against theism.' A theistic philosopher gives a specific reply. Which is it?
answer: Skeptical theism — Bergmann argues that the move from 'we see no good justifying this evil' to 'there is no such good' presupposes we would see it if it existed, which our cognitive limits relative to God do not warrant.
choices: Skeptical theism — Bergmann argues that the move from 'we see no good justifying this evil' to 'there is no such good' presupposes we would see it if it existed, which our cognitive limits relative to God do not warrant.

Free-will defense — Plantinga argues that if creating free agents is possibly a great good, moral evil is logically compatible with God's goodness, but forest-animal suffering is not moral evil generated by free choice.

Soul-making theodicy — Hick argues evil is the environment for moral-spiritual growth, but animal suffering with no soul present to be made does not fit the theodicy's account of why suffering serves character formation.

Privation theory — Augustine treats evil as the corruption of good rather than a positive thing in itself, but the metaphysics does not address whether particular sufferings are gratuitous on the evidence we actually have.
context: William Rowe's 'The Problem of Evil and Some Varieties of Atheism' (1979) formulated the modern evidential problem of evil, using the example of a fawn dying slowly in an unobserved forest fire. Skeptical theism (Wykstra, Bergmann, Howard-Snyder, Alston) replies by challenging the noseeum inference: from 'we see no justifying good' to 'there is none.'

question: A philosopher of religion argues: 'Belief in God can be rational without being inferred from any argument — it can be a properly basic belief, formed by the right kind of cognitive faculties operating in the right circumstances, on a par with belief in the external world or other minds.' Which view is she defending?
answer: Reformed epistemology — Plantinga (Warranted Christian Belief, 2000) argues theistic belief can be properly basic, warranted by a cognitive faculty (the sensus divinitatis) operating rightly, not requiring inferential support.
choices: Reformed epistemology — Plantinga (Warranted Christian Belief, 2000) argues theistic belief can be properly basic, warranted by a cognitive faculty (the sensus divinitatis) operating rightly, not requiring inferential support.

Natural theology — Swinburne argues theistic belief is supported by a cumulative case of inductive arguments from cosmology, design, and experience; on this view belief rests on inference rather than being properly basic.

Religious experientialism — Alston (Perceiving God, 1991) argues religious experience is itself a doxastic practice yielding prima facie justified belief, but the route runs through experience as evidence, not basicality.

Fideism — Kierkegaard treats faith as a leap beyond the reach of reason; the move places religious belief outside epistemic justification, whereas reformed epistemology insists belief can be warranted on the proper account.
context: Alvin Plantinga's reformed epistemology, developed across Faith and Rationality (1983) and culminating in the warrant trilogy (Warranted Christian Belief, 2000), draws on Calvin's sensus divinitatis. Belief in God need not be based on argument to be warranted; it can be produced by a properly functioning cognitive faculty aimed at truth in suitable conditions.

question: A theologian on stage argues: 'When someone perceives God in a religious experience, that perceptual experience carries prima facie evidential weight in the same way ordinary sense perception does — the burden falls on anyone who claims religious perception is uniquely unreliable.' Which view is she defending?
answer: Alstonian religious experientialism — Alston argues mystical perception is a doxastic practice yielding prima facie justified belief, parallel to sense perception, until specific defeaters arise.
choices: Alstonian religious experientialism — Alston argues mystical perception is a doxastic practice yielding prima facie justified belief, parallel to sense perception, until specific defeaters arise.

Reformed epistemology — Plantinga argues theistic belief can be properly basic, warranted by the sensus divinitatis functioning rightly, but the route is through cognitive faculty design rather than through perception.

Evidentialism — Clifford insists every belief must rest on sufficient evidence; religious belief must survive critical evaluation by shared epistemic norms, but the position is the target of Alston's defense, not its ground.

Fideism — Kierkegaard treats faith as a leap beyond reason; the move places religious commitment outside ordinary epistemic evaluation entirely, whereas Alston defends the experience itself as ordinary epistemic evidence.
context: William Alston's Perceiving God (1991) frames religious experience as a doxastic practice — Christian mystical practice — yielding prima facie justified belief on analogy with sense-perceptual practice. Richard Swinburne's principle of credulity (The Existence of God, 1979) gives a related defense: experiences are prima facie evidence for what they appear to be of.

question: A physicist-philosopher on a panel argues: 'The dimensionless physical constants — the cosmological constant, the ratios that govern atomic stability — fall within ranges so narrow that the existence of complex life is extraordinarily improbable on chance; design is a better explanation.' Which argument is she advancing?
answer: Fine-tuning argument — Collins (Blackwell Companion to Natural Theology) argues the calibration of physical constants for life is far more probable on design than on chance, taking design as the inference to best explanation.
choices: Fine-tuning argument — Collins (Blackwell Companion to Natural Theology) argues the calibration of physical constants for life is far more probable on design than on chance, taking design as the inference to best explanation.

Kalam cosmological argument — the universe began to exist; what begins to exist has a cause; the cause transcends the universe, but the argument turns on the universe's beginning rather than on the calibration of laws.

Thomistic teleological argument — natural processes exhibit ordered ends toward which they tend; ordered processes presuppose directing intelligence, but the argument concerns directedness within nature, not initial parameters.

Modal ontological argument — Plantinga uses possible-worlds logic to infer necessary existence from possible maximal greatness, but the move is purely modal and does not involve probability or physical evidence at all.
context: Robin Collins, William Lane Craig, and John Leslie develop the fine-tuning argument as a modern teleological argument. The argument compares the probability of the calibration on design with its probability on chance or necessity; the multiverse response (Susskind, Tegmark) is the leading naturalistic alternative, generating ongoing debate over comparative probabilities.

question: A philosopher of religion argues: 'The wrongness of cruelty consists in its being contrary to the commands of a loving God — but God's commands are not arbitrary, because they flow from God's essential moral character, which itself is the standard of goodness.' Which view of moral foundations is she defending?
answer: Modified divine command theory — Adams grounds moral wrongness in being contrary to a loving God's commands while grounding goodness in God's character, dissolving Euthyphro's force.
choices: Modified divine command theory — Adams grounds moral wrongness in being contrary to a loving God's commands while grounding goodness in God's character, dissolving Euthyphro's force.

Classical divine command theory — moral facts just are what God commands; on this stricter view God could in principle command cruelty and it would thereby be right, which is the Euthyphro horn modified DCT is built to avoid.

Natural law theory — Aquinas grounds moral wrongness in the inclinations of human nature toward proper ends; wrongness tracks what frustrates rational nature, but the foundation is teleological rather than command-based.

Strong theological voluntarism — Ockham's strongest form treats divine will as the unconstrained source of moral facts, but the view collapses moral arbitrariness into divine sovereignty, which Adams's modified theory resists.
context: Robert Adams's Finite and Infinite Goods (1999) develops modified divine command theory. The Euthyphro dilemma (Plato, Euthyphro 10a): is the pious loved by the gods because it is pious, or pious because it is loved? Adams's reply: God's commands constitute wrongness because God's character constitutes goodness; the dilemma's two horns are dissolved rather than chosen between.

question: A philosopher of religion argues: 'The great world religions are alternative human responses to a Real beyond all our concepts; their conflicting doctrines are conceptually constrained images of a single transcendent Reality, none of which captures the Real as it is in itself.' Which view is she defending?
answer: Hickian religious pluralism — Hick (An Interpretation of Religion, 1989) treats the major religions as alternative culturally-shaped responses to a single noumenal Real, so doctrinal conflict reflects perspective, not truth.
choices: Hickian religious pluralism — Hick (An Interpretation of Religion, 1989) treats the major religions as alternative culturally-shaped responses to a single noumenal Real, so doctrinal conflict reflects perspective, not truth.

Religious exclusivism — Plantinga ('A Defense of Religious Exclusivism', 1995) holds that the defining claims of a religion can be true and contrary claims of other religions false without epistemic or moral fault by holding so.

Religious inclusivism — Rahner argues salvation is mediated through Christ but accessible to sincere adherents of other religions ('anonymous Christians'); the view treats one tradition as uniquely true while accommodating others.

Religious naturalism — apparent religious diversity reflects naturalistic causes (culture, psychology, evolution) rather than alternative responses to a transcendent Real; the framework dispenses with the noumenal entirely.
context: John Hick's An Interpretation of Religion (1989) develops the pluralist hypothesis: the world religions are different lenses on a transcendent Real (Hick uses Kant's noumenon/phenomenon distinction). The view's main critics: Plantinga, Alston (defending exclusivism); Karl Rahner (inclusivism); Gavin D'Costa (developing alternatives within Christian theology).

question: A philosopher of religion argues: 'A Christian who holds that the central claims of Christianity are true, and that incompatible claims of other religions are false, is not thereby being epistemically irresponsible or morally arrogant; truth-claims about the world commit one to thinking incompatible alternatives false.' Which position is she defending?
answer: Religious exclusivism — Plantinga argues holding central religious claims as true while taking incompatible alternatives as false is no more arrogant than analogous moves elsewhere.
choices: Religious exclusivism — Plantinga argues holding central religious claims as true while taking incompatible alternatives as false is no more arrogant than analogous moves elsewhere.

Religious pluralism — Hick treats the major religions as alternative culturally-shaped responses to a single transcendent Real, so doctrinal disagreement reflects perspective rather than competing truth-claims at all.

Religious inclusivism — Rahner holds salvation is mediated through Christ but accessible to sincere adherents of other religions; the view affirms uniqueness while extending reach, a middle path between Hick and Plantinga.

Religious agnosticism — the proper response to apparent diversity is suspension of judgment about which tradition's claims are true, but the position treats the question as unsettled rather than rationally settleable.
context: Alvin Plantinga's 'A Defense of Religious Exclusivism' (1995, reprinted in The Rationality of Belief and the Plurality of Faith). The argument: exclusivism is the natural epistemic stance for anyone who holds substantive claims about reality; pluralism's egalitarianism cannot be sustained without itself becoming an exclusivist position about religious truth.

question: A philosopher on a debate panel argues: 'If the question of God's existence cannot be settled by reason, and the stakes are infinite gain versus finite loss, then prudence itself recommends belief — even granting epistemic uncertainty, the expected value of belief swamps the expected value of unbelief.' Which classic argument is she advancing?
answer: Pascalian wager — Pascal (Pensees, 1670) argues that under epistemic uncertainty about God's existence the expected-value calculation favors belief, since the infinite gain on theism dominates any finite cost of believing.
choices: Pascalian wager — Pascal (Pensees, 1670) argues that under epistemic uncertainty about God's existence the expected-value calculation favors belief, since the infinite gain on theism dominates any finite cost of believing.

Kierkegaardian leap of faith — Fear and Trembling (1843) treats faith as a passionate commitment beyond the reach of reason; the move is qualitatively different from Pascal's, treating calculative framing as a category mistake.

Jamesian will to believe — James (The Will to Believe, 1896) argues some genuine options let the passional nature decide where evidence is balanced, but the case rests on psychological grounds, not on expected value.

Reformed epistemology — Plantinga argues theistic belief can be properly basic, warranted by the sensus divinitatis functioning rightly, but the route dispenses with the calculative-decision picture the wager presupposes.
context: Blaise Pascal's Pensees (published posthumously 1670) presents the wager argument in fragments 233 and neighboring sections. Standard critiques: the many-gods objection (Hick), the problem of inauthentic belief, whether infinite utilities can be coherently compared. Defenders (Jordan, Rota, 2016) reformulate the argument to address these standard objections.

question: A theologian on stage argues: 'Faith is not the conclusion of a probabilistic argument; it is a passionate commitment in the face of objective uncertainty — a leap beyond the reach of speculative reason, into a relation with the eternal that calculation cannot reach.' Which view of religious commitment is she defending?
answer: Kierkegaardian fideism — Fear and Trembling and Concluding Unscientific Postscript treat faith as a leap beyond reason, a passionate inwardness incommensurable with the speculative reason that argument employs.
choices: Kierkegaardian fideism — Fear and Trembling and Concluding Unscientific Postscript treat faith as a leap beyond reason, a passionate inwardness incommensurable with the speculative reason that argument employs.

Plantingan reformed epistemology — theistic belief can be properly basic, warranted by a cognitive faculty functioning rightly, but the view treats belief as within the framework of epistemic warrant, not as a leap beyond.

Swinburnian natural theology — religious belief rests on a cumulative inductive case from cosmology, design, and experience; the framework treats faith as continuous with reasonable inquiry, not discontinuous with it.

Pascalian wager — under epistemic uncertainty about God's existence the expected-value calculation favors belief; but the calculation is the very kind of calculative framing Kierkegaard treats as a category mistake.
context: Soren Kierkegaard's Fear and Trembling (1843) and Concluding Unscientific Postscript (1846) develop the leap of faith and the category of the Knight of Faith. Faith is a passionate inwardness sustained in objective uncertainty; the position is distinguishable both from rational theology and from arbitrary belief, though critics (Russell, Adams) press at the distinctions.

question: A philosopher of religion argues: 'No single argument settles the question of God's existence, but a series of inductive arguments — from the universe's existence, its order, fine-tuning, consciousness, religious experience — each raises the probability somewhat, and together they make theism the better hypothesis.' Which framework is she defending?
answer: Swinburnian natural theology — Swinburne builds a cumulative inductive case: multiple arguments each raise theism's probability somewhat, and their joint effect makes theism the better hypothesis.
choices: Swinburnian natural theology — Swinburne builds a cumulative inductive case: multiple arguments each raise theism's probability somewhat, and their joint effect makes theism the better hypothesis.

Reformed epistemology — Plantinga argues theistic belief can be properly basic, warranted by the sensus divinitatis functioning rightly, but the route dispenses with the inferential-cumulative-case framework Swinburne defends.

Kalam cosmological argument — Craig argues that the universe began to exist, that whatever begins has a cause, and that the cause transcends the universe; the argument is a single deductive line rather than a cumulative case.

Fideism — Kierkegaard treats faith as a leap beyond the reach of reason, but the move treats the calculative-inductive framework as a category mistake about faith, whereas Swinburne defends that framework as fully appropriate.
context: Richard Swinburne's trilogy — The Coherence of Theism (1977), The Existence of God (1979), Faith and Reason (1981) — develops the cumulative inductive case using Bayesian probability. Each argument (cosmological, teleological, moral, religious experience) raises P(theism | evidence) somewhat; Swinburne argues the joint posterior is greater than 0.5.

question: An atheist philosopher argues: 'It is wrong, always, everywhere, and for anyone, to believe anything upon insufficient evidence — and the standard arguments offered for God's existence do not meet that evidential burden. The duty of honest inquiry rules belief out, not theology in.' Which classical position is she defending?
answer: Cliffordian evidentialism — Clifford argues every belief must rest on sufficient evidence as an intellectual duty, so religious belief without evidential support is morally and epistemically faulty.
choices: Cliffordian evidentialism — Clifford argues every belief must rest on sufficient evidence as an intellectual duty, so religious belief without evidential support is morally and epistemically faulty.

Logical positivism — religious claims are cognitively meaningless because unverifiable, so the question of evidence does not arise; the position is stronger and historically distinct from Clifford's epistemic-duty evidentialism.

Pragmatist atheism — religious belief should be evaluated by consequences for human flourishing rather than by abstract evidential standards; the position frames the question differently from Clifford's duty-of-evidence rule.

Mackiean atheism — the existence of evil counts decisively against theism, making belief in God irrational given the evidence we actually have, but the argument is substantive rather than about evidential duty as a general norm.
context: W.K. Clifford's 'The Ethics of Belief' (1877) opens with the parable of the shipowner: a man who sends a rusting ship to sea on insufficient evidence of its seaworthiness is guilty of the deaths even if the ship arrives. The principle generalizes: belief on insufficient evidence is morally and epistemically faulty. William James's 'The Will to Believe' (1896) is the locus classicus reply.

question: An atheist philosopher argues: 'There exist instances of intense suffering an omnipotent being could prevent without losing some greater good. An omniscient and wholly good being would prevent any such suffering. So probably no omniscient, wholly good, omnipotent being exists.' Which argument shape is she defending?
answer: Evidential problem of evil — Rowe (1979) builds the inductive case: apparently gratuitous suffering makes theism less probable than its denial, even granting the logical compatibility Plantinga's free-will defense secured.
choices: Evidential problem of evil — Rowe (1979) builds the inductive case: apparently gratuitous suffering makes theism less probable than its denial, even granting the logical compatibility Plantinga's free-will defense secured.

Logical problem of evil — Mackie (1955) argues the existence of any evil is logically incompatible with an omnipotent and wholly good God; Plantinga's free-will defense is treated as defusing the stronger logical claim.

Hume's argument from natural evil — Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion (1779) presses on the systematic character of natural suffering; the position overlaps with Rowe's but predates the inductive-probabilistic apparatus.

Cliffordian evidentialism — the duty of honest inquiry rules out belief without sufficient evidence; the move is methodological rather than substantive about evil, and Rowe's argument is substantive, not about a general norm.
context: William Rowe's 'The Problem of Evil and Some Varieties of Atheism' (1979) gave the modern evidential problem its canonical form, using the example of a fawn suffering in an unobserved forest fire. The argument is probabilistic rather than deductive; replies include skeptical theism (Wykstra, Bergmann), the greater-goods defense, and Hick's soul-making theodicy.

question: A Catholic theologian on a panel argues: 'Salvation is mediated through Christ alone, yet the sincere adherent of another tradition may participate in that salvation without explicit acknowledgment — the grace operative in Christianity reaches further than the visible boundaries of the church.' Which position is he defending?
answer: Rahnerian inclusivism — Karl Rahner (Theological Investigations) holds salvation is mediated through Christ but extends to sincere adherents of other traditions ('anonymous Christians'), a path between exclusivism and pluralism.
choices: Rahnerian inclusivism — Karl Rahner (Theological Investigations) holds salvation is mediated through Christ but extends to sincere adherents of other traditions ('anonymous Christians'), a path between exclusivism and pluralism.

Religious exclusivism — Plantinga argues the defining claims of one religion can be true and incompatible claims of others false without epistemic fault; the view holds salvation requires accepting those defining claims directly.

Religious pluralism — Hick treats the major religions as alternative culturally-shaped responses to one transcendent Real; the framework dispenses with the asymmetry the inclusivist retains between one tradition and others.

Religious naturalism — apparent religious diversity reflects naturalistic causes (culture, psychology, evolution) rather than alternative paths to salvation; the framework treats salvation-language as fundamentally inapplicable.
context: Karl Rahner's Theological Investigations (multi-volume, 1961-92) and the documents of the Second Vatican Council (1962-65, especially Lumen Gentium and Nostra Aetate) shape the modern Catholic inclusivist position. Critics include both Christian exclusivists (Hendrik Kraemer, Cornelius Van Til) and Hickian pluralists who argue inclusivism remains exclusivist beneath its accommodation.

question: A medieval-philosophy seminar discusses an argument: 'Evil is not a positive thing alongside good — it is the corruption or privation of a good that should be present. Blindness is not a thing but the absence of sight in something that ought to see. So evil is not part of what God created.' Which view is this?
answer: Augustinian privation theory — Augustine (Confessions VII; Enchiridion) treats evil as the corruption or privation of goods properly belonging to a created nature, so evil is not a positive thing God created alongside good.
choices: Augustinian privation theory — Augustine (Confessions VII; Enchiridion) treats evil as the corruption or privation of goods properly belonging to a created nature, so evil is not a positive thing God created alongside good.

Manichaean dualism — evil is a positive principle of darkness ontologically equal to good, opposed in permanent cosmic struggle; the view is exactly what Augustine spent his post-conversion career arguing against.

Free-will defense — Plantinga argues moral evil is the consequence of created freedom, but the position is about why evil exists given creation, whereas the privation account is about what evil ontologically is.

Soul-making theodicy — Hick treats evil as the necessary environment for moral and spiritual development, but the position is teleological about suffering's purpose, distinct from the metaphysical claim about evil's status.
context: Augustine's privation theory, developed against the Manichaeans in works including Confessions VII, On the Nature of the Good (399), and the Enchiridion (421), shaped medieval philosophy through Aquinas (Summa I.48-49). The theory holds evil has no positive ontological status — it is the corruption or privation of a good in something whose nature includes that good.

question: A philosopher of religion argues: 'A Christian who believes the central claims of Christianity on the basis of trustworthy testimony — the canonical scriptures, the witness of the church, the experience of a community across time — can be rationally justified even without working through philosophical arguments.' Which view is she defending?
answer: Testimonial religious epistemology — Mavrodes, Coady, and later Plantinga argue trustworthy religious testimony (scriptures, community, tradition) yields prima facie justified belief, parallel to ordinary testimony in general.
choices: Testimonial religious epistemology — Mavrodes, Coady, and later Plantinga argue trustworthy religious testimony (scriptures, community, tradition) yields prima facie justified belief, parallel to ordinary testimony in general.

Swinburnian natural theology — religious belief rests on a cumulative inductive case from cosmology, design, consciousness, and experience, but the framework treats testimony as one strand among many rather than the primary route.

Reformed epistemology — Plantinga argues theistic belief can be properly basic, warranted by the sensus divinitatis functioning rightly, but the foundational route is cognitive faculty design rather than testimonial transmission.

Fideism — Kierkegaard treats faith as a leap beyond reason; the view places religious commitment outside epistemic justification, whereas the testimonial position holds religious belief is within ordinary epistemic norms.
context: C.A.J. Coady's Testimony (1992) re-established testimony as a fundamental source of justified belief in general epistemology. George Mavrodes and Plantinga extend testimony-based justification to religious belief: scripture, church community, and tradition can yield rational belief without each believer having to work through arguments from natural theology.
